# AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on Intragastric Balloons in the Management of Obesity (2021)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Muniraj T, Day LW, Teigen LM, Ho EY, Sultan S, Davitkov P, Shah R, Murad MH. AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on Intragastric Balloons in the Management of Obesity (2021). Gastroenterology 2021;160:1799–1808. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.03.003.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.03.003)
- **Authors:** Muniraj T, Day LW, Teigen LM, Ho EY, Sultan S, Davitkov P, Shah R, Murad MH
- **Year:** 2021 (April)
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2021;160:1799–1808. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.03.003
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2021.03.003](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.03.003)
- **Type:** GRADE-based clinical practice guideline (AGA Institute), accompanied by a separate Technical Review (Shah et al, Gastroenterology 2021;160:1811–1830)

---

## Summary

This AGA guideline addresses the use of [[intragastric-balloon|intragastric balloons]] (IGBs) for weight loss in adults with [[obesity]]. Obesity affects roughly 40% of US adults, yet only ~1.1% of eligible patients receive primary bariatric surgery and <5% of patients seeking weight loss are aware of endoscopic options. IGBs (on the US market since 1982, withdrawn in the 1980s–90s after devastating adverse events, then re-introduced with newer models) are endoscopically placed, restrictive devices that augment lifestyle modification over a 6–12 month implantation period.

Using GRADE methodology, the panel issued **7 recommendations** (2 strong, 5 conditional). The central finding is that IGB therapy combined with lifestyle modification produces greater short-term weight loss than lifestyle modification alone across multiple measures (%TBWL, percent excess weight loss, achievement of 5% and 10% TBWL), with the greatest effect at 6–8 months and incrementally smaller benefit thereafter. IGBs also improve metabolic parameters (HbA1c, fasting glucose, LDL trend, transaminases) and increase remission of diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia versus standard of care.

Serious adverse events are uncommon but higher than SOC (5.6% vs 1.1%; RR 3.07): perforation 0.3%, esophageal mucosal injury 0.8%, gastric ulcer/bleeding 0.76%, gastric outlet/bowel obstruction 0.12%; no deaths in the 7 pooled RCTs, though post-marketing surveillance reports rare hyperinflation, acute pancreatitis, and death. Early removal for intolerance occurred in 9.4%. Fluid-filled balloons achieve ~3% more weight loss than gas-filled but with higher adverse-event rates and lower tolerability; the panel makes no recommendation on a specific device, deferring to shared decision-making.

The guideline also covers concomitant lifestyle intensity, PPI prophylaxis, peri-procedural antiemetics, nutritional screening and multivitamin supplementation, and post-removal maintenance strategies.

---

## Recommendations (verbatim, with strength and certainty)

**Recommendation 1.** In individuals with obesity seeking a weight-loss intervention who have failed a trial of conventional weight-loss strategies, AGA suggests the use of IGB therapy with lifestyle modification over lifestyle modification alone. *(Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty)*
- *Implementation remark:* Trials in the United States were limited to a body mass index (BMI) range between 30 and 40 kg/m². Individuals with BMI values outside this range were sometimes included in international trials.
- *Implementation remark:* Fluid-filled balloons may be associated with more weight loss, lower tolerability, and less favorable safety profile than gas-filled balloons. Shared decision-making is suggested for determining device choice.

**Recommendation 2.** In individuals with obesity undergoing IGB therapy, AGA recommends moderate- to high-intensity concomitant lifestyle modification interventions to maintain and augment weight loss. *(Strong recommendation, moderate certainty)*

**Recommendation 3.** In individuals undergoing IGB therapy, AGA recommends prophylaxis with PPIs. *(Strong recommendation, moderate certainty)*

**Recommendation 4.** In individuals undergoing IGB therapy, AGA suggests using the intraoperative anesthetic regimens associated with the lowest incidence of nausea along with perioperative antiemetics. AGA suggests a scheduled antiemetic regimen for 2 weeks after IGB placement. *(Conditional recommendation, low certainty)*
- *Implementation remark:* Evidence is insufficient to recommend a specific antiemetic regimen. The choice of regimen is based on institutional policy, clinical context, and availability.

**Recommendation 5.** In individuals undergoing IGB therapy, AGA suggests against perioperative laboratory screening for nutritional deficiencies. *(Conditional recommendation, low certainty)*

**Recommendation 6.** AGA suggests daily supplementation with 1–2 adult dose multivitamins after IGB placement. *(Conditional recommendation, very low certainty)*

**Recommendation 7.** After IGB removal, AGA suggests subsequent weight-loss or maintenance interventions that include dietary interventions, pharmacotherapy, repeat IGB, or bariatric surgery. The choice of weight-loss or maintenance method after IGB is determined based on patient's context and comorbidities following a shared decision-making approach. *(Conditional recommendation, low certainty)*

---

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Weight loss vs SOC (pooled RCTs):** ~15.46 lbs at 6 mo (7 RCTs; 95% CI 10.42–20.51), ~13.12 lbs at 9 mo (3 RCTs; 10.53–15.70), ~9.76 lbs at 12 mo (2 RCTs; 6.38–13.14) — benefit declines with time.
- **%TBWL:** greatest at 6–8 mo (MD 6.89%; 95% CI 4.09–9.70). **Percent excess weight loss:** greatest at 9 mo (MD 20.43%; 16.09–24.77).
- **Responder rates (6–8 mo):** ≥5% TBWL in 85.1% (IGB) vs 34.6% (SOC), RR 2.44; ≥10% TBWL in 61.9% vs 13.7%, RR 4.31.
- **Metabolic:** lowers HbA1c and fasting glucose (esp. glucose >100, HbA1c >6.5%, BMI >40); ALT −9 U/L, AST −3 U/L; waist circumference −4.1 cm; greater remission of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia; LDL downward trend; no triglyceride benefit.
- **Safety:** serious AE 5.6% (IGB) vs 1.1% (SOC), RR 3.07 (95% CI 1.16–8.11); perforation 0.3%, esophageal mucosal injury 0.8%, gastric ulcer/bleeding 0.76%, gastric outlet/bowel obstruction 0.12%. No deaths in 7 pooled RCTs; post-marketing: rare hyperinflation, acute pancreatitis, death. Early removal 9.4% (intolerance: fullness, epigastric pain, reflux, nausea, emesis).
- **Device type:** meta-analysis of 22 RCTs — fluid-filled IGBs ~3% more weight loss than gas-filled but numerically higher AE rates; gas-filled better tolerated/safer. No device-specific recommendation made.
- **Lifestyle (Rec 2):** high-intensity very-low-calorie ketogenic diet > low-calorie diet after IGB (MD 7.1 kg; 12% greater excess weight loss); ongoing diet sustains loss after removal.
- **PPI (Rec 3):** no direct RCT; indirect evidence — PPIs reduce rebleeding risk and IGB+PPI arms had fewer serious upper GI bleeding events. Use lowest dose/frequency/duration given PPI risks (C. difficile, pneumonia, fracture, kidney disease, micronutrient deficiency).
- **Post-removal (Rec 7):** sibutramine and liraglutide 3 mg trials showed maintained/added loss; sequential IGB gave greater BMI reduction (MD 5.49 kg/m²) but more complications; bariatric surgery after IGB and IGB-before-surgery both supported by limited data.
- **BMI eligibility note:** US trials limited to BMI 30–40 kg/m².

---

## Relevance to Wiki

- Anchors the new advanced-procedure page [[intragastric-balloon]] (endoscopic bariatric therapy).
- Connects to [[obesity]] management alongside the pharmacotherapy guideline [[aga-2022-obesity-pharm]] and the GLP-1 agent [[semaglutide]] (liraglutide 3 mg also studied as post-IGB adjunct).
- Establishes IGB-related PPI prophylaxis and links to [[upper-gi-bleeding]] risk and bariatric surgery as a sequential/maintenance option.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No long-term (>1 yr) efficacy data vs SOC; weight-loss benefit declines 6–12 mo.
- No direct RCT for PPI prophylaxis, antiemetic regimen, nutritional screening, or multivitamin dosing — several recommendations rest on indirect/very-low-certainty evidence.
- No device-specific recommendation despite fluid- vs gas-filled trade-offs.

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [AGA 2022: Diagnosis and Management of AKI in Cirrhosis.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.08.033)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2022.08.033](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.08.033)
Flamm SL, Wong F, Ahn J, Kamath PS. "AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Evaluation and Management of Acute Kidney Injury in Patients With Cirrhosis: Expert Review." *Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology* 2022;20:2707–2716. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.08.033>

- Type: Expert review / Best Practice Advice (not a formal systematic review)
- Commissioned by the AGA Institute Clinical Practice Updates Committee
- Authors: Rush University, Toronto General, Oregon Health & Science University, Mayo Clinic

## Summary

This AGA expert review provides 14 Best Practice Advice (BPA) statements on AKI in patients with cirrhosis, covering diagnosis (KDIGO criteria), classification of AKI subtypes, initial evaluation, pharmacological treatment of HRS-AKI (albumin plus vasoconstrictors), indications for renal replacement therapy, and [[liver-transplantation|liver transplantation]] as definitive therapy. The document also reflects the updated International Club of Ascites (ICA) nomenclature replacing HRS Type 1/2 with HRS-AKI and HRS-NAKI.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Epidemiology**

- AKI occurs in ~47% of hospitalized patients with complications of cirrhosis and ~30% of outpatients with cirrhosis
- Associated with a 7-fold increase in morbidity and mortality vs. those without AKI
- ~$4 billion in total US hospitalization costs annually
- Repeated AKI episodes increase risk of progression to CKD

**Diagnosis**

- AKI defined by KDIGO criteria: SCr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, OR ≥50% increase from baseline within 7 days, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 hours
- Baseline SCr: use most recent value within prior 3 months if no value within 7 days
- Serum creatinine underestimates true GFR reduction in cirrhosis (reduced muscle mass, impaired hepatic creatine production, hyperbilirubinemia interfering with colorimetric assays)

**AKI Classification (Updated ICA Nomenclature)**

| Old Term | New Term | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|
| HRS Type 1 | HRS-AKI | Meets AKI criteria + functional, no response to 2-day albumin challenge |
| HRS Type 2 | HRS-NAKI / HRS-AKD | GFR <60 mL/min for <3 months without meeting AKI criteria |
| — | HRS-CKD | GFR <60 mL/min for ≥3 months |

HRS-AKI diagnostic criteria (current):

- SCr increase ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48h OR ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days
- Cirrhosis with [[ascites]]
- No response to 2-day albumin volume challenge (1 g/kg/d)
- Absence of shock
- No current/recent nephrotoxic drug use
- No structural kidney injury markers (proteinuria >500 mg/d, hematuria >50 RBCs/HPF, abnormal renal US)

**Urine Studies**

- Urine Na <10 mEq/L in HRS (but may be higher post-diuretics)
- FENa <1%: suggests prerenal/HRS; sensitivity 100%, specificity only 14% in cirrhosis
- FEUrea <28.16%: sensitivity 75%, specificity 83% for separating HRS from non-HRS — preferred over FENa in cirrhosis
- Urinary NGAL: most studied biomarker; levels in HRS-AKI much lower than ATN; cutoff 220–244 mcg/g creatinine distinguishes ATN from HRS/prerenal; not widely available in US clinically

**Prevention**

- Avoid NSAIDs, excessive diuretics, nonselective beta-blockers
- Albumin 1 g/kg with large-volume paracentesis
- Antibiotics with GI bleeding and [[spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis|SBP]] prophylaxis
- Counsel against alcohol use

**Initial Management (BPA 5)**

- Hold diuretics and nonselective beta-blockers
- Discontinue NSAIDs
- Treat precipitating cause
- Replace fluid losses
- If SCr doubles from baseline: albumin 1 g/kg/d for 2 days

**HRS-AKI Treatment (BPA 6)**

- If SCr remains >2× baseline after initial measures: start vasoconstrictors + albumin
- Albumin: 1 g/kg IV on day 1, then 20–40 g/day
- Continue until SCr returns to within ≤0.3 mg/dL of baseline for 2 consecutive days, OR for maximum 14 days

**Terlipressin (BPA 7)**

- Bolus: 1 mg IV q4–6h (total 4–6 mg/d)
- Escalate to 2 mg q4–6h (total 8–12 mg/d) if SCr does not decrease ≥25% by day 3
- Continuous infusion alternative: start 2 mg/d, titrate by 24–48h intervals to max 12 mg/d
- FDA restrictions: contraindicated if SCr ≥5 mg/dL or O2 sat <90%
- Predictors of response: bilirubin <10 mg/dL, SCr <5 mg/dL, lower ACLF grade, sustained MAP increase of 5–10 mmHg
- Response rate in RCTs: 36–44% (CONFIRM: 29% reversed HRS and survived 10 days post-treatment without RRT)
- Risk of respiratory failure: ~30% in CONFIRM terlipressin arm, especially with concomitant organ failure

**Midodrine + Octreotide (BPA 8)**

- Midodrine: start 7.5 mg PO TID, titrate to 12.5 mg TID
- Octreotide: start 100 mcg SQ TID, titrate to 200 mcg TID
- Inferior to terlipressin; works slowly; widely used when terlipressin unavailable and ICU not available

**Norepinephrine (BPA 9)**

- Start 0.5 mcg/h IV, increase by 0.5 mcg/h q4h, max 3 mcg/h
- Goal: MAP increase ≥10 mmHg and/or urine output >50 mL/h for ≥4 hours
- Must be administered in ICU (feasibility study outside ICU exists but not standard)
- Similar efficacy to terlipressin except in ACLF (bilirubin >5 mg/dL, INR >1.5, with encephalopathy or ascites onset within 4 weeks): terlipressin superior

**Renal Replacement Therapy (BPA 12)**

- Indicated in ATN
- Indicated in HRS-AKI only as bridge to liver transplantation — NOT in non-transplant candidates
- Continuous RRT preferred over intermittent (less hemodynamic instability)
- ~2/3 of HRS-AKI patients on pretransplant RRT recover renal function post-LT
- Duration >14 days pretransplant associated with renal non-recovery
- Each additional day of dialysis pretransplant: 3.6–6% increased risk of renal non-recovery post-LT
- Mortality with >7 days RRT: 59%

**TIPS**

- Not recommended for treatment of HRS-AKI (insufficient data)

**Liver Transplantation (BPA 14)**

- Most effective treatment for HRS-AKI (reverses underlying hepatic dysfunction)
- Treat HRS-AKI pharmacologically before LT — may improve post-LT outcomes
- MELD paradox: successful treatment lowers SCr, reducing MELD-Na score and transplant priority
- Simultaneous liver-kidney transplant criteria (OPTN/UNOS 2017): dialysis dependence OR GFR ≤25 mL/min for ≥6 consecutive weeks

## Recommendations

| Recommendation | Strength | Evidence Quality |
|---|---|---|
| **Diagnosis** | | |
| Diagnose AKI using KDIGO criteria: SCr rise >=0.3 mg/dL within 48h OR >=50% increase from baseline within 7 days OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 hours | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Use FEUrea <28.16% (rather than FENa) to differentiate HRS from non-HRS AKI in cirrhosis | Best Practice Advice | — |
| **Prevention** | | |
| Avoid NSAIDs, excessive diuretics, and nonselective beta-blockers; use albumin with large-volume paracentesis; provide antibiotic prophylaxis with GI bleeding and SBP | Best Practice Advice | — |
| **Initial Management** | | |
| Hold diuretics and NSBBs; treat precipitating cause; replace fluid losses; if SCr doubles from baseline, give albumin 1 g/kg/d for 2 days | Best Practice Advice | — |
| **HRS-AKI Treatment — Vasoconstrictors** | | |
| If SCr remains >2x baseline after initial measures: start vasoconstrictors + albumin (1 g/kg IV on day 1, then 20-40 g/day for up to 14 days) | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Use terlipressin 1 mg IV q4-6h; escalate to 2 mg q4-6h if SCr does not decrease >=25% by day 3 (contraindicated if SCr >=5 mg/dL or O2 sat <90%) | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Use midodrine 7.5 mg TID (titrate to 12.5 mg TID) + octreotide 100 mcg TID (titrate to 200 mcg TID) if terlipressin unavailable and ICU not available | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Use norepinephrine 0.5 mcg/h IV (increase by 0.5 mcg/h q4h to max 3 mcg/h) in ICU when terlipressin unavailable | Best Practice Advice | — |
| **Renal Replacement Therapy** | | |
| Use RRT in ATN; use RRT in HRS-AKI only as bridge to liver transplantation (not in non-transplant candidates) | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Prefer continuous RRT over intermittent RRT for hemodynamic stability | Best Practice Advice | — |
| **Liver Transplantation** | | |
| Treat HRS-AKI pharmacologically before liver transplantation to optimize post-transplant outcomes | Best Practice Advice | — |
| Apply simultaneous liver-kidney transplant criteria (dialysis dependence OR GFR <=25 mL/min for >=6 consecutive weeks) per OPTN/UNOS 2017 | Best Practice Advice | — |

## Relevance to Wiki

Primary source for `[[aki-in-cirrhosis]]` disease script. Provides:

- Current KDIGO/ICA-AKI diagnostic thresholds
- Updated HRS-AKI vs. HRS-NAKI nomenclature (replaces HRS Type 1/2)
- Specific vasoconstrictor dosing regimens for terlipressin, midodrine/octreotide, norepinephrine
- RRT indications and transplant decision framework
- Prevention strategies relevant to patients with [[alcohol-associated-liver-disease]] and [[chronic-hepatitis-b]]

## Contradictions / Open Questions

1. MELD paradox: successful pharmacological reversal of HRS-AKI lowers SCr, decreasing transplant priority — not yet resolved by allocation policy
2. Long-term albumin for HRS prevention: ANSWER trial positive, but not replicated in subsequent trials
3. FENa has poor specificity (14%) in cirrhosis — limited discriminatory value despite widespread use
4. Terlipressin respiratory failure rate (30% in CONFIRM) raises safety concerns, especially in ACLF with multi-organ failure
5. Simultaneous liver-kidney vs. liver-alone transplantation: biomarkers needed to identify best candidates
6. No studies using patient-reported outcomes in AKI in cirrhosis

# US Multi-Society Task Force: GI Hamartomatous Polyposis Syndromes (2022)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [US Multi-Society Task Force Guideline: GI Hamartomatous Polyposis Syndromes (2022). American Journal of Gastroenterology / Gastroenterology (USMSTF).](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.02.021)
- **Year:** 2022
- **Journal:** American Journal of Gastroenterology / Gastroenterology (USMSTF)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2022.02.021](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.02.021)
- **Type:** GRADE-based multi-society guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline provides diagnosis, management, and **surveillance** recommendations for the hamartomatous polyposis syndromes — **Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS)**, **juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS)**, and **PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (Cowden)** — addressing GI polyp burden and extraintestinal cancer risk.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **[[peutz-jeghers-syndrome|Peutz-Jeghers (PJS)]]:** baseline **upper endoscopy + colonoscopy at age 8–10**, repeat every ~3 years (resume at 18 if negative at baseline); lifelong **small-bowel surveillance** (capsule/MRE) for intussusception risk; extraintestinal screening (breast, pancreas, gynecologic, testicular).
- **[[juvenile-polyposis-syndrome|Juvenile polyposis (JPS)]]:** begin **colonoscopy + upper endoscopy at age 12–15** (or earlier if symptomatic), with intervals by polyp burden; evaluate for *SMAD4* (HHT overlap) and *BMPR1A*.
- **PTEN/[[cowden-syndrome|Cowden]]:** **colonoscopy starting at age 35** (earlier if symptomatic); coordinate intensive extraintestinal cancer surveillance (breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal).
- Manage symptomatic/large polyps endoscopically; refer for genetic testing and family cascade screening.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Sets concrete surveillance start ages and intervals across PJS, JPS, and Cowden, integrating small-bowel and extraintestinal cancer screening. Complements the vault's hereditary syndrome notes and [[colorectal-cancer]] prevention.

---

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [AGA Clinical Practice Guideline: Systemic Therapy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (2022). Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline).](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.12.276)

- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2021.12.276](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2021.12.276)
- **Type:** GRADE-based guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline sequences **systemic therapy for advanced [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]]** (not amenable to resection, transplant, or locoregional therapy), reflecting the shift to immunotherapy-based first-line treatment.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **First-line:** **atezolizumab + bevacizumab** over sorafenib in eligible patients (preserved liver function, no high-risk varices/uncontrolled bleeding — screen and manage varices before bevacizumab). **Lenvatinib or sorafenib** where immunotherapy/bevacizumab is contraindicated.
- **Second-line:** tyrosine kinase inhibitors (**regorafenib, cabozantinib**) and **ramucirumab** (for AFP ≥400 ng/mL), or **nivolumab**, depending on prior therapy and tolerance.
- Reserve systemic therapy for **advanced/unresectable** disease with adequate hepatic reserve; integrate with [[hcc-surveillance]] and multidisciplinary staging.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Establishes **atezolizumab + bevacizumab** as preferred first-line for advanced [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]] (with mandatory variceal screening), TKIs/ramucirumab/nivolumab as later lines. Connects to [[portal-hypertension]] (bleeding risk) and surveillance via [[hcc-surveillance]]. (Note: newer regimens, e.g. durvalumab+tremelimumab, post-date this 2022 guideline.)

## Summary

This guideline ranks drug therapy for constipation-predominant [[irritable-bowel-syndrome]] (IBS-C), a [[disorders-of-gut-brain-interaction|disorder of gut–brain interaction]]. Only **linaclotide** earned a strong recommendation; the remainder are conditional.

---

- **[[linaclotide]]** — *recommended* (strong).
- **Tenapanor**, **[[plecanatide]]**, **tegaserod**, and **[[lubiprostone]]** — *suggested* (conditional).
- **PEG laxatives** — suggested (low-cost option, though limited effect on global IBS symptoms/pain).
- **Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)** — suggested for IBS (central neuromodulation).
- **Antispasmodics** — suggested; **against routine SSRIs** for IBS.

Linaclotide is the only strongly recommended agent for IBS-C; secretagogues (tenapanor, plecanatide, lubiprostone) and the prokinetic tegaserod are conditional alternatives, with TCAs for pain-predominant disease. Distinguish IBS-C from [[chronic-idiopathic-constipation]] (overlapping drugs, different targets).

## Summary

This guideline ranks drug therapy for diarrhea-predominant [[irritable-bowel-syndrome]] (IBS-D). All recommendations are conditional.

---

## Key Recommendations (conditional)

- **[[rifaximin]]** — suggested; **retreatment with rifaximin** suggested for recurrent symptoms after initial response.
- **Eluxadoline** — suggested (avoid in patients without a gallbladder, with sphincter-of-Oddi dysfunction, or heavy alcohol use — pancreatitis risk).
- **Alosetron** — suggested for women with severe IBS-D (REMS due to ischemic colitis/constipation risk).
- **Loperamide** — suggested for diarrhea control (limited effect on global symptoms).
- **TCAs** — suggested (central neuromodulation); **antispasmodics** suggested; **against routine SSRIs**.

---

## Clinical Relevance

[[rifaximin]] (with retreatment), eluxadoline, and alosetron are the disease-modifying options for IBS-D, layered with loperamide for symptom control and TCAs for pain. Mirrors the IBS-C guideline within the [[disorders-of-gut-brain-interaction]] framework.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Strand DS, Law RJ, Yang D, Elmunzer BJ. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Endoscopic Approach to Recurrent Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2022;163:1107–1114.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.07.079)
- **Authors:** Daniel S. Strand, Ryan J. Law, Dennis Yang, B. Joseph Elmunzer
- **Year:** 2022
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2022.07.079](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.07.079)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

AGA Expert Review giving practical, evidence-based guidance on the **role of endoscopy in recurrent acute pancreatitis (RAP) and chronic pancreatitis (CP)**, framed around **8 Best Practice Advice statements**. RAP is defined as **≥2 distinct episodes of acute pancreatitis with complete interceding resolution, separated by ≥3 months**; ~10–30% of patients develop RAP after an index AP episode, and ~35% of RAP patients progress to CP.

For **evaluation of unexplained AP/RAP** (etiology unrevealed in 16–27% of cases despite history, medication review, labs, and noninvasive imaging), **EUS is the preferred initial diagnostic test** (yields a potential etiology in 29–88%; most common finding is occult biliary lithiasis; occult ampullary/pancreatobiliary malignancy found in up to 5% after single unexplained AP and up to 12% with RAP). MRI/MRCP with contrast is a reasonable complementary/alternative test — EUS is more likely than MRI to give a probable cause (OR 3.79, driven by sensitivity for occult biliary stones), while MRCP better identifies ductal etiologies (pancreas divisum, anomalous pancreaticobiliary union). Optimal EUS timing is a short delay (2–6 weeks) after AP resolution.

The **role of ERCP to reduce AP frequency is controversial** in both pancreas divisum (PD) and standard-anatomy unexplained RAP. In PD, minor papilla endotherapy may be considered mainly with objective outflow obstruction (dilated dorsal duct and/or santorinicele); there is no role for ERCP for pain alone. In standard anatomy, ERCP is even more controversial and should follow shared decision-making about uncertain benefit and severe adverse-event risk; biliary sphincterotomy alone may be preferable to dual sphincterotomy (Coté RCT).

For **CP**, surgery is favored over endoscopy for long-term treatment of painful obstructive CP (ESCAPE and 2 prior RCTs), with endoscopy a reasonable alternative for poor operative candidates. Endoscopic techniques covered: MPD stones (conventional extraction for ≤5 mm; ESWL and/or pancreatoscopy-guided intraductal lithotripsy for larger), MPD strictures (prolonged 6–12 month plastic-stent upsizing; FCSEMS emerging), CP-related biliary strictures (FCSEMS favored over multiple plastic stents, with a cholecystitis caveat when gallbladder in situ), and EUS-guided celiac plexus block (not routine; case-by-case for debilitating refractory pain).

## Key Findings / Claims

Verbatim/near-verbatim Best Practice Advice statements:

- **Best Practice Advice 1:** After an unrevealing initial evaluation, EUS is the preferred diagnostic test for unexplained acute and recurrent pancreatitis. MRI/MRCP is a reasonable complementary or alternative test to EUS, based on local expertise and availability.

- **Best Practice Advice 2:** The role of ERCP for reducing the frequency of AP episodes in patients with PD is controversial, but minor papilla endotherapy may be considered, particularly for those with objective signs of outflow obstruction, such as a dilated dorsal pancreatic duct and/or santorinicele. There is no role for ERCP to treat pain alone in patients with PD.

- **Best Practice Advice 3:** The role of ERCP for reducing the frequency of pancreatitis episodes in patients with unexplained RAP and standard pancreatic ductal anatomy is controversial and should only be considered after a comprehensive discussion of the uncertain benefits and potentially severe procedure-related adverse events. When pursued, ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy alone may be preferable to dual sphincterotomy.

- **Best Practice Advice 4:** Surgical intervention should be considered over endoscopic therapy for long-term treatment of patients with painful obstructive CP. Endoscopic intervention is a reasonable alternative to surgery for suboptimal operative candidates or those who favor a less invasive approach, assuming they are clearly informed that the best practice advice primarily favors surgery.

- **Best Practice Advice 5:** When ERCP is pursued, small (≤5 mm) MPD stones can be treated with pancreatography and conventional stone extraction maneuvers. For larger stones, ESWL and/or pancreatoscopy with intraductal lithotripsy may be required.

- **Best Practice Advice 6:** When ERCP is pursued, prolonged stent therapy (6–12 months) is effective for treating symptoms and remodeling MPD strictures. The preferred approach is to place and sequentially add multiple plastic stents in parallel (upsizing); emerging evidence suggests that FCSEMS may have a role for this indication, but additional research is necessary.

- **Best Practice Advice 7:** ERCP with stent insertion is the preferred treatment for benign biliary stricture due to CP. FCSEMS placement is favored over multiple plastic stents whenever feasible, given similar efficacy but significantly reduced need for stent exchange procedures during the treatment course.

- **Best Practice Advice 8:** CPB should not be routinely performed for the management of pain due to CP. The decision to proceed with CPB in selected patients with debilitating pain in whom other therapeutic measures have failed can be considered on a case-by-case basis, but only after discussion of the unclear outcomes of this intervention and its procedural risks.

**Supporting data points:**
- RAP definition: ≥2 distinct AP episodes with complete interceding resolution, separated by ≥3 months. ~10–30% develop RAP after index AP; ~35% of RAP progress to CP.
- Unexplained AP: etiology remains unknown in 16–27% despite standard workup. EUS uncovers etiology in 29–88%; most common = occult biliary lithiasis. Occult ampullary/pancreatobiliary malignancy up to 5% after single unexplained AP, up to 12% with RAP.
- EUS vs MRI: EUS more likely to give probable cause (OR 3.79). EUS timing: 2–6 week delay after AP resolution.
- Pancreas divisum: most common congenital pancreatic anomaly, ~6–10% of individuals; most asymptomatic. Endotherapy reduces/eliminates RAP in ~60–80% in uncontrolled series. Only RCT (n=19): minor papilla stenting reduced future AP (10% vs 67%, P<.05). Risks: post-ERCP pancreatitis 10–15%; post-papillotomy stenosis up to 19% (1 in 5).
- Standard-anatomy RAP: Jacob RCT — PD stenting reduced RAP (11% vs 53%, P<.02). Coté RCT — pancreatic sphincterotomy no incremental benefit over biliary sphincterotomy alone.
- Painful obstructive CP: 3 RCTs favor early surgery over endotherapy. ESCAPE (n=88, dilated MPD): complete/partial pain relief 58% (surgery) vs 39% (endotherapy) at 18 months. Endotherapy typically requires serial ERCPs over up to 12 months; surgery is one-time.
- MPD stones: occur in ~60% of CP (more with alcohol >80 g/d, tobacco >20 cig/d). ESWL fragmentation >90%; complete PD clearance by ERCP achievable in >⅔; >½ pain-free at 2 years; up to 89% report QoL improvement. Pancreatoscopy-directed lithotripsy technical success 88%, adverse events 12%.
- MPD strictures: pain relief up to 85% with stent across stricture. Durable remodeling with plastic stents needs 6–12 months incremental upsizing. FCSEMS vs multiple plastic stents meta-analysis: no difference in pain improvement (88% vs 89%) or stricture recurrence (8% vs 11%); fewer ERCPs with FCSEMS but higher adverse event rate (39% vs 14%).
- CP biliary strictures: occur in ~15% of advanced CP. Plastic-stent therapy clinically successful up to 90% but requires several sessions (every 10–12 weeks). FCSEMS: similar success/safety, fewer procedures; caveat — increased cholecystitis risk if gallbladder in situ and stent covers cystic duct orifice → reasonable to avoid FCSEMS then. Stent therapy 6–12 months depending on stricture severity/type/response.
- EUS-guided celiac plexus block: local anesthetic + corticosteroid. Pain relief in 50–60% with duration ≤6 months; weak evidence. Almost all patients need additional analgesics. Diarrhea and orthostatic hypotension most common AEs; major AEs (abscess, intravascular injection, paralysis) <1%.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[recurrent-acute-pancreatitis]]** (new diagnostic schema) — home for the RAP definition, EUS-first evaluation algorithm, and ERCP controversy (BPA 1–3).
- **[[pancreas-divisum]]** (new disease script) — definition, epidemiology, minor papilla endotherapy indications/risks (BPA 2).
- **[[acute-pancreatitis]]** — EUS-preferred evaluation of unexplained/idiopathic AP; occult malignancy yield; timing.
- **[[chronic-pancreatitis]]** — endoscopic therapy detail (stone-size thresholds, stent durations, FCSEMS vs plastic for MPD & biliary strictures), surgery-over-endoscopy for painful obstructive CP, celiac plexus block (BPA 4–8).
- **[[ercp]]** — pancreatic indications: PD minor papilla endotherapy, MPD stones/strictures, CP biliary strictures.
- **[[endoscopic-ultrasound]]** — evaluation of unexplained AP/RAP; EUS-guided celiac plexus block.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Painful obstructive CP — surgery vs endoscopy:** this CPU (2022) explicitly favors **surgery over endoscopy** for long-term pain in obstructive CP (ESCAPE + 2 RCTs), while several prior guidelines (and the existing CP page's pain ladder) frame endoscopy as the initial intervention. Higher-priority resolution: newer ASGE 2024 CP-endoscopy guideline and this AGA CPU both temper the endoscopy-first stance; the CP page notes surgery superiority for long-term pain — consistent.
- **FCSEMS for MPD strictures:** benefit (fewer ERCPs) offset by higher adverse-event rate (39% vs 14%) — role remains "emerging," not standard. For CP biliary strictures FCSEMS is favored, except gallbladder-in-situ cholecystitis caveat.
- Definitive role of ERCP in unexplained RAP (± PD) awaits ongoing sham-controlled minor-papilla-sphincterotomy RCT.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2023;164:484–491.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.11.034)
- **Authors:** Bruce Wang, Herbert L. Bonkovsky, Joseph K. Lim, Manisha Balwani
- **Year:** 2023 (published March 2023; accepted November 20, 2022)
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology, Vol. 164, Iss. 3, pp. 484–491. AGA Institute (open access, CC BY)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2022.11.034](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.11.034)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

The acute hepatic porphyrias (AHP) are rare inborn errors of heme metabolism comprising **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)**, **hereditary coproporphyria (HCP)**, **variegate porphyria (VP)**, and **5-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency porphyria (ALAD)**. Partially defective activity of heme-synthesis enzymes causes accumulation of the porphyrin precursors δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG), producing acute neurovisceral attacks — severe abdominal pain without peritoneal signs or cross-sectional imaging abnormalities, plus nausea, vomiting, constipation, muscle weakness, neuropathy, tachycardia, and hypertension. AIP is the most common form; symptomatic AHP has an estimated prevalence of ~1 in 100,000, though population genetic data suggest AIP pathogenic-variant prevalence of 1 in 1300–1785. About 90% of symptomatic patients are women aged 15–50 years; attacks are rare before menses and after menopause. Diagnosis is frequently delayed (~15 years on average).

Because systematic reviews were not performed, the 12 **Best Practice Advice (BPA)** statements carry no formal ratings of evidence quality or strength; they derive from published literature and expert opinion. The CPU addresses when to screen (women 15–50 y with unexplained recurrent severe abdominal pain), how to diagnose biochemically (random urine ALA, PBG, creatinine — elevated ≥5-fold ULN during attacks), how to confirm the specific type genetically (sequencing ALAD, HMBS, CPOX, PPOX), and how to manage acute attacks and provide long-term care.

Acute-attack cornerstones: discontinuation of porphyrinogenic drugs/chemicals, IV or oral dextrose, IV hemin (3–4 mg/kg/day, high-flow central vein), and analgesics/antiemetics with correction of hypertension, tachycardia, hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia. Patients with recurrent attacks (≥4/year) should be considered for prophylaxis with IV hemin or subcutaneous givosiran (an ALAS1-targeting siRNA). Liver transplantation is curative but reserved for intractable, refractory disease. AHP carries long-term risks of systemic arterial hypertension, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), mandating ongoing surveillance.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Four AHP types** (Table 1): AIP (AD, *HMBS*), HCP (AD, *CPOX*), VP (AD, *PPOX*), ALAD (autosomal recessive, *ALAD*; <12 reported cases worldwide). AIP/HCP/VP autosomal dominant; AHP pathogenic variants cause ≥50% reduction in the corresponding enzyme's activity.
- **Penetrance is low:** ~1% of AIP gene carriers become symptomatic; >20% in families with symptomatic patients. HCP and VP have lower penetrance than AIP. >90% of symptomatic patients experience only 1 or a few lifetime attacks; 3%–5% have recurrent attacks (≥4/year).
- **Biochemical diagnosis:** random (spot) urine ALA, PBG, and creatinine. During acute attacks both ALA and PBG are elevated ≥5-fold ULN, normalized to creatinine; 24-hour collection not recommended. In ALAD porphyria only ALA is elevated (PBG normal). Urine porphyrins alone should NOT be used to screen — secondary porphyrinurias cause overdiagnosis.
- **Timing matters:** testing most useful during an acute attack; ALA/PBG remain elevated for months–years after an AIP attack but fall quickly after HCP/VP attacks. In asymptomatic sporadic AIP, 15%–44% have normal ALA/PBG. In recurrent attackers, ALA/PBG are usually elevated at baseline; normal levels likely rule out AHP.
- **Genetic confirmation:** sequence *ALAD, HMBS, CPOX, PPOX* → ALAD, AIP, HCP, VP respectively; whole-gene sequencing identifies 95%–99%. Screen first-degree relatives once the familial variant is known. Not for initial screening.
- **Acute-attack treatment:** IV hemin 3–4 mg/kg/day, once daily, typically 4 days (3–5 days), via high-flow central vein (PICC/central port) due to thrombophlebitis; heme bound to human serum albumin preferred. Collect random urine ALA/PBG/creatinine before starting hemin. Symptom relief typically 48–72 h.
- **Supportive care:** stop CYP450-inducing precipitants; analgesics and antiemetics; IV carbohydrate loading ~300 g/day; monitor/correct hyponatremia (SIADH — correct slowly) and hypomagnesemia. Seizures: barbiturates, hydantoins, carbamazepine, and valproic acid are contraindicated; magnesium sulfate, benzodiazepines, and levetiracetam appear safe.
- **Trigger avoidance:** alcohol, porphyrinogenic (CYP450-inducing) medications, sex hormones (progesterone), acute illness/infection, physical/psychological stress, tobacco, caloric deprivation. Safe/unsafe drug databases: porphyria.org and drugs-porphyria.org.
- **Prophylaxis (≥4 attacks/year):** off-label prophylactic IV hemin (monitor iron overload) or subcutaneous givosiran (ALAS1-specific siRNA-GalNAc; FDA/EMA approved — adults in US, ≥12 y in EU). Prescribe givosiran only for biochemically AND genetically confirmed recurrent attacks; avoid in pregnancy/pregnancy planning; monitor liver enzymes, BUN/creatinine, homocysteine, amylase, lipase. Menstrual-associated attacks: GnRH agonists (limited success).
- **Liver transplantation:** curative (corrects hepatic HMBS deficiency, normalizes ALA/PBG); reserved for intractable symptoms refractory to pharmacotherapy. European Liver Transplant Registry: 38 recipients; 1- and 5-year survival 92% and 82%; poorer outcomes with severe neuropathy/renal dysfunction. Genetically screen related living donors (asymptomatic *HMBS* variant donors → poor outcomes).
- **Long-term surveillance:** monitor liver disease annually (baseline aminotransferase elevations in 28% in ENVISION; abnormal LFTs warrant alternative-etiology workup). Chronic hemin (9% iron by weight) → iron overload; on ≥monthly prophylactic hemin check ferritin/iron every 3–6 months and consider therapeutic phlebotomy if ferritin >1000 ng/mL. Givosiran: ALT >3× ULN in first 3–6 months → monthly liver enzymes during that period.
- **HCC surveillance:** risk 1.5%–1.8%; begin at age 50 y with liver ultrasound every 6 months regardless of symptom severity. Female predominance 2.5×; HCC may occur without fibrosis/cirrhosis; AFP role unclear.
- **CKD surveillance:** annual serum creatinine and eGFR (more frequent on givosiran). CKD 29% and hypertension 43% (US Porphyrias Consortium); porphyria-associated kidney disease up to 59% of symptomatic AIP (eGFR decline ~1 mL/min/1.73 m²/year); EXPLORE — 68% reduced eGFR, 28% stage 3a/3b/4 CKD. Kidney transplant for ESRD; optimize blood pressure.

## Best Practice Advice Statements (verbatim)

The 12 BPA statements carry **no formal ratings** of evidence quality or strength (no systematic review performed).

1. **Best Practice Advice 1:** Women aged 15–50 years with unexplained, recurrent severe abdominal pain without a clear etiology after an initial workup should be considered for screening for an AHP.
2. **Best Practice Advice 2:** Initial diagnosis of AHP should be made by biochemical testing measuring δ-aminolevulinic acid, porphobilinogen, and creatinine on a random urine sample.
3. **Best Practice Advice 3:** Genetic testing should be used to confirm the diagnosis of AHP in patients with positive biochemical testing.
4. **Best Practice Advice 4:** Acute attacks of AHP that are severe enough to require hospital admission should be treated with intravenous hemin, given daily, preferably into a high-flow central vein.
5. **Best Practice Advice 5:** In addition to intravenous hemin, management of acute attacks of AHP should include pain control, antiemetics, management of systemic arterial hypertension, tachycardia, and hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia, if present.
6. **Best Practice Advice 6:** Patients should be counseled to avoid identifiable triggers that may precipitate acute attacks, such as alcohol and porphyrinogenic medications.
7. **Best Practice Advice 7:** Prophylactic heme therapy or givosiran, administered in an outpatient setting, should be considered in patients with recurrent attacks (4 or more per year).
8. **Best Practice Advice 8:** Liver transplantation for AHP should be limited to patients with intractable symptoms and significantly decreased quality of life who are refractory to pharmacotherapy.
9. **Best Practice Advice 9:** Patients with AHP should be monitored annually for liver disease.
10. **Best Practice Advice 10:** Patients with AHP, regardless of the severity of symptoms, should undergo surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma, beginning at age 50 years, with liver ultrasound every 6 months.
11. **Best Practice Advice 11:** Patients with AHP on treatment should undergo surveillance for chronic kidney disease annually with serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate.
12. **Best Practice Advice 12:** Patients should be counseled on the chronic and long-term complications of AHP, including neuropathy, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma, and need for long-term monitoring.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates the disease script [[acute-hepatic-porphyria]] (hepatology-diseases) — the primary page this source builds.
- Introduces med stubs [[givosiran]] (ALAS1 siRNA) and [[hemin]] (heme therapy) referenced by the disease page.
- Connects to [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]] (HCC surveillance from age 50 with 6-monthly ultrasound) and [[liver-transplantation]] (curative, refractory disease).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No direct conflict with existing wiki content (new topic area).
- Internal open questions noted by the source: cause of AHP-associated liver enzyme elevation/fibrosis is undefined; role of AFP in HCC surveillance is unclear; mechanism of chronic symptoms (persistent ALA elevation vs incomplete neurologic recovery) remains uncertain; givosiran may worsen eGFR in a subset of patients.

# AGA CPU on the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Colon Polyp Diagnosis and Management (2023)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Samarasena J, Yang D, Berzin TM. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Colon Polyp Diagnosis and Management: Commentary. *Gastroenterology* 2023;165:1568–1573.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.010)
- **Authors:** Jason Samarasena, Dennis Yang, Tyler M. Berzin
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.010](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.010)
- **Type:** Clinical Practice Update — Expert Commentary (no formal Best Practice Advice statements)

---

## Summary

This AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update is an **Expert Commentary** (not a formal GRADE or Best Practice Advice document) reviewing the current landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) for [[colonoscopy]]. It frames AI computer-vision tools into three groups: **computer-aided detection (CADe)** for finding polyps, **computer-aided diagnosis (CADx)** for optical histology prediction, and **computer-aided quality assessment** for measuring/improving withdrawal technique.

CADe was the first target: meta-analytic data show it significantly raises adenoma detection rate (ADR) and adenomas detected per colonoscopy (APC), but the gains are mainly in small, non-advanced adenomas, and several recent pragmatic/observational studies (Ladabaum, Levy, a UK RCT) found **no ADR benefit** — attributed to ceiling effects in high performers, unconscious degradation of mucosal exposure, and unblinding/performance bias. CADx aims to enable "resect-and-discard" and "diagnose-and-leave" strategies, which require meeting the ASGE PIVI thresholds; a real-time white-light CADx study exceeded the ≥90% NPV threshold for diminutive rectosigmoid lesions. Adoption remains slower than expected because of cost/reimbursement, lack of integration into scopes, and false-positive distraction.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

**AI and computer vision — framework**
- Three application classes in colonoscopy: **CADe** (detection), **CADx** (optical diagnosis/histology prediction), and **computer-aided quality assessment** (a third, emerging class targeting exposure errors).
- Contemporary tools use deep-learning convolutional neural networks trained on large datasets, running in real time on live video (earlier systems were still-image, hand-engineered feature detectors).

**Rationale / detection variability**
- CRC is the 2nd most common cause of cancer death worldwide; screening colonoscopy reduces CRC risk by removing precancerous polyps.
- Polyp detection is operator-dependent: **ADR ranges 7%–53%** across colonoscopists.
- A **1% increase in ADR** is associated with a **3% decrease in future CRC risk**; missed neoplastic polyps drive post-colonoscopy interval CRC (~8% of all diagnosed CRC).
- Most detected polyps are diminutive and non-neoplastic; unnecessary resection/pathology of these adds cost and adverse-event risk.

**CADe — computer-aided detection**
- Early CNN CADe (Urban et al): 97% sensitivity, 95% specificity, 96% accuracy; detected 92% of polyps the endoscopists had missed.
- Meta-analysis (Huang et al, 10 RCTs, 6629 patients): AI-aided vs routine colonoscopy — **ADR RR 1.43** (P<.001) and **polyp detection rate RR 1.44** (P<.001); APC and PDC also significantly higher.
- **Negative/neutral studies:** Ladabaum (retrospective pragmatic trial — no improvement in ADR/APC); Levy (retrospective observational — **lower** ADR with CADe, 30.3% vs 35.2%, P=.001); a UK RCT — no ADR difference.
- Proposed explanations for lack of benefit: ceiling effect in high-ADR endoscopists; unconscious degradation of mucosal-exposure quality (false sense of security); unblinding/performance bias in most RCTs.
- **Cost concerns:** ADR gains are mostly small non-advanced adenomas → risk of more unnecessary resections; Shaukat US multicenter RCT (677 standard vs 682 CADe) showed **APC 0.83 → 1.05** with **no decrease in true-histology rate** (i.e., CADe raised APC without more resection of non-neoplastic lesions).
- **Surveillance burden:** Mori et al estimated CADe increases the proportion needing intensive surveillance by ~35% (US) and ~20% (Europe) (absolute +2.9% and +1.3%).
- **Cost-effectiveness modeling (Areia):** CRC-incidence reduction vs no screening was 44.2% (colonoscopy without AI) vs 48.9% (with AI); AI lowered discounted cost per screened individual from $3400 to $3343; at US-population level, ~7194 additional CRC cases and ~2089 deaths prevented per year, ~$290 million saved per year — contingent on real-world ADR gains.
- Human–AI interaction: false positives are a major deterrent; formalized training and better algorithms proposed; a physician learning curve exists.

**CADx — computer-aided diagnosis (optical histology)**
- Goal: enable **resect-and-discard** and **diagnose-and-leave** strategies for diminutive polyps, reducing polypectomy/pathology.
- **ASGE PIVI thresholds:** to *diagnose-and-leave* suspected hyperplastic polyps <5 mm in the rectosigmoid, technology must provide **≥90% negative predictive value** for adenomatous histology; to *resect-and-discard* polyps <5 mm, the technology must provide **>90% agreement** on post-polypectomy surveillance intervals vs pathology-based assignment.
- Adenomas <5 mm + rectosigmoid hyperplastic polyps <5 mm account for **>80%** of all polyps found at screening/surveillance; broad adoption could save an estimated **$33–150 million/year**.
- Hassan et al (simultaneous CADe + CADx, white-light unmagnified): CADx feasible in 98.6% of polyps; **NPV 97.6%** for rectosigmoid lesions <5 mm; 82% amenable to leave-in-situ; 39% amenable to resect-and-discard; 95.9% agreement with histology-based surveillance intervals — exceeding the PIVI ≥90% NPV bar in standard white-light endoscopy.
- Barua et al: CADx (requiring a magnifying colonoscope) did not raise diagnostic sensitivity but **improved endoscopist confidence** (high-confidence diagnosis 74.2% → 92.6%).
- Barriers to CADx adoption: need for workflow-integrated tools without image enhancement/magnification; reimbursement (pathology fees are revenue), and medical-legal concerns of leaving/discarding polyps.

**Computer-aided quality assessment**
- Missed adenomas arise from **cognitive errors** (fails to recognize a visualized adenoma) and **exposure errors** (blind spots/incomplete mucosal exposure from withdrawal speed, skill, cleansing). Current CADe does **not** address exposure errors.
- Four complementary skills improve inspection quality against exposure errors: **fold examination, mucosal cleaning, luminal distension, adequacy of viewing time.**
- Liu et al AI fold-evaluation-quality (FEQ) system: correlated with expert scores, historical ADR, and withdrawal time; for low-ADR (<25%) colonoscopists, AI assistance significantly improved FEQ.
- Other emerging tools: withdrawal "speedometers," colon-surface "painting"/coverage maps, mucosal-exposure scoring.

**Challenges & future directions**
- Despite robust early data, clinical adoption is slower than expected (Rex et al): history of underused add-on detection devices (low value ascribed by colonoscopists); **no separate reimbursement** for CADe; not yet integrated into scopes/processors (currently a separate add-on); false-positive distraction.
- Authors predict a future **hybrid model** — an AI "suite" (CADe + CADx + quality assessment + automated note generation) integrated into practice.

---

## Relevance to Wiki

- Primary home: [[artificial-intelligence-endoscopy]] (new concept page — CADe / CADx / computer-aided quality assessment).
- Updates [[colonoscopy]] — AI adjuncts within quality metrics (ADR, APC, withdrawal quality).
- Touches [[colorectal-cancer-screening]] and [[polypectomy-emr]] (resect-and-discard / diagnose-and-leave strategies, PIVI thresholds).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Source priority note:** the later **[[aga-2025-cade-colonoscopy]]** AGA *living guideline* (GRADE) makes **no recommendation for or against** routine CADe (very low certainty). This 2023 CPU is an enthusiastic *commentary* summarizing positive early data; where they meet (CADe for detection), the newer 2025 guideline's cautious framing governs the wiki's primary assertion. The 2023 CPU remains the home for the CADx and quality-assessment content the 2025 CADe-only guideline does not cover.
- CADe ADR benefit is inconsistent across real-world/pragmatic studies (positive RCT meta-analysis vs neutral/negative pragmatic and UK RCT data).
- Cost-effectiveness hinges on unproven assumptions that ADR gains persist in routine practice.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [McGill SK, Hashash JG, Platts-Mills TA. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Alpha-Gal Syndrome for the GI Clinician: Commentary. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023;21:891–896.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.035)
- **Authors:** Sarah K. McGill, Jana G. Hashash, Thomas A. Platts-Mills
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2023;21(4):891–896
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.035](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.035)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Commentary; narrative, no formal Best Practice Advice statements or evidence ratings)

## Summary

Commentary to increase awareness among gastroenterologists of alpha-gal syndrome, an emerging IgE-mediated allergy to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (an oligosaccharide on the cells of all nonprimate mammals). Reactions occur **1 to several hours after** ingestion of mammalian meat or mammalian-derived products and can cause anaphylaxis, GI symptoms, and skin changes. Sensitization is understood to follow a **tick bite** (Lone Star tick / *Amblyomma americanum* in the US) or parasitic infection. In the US, reports cluster in the range of the Lone Star tick (New York and Iowa to Texas and Florida).

The CPU focuses on the increasingly recognized **GI phenotype**: nonspecific abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting **without** predominant skin, respiratory, or circulatory symptoms. These patients often present to primary care, ERs, or GI clinics and are commonly misdiagnosed as IBS or other functional GI illness unless the specific alpha-gal IgE blood test is sent. Research on GI alpha-gal is nascent; formal ratings of evidence quality/strength were not performed because no systematic review was done.

Mechanism (Figure 1): the ingested alpha-gal antigen binds to fat in a glycolipid, is absorbed and incorporated into chylomicrons, and enters the circulation in ~2 hours; it then binds IgE on GI mast cells, which degranulate and release histamine and other mediators acting on sensory nerves (pain), smooth muscle (contraction), and mucous glands. Two GI observational studies (16 patients in North Carolina; 359 in Virginia) found ~three-quarters of alpha-gal IgE+ GI patients improved on an avoidance diet. Among 91 oral-food-challenge–proven patients, abdominal pain (71%) and vomiting (22%) were most common, and 40.7% had GI symptoms alone.

## Key Findings / Claims (narrative — no numbered Best Practice Advice)

- **Antigen / mechanism:** allergy is to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal), present on all nonprimate mammals. IgE-mediated; delayed (hours) because antigen must be absorbed on fat via chylomicrons (~2 h to circulation) before binding GI mast cell IgE.
- **Sensitization:** occurs after tick bite (US: Lone Star tick, *Amblyomma americanum*; principal host deer) or parasitic infection (e.g., *Ascaris*). Lone Star tick is the only US tick that bites humans in the larval phase.
- **Geography (US):** range of *Amblyomma americanum* — Southeast, mid-Atlantic, Midwest, East Central Census regions (NY/Iowa → TX/FL). International reports: Australia, South Africa, Western Europe, Japan (all continents except Antarctica).
- **GI presentation:** abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting without predominant skin/respiratory/circulatory symptoms. Symptom stats from OFC-proven cohorts: abdominal pain 71%, vomiting 22%, GI-only reactions 40.7%. Delayed reactions (hives/anaphylaxis) typically occur 3–5 hours after eating mammalian meat.
- **When to consider it:** unexplained GI symptoms (abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) in patients who live/have lived in an alpha-gal–prevalent area → send **serum alpha-gal IgE**. Features raising likelihood: **nighttime awakening from sleep with GI distress**, history of tick bites, outdoor pursuits.
- **When NOT to test / red flags:** consider not testing patients with **anemia, GI bleeding, or weight loss** — the allergy does not cause these. Skin symptoms (urticaria, angioedema) may or may not be present.
- **Diagnosis (clinical + supporting labs):** requires (1) consistent symptoms, (2) **increased alpha-gal IgE titer**, and (3) **symptom resolution/improvement after an alpha-gal–avoidance diet**. A positive alpha-gal IgE **alone is not sufficient**, especially with isolated GI distress, because sensitized individuals are often asymptomatic (seroprevalence 31% in a NC colonoscopy screening cohort; 35% in German hunters/forest workers). *(No specific numeric IgE cutoff is given in this CPU.)*
- **Diagnostic trial:** alpha-gal–avoidance diet eliminating mammalian meat (beef, pork, venison) and related products (lard, dairy, ice cream) for **at least a month**, avoiding restaurants (cross-contamination) and processed foods (additives); re-evaluate after the trial. Oral food challenge is the formal allergy diagnostic but is impractical here (hours-long delay, inconsistent reactions).
- **Management cornerstone = dietary elimination.** Avoid pork, beef, venison, and any mammal ("any animal with hair") and their products: lard, butter, milk. Dairy contains smaller amounts (higher with high-fat: **ice cream, cream, cream cheese**). **Gelatin** (pig/cow bone collagen) → marshmallows, gummy bears, gelatin candies, desserts may be problematic. Processed foods and restaurant cross-contamination are risks; some react to **aerosolized alpha-gal** (frying bacon/beef). **Acceptable:** fish, seafood, turkey, chicken, other fowl. Work with dieticians.
- **Accidental exposure:** inform a reliable person; take **1–2 diphenhydramine 25 mg tablets**; ensure access to **self-injectable epinephrine**, especially if respiratory compromise. No evidence supports acupuncture.
- **Tick-bite avoidance** (further bites raise IgE titers and worsen allergy): tick checks and showering after wooded areas, tight mesh socks pulled over pant cuffs, treat clothes/boots with **permethrin**.
- **Alpha-gal in medical products:** cetuximab (severe infusion anaphylaxis — original 2007 signal), porcine **pancreatic enzymes**, and bioprosthetic (bovine/porcine) **cardiac valves/patches/veins** (in-vitro IgE affinity; ≥2 anaphylaxis reports post-valve; no proven early device failure). Revivicor makes alpha-gal–free devices and pork (FDA-approved, not yet widely available); alpha-gal–knockout pig kidneys xenotransplanted without hyperacute rejection.
- **Follow-up (dynamic condition):** if tick bites avoided, **repeat alpha-gal IgE at 6–12 months**; as levels fall/negative, may resume first dairy then mammalian meat in small portions. Self-challenge only with modest doses (**quarter serving of meat**), antihistamines + autoinjectable epinephrine available, another person present; patients with systemic symptoms (itching, hives) should work with an allergist first.
- **Refer to allergist** when skin/systemic changes occur (facial/throat swelling, voice changes, difficulty breathing, hives, fainting) — anaphylaxis risk; need epinephrine-autoinjector counseling. No established desensitization protocol exists.
- **Cofactors** increasing risk/severity of reaction: fatty cuts of meat, NSAIDs, exercise, alcohol. A sensitized person who tolerates meat once can still be allergic (reactions don't occur after every exposure).
- **Asymptomatic sensitization:** mostly asymptomatic and not associated with decreased meat intake or higher rates of abdominal pain/diarrhea; but continued mammalian-meat intake in sensitized individuals may raise **coronary artery disease** risk (noncalcified plaque, obstructive CAD).

**Take-Home Messages (verbatim):** "Gastroenterology clinicians should be aware of the diagnosis and management of alpha-gal syndrome because a subset of alpha-gal allergic patients show GI symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting without skin changes or anaphylaxis. The diagnosis of alpha-gal syndrome can be made among patients with GI distress and increased serum alpha-gal IgE antibodies whose symptoms are relieved adequately on an alpha-gal–avoidance diet that eliminates pork, beef, and mammalian-derived products. Patients with suspected alpha-gal allergy should be counseled on an alpha-gal–avoidance diet because that is the primary management. Counseling also should include measures to avoid tick bites because further bites can drive alpha-gal IgE titers higher and worsen the allergy. Patients who also have reactions such as facial swelling, urticaria, and respiratory difficulty should be referred to allergists. GI alpha-gal syndrome recently was described, and prospective studies are needed to better understand this condition."

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[alpha-gal-syndrome]] — new disease-script page (route: `1-disease-scripts/other/`).
- [[irritable-bowel-syndrome]] — key differential; alpha-gal is a departure from functional-GI paradigms and can be misdiagnosed as IBS.
- [[chronic-diarrhea]] — diagnostic-schema workup context for unexplained diarrhea.
- [[colorectal-cancer]] — cetuximab (anti-EGFR) infusion reactions were the original alpha-gal signal.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **No formal evidence grades** (commentary; no systematic review). Prospective studies on GI alpha-gal do not yet exist.
- **No numeric alpha-gal IgE cutoff** is specified for diagnosis — the CPU relies on an "increased" titer plus symptom response, explicitly noting a positive IgE alone is insufficient.
- Consequences of continued mammalian-meat intake in asymptomatic sensitized individuals are unclear; cardiovascular (CAD) association is reported but causation/device-failure not established.

- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline)

- **Type:** GRADE-based guideline

## Summary

This guideline defines how **fecal calprotectin, CRP, and the Endoscopic Healing Index** can substitute for or triage endoscopy in monitoring [[crohns-disease]], supporting a **biomarker- and symptom-based** treat-to-target strategy over symptoms alone.

---

## Key Recommendations

- Use a **biomarker- and symptom-based monitoring** strategy rather than symptoms alone.
- In patients in **symptomatic remission:** a **fecal calprotectin <150 µg/g** plus **normal CRP** rules out active inflammation and **avoids routine endoscopy**.
- In patients with **active symptoms:** elevated **fecal calprotectin / CRP** supports active inflammation and the need for treatment adjustment; normal biomarkers with persistent symptoms warrant endoscopic evaluation to confirm.
- Thresholds guide escalation/de-escalation within a treat-to-target framework.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Embeds noninvasive biomarkers (calprotectin <150, CRP) into [[crohns-disease]] monitoring, reducing unnecessary colonoscopy while catching subclinical inflammation. Complements the IBD pharmacologic guidelines and the [[inflammatory-bowel-disease]] treat-to-target paradigm.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Moshiree B, Drossman D, Shaukat A. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Evaluation and Management of Belching, Abdominal Bloating, and Distention: Expert Review. Gastroenterology. 2023;165(3):791–800.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.04.039)
- **Authors:** Baha Moshiree, Douglas Drossman, Aasma Shaukat
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.04.039](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.04.039)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

AGA Expert Review covering three highly prevalent, often-overlapping GI symptoms — **belching, abdominal bloating, and abdominal distention** — which, when frequent/severe enough to impair daily activity, are categorized as **disorders of gut–brain interaction (DGBIs)**. Because systematic reviews were not performed, the best-practice-advice statements carry **no formal GRADE ratings**; where evidence was insufficient, level-5 (expert opinion) guidance is given.

Belching is separated from bloating/distention given differing location, pathophysiology, and diagnostic/treatment pathways. **Belching** is subdivided into **gastric** (a true transient LES relaxation letting gastric air escape; associated with GERD) and **supragastric** (a learned behavior — air sucked/injected into the esophagus and immediately expelled, independent of peristalsis; associated with anxiety, stops during sleep/distraction/speaking). **Aerophagia** (excess air swallowing) is distinct and presents mainly with bloating/flatulence. High-resolution manometry with impedance/impedance-pH differentiates the belching syndromes. Supragastric belching is a behavioral disorder → treated with brain–gut behavioral therapies (CBT, diaphragmatic breathing), speech therapy, and central neuromodulators, not PPIs.

**Abdominal bloating** (subjective sensation of fullness/gas/tightness) and **distention** (objective, visible increase in girth) have interrelated pathophysiology and are diagnosed by **Rome IV** criteria as primary DGBIs only when IBS, functional constipation/diarrhea, and functional dyspepsia are excluded. Prevalence of primary functional bloating/distention is ~3.5% (higher in women), but bloating/distention are >50% prevalent when overlapping other DGBIs. Diagnostic testing is **algorithmic and symptom-driven** — most patients need no labs/imaging/endoscopy absent alarm features. Management combines dietary (low-FODMAP, fructan/gluten avoidance with dietitian), treatment of underlying constipation/pelvic-floor dyssynergia (biofeedback), and central neuromodulators + brain–gut behavioral therapies for visceral hypersensitivity. **Probiotics are not recommended** for bloating/distention.

## Key Findings / Claims (Best Practice Advice — verbatim)

1. **BPA 1:** Clinical history and physical examination findings and impedance pH monitoring can help to differentiate between gastric and supragastric belching.
2. **BPA 2:** Treatment options for supragastric belching may include brain–gut behavioral therapies, either separately or in combination, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, diaphragmatic breathing, speech therapy, and central neuromodulators.
3. **BPA 3:** Rome IV criteria should be used to diagnose primary abdominal bloating and distention.
4. **BPA 4:** Carbohydrate enzyme deficiencies may be ruled out with dietary restriction and/or breath testing. In a small subset of at-risk patients, small bowel aspiration and glucose- or lactulose-based hydrogen breath testing may be used to evaluate for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
5. **BPA 5:** Serologic testing may rule out celiac disease in patients with bloating and, if serologies are positive, a small bowel biopsy should be done to confirm the diagnosis. A gastroenterology dietitian should be part of the multidisciplinary approach to care for patients with celiac disease and nonceliac gluten sensitivity.
6. **BPA 6:** Abdominal imaging and upper endoscopy should be ordered in patients with alarm features, recent worsening symptoms, or an abnormal physical examination only.
7. **BPA 7:** Gastric emptying studies should not be ordered routinely for bloating and distention, but may be considered if nausea and vomiting are present. Whole gut motility and radiopaque transit studies should not be ordered unless other additional and treatment-refractory lower gastrointestinal symptoms exist to warrant testing for neuromyopathic disorders.
8. **BPA 8:** In patients with abdominal bloating and distention thought to be related to constipation or difficult evacuation, anorectal physiology testing is suggested to rule out a pelvic floor disorder.
9. **BPA 9:** When dietary modifications are needed (eg, low-FODMAP diet), a gastroenterology dietitian should preferably monitor treatment.
10. **BPA 10:** Probiotics should not be used to treat abdominal bloating and distention.
11. **BPA 11:** Biofeedback therapy may be effective for bloating and distention when a pelvic floor disorder is identified.
12. **BPA 12:** Central neuromodulators (eg, antidepressants) are used to treat bloating and abdominal distention by reducing visceral hypersensitivity, raising sensation threshold, and improving psychological comorbidities.
13. **BPA 13:** Medications used to treat constipation should be considered for treating bloating if constipation symptoms are present.
14. **BPA 14:** Psychological therapies, such as hypnotherapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, and other brain–gut behavior therapies may be used to treat patients with bloating and distention.
15. **BPA 15:** Diaphragmatic breathing and central neuromodulators are used to treat abdominophrenic dyssynergia.

**Additional decision-relevant detail:**
- Rome IV **belching** = audible escape of air from esophagus/stomach into pharynx; "excessive belching" when bothersome and >3 days/week.
- Rome IV **functional bloating/distention** = recurrent fullness/pressure or visible girth increase ≥1 day/week, active ≥3 months, onset ≥6 months prior, without predominant pain or altered bowel habits, and not meeting IBS/functional constipation/diarrhea/FD criteria.
- Supragastric belching before reflux does **not** respond to PPI; after a reflux episode it may.
- Baclofen not advocated for supragastric belching alone; may be considered for gastric belching due to GERD (reduces LES relaxations).
- SIBO testing **not** advocated routinely for bloating/distention unless clear risk factors or severe symptoms (chronic watery diarrhea, malnutrition/weight loss, small-bowel dysmotility diseases — cystic fibrosis, Parkinson, scleroderma, diabetes).
- Fructose intolerance (60%) more common than lactose (51%) across DGBIs.
- Bloating/fullness can be a presenting symptom of **ovarian cancer** (highest risk women ≥50) — alarm-feature imaging caveat.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Creates `[[abdominal-bloating-and-distention]]` diagnostic schema (belching, bloating, distention; Rome IV criteria; symptom-driven workup; neuromodulator/behavioral therapy).
- Links to `[[disorders-of-gut-brain-interaction]]`, `[[small-intestinal-bacterial-overgrowth]]`, `[[intestinal-methanogen-overgrowth]]`, `[[irritable-bowel-syndrome]]`, `[[celiac-disease]]`, `[[chronic-idiopathic-constipation]]`, `[[defecation-disorders]]`, `[[gastroparesis]]`, `[[dyspepsia]]`.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- SIBO breath-test cutoffs/substrate doses remain non-standardized and controversial; authors decline to endorse routine testing — consistent with `[[acg-2020-sibo]]` caution.
- No formal evidence grades (expert review); most treatment evidence is single-center or observational.

title: "AGA Clinical Practice Update on Risk Stratification for Colorectal Cancer Screening and Post-Polypectomy Surveillance: Expert Review (2023)"

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Issaka RB, Chan AT, Gupta S. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Risk Stratification for Colorectal Cancer Screening and Post-Polypectomy Surveillance: Expert Review. *Gastroenterology* 2023;165(5):1280–1291.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.033)
- **Authors:** Rachel B. Issaka, Andrew T. Chan, Samir Gupta
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.033](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.033)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review; Best Practice Advice, unrated)

## Summary

AGA CPU Expert Review on how to **risk-stratify adults for CRC screening initiation and post-polypectomy surveillance**, framed around age, family history, and predisposing conditions. Nine Best Practice Advice (BPA) statements; because no systematic review was performed, statements carry **no formal evidence grade**.

Core framework: fibrosis of the field — **average risk** (no personal/family history of CRC, IBD, hereditary syndrome, or other predisposing condition) vs **increased risk** (chiefly a first-degree relative [FDR] with CRC, or a family history of advanced adenoma). Average-risk screening begins at **age 45**. For an FDR with CRC, screening begins **10 years before the youngest affected relative's diagnosis age, or age 40, whichever is earlier**. Colonoscopy is the strategy of choice for increased-risk individuals (highest sensitivity for neoplasia); average-risk individuals may choose among colonoscopy, FIT, flexible sigmoidoscopy + FIT, multitarget stool DNA-FIT, and CT colonography by availability/preference.

For adults **>75 years**, both continued screening and continued post-polypectomy surveillance should be **individualized** on risks/benefits/comorbidities and screening history — colonoscopy harms rise with age (3.8%–6.8% emergency visit/hospitalization within 30 days in older adults) and a **≥5-year "lag time to benefit"** means those with life expectancy <5 years are unlikely to benefit. Emerging multifactorial risk-stratification tools (demographics, lifestyle, genetics) should be validated for real-world and cost-effectiveness across diverse populations before adoption.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice (verbatim intent, 9 statements):**

1. All individuals with a **first-degree relative** (parent, sibling, or child) diagnosed with CRC — **particularly before age 50** — should be considered at increased risk for CRC.
2. All individuals **without** a personal history of CRC, IBD, hereditary CRC syndromes, other CRC-predisposing conditions, or a family history of CRC should be considered at **average risk**.
3. Average-risk individuals should **initiate screening at age 45**; those at increased risk due to an FDR with CRC should initiate **10 years before the age at diagnosis of the youngest affected relative, or age 40, whichever is earlier**.
4. Risk stratification for **initiation** should be based on age, known/suspected predisposing hereditary CRC syndrome, and/or family history of CRC.
5. The decision to **continue CRC screening in individuals >75 years** should be individualized on risks, benefits, screening history, and comorbidities.
6. Screening options for **average-risk** individuals: colonoscopy, FIT, flexible sigmoidoscopy + FIT, multitarget stool DNA-FIT, and CT colonography — based on availability and individual preference.
7. **Colonoscopy** should be the screening strategy used for individuals at **increased** CRC risk.
8. The decision to **continue post-polypectomy surveillance in individuals >75 years** should be individualized on risks, benefits, and comorbidities.
9. Risk-stratification tools emerging from research should be examined for real-world and cost-effectiveness in diverse populations before widespread implementation.

**Supporting data:**
- Lifetime CRC risk ~4% (average risk); ~20% of CRC shows familial clustering, ~5% due to hereditary syndromes.
- Pooled RR of CRC with ≥1 affected FDR ~1.76–2.26; substantially higher when the FDR was diagnosed **<50 years** (pooled cohort RR 3.26; 95% CI 2.82–3.77) vs ≥50 years (RR 1.83).
- FDR with any adenoma → ~1.8-fold increased CRC risk; siblings of patients with advanced adenoma had 11.5% vs 2.5% prevalence of advanced adenoma (OR 6.05).
- NORDICC (only screening-colonoscopy RCT): invited-to-colonoscopy RR of CRC 0.82 (0.70–0.93); per-protocol (completed colonoscopy) RR 0.69 for incidence and 0.50 for mortality; only 42% completed.
- Multitarget stool DNA-FIT sensitivity for CRC ~92% vs conventional FIT ~74%, but lower specificity; annual FIT more effective and less costly than mt-sDNA-FIT in cost-effectiveness analysis.
- Older adults: 1.5–3.7-fold increase in post-colonoscopy complications vs younger.

**Table 1 (guideline comparison — CRC screening initiation, family-history strata):** ACG 2021, ACS 2018, NCCN 2022, USMSTF 2021/2017, USPSTF 2021 for average risk (begin 45, "any test"); for increased risk (FDR with CRC/advanced adenoma), all recommend beginning **age 40 or 10 years before earliest CRC diagnosis**, colonoscopy every 5 y (ACG: CRC/advanced adenoma in 1 FDR <60 y or ≥2 FDRs any age → colonoscopy q5y; single FDR ≥60 y → begin age 40, any test).

**Table 2 (research priorities):** validate multifactorial and ancestry-inclusive risk models; studies in adults >75 y for stop-age; family-history documentation interventions; AI incorporation of colonoscopy-quality factors into surveillance risk.

## Relevance to Wiki

- **[[colorectal-cancer-screening]]** — supplies the family-history risk-stratification strata and initiation ages (average 45; FDR-with-CRC begins 40 or 10 y before youngest relative's diagnosis); increased-risk → colonoscopy.
- **[[colonoscopy-surveillance]]** — >75 y individualization of surveillance; lag-time-to-benefit (≥5 y); harms rising with age.
- **[[colorectal-cancer]]** — family-history/predisposing-condition risk context.
- Cross-links to **[[lynch-syndrome]]**, **[[familial-adenomatous-polyposis]]**, FIT/**[[colonoscopy]]** modalities.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- This CPU **broadens** the increased-risk definition: it advises treating **any** FDR with CRC as high-risk regardless of the relative's age at diagnosis (until better data), whereas ACG 2021 / NCCN differentiate FDR <60 y vs ≥60 y for interval intensity. Higher-priority/newer formal guidelines (USMSTF/ACG) still govern specific surveillance intervals; this CPU adds the simplified initiation heuristic.
- No RCTs inform the optimal **stop age**; all >75 y guidance is individualized expert advice.
