## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Whitcomb DC, Buchner AM, Forsmark CE. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Management of Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2023;165:1292–1301.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.007)
- **Authors:** David C. Whitcomb, Anna M. Buchner, Chris E. Forsmark
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2023;165:1292–1301
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.007](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.007)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review; Best Practice Advice, no formal GRADE ratings)

## Summary

Expert Review on exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) — failure of the pancreas to deliver a threshold level of digestive enzymes to the intestine, causing maldigestion, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and protein-calorie malnutrition. EPI is frequently underdiagnosed and undertreated. The update frames EPI as a syndrome to be **suspected** in high-risk conditions and **considered** in moderate-risk conditions, diagnosed primarily by **fecal elastase-1 (FE-1)** on a formed stool, and treated with **pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT)** plus fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and nutritional monitoring.

Fifteen Best Practice Advice (BPA) statements carry no formal evidence grade (drawn from literature review and expert opinion).

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice statements (verbatim/near-verbatim):**

1. EPI should be **suspected** in high-risk clinical conditions: chronic pancreatitis, relapsing acute pancreatitis, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, cystic fibrosis, and previous pancreatic surgery.
2. EPI should be **considered** in moderate-risk conditions: duodenal diseases (celiac and Crohn's disease), previous intestinal surgery, longstanding diabetes mellitus, and hypersecretory states (e.g., Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).
3. Clinical features of EPI: steatorrhea with or without diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, excessive flatulence, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, and protein-calorie malnutrition.
4. **Fecal elastase test is the most appropriate initial test** and must be performed on a semi-solid or solid stool specimen. FE-1 **<100 µg/g** stool = good evidence of EPI; **100–200 µg/g = indeterminate**.
5. Fecal elastase testing **can be performed while on PERT** (FE-1 does not cross-react with porcine enzymes).
6. Fecal fat testing is rarely needed and must be performed on a high-fat diet; quantitative testing is generally not practical for routine clinical use.
7. **Response to a therapeutic trial of pancreatic enzymes is unreliable for EPI diagnosis.**
8. Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI, EUS) **cannot identify EPI**, though it is important for diagnosis of benign and malignant pancreatic disease.
9. Breath tests and direct pancreatic function tests hold promise but are not widely available in the United States.
10. Once EPI is diagnosed, **PERT is required**; untreated EPI causes complications of fat malabsorption and malnutrition and reduces quality of life.
11. PERT formulations are all porcine-derived and equally effective at equivalent doses; **non–enteric-coated preparations require concurrent H2 blocker or PPI**.
12. PERT should be taken **during the meal**; initial dose **≥40,000 USP units of lipase per meal** in adults and **one-half that with snacks**; titrate to meal size and fat content.
13. Routine supplementation and monitoring of fat-soluble vitamins is appropriate; dietary modification = low-to-moderate fat diet with frequent smaller meals; **avoid very-low-fat diets**.
14. Markers of successful PERT: reduction in steatorrhea and GI symptoms; gain of weight, muscle mass, and muscle function; improvement in fat-soluble vitamin levels.
15. Monitor EPI with baseline nutritional status (BMI, quality-of-life measure, fat-soluble vitamin levels) and a **baseline DXA scan repeated every 1–2 years**.

**Supporting detail:**
- EPI develops in >½ of chronic pancreatitis patients; risk >80% with chronic alcohol/smoking, ductal obstruction, atrophy, calcifications, or diabetes; typically after 5–10 yr of disease.
- Pooled EPI prevalence after acute/recurrent acute pancreatitis 27%–62%. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: 50%–92% (unresectable), 40%–50% (resectable pre-treatment), 75% post-treatment. Cystic fibrosis: 85% at birth/infancy.
- Type 3c diabetes (pancreatogenic) results from loss of islet α and β cells in pancreatitis.
- DDx / mimics that overlap and blunt PERT response: celiac disease, SIBO, longstanding diabetes, Crohn's, disaccharidase deficiencies, bile acid diarrhea, giardiasis.

- [[exocrine-pancreatic-insufficiency]] — new disease-script page (home for FE-1 thresholds, PERT dosing, monitoring).
- Updates [[chronic-pancreatitis]], [[pancreatic-cancer]], [[hereditary-pancreatitis]] (EPI as sequela), and [[chronic-diarrhea]] (fatty-diarrhea workup).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No formal evidence ratings (expert opinion). FE-1 indeterminate zone (100–200 µg/g) requires clinical correlation; false-positives with watery/diarrheal stool (dilution).

# AGA 2023 Clinical Practice Update on Role of EUS-Guided Gallbladder Drainage in Acute Cholecystitis

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Irani SS, Sharzehi K, Siddiqui UD. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Role of EUS-Guided Gallbladder Drainage in Acute Cholecystitis: Commentary. *Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2023;21(5):1141–1147. doi:10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.039.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.039)
- **Authors:** Shayan S. Irani, Kaveh Sharzehi, Uzma D. Siddiqui
- **Year:** 2023 (May)
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology* 2023;21(5):1141–1147 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Commentary)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.039](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2022.12.039)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — expert commentary (literature review; **not a systematic review — no formal rating of evidence quality or strength** of considerations)

---

## Summary

[[acute-cholecystitis|Acute cholecystitis]] is definitively treated by cholecystectomy, but comorbid patients may be inoperable. Percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PT-GBD) is the most common nonsurgical decompression method but carries **50%–75% morbidity** and **recurrent cholecystitis in up to 15.4%**, driving development of endoscopic alternatives: **endoscopic transpapillary gallbladder drainage (ET-GBD)** at [[ercp|ERCP]] (cystic duct cannulation + plastic stent) and **[[eus-guided-gallbladder-drainage|EUS-guided gallbladder drainage (EUS-GBD)]]** — transmural stenting from duodenum or stomach into the gallbladder, now facilitated by lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS).

The Update's core message: endoscopic GBD is a feasible, efficacious alternative to percutaneous drainage for **high-risk surgical candidates**; choosing the optimal drainage route depends on individual patient characteristics (comorbidities, gallbladder position/cystic duct anatomy, in-dwelling metal biliary stents, ascites, future surgical candidacy) and local expertise; EUS-GBD must be done by experts in advanced therapeutic [[endoscopic-ultrasound|EUS]]; and multidisciplinary collaboration with interventional radiology and surgery is paramount. Comparative data (5 studies, 488 patients, incl. the DRAC-1 RCT) show EUS-GBD has technical/clinical success comparable to PT-GBD with shorter stays, less pain, fewer reinterventions, and less recurrent cholecystitis; EUS-GBD also outperforms ET-GBD for technical/clinical success when cystic duct pathology is present.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

**Description statement (verbatim):** "Endoscopic gallbladder drainage is a feasible and efficacious alternative to percutaneous drainage in the management of acute cholecystitis for high-risk surgical candidates. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided gallbladder drainage and per-oral cholecystoscopy is facilitated by the use of lumen-apposing metal stents. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided gallbladder drainage should be performed by those expert in advanced therapeutic endoscopic ultrasound. Multidisciplinary collaboration between interventional radiology and surgery is paramount in the care of these patients. Choosing the optimal drainage method is dependent on individual patient characteristics."

**Indications for EUS-GBD:**

1. Gallbladder drainage in high-surgical-risk patients with acute cholecystitis
2. Removal of percutaneous cholecystostomy drains in non-cholecystectomy candidates (conversion to internal drainage)
3. Drainage of malignant biliary obstruction in select patients with failed ERCP **and** failed EUS-guided biliary drainage (rescue)

**Patient selection:**

- EUS-GBD candidates: high surgical risk, **no free gallbladder perforation**, able to tolerate anesthesia and a therapeutic endoscopic procedure.
- Favor **ET-GBD first** when: already requiring ERCP for other reasons ([[choledocholithiasis]], suspected cholangitis); potential **future surgical candidate** (preserves normal anatomy); coagulopathy; large-volume [[ascites]]; comorbidities precluding optimal percutaneous drain or EUS-GBD.
- Favor **EUS-GBD** when: in-dwelling **uncovered metal biliary stent obstructing the cystic duct takeoff**; malignant cystic duct obstruction; **large burden of cholelithiasis** or other indication for per-oral cholecystoscopy; poor candidate for repeat interventions.
- **Contraindications to EUS-GBD:** gallbladder perforation, biliary peritonitis, large-volume ascites, significant coagulopathy; intolerance of anesthesia contraindicates all endoscopic GBD.
- **Surgical discussion before EUS-GBD is imperative** — cholecystectomy after EUS-GBD requires fistula repair with postoperative leak risk; clarify future surgical candidacy first.

**Table 1 — PT-GBD vs ET-GBD vs EUS-GBD (recreated):**

| | PT-GBD | ET-GBD | EUS-GBD |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Description** | Ultrasound- (or CT-) guided percutaneous drain placement into the gallbladder | ERCP with selective cannulation of the cystic duct and transpapillary stent placement | EUS-guided placement of a stent from the duodenum or the stomach into the gallbladder |
| **Patient selection** | Conventional treatment in patient with acute cholecystitis and significant medical comorbidities that would make laparoscopic cholecystectomy excessively risky | Consider: patients requiring ERCP for other indications; future cholecystectomy candidates; large-volume ascites; coagulopathy | Consider: in-dwelling uncovered metal biliary stent; malignant obstruction of the cystic duct takeoff; large burden of cholelithiasis |
| **Advantages** | Widely available | Safer in patients with ascites; can simultaneously address choledocholithiasis and cholangitis | Least likely to need reintervention; can simultaneously address gallstones (cholecystoscopy) |
| **Disadvantages** | Higher reintervention rate (drain exchanges); higher risk of recurrent cholecystitis; dyscosmesis | Lower technical success; lowest clinical success; risk of pancreatitis; may need stent changes or replacement if migration occurs | May require fistula closure if patient undergoes cholecystectomy; may become occluded with food; contraindicated in gallbladder perforation |

**Technique of EUS-GBD:**

- LAMS overcame limitations of pigtail plastic/biliary SEMS (leak, contralateral wall injury, migration): short saddle, large flanges, diameters 6–20 mm — allow stone passage and endoscope passage for therapeutic cholecystoscopy. Three LAMS designs in Europe/Asia; only 1 commercially available in the US (Axios, Boston Scientific; fully covered, 10.5F delivery catheter, needs 3.7-mm channel therapeutic echoendoscope; saddle lengths 10 and 15 mm; inner diameters 10, 15, 20 mm; flanges 21, 24, 29 mm).
- **Two techniques:** (1) non–cautery-enhanced: 19-gauge FNA puncture → guidewire → tract dilation → stent under fluoroscopy; (2) direct (cautery-enhanced LAMS): freehand entry and deployment without guidewire/exchange — can be done entirely under EUS guidance without fluoroscopy.
- **Enteral puncture site–to–gallbladder distance must be <10 mm** for safe deployment.
- Prefer **over-the-wire technique** (retained access if misdeployment) in fibrotic/contracted gallbladders, existing percutaneous drains, or difficult scope positions.
- Duodenum vs stomach: no significant AE difference; authors prefer **duodenal** placement (antral LAMS occlude with food more easily; higher inward migration from gastric contraction), but the most important factor is the site of closest gallbladder–GI wall apposition. Distal stomach is easier for surgeons to access if the site later needs closure.
- Coaxial **double-pigtail plastic stent through the LAMS** is routine in the authors' practice (mitigates bleeding, stent obstruction, contralateral wall injury).
- Informed consent: LAMS for GBD is **off-label**; specific AEs = puncture hemorrhage, bile leak with peritonitis, GB perforation, stent migration; late relapsing cholecystitis with migration/occlusion; future cholecystectomy may be harder or impossible.

**Outcomes:**

- EUS-GBD technical success 90%–98.7%; clinical success 89%–98.4%; adverse events 4.8%–22% (bleeding, recurrent cholecystitis, stent migration, occlusion). Meta-analysis: morbidity 20.4%, mortality 3.9% (mostly ongoing sepsis).
- **vs PT-GBD** (5 studies, 488 pts, incl. DRAC-1 RCT): comparable technical/clinical success; PT-GBD had longer stays, longer time to resolution, more reinterventions, higher pain scores, trend to more AEs at 30 d and 1 y; recurrent cholecystitis 20% (8/40) PT-GBD vs 2.6% (1/39) EUS-GBD (P = .029); PT-GBD readmissions from drain leaks/obstruction/dislodgement.
- **vs ET-GBD:** ET-GBD has lower technical (84% vs 98%) and clinical (91% vs 97%) success — cystic duct occlusion (tumor, stone, uncovered metal stent) is the main ET-GBD failure mode; EUS-GBD has lowest recurrent-cholecystitis risk of the 3 modalities (network meta-analysis RR: EUS 1.089 vs PT 2.02 vs ET 2.891), while **ET-GBD had the lowest mortality** (RR: EUS 2.62 vs PT 2.09 vs ET 1.29).

**Follow-up after EUS-GBD — 2 options:**

1. **Per-oral cholecystoscopy at 4–6 weeks** for stone clearance + exchange LAMS for double-pigtail plastic stents to maintain the fistula long-term (technical success 93.1%; 56% spontaneous stone passage; overall stone clearance 88% after mean 1.25 sessions).
2. **Leave LAMS in permanently** (frail patients, refuse second procedure): delayed AEs 7.1% at median 275 d; 3-year stent patency 86%.

**Training:** limited to high-volume centers; minimum ~**19–25 procedures** for competency (published estimates); authors' pathway = master LAMS in pancreatic fluid collections (the FDA-approved indication; ≥10 independent deployments) before EUS-GBD, starting with distended gallbladders without intervening tissue.

**Figure 3 — approach to cholecystitis in high-surgical-risk patients (algorithm):** perforation suspected on imaging or unable to tolerate sedation → PT-GBD. No perforation + tolerates sedation → ET(P)-GBD initially if uncontrolled ascites, potential future surgical candidate, undergoing ERCP for other reasons, or GB >10 mm from GI tract wall; EUS-GBD initially (after surgeon discussion) if duodenal obstruction/gastric outlet obstruction, in-dwelling metal stent occluding cystic duct, or large gallbladder stone burden; each rescues the other on failure, then PT-GBD if both fail. Image embedded on [[acute-cholecystitis]].

- Creates [[acute-cholecystitis]] (disease script — drainage decision pathway for high-surgical-risk patients; Figure 3 algorithm).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Consistent with [[asge-2024-therapeutic-eus-biliary]] (EUS-GBD favored over percutaneous cholecystostomy in nonsurgical candidates where expertise exists) — this CPU adds the ET-GBD arm and the selection criteria between all 3 routes.
- **Mortality signal diverges from recurrence signal:** network meta-analysis found lowest recurrent cholecystitis with EUS-GBD but lowest mortality with ET-GBD — no head-to-head RCT of ET-GBD vs EUS-GBD; the authors call for randomized/prospective comparisons incl. cost analysis.
- LAMS for gallbladder drainage remains **off-label** (FDA approval pending more outcome/safety data).
- No formal evidence grading (commentary format).

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Chen JW, Vela MF, Peterson KA, Carlson DA. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Diagnosis and Management of Extraesophageal Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease: Expert Review. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023;21(6):1414–1421.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.01.040)
- **Authors:** Joan W. Chen, Marcelo F. Vela, Kathryn A. Peterson, Dustin A. Carlson
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2023.01.040](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.01.040)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

This AGA Clinical Practice Update addresses suspected **extraesophageal reflux (EER)** — laryngitis, chronic cough, asthma, and dental erosions attributed to GERD. The central problem: **there is no single test that conclusively proves GER causes extraesophageal symptoms**, and 50–60% of patients with EER symptoms do not actually have GERD and will not respond to anti-reflux therapy. Diagnosis therefore rests on a global clinical impression integrating symptoms, endoscopy, reflux monitoring, and treatment response, ideally within a multidisciplinary framework (pulmonology, otolaryngology, dentistry).

Two mechanisms are postulated: the **reflux pathway** (micro-aspiration/direct mucosal injury by acid or non-acid refluxate) and the **reflex pathway** (vagally-mediated airway reactions). Because of the reflex mechanism, symptom improvement on a PPI may occur through effects other than acid suppression and should not be taken as proof of GERD.

Key management shifts: consider objective reflux testing **before** starting empiric PPI in patients with EER symptoms but **without** typical GERD symptoms; a single-dose PPI trial titrated up to twice daily is reasonable in those with typical symptoms. After one PPI trial (up to 12 weeks) fails, additional trials of different PPIs are low-yield — pursue objective testing instead. Anti-reflux surgery should only be considered with clear, objectively-defined GERD, and a lack of PPI response predicts lack of surgical response.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice statements (verbatim):**

1. Gastroenterologists should be aware of potential extraesophageal manifestations of GERD and should inquire about such disorders including laryngitis, chronic cough, asthma, and dental erosions in GERD patients to determine whether GERD may be a contributing factor to these conditions.
2. Development of a multidisciplinary approach to extraesophageal (EER) manifestations is an important consideration because the conditions are often multifactorial, requiring input from non-gastroenterology (GI) specialties. Results from diagnostic testing (ie, bronchoscopy, thoracic imaging, laryngoscopy, etc) from non-GI disciplines should be taken into consideration when gastroesophageal reflux (GER) is considered as a cause for extraesophageal symptoms.
3. Currently, there is no single diagnostic tool that can conclusively identify GER as the cause of EER symptoms. Determination of the contribution of GER to EER symptoms should be based on the global clinical impression derived from patients' symptoms, response to GER therapy, and results of endoscopy and reflux testing.
4. Consideration should be given toward diagnostic testing for reflux before initiation of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy in patients with potential extraesophageal manifestations of GERD, but without typical GERD symptoms. Initial single-dose PPI trial, titrating up to twice daily in those with typical GERD symptoms, is reasonable.
5. Symptom improvement of EER manifestations while on PPI therapy may result from mechanisms of action other than acid suppression and should not be regarded as confirmation for GERD.
6. In patients with suspected extraesophageal manifestation of GERD who have failed one trial (up to 12 weeks) of PPI therapy, one should consider objective testing for pathologic GER, because additional trials of different PPIs are low yield.
7. Initial testing to evaluate for reflux should be tailored to patients' clinical presentation and can include upper endoscopy and ambulatory reflux monitoring studies of acid suppressive therapy.
8. Testing can be considered for those with an established objective diagnosis of GERD who do not respond to high doses of acid suppression. Testing can include pH-impedance monitoring while on acid suppression to evaluate the role of ongoing acid or non-acid reflux.
9. Alternative treatment methods to acid suppressive therapy (eg, lifestyle modifications, alginate-containing antacids, external upper esophageal sphincter compression device, cognitive-behavioral therapy, neuromodulators) may serve a role in management of EER symptoms.
10. Shared decision-making should be performed before referral for anti-reflux surgery for EER when the patient has clear, objectively defined evidence of GERD. However, a lack of response to PPI therapy predicts lack of response to anti-reflux surgery and should be incorporated into the decision process.

**Additional detail:**
- Conditions commonly attributed to EER (Table 1): chronic cough, laryngeal hoarseness/dysphonia, pulmonary fibrosis, asthma, dental erosions, sinus disease, ear disease, post-nasal drip, throat clearing. Each has a large non-reflux differential and benefits from multidisciplinary evaluation (pulmonary, ENT, dentistry, allergy).
- 50–60% of patients with EER symptoms will not have GERD and will not respond to anti-reflux therapies — the rationale for objective testing before/instead of prolonged empiric PPI.
- Excluding GERD lowers the probability that symptoms are reflux-caused; objectively supporting GERD keeps reflux as a possible causal factor but does not prove causation.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[extraesophageal-reflux]]** — new diagnostic-schema page; this CPU is its primary source (umbrella EER framework, diagnostic algorithm, Table 1 manifestations).
- **[[gerd]]** — enriches the Extraesophageal GERD Manifestations section (test-before-PPI, PPI improvement ≠ confirmation, one 12-week trial then objective testing, surgery caveat).
- **[[laryngopharyngeal-symptoms]]** — LPR is the dominant EER manifestation; consistent test-before-empiric-PPI approach for isolated symptoms.
- **[[ambulatory-reflux-monitoring]]**, **[[reflux-testing]]** — supports on- vs off-therapy testing choices and pH-impedance for non-acid reflux.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No single gold-standard test for EER; causal attribution remains probabilistic. Salivary pepsin and oropharyngeal pH testing are not endorsed (consistent with [[acg-2021-gerd|ACG 2021]] and [[san-diego-2025-lprd|San Diego 2025]]).
- Softer on empiric PPI than older practice: emphasizes testing before/instead of prolonged empiric therapy, especially without typical GERD symptoms.

# AGA 2023 CPU: Gastric Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy for Gastroparesis (Commentary)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Khashab MA, Wang AY, Cai Q. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Gastric Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy for Gastroparesis: Commentary. *Gastroenterology* 2023;164(7):1329–1335. doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2023.02.027.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.02.027)
- **Authors:** Mouen A. Khashab, Andrew Y. Wang, Qiang Cai
- **Year:** 2023 (received October 29, 2022; accepted February 18, 2023)
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastroenterology* 2023;164(7):1329–1335 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Commentary)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.02.027](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.02.027)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — expert **Commentary** (no numbered Best Practice Advice statements and **no formal evidence/strength ratings**; expert advice on cognitive, procedural, and post-procedural aspects of G-POEM)

---

## Summary

Expert commentary on **gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM**, also called peroral endoscopic pyloromyotomy**)** for medically refractory [[gastroparesis]]. Medically refractory gastroparesis = "persistent symptoms in the context of objectively confirmed gastric emptying delay, despite the use of dietary adjustment and metoclopramide as a first-line therapeutic agent." G-POEM — a natural extension of [[endoscopic-submucosal-dissection|ESD]] and esophageal [[poem|POEM]] (first described in a porcine model by Kawai 2012; first human case by Khashab 2013) — is efficacious for **diabetic, post-surgical, and idiopathic** gastroparesis.

The core selection advice: offer G-POEM to adults with refractory gastroparesis who have (1) EGD excluding mechanical gastric-outlet obstruction, (2) solid-phase gastric emptying scan (GES) confirming delay — preferably **retention >20% at 4 hours**, and (3) **moderate-to-severe symptoms** (GCSI total >2), preferably **nausea/vomiting-dominant**. Baseline GCSI >2.6 and baseline 4-hour retention >20% independently predict 12-month clinical success; pain-predominant patients respond less well; most **post-infectious** gastroparesis should *not* be offered G-POEM; nonselective use is discouraged. Durable 1-year clinical success is in the **50%–60% range** (pooled 1-year 61%) — more modest than earlier pooled short-term estimates of 71%–82% — but a European sham-controlled RCT showed clear superiority of G-POEM over sham (71% vs 22% at 6 months, ITT). AEs are uncommon (6.2%–14%; most mild). The commentary also covers technique (greater-curvature approach, full-thickness pyloromyotomy sparing serosa, closure), post-procedural care (diet ladder, 8 weeks PPI), follow-up (GCSI each visit; GES no sooner than 4–8 weeks), the double-myotomy variation, and the lack of an effective salvage strategy after failed G-POEM.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

*No numbered BPA statements in this CPU format; the following captures every "we suggest/advise" near-verbatim, grouped by section.*

**Patient selection:**

- G-POEM should be considered for patients with **medically refractory gastroparesis** (persistent symptoms + objectively confirmed gastric-emptying delay despite dietary adjustment and metoclopramide first-line).
- Efficacious for gastroparesis from **diabetes, prior surgery, and idiopathic** causes.
- **We suggest offering G-POEM to adult patients with refractory gastroparesis who:** (1) have undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy to confirm **no mechanical gastric-outlet obstruction**; (2) had a **solid-phase gastric emptying scan (GES)** confirming delayed gastric emptying, preferably with **retention >20% at 4 hours**; and (3) have **moderate-to-severe symptoms**, preferably with **nausea and vomiting as the dominant symptoms**.
- Normal gastric retention at 4 hours is **<10%** (scintigraphy with low-fat [2%] chicken-egg-white meal). Retention >20% at 4 h suggested as the offer threshold — baseline retention >20% at 4 h was an independent predictor of clinical success in a large prospective study.
- **GCSI**: scale 0 (none)–5 (very severe), 2-week recall, 9 symptoms in 3 subscales — nausea/vomiting (3 items), postprandial fullness/early satiety (4 items), bloating (2 items); total score = average of the 3 subscale means. Moderate-to-severe symptoms often correspond to **GCSI total >2**.
- Patients who failed gastric electrical stimulation, pyloric stenting, or botulinum toxin injection should also be offered G-POEM — **failure of these therapies is not a prerequisite**. Published studies do not inform whether improvement after botulinum toxin or transpyloric stenting predicts G-POEM success.
- **Opioid dependence:** wean off opioids whenever possible and re-evaluate gastric emptying first.
- Most patients with **post-infectious gastroparesis should not be offered G-POEM** (usually self-limited).
- The ultimate decision should be based on the **full clinical picture**, not GES results or GCSI score alone. Nausea/vomiting-predominant patients are more likely to respond; **abdominal-pain-predominant patients are less likely to respond**.
- Pyloric **cross-sectional area and distensibility index** on [[flip-panometry|impedance planimetry (FLIP)]] may have a role in patient selection (data limited). **Nonselective use of G-POEM should be discouraged.**
- **Pediatrics:** insufficient evidence for G-POEM in children with gastroparesis (though used for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis). **Post-lung-transplant** severe gastroparesis: emerging evidence, promising minimally invasive option.

**Table 1 — Potential causes of gastroparesis:**

| Cause | Details |
|---|---|
| Endocrine | Diabetes accounts for ~25% of gastroparesis cases |
| Post-surgical | Typically partial/complete vagotomy, intended or unintended (esophagectomy, Billroth II gastrectomy, fundoplication or hernia repair); symptomatic gastroparesis is a common adverse event after lung or heart–lung transplantation (may promote microaspiration into the allograft → graft failure) |
| Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty | May delay gastric emptying by constraining the middle and distal stomach |
| Medications | Anticholinergics, GLP-1 receptor agonists; opioids induce pyloric dysfunction and gastric stasis — a common, iatrogenic, potentially reversible cause |
| Post-viral | Usually self-limited; course can be prolonged in some |
| Idiopathic | The most common form |

**Procedural considerations:**

- G-POEM should **only be performed by interventional endoscopists with expertise or training in third-space endoscopy**; ESD experience not mandatory but shortens the learning curve; E-POEM + ESD expertise immensely beneficial.
- Prep: **liquid diet ≥24 hours** pre-procedure; **periprocedural antibiotics** with efficacy against enteric pathogens; **general anesthesia**, supine or left-lateral (authors favor **supine** — easier examination for capnoperitoneum; tension pneumoperitoneum managed with percutaneous needle decompression).
- Equipment: high-definition gastroscope with waterjet + clear distal cap; **low-flow CO₂ insufflation required — room air completely avoided**; modern electrosurgical generator modulating power by tissue resistance/impedance.
- Steps: submucosal bleb **4–5 cm proximal to the pylorus**, typically **greater curvature** (saline + ~0.25% indigo carmine/methylene blue) → longitudinal or transverse **1.5–2 cm mucosal incision** → submucosal tunnel by repeated injection/dissection until the **pyloric ring is exposed** (blended-cutting current for incision, blended-coagulation for tunnel; hemostatic forceps for large vascular complexes; intermittent stomach deflation reduces looping) → **single myotomy** extended **1–3 cm proximally into the antrum**; insulated-tip knife may increase the safety margin (difficult situations / early learning curve). **At minimum incise the inner circular muscularis; authors advise full-thickness pyloromyotomy of the circular and oblique bundles with preservation of the serosa** (do not breach serosa) → close mucosal incision with **endoscopic clips or suturing**. Fluoroscopy optional, not mandatory.
- **Variations:** lesser-curvature approach described with similar outcomes but pyloromyotomy is more challenging. **Double myotomy** (2nd incision near the 1st) superior to single myotomy at 6 months in a single study; technically easy, adds little time — but additional long-term comparative data required before deeming it routinely necessary.

**Post-procedural care:**

- Often admitted overnight. If no AEs → clear-liquid diet. Optional upper-GI study next day to exclude contrast leak → advance to full liquids. **Considerable abdominal pain, tachycardia, and/or fever → CT or upper-GI study.**
- Generally: **full-liquid diet 5–7 days**, then **5–6 small meals/day of a low-fiber, low-fat solid gastroparesis diet**.
- **8 weeks of PPI** (mucosal healing) + a short course of oral antibiotics suggested.
- **Same-day discharge** possible at experienced centers for reliable patients with ED access if: high-confidence mucosal closure, no intraoperative AEs, no major comorbidities, pain controlled with oral meds, liquids tolerated without nausea/vomiting.
- **Aspirin** with strong indication may be continued irrespective of G-POEM; resumption of clopidogrel/warfarin/other antithrombotics individualized.

**Follow-up and efficacy definitions:**

- Clinic follow-up ~**1–3 months**; **repeat solid-phase GES no sooner than 4–8 weeks** post-G-POEM; obtain **GCSI before G-POEM and at each visit**.
- **Clinical success** (recent definition): decrease in total GCSI ≥1, typically with **>25% decrease in ≥2 GCSI subscales**. **Recurrence**: clinical return of gastroparesis symptoms + GCSI back to baseline or ≥3 after initial response. Desirable signs: relief of nausea/vomiting, increased meal size, weight gain.

**Efficacy data:**

- Pooled meta-analyses (largely short-term): clinical success **71%–82%**; recent meta-analysis: **1-year pooled clinical success only 61%**; French multicenter retrospective: **66% at 1 year**; long-term retrospective (4–5 y): only **50% sustained efficacy**. Durable clinical success is in the **50%–60% range** — still a major benefit given the paucity of effective gastroparesis therapies.
- **International prospective study (n=80,** all failed prokinetics, 70% also failed botulinum toxin and/or transpyloric stenting; mean 4-h retention 39%; etiology idiopathic 41%, postsurgical 35%, diabetic 24%**):** greater-curve G-POEM, **100% technical success**, median 43 min; at 12 months clinical success **56%**, GCSI <2 in 68%; total GCSI 2.8 → 1.5 (P < .001); success consistent across etiologic subtypes. Follow-up GES (66% of pts, 3 mo): improved 64%, **normalized 47%**. Multivariable **independent predictors of 12-month success: baseline GCSI >2.6 (OR 3.23; P = .04) and baseline 4-h retention >20% (OR 3.65; P = .029)**.
- Single-center retrospective (n=97): 81.1% response at 3–6 months but **loss of response 12.9% per year**.
- **Sham-controlled RCT** (European, single-blinded, n=41: 17 diabetic, 13 post-surgical, 11 idiopathic; terminated early for G-POEM superiority): success (GCSI decrease ≥50% at 6 mo) **71% G-POEM vs 22% sham** (P = .001; OR 9.0 favoring G-POEM, P = .005); by GCSI decrease ≥1 definition, **95% vs 37%**. **Diabetic gastroparesis had the highest success (89%)**. 4-h retention fell 22% → 12% after G-POEM (no change post-sham). 12 sham patients crossed over; 75% achieved success.
- Mexico City retrospective (n=374; 102 completed 48 months): **4-year clinical success 77.5%**; diabetic gastroparesis had the best long-term outcomes and fewest recurrences.
- A US sham-controlled trial (NCT04869670) in diabetic/idiopathic gastroparesis is planned.

**Adverse events:**

- Uncommon when performed by trained/experienced endoscopists, but serious AEs occur.
- International prospective (n=80): AEs **6.2%, all mild** — capnoperitoneum ×3 (needle decompression), mucosotomy ×1 (stented), thermal mucosal injury ×1 (clipped).
- Retrospective n=216: AEs **14%** (77% mild, 16% moderate, 6% severe); most common abdominal pain (n=16), inadvertent mucosotomy (n=5), capnoperitoneum (n=4); the 2 severe = post-procedural pain → negative exploratory laparoscopy, and a 2-mm anterior stomach/pylorus perforation → laparoscopic omental patch.
- Retrospective n=374: AEs **8.6%; bleeding most common**; all managed endoscopically/conservatively. Also reported: gastric ulceration, dumping syndrome.

**After failed G-POEM:**

- A sizable minority will not achieve satisfactory response; **redo G-POEM is very challenging (dense fibrosis)** and data are sparse. Gastric electrical stimulation might be attempted if not already failed (no published guidance). **No proven medical or minimally invasive salvage strategy** → set realistic expectations; refine patient selection; intraprocedural impedance planimetry may help gauge myotomy adequacy.

**Comparative data (supplementary):**

- vs **laparoscopic pyloroplasty** (propensity-matched, 30 vs 30): LP had longer stay (4.6 vs 1.4 d; P = .003), longer operative time (99.3 vs 33.9 min; P < .001), more AEs (16.7% vs 3.3%; P = .086) — comparable functional outcomes, less perioperative morbidity with G-POEM.
- Meta-analysis (332 G-POEM vs 376 surgical pyloroplasty): pooled GCSI-based clinical success **76% vs 77%** (NS); comparable AEs.
- vs **gastric electrical stimulation** (propensity-matched 23 vs 23): G-POEM had better and longer-lasting clinical response.

**Other:**

- Many insurers still consider G-POEM investigational; authors state safety/effectiveness are now well supported and payors should cover it.
- Future: refine selection, prognostic ancillary tests (e.g., intraprocedural FLIP); G-POEM enables gastric muscularis propria biopsy via the tunnel (interstitial-cells-of-Cajal research).

---

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates the procedure page [[g-poem]] (patient selection criteria, predictors of response, technique, post-procedural care, outcomes, adverse events, comparative data).
- Updates [[gastroparesis]] — definition of medically refractory disease, G-POEM selection thresholds (retention >20% at 4 h; GCSI >2; nausea/vomiting-predominant), durability caveat (1-year ~61%), etiology details (diabetes ~25%; post-lung-transplant; endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty; GLP-1 agonists/opioids).
- Cross-links [[poem]] (parent technique), [[endoscopic-submucosal-dissection]], [[flip-panometry]], [[upper-endoscopy]].

---

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Durability vs earlier pooled estimates:** [[acg-2022-gastroparesis]] cites pooled open-label clinical improvement of 88.2% (n=276), whereas this CPU emphasizes more modest durable success — 1-year pooled **61%**, 4–5-year sustained **50%** (both flagged on [[gastroparesis]]). Not a formal contradiction (different endpoints/time horizons), but expectations should be set with the 50%–60% durable figure.
- **Double myotomy:** superior at 6 months in a single study only — not yet routine.
- No validated predictor from response to prior botulinum toxin/stenting; FLIP-based selection promising but unproven.
- No numbered BPA statements or evidence grades (Commentary format) — advice reflects expert experience + literature review.

# AGA 2023 Clinical Practice Update on Interventional EUS for Vascular Investigation and Therapy

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Ryou M, DeWitt JM, Das KK, Shami VM. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Interventional EUS for Vascular Investigation and Therapy: Commentary. *Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2023;21(7):1699–1705. doi:10.1016/j.cgh.2023.03.027.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.03.027)
- **Authors:** Marvin Ryou, John M. DeWitt, Koushik K. Das, Vanessa M. Shami
- **Year:** 2023 (July)
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology* 2023;21(7):1699–1705 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Commentary)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2023.03.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.03.027)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — expert commentary (literature review; **not a systematic review — no formal rating of evidence quality or strength of recommendation**)

---

## Summary

Reviews the evidence for [[interventional-eus-vascular|EUS-guided vascular investigation and therapy]]. The two most widely utilized interventions are **EUS-guided gastric variceal therapy** (coil ± cyanoacrylate glue) and **EUS-guided portosystemic pressure gradient (EUS-PPG) measurement**. Emerging interventions: treatment of ectopic and rectal varices, splenic artery embolization, therapy of arterial bleeding including pseudoaneurysms, and portal venous sampling. Experimental: EUS-guided intrahepatic portosystemic shunt creation.

Bottom line per the authors: **EUS-guided coil injection therapy of gastric varices makes the strongest case for adoption at centers of expertise** — safe, excellent acute hemostasis, low rebleeding, and likely superior to traditional direct endoscopic glue injection (DEI), though supporting data are uncontrolled series and small comparative studies and its place relative to IR endovascular therapies (BRTO, [[tips|TIPS]]) is undefined. **EUS-PPG's strongest indication is when there is another reason for endoscopy** (variceal screening, [[liver-biopsy|liver biopsy]]) — a "one-stop shop." Rectal/ectopic variceal therapy, splenic artery embolization, and arterial/pseudoaneurysm therapy rest on small case series; portal vein sampling appears safe but should stay within research protocols. Two prerequisites for clinical utility of any EUS vascular intervention: a vascular target in/near the GI wall favoring endoscopic over percutaneous access, and efficacy/safety comparable or superior to current alternatives.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

### EUS-guided injection therapy of gastric varices

- Gastric variceal hemorrhage is less prevalent but often more severe than esophageal, with higher mortality; **cardiofundal varices (IGV1, GOV2)** are especially challenging endoscopically (large size, location, retroflexed view needed for DEI, inaccurate intravascular needle placement).
- Advantages of EUS guidance over DEI: injection precision (even during active bleeding with impaired views), expanded options (hemostatic coils), and **real-time Doppler feedback of hemostasis**.
- **Technique:** intubated, left lateral decubitus; instill and retain 100–200 cm³ water in the fundus to delineate intramural varices from extramural collaterals and perforator veins (trace extramural vessels across the muscularis propria into the varix); 19- or 22-gauge FNA needle, transesophageal or transgastric; sequentially place **1–3 coils** (usually Nester or MReye, Cook) as a scaffold; when Doppler flow is significantly reduced/near-absent, inject adjunct cyanoacrylate to minimize embolic events. Fluoroscopy ± varicealography helpful early in the learning curve but not required. No definitive data on targeting the varix itself vs the perforator vein(s).
- **Outcomes:** 3 retrospective series + 2 small RCTs — ~99% technical success and bleeding control; rebleeding 0%–16%; AEs 0%–7%. Meta-analysis: any EUS-guided therapy superior to DEI (treatment efficacy 94% vs 91%; **gastric variceal obliteration 84% vs 63%, P = .02**). **Combination coil + glue is the preferred strategy**: recurrence 5% vs glue or coils alone (subgroup analysis); hemostasis 96%–98% with 10% AEs vs glue alone (96%, 21% AEs) and coils alone (90%, 3% AEs). Coils + absorbable gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) in lieu of cyanoacrylate: similar low rebleeding/reintervention. EUS-guided thrombin: small series only.
- **Open questions:** heterogeneous technique (varix vs perforator target, coil size/number, injectate) — consensus technique needed; larger multicenter data; RCTs vs IR endovascular therapies (BRTO, TIPS); primary prophylaxis vs only acute bleeding/secondary prophylaxis; training pathways. Decisions should be multidisciplinary with hepatology and IR. **Not FDA approved.**

### EUS-guided portal pressure gradient (EUS-PPG) measurement

- HVPG (IR, transjugular) measures the gradient **indirectly** (wedged minus free hepatic vein pressure); drawbacks = radiation/contrast and its indirect nature, which can misdiagnose **noncirrhotic/presinusoidal [[portal-hypertension|portal hypertension]]**. Reference thresholds: HVPG >10 mm Hg correlates with esophageal varix development; >12 mm Hg with variceal bleeding risk.
- **EUS-PPG measures the hepatic vein–portal vein gradient directly**; FDA-approved device (EchoTip Insight, Cook).
- **Technique:** supine, preferably general anesthesia (minimize movement); 1 dose prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin or cefazolin); compact manometer leveled at the midaxillary line/right-heart level throughout; linear echoendoscope; middle or left hepatic vein punctured transgastrically with a **25-gauge needle**; ≥3 consecutive pressure measurements (one-needle-stick approach) averaged; repeat in the intrahepatic portal vein (Doppler-confirmed); **EUS-PPG = mean portal pressure − mean hepatic vein pressure**.
- **Evidence:** first human case 2014; 28-patient pilot showed excellent correlation with endoscopic findings of portal hypertension; 64-patient series — excellent correlation with histologic fibrosis stage, clinical portal hypertension, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, APRI >2, FIB-4 >3.25, **no adverse events**; 83-patient series — correlated with thrombocytopenia and varices, no AEs.
- **Efficiency:** one-stop shop — EGD + EUS + PPG + liver biopsy + evaluation/treatment of endoscopic portal-hypertension features in a single procedure.
- **Indications where helpful:** discordant data on presence/absence of portal hypertension (isolated thrombocytopenia, isolated splenomegaly, normal HVPG but possible presinusoidal PH); supplementing preoperative (incl. pretransplant) clearance in known/suspected [[cirrhosis]]; monitoring response to medications or intervention.
- **Open questions:** whether EUS-acquired values for portal hypertension (HVPG >5 mm Hg) and clinically significant portal hypertension (≥10 mm Hg) map directly onto percutaneous thresholds; effect of general anesthesia vs conscious sedation on absolute pressures; head-to-head EUS-PPG vs HVPG trials needed.

### Emerging interventions

- **Rectal/ectopic varices:** EUS-guided sclerosant/coil/cyanoacrylate for rectal varices — single case reports; duodenal (n=3) and choledochal (n=5) varices treated with glue ± coils in one series. Larger series needed.
- **Splenic artery embolization:** 5 cirrhotic patients with hypersplenism + recent variceal bleeding treated with combinations of variceal ligation and EUS-guided cyanoacrylate and/or coils — all had postprocedure fever and abdominal pain, no splenic abscesses; reduced vein diameter, improved cytopenias, mean splenic embolization rate 65%.
- **Arterial bleeding / pseudoaneurysms (salvage after failed/infeasible IR embolization):** EUS-guided coil + glue in 6 splenic artery pseudoaneurysms (2.5–6.5 cm) — 100% technical success, no AEs, all occluded at 3 months. EUS-guided thrombin in 8 visceral artery aneurysms (1.9–5.0 cm; splenic n=5, left hepatic n=2, gastroduodenal n=1) — 100% technical success; 25% postprocedure abdominal pain; lumen obliteration 7/8 (88%) and recurrence 1/8 (12%) at 12 weeks.
- **Portal vein sampling:** safe and feasible in small series; in 18 suspected pancreaticobiliary cancers, **100% of portal samples contained circulating tumor cells vs <25% of peripheral blood samples** — potential "portal liquid biopsy" for metastasis research. **Should be performed within research protocols.**

### Experimental

- **EUS-guided intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (EUS-IPSS):** preclinical (porcine) only — self-expanding metal stent deployed via EUS bridging hepatic and portal veins; needs a dedicated EUS-compatible endovascular stent and defined clinical scenarios vs TIPS.

**Supplementary Table 1 — published EUS-guided injection therapy series for acute gastric variceal bleeding (condensed):**

| Regimen | Studies (N range) | Technical success | Clinical success | AEs | Rebleeding |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CYA alone | 5 studies, n=19–64 | 89.5%–100% | 79.6%–100% | 5%–57.9% | 5.9%–70.2% |
| Coil + CYA | 5 studies, n=3–152 | 99.3%–100% | 100% | 0%–25%* | 0%–16.6% |
| Coil alone | 3 studies, n=3–29 | 90.9%–100% | 89.7%–100% | 0%–9.1% | 17.2%–33% |
| Coil + Gelfoam | 1 study, n=10 | 100% | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| Thrombin | 1 study, n=8 | 100% | 75% | 0% | 33% |

*25% = asymptomatic pulmonary embolism on per-protocol CT (Lobo 2017 RCT).

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates [[interventional-eus-vascular]] (procedure page: gastric variceal coil/glue, EUS-PPG, portal vein sampling, emerging/experimental interventions).
- Updates [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] (therapeutic EUS — vascular applications).
- Cross-links [[variceal-upper-gi-bleeding]] (EUS-guided option for cardiofundal varices), [[portal-hypertension]] (EUS-PPG vs HVPG), [[tips]], [[liver-biopsy]], [[portal-vein-thrombosis]], [[cirrhosis]].

---

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No formal evidence grading (commentary format); most supporting data are retrospective series and 2 small RCTs.
- EUS-guided gastric variceal therapy is **not FDA approved**; role vs BRTO/TIPS undefined pending RCTs — [[variceal-upper-gi-bleeding]] currently lists cyanoacrylate/BRTO/TIPS for fundal varices without an EUS-guided arm; this CPU positions EUS coil+glue as an expert-center option, not a replacement.
- Whether EUS-PPG values are interchangeable with transjugular HVPG thresholds (>5 / ≥10 mm Hg) is unresolved — anesthesia type may shift absolute pressures.
- Optimal gastric-varix target (intramural varix vs perforator vein), coil number/size, and injectate are unstandardized.

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Wattacheril JJ, Abdelmalek MF, Lim JK, Sanyal AJ. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Role of Noninvasive Biomarkers in the Evaluation and Management of Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: Expert Review. *Gastroenterology* 2023;165(4):1080–1088.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.013)
- **Authors:** Julia J. Wattacheril, Manal F. Abdelmalek, Joseph K. Lim, Arun J. Sanyal
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.013](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.06.013)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review; Best Practice Advice, unrated)

## Summary

AGA CPU Expert Review on using **noninvasive tests (NITs)** to risk-stratify and longitudinally monitor NAFLD, where **fibrosis stage is the strongest predictor of liver-related outcomes** and **advanced fibrosis (AF) = stage F3 (bridging) or F4 (cirrhosis)**. Eight Best Practice Advice statements; no formal evidence grade.

Central algorithm: **FIB-4 as the first-line point-of-care test.** FIB-4 **<1.3** has strong negative predictive value and excludes AF (in patients >65 y, use a **<2.0** cutoff instead, because FIB-4 performs poorly at age extremes — poor in <35 y and low specificity in older adults). FIB-4 **≥1.3** (indeterminate/high) → add a **second NIT** (imaging elastography preferred: VCTE or MRE; ELF as a serum alternative when elastography unavailable). Combining ≥2 NITs is preferred over any single NIT for staging/risk stratification once FIB-4 >1.3. Liver biopsy is reserved for **indeterminate/discordant** NITs, conflict with other data, or suspected alternative etiology.

Downstream: patients with NIT results suggesting **F3/F4** enter complication surveillance — **HCC screening and variceal screening per Baveno criteria** — and are followed with **serial LSM (VCTE or MRE)**, which correlates with clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) and decompensation. Serial NITs also track treatment/lifestyle response.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice (8 statements):**

1. NITs can be used for **risk stratification** in the diagnostic evaluation of NAFLD.
2. A **FIB-4 score <1.3** has strong **NPV** for advanced hepatic fibrosis and may exclude AF.
3. A combination of **≥2 NITs** (serum and/or imaging biomarkers) is preferred over a single NIT for staging and risk stratification when **FIB-4 >1.3**.
4. Use NITs per **manufacturer specifications** (e.g., not in patients with ascites or pacemakers) to minimize discordant results/adverse events.
5. Interpret NITs **in clinical context** (exam, biochemical, radiographic, endoscopic data) to optimize PPV for identifying AF.
6. **Liver biopsy** should be considered when NITs are **indeterminate or discordant**, conflict with other findings, or when alternative etiologies are suspected.
7. **Serial longitudinal monitoring** with NITs may inform management (response to lifestyle/therapy).
8. Patients with NITs suggestive of **AF (F3) or cirrhosis (F4)** should enter surveillance for liver complications (**HCC screening + variceal screening per Baveno**) and be monitored with **serial LSM by VCTE or MRE** (correlates with CSPH and decompensation).

**Table 1 — NIT cutoffs to rule in advanced fibrosis (F3–4), AUROC (95% CI):**

| Noninvasive test | Rule-in cutoff for AF | AUROC (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|
| FIB-4 score | >2.67 | 0.83 (0.79–0.86) |
| NAFLD-FS | >0.676 | 0.75 (0.71–0.79) |
| APRI | >0.84 | 0.76 (0.74–0.79) |
| ELF | >9.8 | 0.81 (0.77–0.85) |
| VCTE (kPa) | >12.0 | 0.93 (0.89–0.96) |
| SWE (kPa) | >8.0 | 0.89 (0.80–0.98) |
| MRE (kPa) | >3.6 | 0.93 (0.90–0.96) |

**Key operative thresholds:**
- FIB-4 **<1.3** rule-out AF (NPV ~90% in specialty populations; rises to ~96% at 10% prevalence, falls to ~73% at 50% prevalence — **NPV/PPV are prevalence-dependent**).
- FIB-4 **>2.67** → associated with AF; **>3.25** → associated with cirrhosis (high specificity/low sensitivity → high PPV, poor NPV).
- **Age adjustment:** in patients **>65 y** use FIB-4 **<2.0** to exclude AF.
- Intermediate FIB-4 **1.3–2.67** → add VCTE; LSM **8–12 kPa** suggests clinically significant fibrosis; **>12 kPa** high-sensitivity threshold for cirrhosis.
- Sequential rule-out (**FIB-4 <1.3 + VCTE <8.0 kPa**) and rule-in (**FIB-4 ≥3.48 + VCTE ≥20 kPa**) reduces biopsies (33% → 19%).
- CSPH: **LSM by VCTE ≥25 kPa** reliably rules in CSPH across cACLD; ANTICIPATE model (platelets and LSM) for stratification.
- Serial testing reduces indeterminate AF stratification by ~20% vs single NIT; MEFIB (MRE + FIB-4) outperformed FAST for at-risk NASH (AUROC 0.90 vs 0.73).

## Relevance to Wiki

- **[[nafld-masld|NAFLD/MASLD]]** — supplies the FIB-4-first sequential algorithm, cutoffs, and F3/F4 → surveillance pathway.
- **[[noninvasive-liver-disease-assessment]]** — FIB-4/VCTE/MRE/ELF cutoffs and AUROCs; prevalence-dependence of NPV/PPV; age adjustment (>65 y → FIB-4 <2.0).
- **[[hcc-surveillance]]**, **[[portal-hypertension]]** (Baveno variceal screening), **[[liver-biopsy]]** (reserved for indeterminate/discordant NITs).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- This is a **2023** CPU under the older **NAFLD/NASH** nomenclature; **AASLD 2024 NILDA** guidances ([[noninvasive-liver-disease-assessment]]) are newer and higher-detail for the same testing questions — where they differ on specific cutoffs, the newer AASLD guidance governs the page; this CPU corroborates the FIB-4-first sequential framework. Also predates **MASLD** nomenclature ([[aasld-2023-masld-nomenclature]]).
- No strong evidence base yet for optimal **monitoring frequency** (expert suggestion: FIB-4 annually in high-risk e.g. T2DM, every 2 y in low-risk).

# AGA 2023 Clinical Practice Update on Management of Ostomies: Commentary

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Hedrick TL, Sherman A, Cohen-Mekelburg S, Gaidos JKJ. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Management of Ostomies: Commentary. *Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2023;21(10):2473–2477. doi:10.1016/j.cgh.2023.04.035.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.04.035)
- **Authors:** Traci L. Hedrick (colorectal surgery), Alexis Sherman (WOC nursing), Shirley Cohen-Mekelburg, Jill K. J. Gaidos (gastroenterology); multidisciplinary panel including an ostomate
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology* 2023;21(10):2473–2477 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Commentary)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2023.04.035](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.04.035)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — expert **Commentary** (no numbered Best Practice Advice statements and no formal evidence ratings; literature review + multidisciplinary expert experience)

---

## Summary

Expert commentary on managing patients with an enteral stoma (colostomy or ileostomy) beyond the immediate perioperative period — a gap area, despite ~750,000 Americans living with an ostomy and ~130,000 new ostomy surgeries/year in the US. Adequate stomal care improves outcomes and reduces hospitalizations.

The update reviews stoma types and configurations (end vs loop vs mucus fistula vs continent ileostomy/Kock pouch), output expectations (colostomy: formed stool ~once daily, appliance change q6–7 days; ileostomy: liquid effluent emptied 3–4×/day, wafer change ~q4 days), and complications by time course. **Early high ostomy output (HOO)** — output exceeding fluid intake, typically **>1.5 L/d**, within 3 weeks of stoma formation — is the key early ileostomy complication; the most important treatment is **hydration to prevent renal failure**, usually IV. **Chronic HOO** (>3 weeks) prompts a search for infection, structural problems, recurrent [[crohns-disease|Crohn's disease]], or other diarrhea etiologies, plus a stepwise medical ladder (bulking → antimotility → antisecretory → anti-inflammatory → GLP-2 analogues → surgical reversal). Long-term complications covered: peristomal dermatoses (leak-related excoriation, appliance allergy, fungal rash, folliculitis, peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum, peristomal varices), parastomal hernia (up to 50% at 5 years), and stomal prolapse (5%–10%). Preoperative wound ostomy continence (WOC) consultation with stoma site marking improves quality of life and reduces peristomal skin/pouching complications.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

*Commentary format — no numbered Best Practice Advice; key advice captured in full below.*

**Ostomy types and output expectations:**

- **Colostomy** (most common enteral stoma): from sigmoid, descending, or transverse colon; right colon avoided (large diameter, liquid effluent → large leak-prone stoma). Indications: [[colorectal-cancer|CRC]], perforated diverticulitis, trauma, Crohn's disease, fecal diversion (for [[fecal-incontinence|fecal incontinence]], sacral wound, spinal cord injury). Output **formed, bowel movements commonly once daily**; appliance changed **once every 6–7 days**.
- **Ileostomy:** constructed from terminal ileum close to the ileocecal valve (maximizes nutrient absorption). Indications: CRC, [[inflammatory-bowel-disease|IBD]], colonic dysmotility. Easier to construct and reverse than colostomy but **more dehydration and skin excoriation**. **Liquid effluent — empty 3–4 times daily**, change wafer **every 4 days on average**.
- Stoma must sit **above skin level** so effluent doesn't seep under the appliance (Brooke technique = suturing to protrude above skin).
- **End ostomy:** intestine divided, proximal end brought out; easiest to pouch; used for permanent stomas and perforation requiring resection. Reversal requires more invasive surgery (locate stapled-off distal end). **Mucus fistula** (distal end also brought out through a separate incision) generally avoided (2 stomas/abdominal wall defects) unless significant leak risk in the stapled-off end (distal obstruction, poor tissue integrity).
- **Loop ostomy:** continuous bowel loop through one aperture, 2 side-by-side openings; proximal end Brooked/dominant. Used for distal obstruction (e.g., obstructing cancer) and temporary diversion (protect distal anastomosis, heal sacral decubitus). Relatively easy to create and reverse.
- **Continent ileostomy (Kock pouch / Barnett Continent Intestinal Reservoir):** internal pleated-intestine pouch with nipple valve; no stool passage until intubated with a catheter; usually no appliance needed. Uncommon — high complication rate leading to revision surgery and intestinal loss.

**High ostomy output (HOO):**

- **Early HOO** = output greater than fluid intake (**typically >1.5 L/d**) within **3 weeks** of stoma formation, resulting in dehydration. Common with ileostomy; rare with colostomy.
- Prompt evaluation for infection (postoperative abdominal infection, [[clostridioides-difficile|C. difficile]]), ileus, or medication-related adverse effects when HOO occurs with a colostomy or is high with an ileostomy.
- **Most important treatment: hydration to prevent renal failure** — repletion volumes are large, so typically **IV**, requiring hospital admission or long-term IV access for home health care.
- Persistent early HOO → consider **early stoma reversal**, but reversal **before 6 weeks** from the index surgery carries increased complication risk.
- **Chronic (late) HOO** = persistent HOO **>3 weeks** after surgery, or new-onset HOO **>3 weeks** after creation. More likely with a jejunostomy, **short bowel (<200 cm small intestine remaining)**, or failed post-surgical adaptation. Ileal adaptation begins over days–weeks (mucosal changes altering electrolyte transport, absorptive capacity, motility). Etiologies of late HOO: infection, structural (stomal stricture/dysfunction, intestinal obstruction, ileus, enteric fistula), recurrent Crohn's disease, and common adult diarrhea causes ([[microscopic-colitis|microscopic colitis]], [[bile-acid-diarrhea|bile acid diarrhea]]).

**Table 1 — Treatment strategies for high ostomy output:**

| Type of treatment | Examples |
|---|---|
| Bulking agents | Psyllium fiber; guar gum; marshmallows |
| Antimotility agents | [[loperamide|Loperamide]]; diphenoxylate + atropine; codeine; tincture of opium |
| Antisecretory agents | Proton pump inhibitors / H2 agonists; somatostatin analogues (octreotide) |
| Anti-inflammatory agents (if from recurrent Crohn's) | Consultation with IBD specialist |
| Adaptation-promoting agents | GLP-2 analogues (teduglutide, elsiglutide, glepaglutide, apraglutide) |
| Surgical | Reversal of the ostomy with restoration of intestinal continuity when possible |

**Short-term complications:**

- **Ostomy leakage** — most common and dreaded. Predisposing: obesity, placement within a skin crease, loop configuration, liquid effluent (ileostomy, chronic diarrhea), flush stoma. Best strategy is prevention (preoperative stomatherapist marking, meticulous technique). Management: thicken stool with antidiarrheals; bolster stoma height (convex appliance, ostomy belt, paste, barrier rings); heat appliance with hair dryer before application; lie flat several minutes after application; dry peristomal skin; stomal powder + skin sealant. Appliance opening cut **one-eighth inch larger than the stoma**; re-measure stoma at each change for the **first 8 weeks** (stoma shrinks). Refractory leakage may need revision.
- **Stomal retraction** — with ischemia or thick abdominal wall (obesity). Early retraction below the abdominal wall → sepsis, emergent surgical revision. Retraction within skin but above fascia → pouching issues/stricture; endoscopy or cross-sectional imaging delineates depth. Temporary stoma: manage symptomatically (convex appliance, belt, barrier ring) until reversal; permanent stoma often needs revision.
- **Mucocutaneous separation** — maturation sutures detach; manage with pouching solutions until healing by secondary intention; immunosuppressed patients at particular risk.

**Long-term complications:**

- **Peristomal skin:** most issues from appliance leakage (manage per above). Appliance **allergy** — itching/redness in the shape of the offending product; skin sealant, pouching-system change, temporary steroid spray. **Fungal infection** (moisture/heat) — itchy maculopapular rash with satellite borders; antifungal powder sealed with sealant; no improvement at 2 weeks → surgeon/enterostomal therapist. Painful ulcers with purple halo (esp. IBD) → assess for **peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum** (interdisciplinary GI/dermatology/wound-care management). Minor bleeding at appliance changes is normal; persistent/severe bleeding or purplish concentric peristomal discoloration → work up **peristomal varices**.
- **Parastomal hernia:** up to **50% of ostomates within 5 years**. Risk factors: obesity, smoking, steroid use, transverse colostomy. Prevention: place stoma **through the rectus**; avoid transverse colon when possible. **Incarcerated hernia** (painful, irreducible → obstruction/ischemia) = **surgical emergency**. Small reducible hernias → hernia belt. Elective repair reserved for significant pouching issues, pain, or recurrent obstruction. Most effective repair = **ostomy reversal**; otherwise minimally invasive repair usually with mesh; recurrence after repair **>25% at 2 years**. Stoma relocation has fallen out of favor (high hernia risk at new site).
- **Stomal prolapse** (elongation of the stoma's intestinal portion): rate **5%–10%**. Acute prolapse with incarceration/ischemia (pain, obstipation, purple/black stoma) = **emergency surgery**. If no ischemia: reduce with patient relaxed, gentle pressure; if irreducible, **table sugar applied to the stoma ×20 minutes** reduces edema and facilitates reduction. Mild, easily reducible, non-interfering prolapse → no surgery; otherwise revision or reversal.

**Perioperative considerations:**

- Address psychological impact (fear of leakage, odor, disclosure, clothing, intimacy, travel, self-care) with pre- and postoperative education.
- **Preoperative education + stoma site marking** improves quality of life and decreases peristomal skin and pouching complications. WOC marking assesses the abdomen in multiple positions for a site within the rectus, away from scars, skin folds, bony prominences, and umbilicus.
- WOC consultation manages expectations (output, appliances, regular mucus passage from the native rectum); community-based and online ostomy support groups exist.

---

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates the concept page [[ostomy-management]] (ostomy types/configurations, output expectations, HOO definitions + treatment ladder, complications and their management, perioperative WOC care).
- Cross-links to [[crohns-disease]], [[ulcerative-colitis]], [[inflammatory-bowel-disease]], [[colorectal-cancer]], [[fecal-incontinence]], [[clostridioides-difficile]], [[microscopic-colitis]], [[bile-acid-diarrhea]], [[loperamide]], [[pouchitis]].

---

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **No numbered BPA statements or evidence grades** — commentary format; advice reflects expert experience + literature review.
- **Medication absorption after ostomy creation is not addressed** (e.g., altered absorption of oral drugs with ileostomy/short bowel) — gap; would need another source.
- Typical daily ileostomy output volumes are not quantified beyond the >1.5 L/d HOO threshold and emptying frequency.
- Figure 1 (schematic of loop ostomy, end ostomy with Hartmann's pouch, end ostomy with mucus fistula, continent ileostomy) is an anatomic schematic, not a decision algorithm.

# AGA Guideline: Endoscopic Eradication Therapy (EET) of Barrett's Esophagus (2024)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [AGA Clinical Practice Guideline: Endoscopic Eradication Therapy of Barrett's Esophagus and Related Neoplasia (2024). Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline).](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.03.019)
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.03.019](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.03.019)
- **Type:** GRADE-based guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline defines when to use **endoscopic eradication therapy (EET)** — endoscopic resection of visible lesions plus ablation (e.g., RFA) — for dysplastic [[barretts-esophagus]] and early neoplasia, and how to survey afterward. It complements the separate Barrett's surveillance guideline and sits within [[endoscopic-oncology]].

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Rec 1 (Strong):** In BE with **high-grade dysplasia (HGD)**, **EET over surveillance**.
- **Rec 2 (Conditional):** In BE with **low-grade dysplasia (LGD)**, suggests **EET over surveillance** (patients prioritizing avoidance of procedural risk may reasonably choose surveillance).
- **Rec 3 (Conditional):** In **non-dysplastic BE (NDBE)**, suggests **against routine EET**.
- **Rec 4–5:** **Endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD) of visible/neoplastic lesions** before/with ablation; post-EET surveillance after complete eradication of intestinal metaplasia (CEIM) at defined intervals (e.g., HGD: 3, 6, 12 months then annually; LGD: years 1 and 3).

---

## Clinical Relevance

EET is standard of care for HGD and favored for LGD; NDBE should not be routinely ablated. Resect visible lesions first, then ablate, then survey. Tightly linked to [[barretts-esophagus]] and dysplasia management via [[endoscopic-oncology]]; upstream control of [[gerd]] remains foundational.

---

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Rubio-Tapia A, McCallum R, Camilleri M. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome: Commentary. Gastroenterology 2024;166:930–934.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.01.040)
- **Authors:** Alberto Rubio-Tapia, Richard McCallum, Michael Camilleri
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2024;166:930–934
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.01.040](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.01.040)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Commentary; narrative expert advice, no formal Best Practice Advice statements)

## Summary

Commentary on cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), a chronic disorder of gut–brain interaction (Rome IV) and a **subtype of cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS)** associated with chronic (typically years), heavy (daily/near-daily) cannabis use, predominantly in males. CHS is rising in prevalence and underrecognized. Diagnosis is clinical (no confirmatory test), resting on stereotyped cyclic vomiting, a defined cannabis-use pattern, and resolution after cannabis cessation; compulsive hot-water bathing is a supportive but non-pathognomonic feature. Management pairs acute antiemetic control (notably topical capsaicin) with long-term cannabis cessation and tricyclic antidepressants.

## Key Findings / Claims

**CVS — Rome IV criteria (adults, Table 1):**
- Stereotypical episodes of vomiting regarding onset (acute) and duration (<1 week).
- ≥3 discrete episodes in the prior year **and** 2 episodes in the past 6 months, occurring ≥1 week apart.
- Absence of nausea/vomiting between episodes (milder symptoms may persist between episodes).
- Supportive: personal or family history of migraine headaches.
- Criteria fulfilled for the last 3 months with onset ≥6 months before diagnosis.

**CHS — proposed diagnostic criteria (Venkatesan et al.):**
1. **Clinical features:** stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling CVS in onset, frequency ≥3 times annually.
2. **Cannabis use pattern:** duration >1 year before symptom onset; frequency >4 times per week on average.
3. **Cannabis cessation:** resolution of symptoms after abstinence for ≥6 months, or ≥ the total duration of 3 typical vomiting cycles in that patient.

- No confirmatory test. Hot-water bathing reported in ~71% of CHS (systematic review, 271 cases: mean age 30 yr, 69% male, mean 6.6 yr of cannabis use before onset, daily use 68%); not pathognomonic (also seen in CVS).
- **4 phases of CVS (Fleisher):** interepisodic, prodromal, emetic, recovery.
- **Complications:** dehydration, acute kidney injury, electrolyte/metabolic imbalance; rarer pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum; death.
- **ED evaluation** must exclude life-threatening mimics: acute abdomen, bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischemia, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction.
- **Outpatient DDx** after excluding structural disease: rumination syndrome, gastroparesis, CVS, pregnancy, migraine, functional chronic nausea and vomiting.

**Management:**
- **Acute/short-term (case series, small trials):** topical **capsaicin 0.1% cream** to the upper abdomen (TRPV1 activation), benzodiazepines, **haloperidol**, promethazine, olanzapine, ondansetron. **Avoid opioids** (worsen nausea, addiction risk).
- **Long-term:** counseling for **cannabis cessation** + **tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline)** as mainstay — start 25 mg at bedtime, titrate weekly to minimal effective dose **75–100 mg at bedtime**; efficacious in ~70%.
- Abrupt ("cold turkey") cessation may trigger cannabinoid withdrawal and high recidivism; co-manage with psychology/psychiatry for refractory disease or psychiatric comorbidity.

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome]] — new disease-script page.
- [[cyclic-vomiting-syndrome]] — new disease-script page (home for CVS Rome IV criteria and 4 phases).
- Updates [[nausea-and-vomiting]] (DDx of episodic vomiting) and [[gastroparesis]] (DDx).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Commentary, no formal evidence ratings; treatment evidence limited to case series/small RCTs. Critical appraisal has questioned the etiologic role of cannabis in CHS. Many patients remain uncertain about the cannabis link, and recidivism is high.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Levinthal DJ, Staller K, Venkatesan T. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome: Commentary. Gastroenterology 2024;167:804–811.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.05.031)
- **Authors:** David J. Levinthal, Kyle Staller, Thangam Venkatesan
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.05.031](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.05.031)
- **Type:** guideline (Clinical Practice Update — expert commentary)

## Summary

AGA expert commentary on the diagnosis and management of **cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS)** in adults — a chronic disorder of gut–brain interaction (DGBI) that is common (~2% US prevalence, more common in women) yet markedly under-diagnosed and under-treated, with most patients enduring years of diagnostic delay, futile investigation, and sometimes unnecessary surgery. Half of patients visit the ED at least annually and 1 in 3 become disabled.

CVS is diagnosed clinically by **Rome IV criteria** and unfolds in **4 phases** — inter-episodic, prodromal, emetic, recovery — each with a distinct treatment goal (see Figure 1 of source). The commentary stratifies patients into **mild** vs **moderate–severe** CVS (ANMS-CVSA criteria), which drives whether prophylaxis is offered. It details a limited diagnostic workup to exclude mimics, the CVS-vs-CHS distinction (cannabis timing/duration), and a full menu of prophylactic and abortive pharmacotherapy (Table 1), all necessarily based on case series and expert opinion given the absence of RCTs.

## Key Findings / Claims

*This CPU is a narrative expert commentary; it does not carry numbered Best Practice Advice statements. Decision-critical content is the diagnostic criteria (Box 1) and the medication table (Table 1).*

**Diagnosis — Rome IV criteria for CVS in adults (Box 1, top):**
- Stereotypical episodes of acute-onset vomiting lasting **<7 days**
- **≥3 discrete episodes in a year**, of which **2 in the prior 6 months**; episodes separated by **≥1 week of baseline health**
- Absence of vomiting between episodes (milder symptoms — nausea, occasional vomiting, dyspepsia — may persist)
- Supportive criterion: personal or family history of **migraine**

**Severity (ANMS-CVSA, Box 1 bottom):**
- **Mild:** <4 episodes/yr, each <2 days, no ED visits/hospitalizations → **abortive therapy only**
- **Moderate–severe:** ≥4 episodes/yr, each >2 days, ≥1 ED visit/hospitalization → **prophylactic + abortive therapy**
- **Coalescent CVS:** worsening trajectory → loss of well periods, may meet chronic nausea vomiting syndrome criteria; offer prophylaxis akin to moderate–severe.

**Clinical clues:** ~65% have a prodrome (median 1 h); abdominal pain present in most episodes (does not exclude CVS); episodes often early-morning; hot-water bathing gives relief in ~48% of non-cannabis users (not specific to CHS). Common triggers: stress (70–80%), sleep deprivation, menses, travel/motion, infection/surgery.

**Comorbidities:** mood/anxiety/panic (50–60%), migraine (20–30%), seizure (~3%), POTS/autonomic imbalance — treating these improves CVS outcomes.

**Workup (to exclude mimics):** CBC, electrolytes, glucose, LFTs, lipase, UA; one-time EGD or upper-GI imaging to exclude obstruction (recognize post-retching epiphenomena as non-causal — don't repeat). **Do not routinely order gastric emptying scans.** Consider Addison's, hypothyroidism, and **acute hepatic porphyria** as mimics; brain imaging + neurology if localizing neuro symptoms.

**CVS vs CHS:** CHS proposed as a CVS subset when heavy (>4×/wk, often daily), prolonged (>1 yr) cannabis use **precedes** symptom onset; retrospective CHS diagnosis requires cannabis cessation for **6 months or ≥3 typical cycle lengths** with symptom resolution. Offer abortive/prophylactic therapy regardless of cannabis use.

**Prophylaxis (moderate–severe only) — Table 1:**
- **First-line: TCAs** (amitriptyline/nortriptyline/doxepin). Start 25 mg qhs → goal 75–150 mg or 1–1.5 mg/kg qhs; slow titration; nortriptyline less anticholinergic than amitriptyline.
- **Second-line:** topiramate (start 25 mg → 100–150 mg/d; kidney stones, avoid in pregnancy, teratogenic), zonisamide (100 → 200–400 mg/d; kidney stones), levetiracetam (500 mg bid → 1000–2000 mg/d; safer in pregnancy), aprepitant (NK-1 antagonist; 125 mg 2–3×/wk if >60 kg), CoQ10/riboflavin supplements.

**Abortive (mild or moderate–severe) — Table 1:** triptans (**sumatriptan** 20 mg intranasal or 6 mg SC, may repeat ×1 at 2 h, max 2/24 h; avoid in ischemic heart disease/pregnancy) + antiemetic (**ondansetron** 8 mg SL q4–6h; promethazine/prochlorperazine; both available PR) ± sedatives (diphenhydramine, benzodiazepines — alprazolam available SL/PR). Nearly all patients need **2-agent combinations**.

**ED management:** treat all regardless of CHS suspicion; IV dextrose-containing fluids + IV antiemetics; **IV ketorolac as first-line non-narcotic analgesic**; benzodiazepines for sedation in a quiet, dark room; narcotics only in most severe refractory cases.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Primary source for `[[cyclic-vomiting-syndrome]]` (previously leaned on `[[aga-2024-chs]]`).
- Reinforces CVS-vs-CHS boundary on `[[cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome]]`.
- Lists `[[acute-hepatic-porphyria]]`, Addison's, and hypothyroidism as mimics — relevant to `[[nausea-and-vomiting]]` / `[[gastroparesis]]` differentials.
- Neuromodulator prophylaxis (TCAs first-line) overlaps the neuromodulator framing used elsewhere in the DGBI cluster.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Diagnostic criteria are **Rome IV**; the wiki now also holds `[[rome-v-2026-dgbi]]` (Rome V, 2026). This CPU predates Rome V — where Rome V revises CVS criteria, the newer consensus governs; flagged for reconciliation when Rome V CVS criteria are ingested.
- All CVS pharmacotherapy rests on case series / expert opinion (no RCTs) — evidence quality is low by design.
