## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Satish Nagula, Sravanthi Parasa, Loren Laine, Shailja C. Shah. AGA 2024: Quality Indicators for Upper GI Endoscopy. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2024;22:933–943.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.10.034)
- **Authors:** Satish Nagula, Sravanthi Parasa, Loren Laine, Shailja C. Shah
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal/Publisher:** Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2024;22:933–943
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2023.10.034](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2023.10.034)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

This AGA Clinical Practice Update (CPU) Expert Review provides 9 best practice advice (BPA) statements on performing a high-quality upper endoscopic examination (EGD). Unlike formal guidelines, these statements are derived from published literature, existing guidelines, and consensus expert opinion without formal evidence rating, per AGA CPU methodology.

The CPU is organized around three phases: preprocedure (appropriate indication and informed consent), intraprocedure (mucosal visualization, imaging technology, inspection time, photodocumentation, standardized terminology, and biopsy protocols), and postprocedure (communication of results and surveillance planning). A major emphasis is placed on reducing missed upper GI cancers — a systematic review of 81,184 patients found 10.7% of upper GI cancers were diagnosed within 3 years of a negative EGD, and 23.9% of esophageal adenocarcinomas in nondysplastic Barrett's patients were diagnosed within 1 year of a negative EGD.

The document provides specific biopsy protocol tables for [[eosinophilic-esophagitis|eosinophilic esophagitis]], [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's esophagus]], [[dyspepsia]]/[[helicobacter-pylori-infection|H. pylori]], gastric preneoplasia, [[peptic-ulcer-disease|peptic ulcer disease]], gastric polyps, and [[celiac-disease|celiac disease]]. It also addresses contemporary issues such as GLP-1 receptor agonist use before endoscopy, simethicone biofilm risk, and AI-assisted detection.

## Key Findings / Claims

### Preprocedure (BPA 1)

- A large meta-analysis of 53,392 patients found 21.7% (95% CI, 21.4–22.1) of upper endoscopies had inappropriate indications
- Appropriate indication associated with higher diagnostic yield (OR 1.42; 95% CI, 1.36–1.49)
- GLP-1 receptor agonists ([[semaglutide]], etc.) are associated with delayed gastric emptying; American Society of Anesthesiologists advises holding 1 dose before endoscopy to reduce aspiration risk

### Mucosal Visualization (BPA 2)

- 10.7% (95% CI, 8.0–13.7%) of upper GI cancers are diagnosed within 3 years of a negative EGD (systematic review, n=81,184)
- 23.9% (95% CI, 15.3–35.4%) of esophageal adenocarcinomas in nondysplastic Barrett's patients occur within 1 year of a negative EGD
- Premedication with simethicone and pronase improves mucosal visualization in most studies; adding N-acetylcysteine to simethicone further improves visualization in some studies
- Simethicone should be used at lowest concentration (0.5%) via working channel (not waterjet), due to biofilm risk in endoscope channels

### High-Definition and Image Enhancement Technologies (BPA 3 and 4)

- HD-WLE is superior to standard-definition WLE for neoplasia detection
- All system components (endoscope chip, processor, monitor, cables) must be HD-compatible for true HD resolution
- Image enhancement technologies (IET): NBI (Olympus), i-Scan (PENTAX), LCI/blue laser imaging (FUJIFILM)
- In Barrett's esophagus: NBI, LCI, or i-Scan improved detection/characterization of dysplastic lesions by 10–20%
- In gastric screening: NBI detected more focal gastric lesions vs. HD-WLE (40.6% vs. 29%; P=.003), and more [[gastric-intestinal-metaplasia|gastric intestinal metaplasia]] (17.7% vs. 7.7%; P=.001) in a large multicenter trial
- LCI tandem trial: significantly lower missed upper GI neoplasia rate vs. HD-WLE (0.67% vs. 3.5%; RR 0.19; 95% CI, 0.07–0.50)

### Inspection Time (BPA 5)

- Total EGD duration >7 minutes associated with increased detection of Barrett's esophagus, gastric intestinal metaplasia, and upper GI cancer
- Barrett's esophagus: Inspection time >1 min/cm of Barrett's segment associated with higher rate of endoscopically suspicious lesions (54.2% vs. 13.3%; P=.04) and trend toward higher advanced neoplasia detection (40.2% vs. 6.7%; P=.06)
- Singapore study (retrospective): endoscopists spending >7 min for entire EGD had 2.5-fold higher odds of detecting high-risk gastric lesions (OR 2.50; 95% CI, 1.52–4.12) and 3.4-fold higher odds of detecting neoplasia (OR 3.42; 95% CI, 1.25–10.38)
- Japan study (n=55,786): inspection time ≥5–7 min associated with higher odds of detecting gastric neoplasia (OR 1.90; 95% CI, 1.06–3.40) vs. <5 min

### Photodocumentation (BPA 6)

- Minimum required anatomic stations: lower esophagus/cardia with SCJ and GEJ, GEJ/fundus in retroflexed view, body and antrum in anterograde view, incisura in retroflexed view, distal extent in duodenum
- ESGE recommends at least 10 landmarks; World Endoscopy Organization recommends 28
- AGA positions minimum set as adequate for average-risk patients; more rigorous photodocumentation recommended for Barrett's esophagus, gastric intestinal metaplasia, or patients referred for endoscopic treatment

### Standardized Terminology (BPA 6 / Classification Systems)

- Los Angeles classification: erosive esophagitis
- Prague C&M criteria: Barrett's esophagus
- Forrest classification: bleeding peptic ulcers
- Paris classification: superficial neoplastic lesions
- Hill grade classification: gastroesophageal flap valve
- Eosinophilic Esophagitis Endoscopic Reference System (EREFS); Index for Severity of EoE (I-SEE) anticipated to become new standard

### Biopsy Protocols (BPA 7)

- **Eosinophilic esophagitis:** ≥6 biopsies total from distal and mid/proximal esophagus
- **Barrett's esophagus:** Seattle protocol — 4-quadrant biopsies every 1–2 cm + targeted biopsies of mucosal abnormalities; ≥8 biopsies significantly improves diagnostic yield even in 1–2 cm segments; avoid routine biopsy of normal or irregular Z-line
- **Dyspepsia/H. pylori:** 5 biopsies from greater and lesser curve of gastric body, incisura, greater and lesser curve of antrum; place in 2 jars (body; antrum/incisura); gastric body biopsies especially important in PPI/PCAB users due to proximal H. pylori migration
- **Gastric preneoplasia (updated Sydney System):** ≥5 biopsies — 2 from antrum (within 2–3 cm of pylorus, lesser and greater curvature), 1 from incisura, 2 from body (lesser curvature ~4 cm proximal to angle, greater curvature ~8 cm distal to cardia); separate into ≥2 jars; targeted biopsies in separate jar; request histologic subtyping of gastric intestinal metaplasia
- **Peptic ulcer disease:** Gastric ulcer biopsies from base and edges; routine duodenal ulcer biopsies not necessary; biopsy remainder of stomach for H. pylori; may individualize gastric ulcer biopsy in very low-risk patients
- **Gastric polyps:** Biopsy or preferably resect solitary polyps; resect largest polyp(s) and sample others if multiple
- **Celiac disease:** ≥4 biopsies from postbulbar duodenum + 1–2 from bulb (place bulb specimens in separate container); bulb biopsies increase sensitivity but may reduce specificity
- **Iron-deficiency anemia:** AGA recommends serologic testing first; duodenal biopsy only if positive serology; H. pylori noninvasive testing (stool antigen) preferred over routine gastric biopsies

### Postprocedure (BPA 8 and 9)

- Document management recommendations based on endoscopic findings
- If recommendations contingent on histopathology (H. pylori, Barrett's, gastric intestinal metaplasia), document that guidance will be provided after results
- Document surveillance indication and appropriate intervals; implement recall system for surveillance-due patients

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Garcia-Tsao G, Abraldes JG, Rich NE, Wong VW-S. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Use of Vasoactive Drugs and Intravenous Albumin in Cirrhosis: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2024;166(1):202–210.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.10.016)
- **Authors:** Guadalupe Garcia-Tsao, Juan G. Abraldes, Nicole E. Rich, Vincent Wai-Sun Wong
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2023.10.016](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2023.10.016)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary

This AGA Clinical Practice Update provides Best Practice Advice on vasoactive drugs and IV albumin across three scenarios of decompensated cirrhosis: **acute variceal hemorrhage (AVH), ascites/SBP, and AKI/HRS**. Because systematic reviews were not performed, the 12 Best Practice Advice statements do not carry formal GRADE ratings.

For AVH, vasoactive drugs (octreotide, somatostatin, or — outside the US — terlipressin) should be started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected, before endoscopy, and continued 2–5 days after hemostasis to prevent early rebleeding. Octreotide is the agent of choice in the US given its safety profile; terlipressin is not FDA-approved for AVH.

For ascites/SBP, IV albumin is indicated at large-volume (>5 L) paracentesis and may be considered in SBP, but should **not** be used in uncomplicated ascites; vasoconstrictors have **no role** in uncomplicated ascites, post-LVP, or SBP. In hospitalized patients with cirrhosis and ascites presenting with AKI, albumin is the volume expander of choice.

For HRS-AKI, vasoactive drugs (terlipressin, norepinephrine, or octreotide+midodrine) reverse HRS-AKI but should not be used for other AKI phenotypes. **Terlipressin is the vasoactive drug of choice**; it does not require ICU monitoring and can be given through a peripheral IV line. Concurrent albumin can be considered accounting for volume status. Terlipressin is contraindicated in hypoxemia and in ongoing coronary/peripheral/mesenteric ischemia, and its benefit may not outweigh risk when SCr >5 mg/dL or MELD ≥35 (listed for transplant) or in ACLF grade 3.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice statements (verbatim):**

1. Vasoactive drugs should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis of variceal hemorrhage is suspected or confirmed, preferably before diagnostic and/or therapeutic endoscopy.
2. After initial endoscopic hemostasis, vasoactive drugs should be continued for 2–5 days to prevent early rebleeding.
3. Octreotide is the vasoactive drug of choice in the management of variceal hemorrhage based on its safety profile.
4. IV albumin should be administered at the time of large-volume (>5 L) paracentesis.
5. IV albumin may be considered in patients with SBP.
6. Albumin should not be used in patients (hospitalized or not) with cirrhosis and uncomplicated ascites.
7. Vasoconstrictors should not be used in the management of uncomplicated ascites, after large-volume paracentesis, or in patients with SBP.
8. IV albumin is the volume expander of choice in hospitalized patients with cirrhosis and ascites presenting with AKI.
9. Vasoactive drugs (eg, terlipressin, norepinephrine, and combination of octreotide and midodrine) should be used in the treatment of HRS-AKI, but not in other forms of AKI in cirrhosis.
10. Terlipressin is the vasoactive drug of choice in the treatment of HRS-AKI and use of concurrent albumin can be considered when accounting for patient's volume status.
11. Terlipressin treatment does not require intensive care unit monitoring and can be administered intravenously through a peripheral line.
12. Terlipressin use is contraindicated in patients with hypoxemia and in patients with ongoing coronary, peripheral, or mesenteric ischemia, and should be used with caution in patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure grade 3. The benefits may not outweigh the risks in patients with serum creatinine >5 mg/dL and in patients listed for transplantation with a MELD ≥35.

**Table 1 — standard AVH regimens (typical daily doses; boluses in μg for octreotide/somatostatin):**

| Drug | Standard regimen | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) | 50 μg IV bolus → continuous IV infusion 50 μg/h; additional boluses for ongoing bleeding | 2–5 d |
| Somatostatin | 250 μg IV bolus → continuous IV infusion 250–500 μg/h; additional boluses for ongoing bleeding | 2–5 d |
| Terlipressin (vasopressin analogue)ᵃ | Initial 48 h: 2 mg IV every 4 h until bleeding controlled; maintenance 1 mg IV every 4 h | 2–5 d |

ᵃ Terlipressin is a standard AVH regimen outside the US, but the FDA label does not include this indication.

- Vasoactive drugs halt AVH in up to 80% of cases; a meta-analysis (3111 patients, 30 RCTs) showed reduced 7-day mortality (RR 0.74), improved hemostasis (RR 1.21), lower transfusion needs, and shorter hospitalization. Stop the drug if endoscopy reveals a non-variceal source.
- Shortening vasoactive therapy to **2 days** may be reasonable in selected low-risk patients (no active bleeding at endoscopy) though data are limited.
- **LVP albumin dose:** 6–8 g/L of ascites removed (lower doses ~4 g/L may suffice); albumin at LVP >5 L mitigates post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (PCD) and AKI.
- **SBP albumin:** empirical regimen 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 (used in 4 of 5 supporting studies); greatest benefit with baseline bilirubin >4 mg/dL and AKI (creatinine >1.0 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL).
- **HRS-AKI terlipressin (US regimen, CONFIRM):** start 1-mg IV boluses every 6 h (peripheral line, no ICU); increase to 2 mg every 6 h on day 4 if insufficient response; continuous infusion (starting 2 mg/d) had fewer complications with similar efficacy. Patients with SCr >5 mg/dL have low response rates. FDA label suggests continuous pulse oximetry; the CPU notes vital-sign assessment (including pulse oximetry) every 2–4 h can substitute.
- Terlipressin (continuous infusion) is superior to or comparable with norepinephrine; NE requires an ICU setting.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[variceal-upper-gi-bleeding]]** — corroborates octreotide-as-first-choice, before-endoscopy initiation, 2–5 day duration; Table 1 regimens.
- **[[ascites]]** — LVP albumin 6–8 g/L (>5 L); adds explicit "no albumin in uncomplicated ascites" and "no vasoconstrictors post-LVP/uncomplicated ascites" decision boundaries.
- **[[spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis]]** — corroborates 1.5 g/kg (d1) / 1 g/kg (d3) albumin; framed as "may be considered," greatest benefit in high-risk.
- **[[aki-in-cirrhosis]]** — terlipressin is drug of choice; adds peripheral-line/no-ICU administration, expanded ischemia contraindications, ACLF-3 caution, and MELD ≥35 / SCr >5 futility caveats.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Frames SBP albumin as "may be considered" (BPA 5), a softer stance than [[aasld-2021-ascites-sbp-hrs|AASLD 2021]], which specifies albumin for high-risk SBP (bilirubin >4, Cr >1.0, BUN >30). Both are guideline-tier and consistent in the high-risk subgroup; wiki pages follow the AASLD high-risk criteria while noting the AGA framing.
- Optimal duration of vasoactive therapy for AVH (2 vs 5 days) remains unsettled; no concrete recommendation.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Orman ES, Fortune BE, John BV, Asrani SK. AGA Clinical Practice Update on the Management of Ascites, Volume Overload, and Hyponatremia in Cirrhosis: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2025;169:1547–1557.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.029)
- **Authors:** Eric S. Orman, Brett E. Fortune, Binu V. John, Sumeet K. Asrani
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.029](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.029)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review)

## Summary
AGA Expert Review on the practical management of three overlapping consequences of decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, volume overload (including hepatic hydrothorax and anasarca), and hyponatremia. Foundations are dietary sodium restriction and the lowest effective diuretic dose, with identification/treatment of decompensation triggers and early liver-transplant referral for refractory disease. The update extends standard ascites care to hepatic hydrothorax (therapeutic thoracentesis; TIPS for refractory cases), to inpatient volume overload (IV loop diuretics by bolus or continuous infusion, with cautious escalation), and to refractory anasarca (nephrology co-management — acetazolamide for contraction alkalosis, second-mechanism agents such as metolazone, or ultrafiltration). Hyponatremia is split into asymptomatic outpatient management (sodium + fluid restriction) and severe/symptomatic inpatient management (albumin, vasoconstrictors, hypertonic saline, vaptans, or renal replacement), all coordinated multidisciplinarily.

## Key Findings / Claims — Best Practice Advice (verbatim)
1. **BPA 1:** Patients with cirrhosis with ascites, hepatic hydrothorax, or volume overload should be managed with dietary sodium restriction and diuretics at the lowest effective dose, with dose escalation guided by symptoms, weight, urine output, and electrolyte/renal monitoring. Education and referral to a dietitian should be provided for dietary management. Triggers of liver decompensation should be identified and addressed.
2. **BPA 2:** Patients with cirrhosis with new-onset ascites, or those admitted to the hospital for symptoms related to ascites or encephalopathy should receive diagnostic paracentesis as soon as possible. Testing should include serum ascites albumin gradient and cell count, Gram stain, and culture.
3. **BPA 3:** Patients with hepatic hydrothorax with dyspnea and/or hypoxemia should undergo a therapeutic thoracentesis for both symptom relief and expansion of the underlying lung.
4. **BPA 4:** All patients with refractory ascites and/or hepatic hydrothorax should be considered for liver transplantation evaluation, regardless of their Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score.
5. **BPA 5:** Refractory ascites and/or hydrothorax should be managed with therapeutic paracentesis and/or thoracentesis, respectively, with the frequency guided by recurrence.
6. **BPA 6:** When the volume of ascites removed is >5 L, 20%–25% intravenous albumin 6–8 g per every total liter removed should be administered. For patients with hypotension, renal insufficiency, or electrolyte abnormalities, albumin should also be considered for removal of smaller volumes.
7. **BPA 7:** Well-selected patients with refractory ascites, hepatic hydrothorax, volume overload, or hyponatremia should be referred for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.
8. **BPA 8:** Diagnostic workup for the etiology of hyponatremia in cirrhosis should include dietary and medication history (diuretics, bowel regimen); review of electrolyte and kidney function; gastrointestinal bleeding assessment; infectious workup, including diagnostic paracentesis; and evaluation of secondary causes (thyroid or adrenal dysfunction).
9. **BPA 9:** Outpatient management of asymptomatic hypervolemic hyponatremia in liver cirrhosis entails both sodium and water restriction (aiming for 1–1.5 L of daily fluid intake), modification of diuretics and laxatives, and monitoring of electrolytes.
10. **BPA 10:** Inpatient management of severe or symptomatic hypervolemic hyponatremia in liver cirrhosis includes both sodium and water restriction; modification or discontinuation of diuretics and laxatives; and additional measures, such as intravenous albumin based on volume assessment or oral vasoconstriction therapy.
11. **BPA 11:** Recurrent or refractory hyponatremia management should involve a multidisciplinary approach (including the liver transplantation team when appropriate) and can consider several therapeutic options, including intravenous vasoconstrictor therapy, infusion of hypertonic saline, use of vasopressin receptor antagonist (vaptans), or use of renal replacement therapy.
12. **BPA 12:** Inpatient management of volume overload includes escalation or trial of intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide or bumetanide) in bolus (2–3 times per day) or continuous fashion. Cautious escalation can be done every 2–3 days with monitoring of volume status, kidney function, daily weights, and symptoms.
13. **BPA 13:** Advanced strategies in refractory anasarca should be coordinated with nephrology for consideration of diuretics in the setting of contraction alkalosis (eg, addition of acetazolamide), second agent with alternate mechanism of action (eg, thiazide diuretics, such as metolazone), or need for ultrafiltration.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[ascites]] — adds hepatic hydrothorax management, inpatient IV loop diuretic strategy, refractory anasarca/nephrology co-management, and an expanded hyponatremia workup/treatment ladder (vasoconstrictors, RRT).
- Corroborates existing AASLD 2021 ascites content (SAAG/cell-count paracentesis, albumin 6–8 g/L for LVP >5 L, TIPS for refractory ascites, LT referral, vaptan cautions).
- Cross-links: [[spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis]], [[aki-in-cirrhosis]], [[hepatic-encephalopathy]], [[portal-hypertension]], [[liver-transplantation]] (TIPS recommended for well-selected refractory cases).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Consistent with [[aasld-2021-ascites-sbp-hrs]]; no material conflict. AGA CPU is the newer same-tier (guideline) source and extends rather than overturns AASLD recommendations.

# AGA Clinical Practice Guideline: Surveillance of Barrett's Esophagus (2025)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Wani S, Zhou MJ, Sawas T, Rubenstein JH, et al. AGA Clinical Practice Guideline: Surveillance of Barrett's Esophagus (2025). Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline).](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.012)
- **Authors:** Wani S, Zhou MJ, Sawas T, Rubenstein JH, et al.
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.012](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.012)
- **Type:** GRADE-based guideline

---

## Summary

This AGA guideline addresses surveillance of non-dysplastic [[barretts-esophagus]] (NDBE) and refinements in sampling technique and acid suppression. It endorses interval surveillance for true intestinal-metaplasia BE, a structured (Seattle-protocol) biopsy approach augmented by chromoendoscopy, and daily PPI therapy — while declining to endorse several adjunctive technologies given limited certainty. Surveillance via [[upper-endoscopy]] aims to detect dysplasia/early neoplasia within the [[endoscopic-oncology]] treatment window.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Rec 1:** In **NDBE**, *suggests* endoscopic surveillance; panel consensus favors high-quality endoscopy roughly **every 3 years** (interval data limited; individualized by segment length).
- **Rec 2:** In **columnar-lined esophagus without intestinal metaplasia or neoplasia**, *suggests against* surveillance endoscopy.
- **Rec 3 (Recommends):** Use a **structured biopsy protocol** (Seattle protocol — 4-quadrant every 1–2 cm + targeted biopsies of visible lesions), with **chromoendoscopy/CE-directed** biopsies as an adjunct.
- **Rec 4:** **No recommendation** for/against **WATS-3D** as an adjunctive sampling technique.
- **Recs 5–6:** No recommendation for/against routine **p53 immunostaining** or **TissueCypher** tissue-based biomarkers.
- **Rec 7:** Suggests **daily PPI** therapy in BE.
- **Rec 8:** Suggests **PPIs over antireflux surgery** for cancer-risk reduction in BE.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Confirms ~3-year surveillance for NDBE with disciplined Seattle-protocol sampling and daily PPI as the chemopreventive backbone; advanced biomarkers/WATS-3D are not yet endorsed for routine use. Tightly linked to [[gerd]] (the upstream driver) and to dysplasia management via [[endoscopic-oncology]]; complements premalignant-mucosa surveillance themes shared with [[gastric-premalignant-conditions]].

# AGA Living Guideline: CADe-Assisted Colonoscopy (2025)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Sultan S, Shung DL, Kolb JM, Foroutan F, Hassan C, Kahi CJ, Liang PS, Levin TR, Siddique SM, Lebwohl B. AGA Living Guideline: Computer-Aided Detection (CADe)-Assisted Colonoscopy (2025). Gastroenterology (AGA Living Clinical Practice Guideline).](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.002)
- **Authors:** Sultan S, Shung DL, Kolb JM, Foroutan F, Hassan C, Kahi CJ, Liang PS, Levin TR, Siddique SM, Lebwohl B
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Living Clinical Practice Guideline)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.002](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.002)
- **Type:** GRADE-based living guideline on AI for [[colonoscopy]]

---

## Summary

This AGA living guideline evaluates **computer-aided detection (CADe)** — real-time AI polyp detection during [[colonoscopy]] — for improving adenoma detection and reducing post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer. Notably, the panel **could make no recommendation for or against** routine CADe use, citing **very low certainty of evidence** for the critical patient-important outcomes and a close balance between desirable and undesirable effects.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

- **No recommendation for or against** CADe-assisted [[colonoscopy]] (very low certainty).
- Modeling suggested a small benefit of roughly **11 fewer colorectal cancers per 10,000** screened and a trivial/no effect on CRC-related mortality (~2 fewer deaths per 10,000 over 10 years).
- CADe **increases adenoma detection rate (ADR)** but with **no clear increase in sessile serrated lesion detection** and at the cost of detecting more diminutive/non-neoplastic lesions, adding **downstream polypectomy and [[colonoscopy-surveillance|surveillance]] burden**.
- The desirable–undesirable tradeoff is **close**, and patient values, costs, and resource implications vary — favoring shared decision-making over a blanket mandate.

---

## Clinical Relevance

CADe is a tool that may modestly raise ADR but, on current evidence, does not warrant a universal "use it" recommendation. Frames AI adjuncts within quality metrics for [[colorectal-cancer-screening]] and [[colorectal-cancer|CRC]] prevention rather than as an established standard. As a *living* guideline, recommendations may change as higher-certainty outcome data (e.g., PCCRC incidence) emerge.

## Summary
AGA Expert Commentary reviewing the current evidence on blood-based tests for CRC screening and their implications, leveraging decision-analytic modeling to identify the test performance, interval, and uptake needed for blood tests to approach the effectiveness of stool tests and colonoscopy. As an Expert Commentary it has no numbered Best Practice Advice; the points below are its key clinical claims.

Two blood tests have population-based clinical-validation data. **Guardant Shield** (cell-free DNA, methylation) — validated in 22,877 adults aged 45–84; CRC sensitivity 83.1%, specificity 89.6%, advanced-precursor-lesion (APL) sensitivity 13.2%; stage 1 CRC sensitivity only 55%. It is FDA-approved (May 2024) and CMS-covered, commercially available. **Freenome** (cell-free DNA methylation) — validated in 48,995 adults aged 45–85; CRC sensitivity 79.2%, specificity 91.5%, APL sensitivity 12.5%; stage 1 sensitivity ~57%; expected to seek FDA/CMS approval. Both detect APLs and early-stage CRC poorly compared with stool tests, limiting cancer prevention and curative-stage detection.

Decision-analytic modeling (4 validated models) projects that triennial Guardant Shield yields substantially smaller reductions in CRC incidence (24%–47%) and mortality (53%–59%) than annual FIT (45%–77% / 67%–81%), triennial Cologuard, or 10-yearly colonoscopy. At its $1450 list price triennial Shield is cost-effective vs no screening ($74,800–$102,300/QALY) but is less effective and more costly than FIT or colonoscopy; even at $300 it would remain inferior to FIT/colonoscopy. For triennial blood-based screening to approximate annual FIT, its APL sensitivity would need to rise to ~50%–80% and cost fall to <$125–$140.

The main attraction is potential improved adherence (only 60%–65% of eligible U.S. adults are up to date; offering a blood test to those who decline other screening increased uptake by 17.5% in one study). But population outcomes are inferior if blood tests *substitute* for FIT/colonoscopy: to match FIT/colonoscopy, participation would need to be ≥35% higher; outcomes are similar only if for every 3 people substituting a blood test there are 2 new screenees. Blood testing requires a *programmatic* approach: abnormal tests must be followed by colonoscopy (almost 50% of patients fail to complete timely colonoscopy within 3–6 months of a positive stool test), and normal tests need repeat testing at appropriate intervals. Multicancer detection tests (e.g., Galleri) remain investigational. The bottom line: novel blood tests may improve participation but could cause net harm if substituted for more effective tests; for patients who decline all other screening, they are an acceptable option.

## Key Findings / Claims
- **Guardant Shield (Guardant):** cell-free DNA methylation blood test. Validation: 22,877 adults, ages 45–84, blood draw ≤60 days before screening colonoscopy; clinical-validation cohort 7861 (65 CRC, 1116 APLs). CRC sensitivity 83.1%, specificity 89.6%, APL sensitivity 13.2%; stage 1 CRC sensitivity 55%. FDA-approved May 2024, CMS-covered, commercially available. List price $1450.
- **Freenome:** cell-free DNA methylation blood test. Validation: 48,995 adults, ages 45–85, blood draw ≤120 days before screening colonoscopy; clinical-validation cohort 27,010 (72 CRC, 2567 APLs). CRC sensitivity 79.2%, specificity 91.5%, APL sensitivity 12.5%; stage 1 sensitivity 57.1%. Expected to seek FDA/CMS approval.
- **APL = advanced precancerous lesion:** adenoma or sessile serrated lesion ≥10 mm, villous histology, high-grade dysplasia, or carcinoma in situ.
- **Both blood tests:** lower sensitivity for stage 1 CRC and for APLs than stool tests → reduced potential for cancer prevention (poor APL detection) and curative treatment (suboptimal early-stage detection). Performance figures are one-time test performances; optimal repeat interval unknown.
- **CMS coverage:** acceptable CRC-screening blood tests covered **every 3 years**; CMS minimum performance threshold is CRC sensitivity 74% and specificity 90% (implies ~10% APL positivity rate).
- **Modeling — reductions in CRC incidence / mortality vs no screening (4 validated models):**
  - Annual FIT: 45%–77% / 67%–81%
  - Triennial MT-sDNA (Cologuard): 40%–73% / 64%–78%
  - Colonoscopy q10y: 57%–81% / 72%–88%
  - Triennial Guardant Shield: 24%–47% / 53%–59% (Freenome similar to Shield)
- **Cost-effectiveness:** Triennial Shield at $1450 = cost-effective vs no screening ($74,800–$102,300/QALY) but less effective and more costly than FIT/colonoscopy. At $300 it could be cost-saving vs no screening but still inferior to FIT/colonoscopy. Shorter intervals (biennial/annual) improve benefit but costs rise faster than benefits.
- **Threshold to match annual FIT:** triennial blood test would need APL sensitivity ~50%–80% AND cost <$125–$140.
- **Substitution vs supplementation:** If blood tests substitute for currently recommended stool tests/colonoscopy, CRC outcomes are inferior. To equal FIT/colonoscopy, participation must be ≥35% higher; population outcomes similar only if for every 3 substituters there are 2 net-new screenees.
- **Adherence:** Only 60%–65% of eligible U.S. adults up to date. In a study of patients who declined other screening, offering a blood test increased CRC screening by 17.5% vs usual care; an RCT showed adherence up to 11% higher for blood vs stool testing.
- **Programmatic requirement:** Abnormal blood test → must complete colonoscopy; normal → repeat at appropriate interval. ~50% of patients do not complete colonoscopy within 3–6 months of a positive stool test; delays raise CRC incidence/mortality. Whether those who decline screening colonoscopy will complete it after a positive blood test is unknown.
- **Multicancer detection tests (MCDs):** Galleri (Grail) — overall cancer sensitivity 51.5%, specificity 99.5%; large NHS validation underway. Investigational; confirmatory imaging imperfect, costs/harms substantial, mortality benefit unproven. Premature for clinical CRC screening.
- **Interval blood tests between screening colonoscopies:** premature to consider.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[colorectal-cancer-screening]]** — primary update: new "Blood-Based CRC Screening" content (Guardant Shield, Freenome performance; CMS 3-year coverage and 74%/90% threshold; modeling-based effectiveness vs FIT/colonoscopy/Cologuard; cost-effectiveness; substitution vs supplementation; programmatic follow-up colonoscopy requirement; MCDs).
- **[[colorectal-cancer]]** — minor: supports that blood tests detect early-stage CRC and precursors poorly relative to stool/colonoscopy.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Positioning of blood tests vs the existing "Not Recommended — Septin-9" note in [[colorectal-cancer-screening]]:** ACG 2021 recommended against the older Septin-9 blood test; this 2025 CPU addresses newer cfDNA tests (Shield FDA/CMS-approved) without endorsing them as equivalent to FIT/colonoscopy — it positions them as acceptable mainly for patients who would otherwise decline all screening. Not a direct contradiction; the newer test class is distinct.
- **USPSTF status:** As of this CPU, blood tests were not yet folded into USPSTF recommendations the way stool tests/colonoscopy are; the table in the screening page lists endorsement status.
- **Unknowns flagged by the source:** optimal repeat interval, real-world uptake, whether improved participation compensates for lower efficacy, and downstream colonoscopy completion after a positive blood test.

- **Type:** GRADE-based living guideline

## Summary

This living guideline ranks advanced therapies for moderate-to-severe [[crohns-disease]] and pushes two practice-changing principles: use a **higher-efficacy agent first** and favor **initial advanced therapy over step-up ("step") therapy**. It positions the newer IL-23 inhibitors (risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab) and the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib alongside established anti-TNF and ustekinumab options. Part of the broader [[inflammatory-bowel-disease]] treatment framework.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Rec 1 (Strong):** Use **infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab, or upadacitinib** over no treatment.
- **Rec 2 (Conditional):** Certolizumab pegol or vedolizumab over no treatment.
- **Recs 3–4 (Conditional):** In **advanced-therapy–naïve** patients, prefer a **higher-efficacy** agent (e.g., infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, upadacitinib) over lower-efficacy options; after prior anti-TNF exposure, again favor higher-efficacy agents (adalimumab, risankizumab, upadacitinib) over lower-efficacy (vedolizumab, certolizumab).
- **Step vs early advanced therapy:** Suggests **initial advanced therapy over step therapy**.
- **Immunomodulators:** Suggests *against* **thiopurine monotherapy** for induction; thiopurines may be used for **maintenance** of remission; prefer **subcutaneous/IM methotrexate** over oral; **infliximab + thiopurine combination** over infliximab monotherapy. No recommendation on infliximab + methotrexate (knowledge gap).

**Implementation:** biosimilars equivalent to originators; SC infliximab/vedolizumab comparable to IV maintenance; dose escalation/extended induction for partial responders.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Reinforces an aggressive, efficacy-first, early-advanced-therapy strategy for moderate-to-severe [[crohns-disease]], with IL-23 inhibitors and upadacitinib now top-tier. Pairs with vaccination/health maintenance per [[ibd-preventive-care]]. As a living guideline, rankings update as comparative data accrue.

# AGA 2025 Clinical Practice Update on Endoscopic Enteral Access: Commentary

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Micic D, Martin JA, Fang J. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Endoscopic Enteral Access: Commentary. *Gastroenterology* 2025;168(1):164–168. doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2024.09.043.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.09.043)
- **Authors:** Dejan Micic, John A. Martin, John Fang
- **Year:** 2025 (received August 27, 2024; accepted September 20, 2024)
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastroenterology* 2025;168(1):164–168 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Commentary)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.09.043](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.09.043)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — expert **Commentary** (no numbered Best Practice Advice statements and no formal evidence ratings)

---

## Summary

Expert commentary to help gastroenterologists choose and manage enteral access — >255,000 US patients annually require enteral nutrition support during hospitalization. Enteral tubes deliver nutrition/medications or decompress the upper GI tract; options are oral/nasal flexible tubes (OG, NG, NJ) and percutaneous tubes (surgical, radiologic, or endoscopic: PEG, PEGJ, DPEJ). Endoscopically placed tubes have a favorable safety profile vs surgical or radiologic placement.

Core selection rules: gastric feeding is preferred (more physiologic, allows bolus or continuous feeds); small-bowel access is reserved for aspiration concerns refractory to prokinetics/rate changes, altered anatomy, gastric outlet obstruction, or severely delayed gastric emptying. Nasal tubes for **short-term (<4 weeks)** access; percutaneous tubes when access is expected **≥4 weeks**. DPEJ gives longer patency and fewer reinterventions than PEGJ (jejunal extension tubes are small caliber, 9F–12F) but is harder to place and leaks more. In severe dementia, tube feeding does not improve survival, infection risk, or functional status vs conscientious hand feeding — realistic goals-of-care conversations required. Periprocedural essentials: single-dose first-generation cephalosporin before percutaneous access (clindamycin/vancomycin if allergic; none if already on systemic antibiotics); PEG placement without interrupting dual-antiplatelet therapy is supported; platelets >50,000/mL and INR <1.5; hold heparin (resume 2–6 h post) and DOACs (resume evening dose). PEG tubes can be used immediately for medications and after 4 hours for feeds. Detailed guidance on placement technique (pull/push/introducer, PEGJ, DPEJ), special situations (ascites, VP shunt, peritoneal dialysis), and complications (peristomal infection, buried bumper, tube migration, occlusion, peristomal leakage, inadvertent removal, persistent gastrocutaneous fistula).

---

## Key Findings / Claims

*Commentary format — no numbered Best Practice Advice; key advice captured in full below.*

**Indications and patient selection:**

- Enteral tubes deliver enteral nutrition and/or medications, or provide GI **decompression** (e.g., malignant obstruction, impaired GI motility).
- Timing: in hospitalized adults at low nutritional risk, pursue enteral access when unable to meet caloric requirements over **5–7 days**; within **24–48 hours** of admission if severely malnourished and unable to maintain adequate oral nutrition.
- Table 1 indications (verbatim list): **Impaired nutrient intake** — neurologic disease (post-CVA, motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, unconscious/ventilated patient, cerebral palsy, select cases of dementia); **upper GI obstruction/motility disorder** (head and neck cancer; head/maxillofacial/mandibular/dental/neck trauma; radiation stomatitis; esophageal cancer; esophageal stricture; esophageal dysmotility; chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction; gastroparesis; superior mesenteric artery syndrome); **altered intestinal anatomy** (bariatric or foregut surgery with impaired intake); **psychiatric disorder** (anorexia nervosa); **increased metabolic requirements** (critical illness, cancer, burn/trauma, cystic fibrosis/chronic lung disease, IBD, liver disease, pancreatitis, renal disease); **increased intestinal losses** (short bowel syndrome).
- Multidisciplinary team advised (speech pathology, dietitians, nutrition nurses, gastroenterologists, co-managing physicians, palliative care when appropriate).
- **Severe dementia:** enteral feeding not associated with improved survival, reduced infection risk, or improved functional status — especially vs a conscientious program of **hand feeding**. Realistic conversations with physicians/families/caregivers about benefits, risks, and complications.

**Tube choice:**

- **Gastric feeding preferred** — more physiologic; allows intermittent bolus or continuous pump feeding. Meta-analyses (mostly critical care) show reduced aspiration pneumonia with small-bowel vs gastric feeding, but small-bowel access is more technically complex; before converting, try prokinetics, reduce bowel-slowing agents, and decrease feeding rates.
- **Duration rule:** nasal route preferred for **short-term (<4 weeks)** access in nonintubated patients; percutaneous tubes typically reserved for expected use of **≥4 weeks** (threshold acknowledged as somewhat arbitrary). Percutaneous devices dislodge less and deliver more adequate/durable feeding than NG tubes, but added placement risk justifies nasoenteral tubes for short-term use.
- **Small-bowel access options:** NJ tube; jejunal extension through a PEG (PEGJ); unitized transgastric jejunostomy tube; DPEJ. **DPEJ > PEGJ for tube patency and reintervention** (jejunal extensions are only 9F–12F) but placement is more complex and **peristomal leakage is increased with DPEJ** (larger-caliber tubes, bumpers in the small bowel).
- Small-bowel access **required** in: altered anatomy (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, partial/total gastrectomy), gastric outlet obstruction, severely delayed gastric emptying.
- Small-bowel feeding requires **reduced and cycled rates** to prevent dumping symptoms (hypertonic formula directly into small bowel).

**Preprocedural considerations:**

- Informed consent from the patient (with capacity) or legally authorized representative; delineate risks, expected benefits, outcomes.
- **Antibiotic prophylaxis:** peristomal infection significantly reduced by preprocedural antibiotics — typically a **single dose of a first-generation cephalosporin immediately before** percutaneous access. Not required if already on systemic antibiotics. Cephalosporin allergy → **clindamycin or vancomycin**.
- **Antithrombotics:** increasing data support PEG placement **without interruption of dual-antiplatelet therapy** (no significant increase in bleeding risk). If antithrombotics are held, resume ASAP considering indication, in consultation with the initiating service.
- **Laboratory thresholds:** platelet count **>50,000/mL**, INR **<1.5**. **Unfractionated heparin** should be held for percutaneous placement, and can be given **2–6 hours after** the procedure. **DOACs** held for placement, resumed with the **evening dose** after placement.

**Placement technique:**

- OG/NG tubes: bedside, blind, 8F–12F. Bedside nasoenteric (postpyloric) placement harder; electromagnetic tracking improves success. **Radiographic confirmation for all blind enteric placements** (and after guided placement if concern). Endoscopic NJ placement most secure (drag, over-guide-wire, and through-the-scope techniques all effective) but more resource-intensive.
- Percutaneous gastrostomy routes: **transoral** (pull or push) and **transabdominal**. Transabdominal (radiologic or endoscopic "introducer"/Russell technique: T-tack gastropexy → tract dilation → tube through dilated tract) typically reserved for **head and neck cancer** (minimize tumor seeding) and upper GI strictures/obstruction.
- PEG (pull) technique: insufflate stomach to appose to abdominal wall; site typically **2 cm below the costal margin** at maximal transillumination; "one-to-one" finger indentation; **"safe track"** — anesthetic-filled small-bore needle advanced under aspiration to exclude interposed bowel; trocar → guide wire → snared and pulled out mouth → tube pulled out through abdominal wall. Push technique similar (tube with dilator pushed over the wire from the mouth).
- **PEGJ:** place PEG directed toward/closer to the pylorus; choose extension size (**12F via 24F PEG, 9F via 20F PEG** — smaller sizes clog more); drag with suture + forceps/clip, or pass over a guide wire (pediatric colonoscope, ideally past the ligament of Treitz; ultrathin-endoscope guide-wire techniques also used).
- **DPEJ:** like a pull-PEG but harder (mobile small bowel, narrow angulated lumen); needs transillumination + finger indentation; snare-grasp the sounding needle to stabilize the loop before incision/trocar. Thin habitus, altered surgical anatomy, and **glucagon** (reduces small-bowel contractility) facilitate. 14F–20F tubes possible; authors prefer **14F** (less obstruction of intestinal flow, easier snare capture at removal).

**Procedural considerations / contraindications:**

- **Only absolute contraindication** to enteral access for feeding: **mechanical small-bowel obstruction** (unless tube placed for decompression).
- Avoid **nasal** access with abnormal nasal anatomy, facial trauma, or recent oronasal surgery.
- **Relative contraindications** to percutaneous insertion: active GI bleeding from peptic ulcer; hemodynamic or respiratory instability.
- Large midline wounds, chest tubes, abdominal mesh, and ostomies complicate but do not necessarily preclude PEG. Morbid obesity, large hiatal or abdominal wall hernias, peritoneal carcinomatosis, severe dysmotility, and esophageal varices are **not absolute contraindications** but complicate siting or raise aspiration risk; anesthesia support helps.
- **Ascites:** impairs wound healing and gastric-abdominal wall apposition — **drain via paracentesis or intraperitoneal drain**, and use T-tacks to improve tract formation.
- **VP shunt:** place gastrostomy **concurrently with or before** VP shunt rather than within 15 days after shunt placement; consider longer perioperative antibiotics with an existing shunt.
- **Peritoneal dialysis:** converting to (or maintaining) **hemodialysis for 6 weeks** reduces, but does not eliminate, peritonitis risk.

**Postprocedural care:**

- NG/NJ: use immediately after confirmation (usually abdominal radiography). **PEG: medications immediately; tube feeds after 4 hours.**
- Multidisciplinary follow-up (dietitians for formula/volume/free water/delivery method; nursing/APCs for site assessment).
- **Bridling** transnasal tubes reduces unintentional dislodgement, allows greater caloric intake. Transnasal tubes typically **≤3–4 weeks** (sinusitis risk); rarely longer with close monitoring.
- Percutaneous devices replaced at **6- to 12-month intervals** (sooner if breakdown). Avoid overlying gauze/tape/abdominal pads (retain moisture, injure skin).
- After permanent removal, spontaneous tract closure typically within **72 hours**. Risk factors for **persistent gastrocutaneous fistula**: immune suppression, prior gastrostomy-site infection, malnutrition, delayed gastric emptying → endoscopic closure with over-the-scope clips or suturing.
- **Inadvertent tube removal:** if placed within the previous **4 weeks**, do **not** blindly replace (stomach may not be adhered to the abdominal wall) — give antibiotics, serial abdominal exams for peritonitis, replace under radiographic or endoscopic guidance. If **>4 weeks**, routine clinic/bedside replacement through the mature tract — act fast (tract can close within hours); confirm intraluminal position with water-soluble contrast through the tube (or endoscopy).

**Complications:**

- Sinusitis (nasal tubes, duration-related). Peristomal infection (reduced by preprocedural antibiotics). Cellulitis, rarely **necrotizing fasciitis** (surrounding-skin inflammation ± subcutaneous gas on imaging).
- Self-extraction: bridles for nasal tubes; gloves/mitts, abdominal binders, or low-profile tubes for percutaneous tubes in altered consciousness.
- **Tube occlusion:** small-bore tubes (8F–12F, oral/nasal/jejunal extensions) clog sooner. Prevent with **30 mL water flush every 4 hours** during continuous feeding plus flushes before/after feedings; eliminate crushed-medication administration.
- **Buried bumper:** from excessive external traction (external bumper too tight); prevent with routine tube assessment and **1-cm breadth between external bumper and skin**. Presents with pain, inability to rotate/advance the tube, difficulty feeding/flushing, or increased leakage/infection at the site. Identify with cross-sectional imaging or endoscopy → **replace under endoscopic or radiologic guidance**.
- **Internal migration** (external bumper too loose): internal bumper/balloon obstructs pylorus or proximal duodenum — tube tight to skin and/or severe bilious leakage.
- **Peristomal leakage** of gastric/bilious contents: do **not** upsize the tube (enlarges the hole, worsens leakage). Assess for motility-altering medications (opiates), gastroparesis risk factors, vagal nerve injury. Trial promotility agents with intermittent feeds and/or continuous pump feeding at reduced rate; if unsuccessful, **convert gastric to jejunal feeding** (vent stomach while feeding); rarely remove the tube temporarily for partial stoma closure or re-site.

- **No numbered BPA statements or evidence grades** — commentary format.
- **Duration threshold:** this CPU uses **<4 weeks nasal / ≥4 weeks percutaneous** ("somewhat arbitrarily defined"); [[asge-2011-enteral-feeding]] frames it as peroral nutrition expected **within 30 days** → nasoenteric. Functionally concordant.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Ngamruengphong S, Othman MO, Wang AY, Yang D. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Endoscopic Resection for Early Colorectal Cancer: Commentary. Gastroenterology 2025;169:1558–1564.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.001)
- **Authors:** Saowanee Ngamruengphong, Mohamed O. Othman, Andrew Y. Wang, Dennis Yang
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2025;169(7):1558–1564
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.001](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.09.001)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Commentary; no formal Best Practice Advice statements)

## Summary
AGA Expert Commentary on the endoscopic management of T1 colorectal cancer (CRC) — cancer with invasion confined to the submucosa, without invasion of the muscularis propria. It reviews the definition of early CRC, the role of endoscopic resection, histopathologic factors driving risk of lymph node metastasis (LNM) and recurrence, and post-resection management (surveillance vs adjuvant surgery). This is an Expert Commentary, so it contains no numbered Best Practice Advice; the points below are its key clinical claims, drawn largely from USMSTF, ESGE, and JGES/JSCCR guidance.

Optical lesion assessment is the first critical step. Endoscopists should recognize features suggesting submucosal invasion (SMI) — depressed/excavated lesions, irregular pit/vascular pattern, NICE type 3, and lateral-spreading granular-mixed or nongranular lesions. Optical diagnosis alone is highly operator-dependent (real-world sensitivity often only 40%–50%); when diagnosis is unclear or CRC is highly suspected, refer to a high-volume center with resection and pathology expertise. Suspected T1 CRC should ideally be removed **en bloc**, because piecemeal resection prevents accurate histologic assessment and is itself an independent risk factor for luminal recurrence.

Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), with its higher en-bloc rate than EMR regardless of size, is often the preferred strategy for suspected superficially invasive T1 CRC; endoscopic full-thickness resection (EFTR) is a reasonable alternative for select T1 CRCs <2 cm where deep SMI is suspected. Resection is considered curative when all five criteria are met. Importantly, emerging data downgrade deep SMI as a solitary risk factor: in a meta-analysis (Zwager et al), SMI alone carried an absolute LNM risk of only ~2.6% and was **not** an independent predictor of LNM. LVI is the strongest predictor of LNM; tumor budding (Bd 2/3) and adverse histology (G3/G4, signet ring, mucinous) also confer high risk.

Recurrence after curative endoscopic resection of low-risk T1 CRC is low (~0.7%) vs 7.0% for high-risk (noncurative) T1 CRC; most recurrences occur within 36 months and 96% within 72 months. For high-risk T1 CRC surgery remains standard, but >80% of "high-risk" cases have no LNM at surgery, so the decision should be individualized against operative morbidity. Rectal T1 CRC carries higher local-recurrence and LNM risk than colonic, but rectal surgery is more morbid — favoring organ-preserving strategies. Full-thickness scar resection (EFTR, TAMIS, combined endo-lap) is an emerging alternative to completion surgery after R1/Rx margins without other risk factors.

## Key Findings / Claims
- **Definitions:** T1 CRC = neoplastic invasion through muscularis mucosae into submucosa, without muscularis propria invasion ("malignant polyp"). Without SMI, the word "cancer" should be avoided; terms *intramucosal adenocarcinoma* / *in situ adenocarcinoma* should be avoided (no LNM risk).
- **En-bloc imperative:** Suspected T1 CRC should be approached with en-bloc resection (USMSTF/ESGE/JGES). Piecemeal resection impairs histology and is an independent risk factor for luminal recurrence; NCCN states piecemeal-removed T1 inevitably requires adjuvant surgery.
- **Resection modality:** ESD preferred for suspected superficial T1 CRC (higher en-bloc rate irrespective of size); limited by complexity, learning curve, and inability to confidently resect deep SMI. EFTR reasonable for select T1 CRC <2 cm with suspected deep SMI.
- **Curative resection criteria (USMSTF/ESGE/JGES) — ALL five required:** (1) complete resection with histopathologic margins free of tumor; (2) superficial SMI (<1000 μm); (3) absence of lymphovascular invasion (LVI); (4) well-to-moderately differentiated histology (G1/G2); (5) low or absent tumor budding.
- **Depth of SMI:** Measured in μm per JSCCR — for nonpedunculated lesions from bottom of muscularis mucosae (or surface if not identifiable) to invasive front; pedunculated lesions use Haggitt classification (levels 0–4). Deep SMI = ≥1000 μm.
- **Deep SMI is a weaker solitary risk factor than historically believed:** >95% of patients with deep SMI as the *only* high-risk criterion have no LNM. Meta-analysis (Zwager et al, 8 studies, 1146 pts): SMI as solitary risk factor → absolute LNM risk 2.6% (pooled incidence 2.83; 95% CI 1.66–4.78); deep SMI was NOT an independent predictor of LNM; 37.9% of deep-SMI cancers had no other high-risk feature.
- **Operative risk:** Population cohort of 5170 surgical T1 CRC pts — 30-day mortality 1.7%, severe adverse events requiring re-intervention 8.3%.
- **LVI:** Strongest independent predictor of LNM (RR 5.2; 95% CI 4.0–6.8). Small-vessel involvement more strongly associated with LNM than large. USMSTF/JSCCR/ESGE all consider LVI a high-risk criterion prompting surgery. Perineural invasion also a risk factor.
- **Tumor budding:** Single tumor cell or cluster of ≤4 cells at invasive margin. Bd1 = 0–4 buds (low); Bd2 = 5–9 (intermediate); Bd3 = ≥10 (high). Bd2/Bd3 → increased LNM (OR 2.83 per Zwager). High-risk criterion (USMSTF/JSCCR/ESGE).
- **Adverse histology:** Poorly differentiated (G3), undifferentiated (G4), signet ring cell, mucinous → worse prognosis; adverse histology independent LNM risk factor (OR 2.14, meta-analysis of 67 studies/21,238 pts). WHO grades by lowest level of differentiation; JSCCR by predominant.
- **Resection margins:** R0 = both horizontal and vertical margins microscopically free. Lateral/horizontal positivity → local recurrence risk; vertical/deep positivity → deeper invasion + LNM risk. Margin <1 mm traditionally a risk, but a recent multicenter study found local recurrence not significantly higher at 0.1–1 mm (0.8%; 95% CI 0.1%–4.4%) vs >1 mm absent tumor budding. ESGE prefers vertical margin ≥1 mm.
- **Surveillance after curative low-risk T1 CRC:** Recurrence ~0.7% (low-risk) vs 7.0% (high-risk/noncurative); 60% of recurrences within 36 mo, 96% within 72 mo. Surveillance colonoscopy alone (no nodal/distant imaging) is reasonable after curative resection of low-risk T1 CRC. JSCCR and ESGE recommend surveillance colonoscopy within 1 year; NCCN recommends 1-year colonoscopy after curative colon resection but more frequent for rectal. Rectal T1 may warrant sooner/more frequent surveillance.
- **High-risk T1 CRC:** Surgery is standard of care, but >80% of "high-risk" cases have no LNM at surgery → individualize. Rectal T1 CRC: higher local recurrence and LNM than colon, but higher surgical morbidity → favor organ-preserving options.
- **R1/Rx margins without other risk factors:** Risk of intramural residual cancer 5%–11% and LNM 8%–9%. ESGE/JSCCR recommend endoscopic surveillance at 3–6 months for isolated lateral margin positivity. Full-thickness scar resection (EFTR / TAMIS / combined endoscopic-laparoscopic) is an emerging alternative to completion surgery; retrospective long-term data showed recurrence 2.2% (adjuvant surgery) vs 9.0% (EFTR) with similar 5-year metastasis-free and overall survival.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[polypectomy-emr]]** — primary update: en-bloc imperative for suspected T1 CRC; ESD-preferred and EFTR (<2 cm deep SMI) framing; unified 5-point curative-resection criteria (USMSTF/ESGE/JGES); updated deep-SMI LNM data (Zwager: ~2.6% absolute risk, not independent predictor); post-resection surveillance for low-risk vs high-risk/noncurative T1; R1/Rx scar-resection alternative.
- **[[colorectal-cancer]]** — corroborates and dates the endoscopic-vs-surgical decision for early T1 CRC; adds individualization for high-risk T1 (>80% have no LNM) and rectal-vs-colonic distinctions.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Deep SMI as a surgical trigger:** Historically (and in the existing [[polypectomy-emr]] "Favorable vs Unfavorable" table) deep SMI (≥1 mm) is an unfavorable criterion prompting surgical evaluation. This 2025 CPU nuances that — deep SMI *in isolation* carries only ~2.6% LNM risk and is not an independent predictor — supporting individualized, organ-preserving decisions rather than automatic surgery. Surfaced inline on the entity page; existing guideline-based criteria remain the page's primary recommendation.
- **Margin <1 mm:** Traditional ≥1 mm clear-margin threshold (USMSTF 2020) is questioned by newer multicenter data showing no significantly higher recurrence at 0.1–1 mm absent tumor budding; still unsettled.
- **Surveillance intervals after curative endoscopic resection of T1 CRC are not well defined** (no clear evidence); most data originate from Europe/Asia — generalizability to North American populations is uncertain.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Nguyen AD, Carlson DA, Patel A, Gyawali CP. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Incorporating Functional Lumen Imaging Probe Into Esophageal Clinical Practice: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2025;169:726–736.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.05.011)
- **Authors:** Anh D. Nguyen, Dustin A. Carlson, Amit Patel, C. Prakash Gyawali
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2025;169:726–736
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.05.011](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.05.011)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review; Best Practice Advice, no formal evidence ratings)

## Summary

Updates the 2017 AGA FLIP CPU. FLIP panometry uses impedance planimetry to measure EGJ distensibility/diameter and esophageal body contractile response to volumetric distention. Positioned as a complementary tool — interpreted alongside symptoms, endoscopy, HRM, and timed barium esophagram — most useful when standard tests are inconclusive, to confirm/refute EGJ outflow obstruction, intraprocedurally during myotomy, and in EoE remodeling and post-treatment symptom evaluation. Not for diagnosing GERD. 10 Best Practice Advice statements.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice (verbatim):**

1. Clinicians should perform a high-quality upper endoscopy evaluating for esophageal pathology immediately prior to considering FLIP.
2. Clinicians should consider performing FLIP if alternate investigations are inconclusive in patients with symptoms of esophageal obstruction (ie, dysphagia, esophageal-type regurgitation, and/or meal-related chest pain), and may consider FLIP as part of index endoscopy for symptomatic patients when the procedure and interpretation expertise are readily available.
3. Clinicians may use common sedation options for endoscopy (ie, propofol, fentanyl, and/or midazolam), as these medications have not been demonstrated to have a clinically significant impact on FLIP findings.
4. Normal esophagogastric junction opening on FLIP has a high negative predictive value for disorders of esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction on high-resolution manometry.
5. If upper endoscopy demonstrates findings strongly supportive of achalasia, clinicians may use FLIP findings to diagnose achalasia.
6. If upper endoscopy does not demonstrate findings supportive of achalasia, abnormal esophagogastric junction opening on FLIP should prompt further diagnostic testing.
7. Clinicians may consider performing FLIP if the mechanism of persisting dysphagia in treated EoE is not apparent on high-quality upper endoscopy or histopathology.
8. Clinicians should not use FLIP findings to diagnose gastroesophageal reflux disease or to determine the necessity for antireflux intervention.
9. When available, clinicians should consider performing FLIP intraprocedurally during myotomy (per-oral endoscopic myotomy or laparoscopic Heller myotomy) to guide adequacy of LES disruption.
10. Clinicians may consider performing FLIP in the evaluation of persisting symptoms of esophageal obstruction (ie, dysphagia, esophageal-type regurgitation, and/or meal-related chest pain) after treatment of achalasia spectrum disorders.

**Technical points:** 8-cm catheter for EGJ metrics; 16-cm catheter adds esophageal body contractile response; key metrics = EGJ-DI (at 60 mL) and max EGJ diameter (at 70 mL). Intraoperative EGJ-DI <2–3 mm²/mm Hg may predict persisting symptoms; high EGJ-DI may associate with post-myotomy reflux. Contraindicated with actively bleeding varices.

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[flip-panometry]] — primary update; adds the 10 BPA on FLIP performance/indications and intraprocedural use.
- [[achalasia]], [[eosinophilic-esophagitis]], [[poem]], [[high-resolution-manometry]] — diagnostic interplay (incl. EGJ outflow obstruction).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Complements (does not replace) HRM/TBE; no consensus EGJ-DI thresholds after myotomy. Aligns with [[dallas-2025-flip-panometry]] Dallas consensus on protocol/interpretation.
