## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Shah SC, Wang AY, Wallace MB, Hwang JH. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Screening and Surveillance in Individuals at Increased Risk for Gastric Cancer in the United States: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2025;168:405–416.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.11.001)
- **Authors:** Shailja C. Shah, Andrew Y. Wang, Michael B. Wallace, Joo Ha Hwang
- **Year:** 2025 (received Sep 19 2024; accepted Nov 2 2024)
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2025;168:405–416
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.11.001](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.11.001)
- **Type:** AGA Clinical Practice Update (CPU) — Expert Review. 15 Best Practice Advice statements. **No formal ratings** — best practice advice drawn from literature review and expert opinion; no systematic review, no GRADE strength/quality ratings.

## Summary

First US-focused best-practice framework for **who to screen and how to survey** for noncardia intestinal-type gastric cancer (GC) in individuals at increased risk. Scope: primary prevention (Helicobacter pylori eradication) + secondary prevention (endoscopic screening/surveillance of premalignant conditions — atrophic gastritis [AG], gastric intestinal metaplasia [GIM], dysplasia). **Cardia GC is explicitly out of scope** (mirrors distal esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma epidemiology). Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer is out of scope for the clinical pathway (Figure 1 footnote).

Core framing: there are **no established US GC screening guidelines** and the evidence base is limited/indirect (mostly East Asian data), so guidance rests on epidemiology + expert opinion rather than direct RCT evidence. Endoscopy (not any noninvasive test) is the only currently acceptable screening modality in the US — simple age-based universal screening is not cost-effective. GC in the US is defined by **disparity**: >40% of the US population is non-White (2020 census); noncardia GC incidence is 2- to >10-fold higher in the 10 most populous non-White groups vs non-Hispanic White; Korean Americans ≥50 have up to 14.5-fold higher incidence; total GC incidence in Korean Americans (25.9/100,000) approaches combined colon+rectal incidence in non-Hispanic White Americans (29.8/100,000).

US 5-year GC survival is a dismal 32% (<25% diagnosed early); contrast Japan/South Korea where programmatic screening drove early-stage diagnosis to 60%–70% and survival >70% overall (95%–99% for early GC). A meta-analysis of 10 Asian observational studies (342,013 individuals) found endoscopic screening associated with a **42% reduction in GC mortality** (RR 0.58; 95% CI 0.48–0.70).

**Age of screening initiation:** not clearly established; **45 years may be an optimal age** — aligns with average-risk CRC screening initiation (allowing EGD at time of screening colonoscopy) and mirrors screening-eligible age in high-risk countries (South Korea ≥40, Japan 40–50). Individualize earlier for first-degree family history of GC (start 10 years earlier than youngest affected relative) and for hereditary syndromes.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice Statements (verbatim, complete):**

1. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 1:** There are identifiable high-risk groups in the United States who should be considered for GC screening. These include first-generation immigrants from high-incidence GC regions and possibly other non-White racial and ethnic groups, those with a family history of GC in a first-degree relative, and individuals with certain hereditary gastrointestinal polyposis or hereditary cancer syndromes.

2. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 2:** Endoscopy is the best test for screening or surveillance in individuals at increased risk for GC. Endoscopy enables direct visualization to endoscopically stage the mucosa and identify areas concerning for neoplasia, as well as enables biopsies for further histologic examination and mucosal staging. Both endoscopic and histologic staging are key for risk stratification and determining whether ongoing surveillance is indicated and at what interval.

3. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 3:** High-quality upper endoscopy for the detection of premalignant and malignant gastric lesions should include the use of a high-definition white-light endoscopy system with image enhancement, gastric mucosal cleansing, and insufflation to achieve optimal mucosal visualization, in addition to adequate visual inspection time, photodocumentation, and use of a systematic biopsy protocol for mucosal staging when appropriate.

4. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 4:** H pylori eradication is essential and serves as an adjunct to endoscopic screening and surveillance for primary and secondary prevention of GC. Opportunistic screening for H pylori infection should be considered in individuals deemed to be at increased risk for GC (refer to Best Practice Advice 1). Screening for H pylori infection in adult household members of individuals who test positive for H pylori (so-called "familial-based testing") should also be considered.

5. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 5:** In individuals with suspected gastric atrophy with or without intestinal metaplasia, gastric biopsies should be obtained according to a systematic protocol (eg, updated Sydney System) to enable histologic confirmation and staging. A minimum of 5 total biopsies should be obtained, with samples from the antrum/incisura and corpus placed in separately labeled jars (eg, jar 1, "antrum/incisura" and jar 2, "corpus"). Any suspicious areas should be described and biopsied separately.

6. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 6:** GIM and dysplasia are endoscopically detectable. However, these findings often go undiagnosed when endoscopists are unfamiliar with the characteristic visual features; accordingly, there is an unmet need for improved training, especially in the United States. Artificial intelligence tools appear promising for the detection of early gastric neoplasia in the adequately visualized stomach, but data are too preliminary to recommend routine use.

7. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 7:** Endoscopists should work with their local pathologists to achieve consensus for consistent documentation of histologic risk-stratification parameters when atrophic gastritis (AG) with or without metaplasia is diagnosed. At a minimum, the presence or absence of H pylori infection, severity of atrophy and/or metaplasia, and histologic subtyping of GIM, if applicable, should be documented to inform clinical decision making.

8. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 8:** If the index screening endoscopy performed in an individual at increased risk for GC (refer to Best Practice Advice 1) does not identify atrophy, GIM, or neoplasia, then the decision to continue screening should be based on that individual's risk factors and preferences. If the individual has a family history of GC or multiple risk factors for GC, then ongoing screening should be considered. The optimal screening intervals in such scenarios are not well defined.

9. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 9:** Endoscopists should ensure that all individuals with confirmed gastric atrophy with or without GIM undergo risk stratification. Individuals with severe atrophic gastritis and/or multifocal/incomplete GIM are likely to benefit from endoscopic surveillance, particularly if they have other risk factors for GC (eg, family history). Endoscopic surveillance should be considered every 3 years; however, intervals are not well defined and shorter intervals may be advisable in those with multiple risk factors, such as severe GIM that is anatomically extensive.

10. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 10:** Indefinite and low-grade dysplasia (LGD) can be difficult to reproducibly identify by endoscopy and accurately diagnose on histopathology. Accordingly, all dysplasia should be confirmed by an experienced GI pathologist, and clinicians should refer patients with visible or nonvisible dysplasia to an endoscopist or center with expertise in the diagnosis and management of gastric neoplasia. Individuals with indefinite or LGD who are infected with H pylori should be treated and have eradication confirmed, followed by repeat endoscopy and biopsies by an experienced endoscopist, as visual and histologic discernment may improve once inflammation subsides.

11. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 11:** Individuals with suspected high-grade dysplasia (HGD) or early GC should undergo endoscopic submucosal dissection with the goal of en bloc, R0 resection to enable accurate pathologic staging with curative intent. Eradication of active H pylori infection is essential, but should not delay endoscopic intervention. Endoscopic submucosal dissection should be performed at a center with endoscopic and pathologic expertise.

12. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 12:** Individuals with a history of successfully resected gastric dysplasia or cancer require ongoing endoscopic surveillance. Suggested surveillance intervals exist, but additional data are required to refine surveillance recommendations, particularly in the United States.

13. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 13:** Type I gastric carcinoids in individuals with atrophic gastritis are typically indolent, especially if <1 cm. Endoscopists may consider resecting gastric carcinoids <1 cm and should endoscopically resect lesions measuring 1–2 cm. Individuals with type I gastric carcinoids >2 cm should undergo cross-sectional imaging and be referred for surgical resection, given the risk of metastasis. Individuals with type I gastric carcinoids should undergo surveillance, but the intervals are not well defined.

14. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 14:** In general, only individuals who are fit for endoscopic or potentially surgical treatment should be screened for GC and continued surveillance of premalignant gastric conditions. If a person is no longer fit for endoscopic or surgical treatment, then screening and surveillance should be stopped.

15. **BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 15:** To achieve health equity, a personalized approach should be taken to assess an individual's risk for GC to determine whether screening and surveillance should be pursued. In conjunction, modifiable risk factors for GC should be distinctly addressed, as most of these risk factors disproportionately impact people at high risk for GC and represent health care disparities.

**Surveillance/management intervals (Figure 1 clinical pathway — for individuals who have undergone high-quality EGD with systematic biopsies + treatment/confirmation of active H pylori):**

| Index finding | Management |
|---|---|
| Absence of AG, GIM, or neoplasia — WITH family history of GC (1° relative) and/or persistent H pylori despite eradication attempts | Screening EGD every **3–5 years** |
| Absence of AG, GIM, or neoplasia — WITHOUT those factors | Further EGDs for GC screening **not advised** |
| Mild AG and/or focal, complete-type GIM | Same branch as above (screen q3–5y if family history / persistent H pylori; otherwise not advised) |
| Moderate to severe AG and/or multifocal or incomplete-type GIM (particularly if other GC risk factors exist) | Surveillance EGD every **3 years** (more frequent could be considered if multiple other GC risk factors present) |
| Visible or nonvisible dysplasia / early GC (EGC) | Confirmation by GI pathologist + referral to center with endoscopic/pathologic expertise (ESD). IND/LGD → repeat EGD in **6 months**; HGD/EGC → repeat EGD **as soon as possible** |

**After second-look confirms residual NONvisible dysplasia (then surveillance EGD):**

| Finding | Interval |
|---|---|
| IND (indefinite for dysplasia) | EGD in **1 year** (12 months) |
| LGD | EGD in **6–12 months** |
| HGD | EGD in **3 months** |
| Nonvisible GC | Multidisciplinary discussion; **consider surgery** |

- If dysplasia or EGC is endoscopically visualized → **en bloc endoscopic resection** (typically ESD; in select scenarios — lesions <1 cm or confirmed IND histology — EMR may be considered). Refer to AGA CPU on ESD for post-curative-ESD surveillance intervals.

**Second-look ("rescue") endoscopy for nonvisible dysplasia (text):** IEE second-look (virtual/dye chromoendoscopy) detects focal neoplasia in ~90% of patients. Nonvisible IND/LGD → repeat high-quality EGD with IEE within **6 months** (ideally after H pylori eradicated). Nonvisible HGD → second-look **as soon as possible** (high risk of synchronous cancer). If second-look again confirms nonvisible dysplasia → repeat in **3 months (HGD), 6–12 months (LGD), 12 months (IND)**.

**High-risk groups / risk factors (Table 1 — personalized screening among individuals ≥45):**

- Early-generation immigrants from moderate-to-high incidence GC regions (GC incidence ≥10–12 per 100,000; includes Eastern Europe, Andean Latin America, East Asia)
- Family history of GC in a first-degree relative (start 10 years earlier than the youngest affected relative)
- Non-White racial/ethnic groups with established moderate-to-high incidence GC
- Personal history of chronic H pylori infection **and** ≥1 of: history of regularly smoking tobacco (>20 pack-years); chronic high-salt diet / red, processed meats and foods; living under persistent poverty in the US (≥20% of residents below federal poverty level over a 4-decade period)
- Certain hereditary GI polyposis syndromes and hereditary cancer syndromes (familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers, juvenile polyposis, MUTYH-associated polyposis, gastric adenocarcinoma and proximal polyposis of the stomach; Lynch syndrome, hereditary breast/ovarian cancer, Li-Fraumeni)

**H pylori (primary prevention):**

- Most common infectious carcinogen worldwide; responsible for ~90% of global GC burden
- Non-US RCT meta-analysis: eradication → **46% reduction in GC incidence** (RR 0.54; NNT 72) and **39% reduction in GC mortality** (RR 0.61; NNT 135)
- **All adults** diagnosed with H pylori warrant eradication, irrespective of symptoms, barring contraindications/limited life expectancy. Confirm eradication in all people ≥4 weeks after treatment course.
- **Familial-based testing:** whole-family test-and-treat had 3-fold higher eradication success (OR 2.93) and ~70% lower recurrence (OR 0.3) vs single-patient treatment
- Taipei Global Consensus suggests screening H pylori between ages 20 and 40 for primary GC prevention (optimal age for diverse US population not established)
- H pylori eradication is an adjunct, not stand-alone — individuals with more advanced histologic changes remain at neoplastic risk even after eradication and should still be considered for endoscopic screening/surveillance

**High-quality endoscopy specifics (BPA 3 text):**

- Endoscopic miss rate for early GC is consistently ~10%, higher among inexperienced endoscopists
- Components: HD white-light + image enhancement (e.g., narrow-band imaging, linked color imaging), mucosal cleansing, insufflation for complete visualization, adequate inspection time, photodocumentation, systematic biopsy protocol when appropriate
- NBI/LCI without magnification: sensitivity/specificity for GIM exceeding 85%–90%

**Biopsy protocol (BPA 5 text):** Updated Sydney System — minimum 5 total biopsies; antrum/incisura and corpus in ≥2 separately labeled jars; suspicious areas described and biopsied separately.

**Type I gastric carcinoids / NETs (BPA 13 text):**

- Type I gNETs account for 70%–80% of all gNETs; typically small (<1 cm), benign, low mitotic/Ki67 indices; arise in corpus atrophy → hypergastrinemia (parietal cell loss–mediated achlorhydria)
- Serum gastrin (elevated vs normal), surrounding mucosa histology, anatomic location, and focality determine type (I/II/III)
- <1 cm: may consider resecting. 1–2 cm: endoscopically resect (by endoscopist with resection expertise; EUS for larger). >2 cm or unfavorable histology (WHO grade ≥II): risk of metastasis → EUS + cross-sectional imaging + multidisciplinary tumor board; surgical resection if submucosa/LN invasion. Type II (Zollinger-Ellison) and type III gNETs out of scope.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates the new concept page [[gastric-cancer-screening]] — the who/how/when framework for GC screening & surveillance, tying together AG, GIM, and dysplasia intervals.
- Third major US guidance on this Correa-cascade cluster alongside [[aga-2020-gastric-intestinal-metaplasia]], [[aga-2021-atrophic-gastritis]], and [[acg-2025-gastric-premalignant]] — this CPU is the **screening/case-finding** framework (who enters surveillance at all), whereas the others focus on managing an established lesion.
- Directly relevant to [[gastric-intestinal-metaplasia]], [[atrophic-gastritis]], [[gastric-premalignant-conditions]], [[helicobacter-pylori-infection]], [[gastric-adenocarcinoma]], and [[upper-endoscopy]].
- Notable **shift vs AGA 2020 GIM:** AGA 2020 recommended *against* routine GIM surveillance (favoring shared decision-making); this 2025 CPU explicitly endorses surveillance q3y for individuals with confirmed AG/GIM who are risk-stratified as high-risk (severe AG and/or multifocal/incomplete GIM), aligning AGA more closely with ACG 2025 GPMC and ESGE.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **No formal ratings** — best practice advice only; no GRADE strength/quality. Evidence is largely indirect (East Asian observational/RCT data extrapolated to the diverse US population).
- **Optimal screening initiation age not established** for the diverse US population (45 proposed but not evidence-established); optimal H pylori screening age for US likewise unknown.
- **Intervals "not well defined"** is a recurring caveat: screening intervals when index EGD is normal but risk factors present (BPA 8); surveillance <3y for multiple risk factors / extensive severe GIM (BPA 9); post-resection surveillance (BPA 12); type I carcinoid surveillance (BPA 13) — all stated as not well defined.
- **AI tools** for early gastric neoplasia detection: promising but data too preliminary for routine use (BPA 6).
- **Biennial EGD** (South Korea/Japan population strategy) is being re-evaluated in the context of declining H pylori prevalence; a risk-stratified approach is now favored over uniform biennial screening.
- **Convergence vs prior AGA 2020 GIM stance** on surveillance (see Relevance) — the wiki's GIM/GPMC pages should note this CPU moves AGA toward endorsing risk-stratified surveillance.

# AGA Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Gastroparesis (2025)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Staller K, Parkman HP, Greer KB, Leiman DA, et al. AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Gastroparesis. *Gastroenterology* 2025;169:828–861.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.004)
- **Authors:** Staller K, Parkman HP, Greer KB, Leiman DA, et al.
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal:** Gastroenterology (AGA Clinical Practice Guideline)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.004](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.08.004)
- **Type:** GRADE-based guideline

---

## Summary

This AGA guideline standardizes diagnosis and pharmacologic/procedural management of [[gastroparesis]]. It favors a properly performed **4-hour gastric emptying scintigraphy**, endorses **metoclopramide** and **erythromycin** as prokinetics, and issues a striking series of *against* recommendations for many commonly used drugs and refractory-disease procedures owing to weak evidence. Diagnostic overlap with [[dyspepsia]] and [[disorders-of-gut-brain-interaction]] is emphasized — rule out alternative/coexisting causes first, especially when pain predominates.

---

## Key Recommendations

**Diagnosis:**
- Use a **4-hour** gastric emptying study rather than a 2-hour (or shorter) study; some patients normal at 2 h are reclassified as delayed at 4 h. Avoid confounders (hyperglycemia, opioids) during testing.

**Pharmacologic (suggests *using*):**
- **Metoclopramide** (conditional).
- **Erythromycin** (conditional).

**Pharmacologic (suggests *against* as first-line):**
- **Domperidone**, **[[prucalopride]]**, **aprepitant**, **nortriptyline**, **buspirone**, and **cannabidiol (CBD)** — the latter except in a clinical trial.

**Refractory disease (suggests *against* routine use):**
- **Gastric per-oral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM)**, **gastric electrical stimulation (GES)**, **intrapyloric botulinum toxin**, and routine initial **surgical pyloromyotomy/pyloroplasty**.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Reaffirms metoclopramide and erythromycin as the evidence-supported prokinetics while explicitly discouraging many off-label drugs and pyloric/stimulation procedures as routine therapy. Reinforces rigorous 4-hour scintigraphy and exclusion of mimics within the [[dyspepsia]] workup. The myotomy theme connects technically to [[poem]] (achalasia) though the guideline does not endorse its gastric analogue routinely.

---

## Summary

This AGA guideline frames hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) risk in patients starting immunosuppressive/immunomodulatory therapy as a **risk-stratified** decision between **antiviral prophylaxis** and **monitoring alone**. Risk depends on serologic status (HBsAg-positive vs anti-HBc–positive/HBsAg-negative) and the immunosuppressive agent (e.g., **rituximab** and B-cell–depleting agents confer the highest risk). Builds on baseline screening and links conceptually to [[chronic-hepatitis-b]] management.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Rec 1 (Strong):** For **high-risk** patients (anticipated HBVr **>10%**), use **antiviral prophylaxis** over monitoring alone — start *before* immunosuppression begins.
- **Rec 2 (Conditional):** For **moderate-risk** (HBVr **1–10%**), the AGA *suggests* antiviral prophylaxis over monitoring alone; shared decision-making, as some patients may reasonably choose monitoring.
- **Rec 3 (Conditional):** For **low-risk** (HBVr **<1%**), the AGA *suggests* **monitoring alone** over routine prophylaxis.
- **Rec 4 (Strong):** For all at-risk individuals, **test for hepatitis B** (HBsAg, anti-HBc, ± anti-HBs) before immunosuppression.

**Risk thresholds:** low <1%, moderate 1–10%, high >10% — determined jointly by serology and the immunosuppressive regimen.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Test-before-treat is universal; prophylaxis is mandatory in high-risk (especially HBsAg-positive and/or anti-HBc–positive patients receiving rituximab/anti-CD20, anthracyclines, high-dose steroids). Practical anchor for hepatology consults on patients starting chemotherapy, biologics, or transplant immunosuppression. Connects to monitoring via [[abnormal-liver-chemistries]] and to underlying [[chronic-hepatitis-b]].

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Aziz Q, Harris LA, Goodman BP, Simrén M, Shin A. AGA Clinical Practice Update on GI Manifestations and Autonomic or Immune Dysfunction in Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome: Expert Review. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2025;23(8):1291–1302.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2025.02.015)
- **Authors:** Qasim Aziz, Lucinda A. Harris, Brent P. Goodman, Magnus Simrén, Andrea Shin
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2025.02.015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2025.02.015)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — expert review, Best Practice Advice)

## Summary

AGA Clinical Practice Update describing the evaluation and management of GI symptoms in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSDs) and their frequently coexisting conditions: postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). hEDS is the most common EDS subtype (80–90% of EDS) and a heritable connective tissue disorder defined by joint hypermobility, tissue fragility, and musculoskeletal symptoms; GI symptoms are highly prevalent and overlap with disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). 16 Best Practice Advice statements, no formal evidence grading.

The mechanistic link between hEDS/HSDs, POTS, and MCAS is theoretical and evolving (altered collagen/extracellular-matrix stiffness, mast-cell–mediated visceral sensitization, autonomic dysfunction, autoimmunity, post-infectious dysautonomia including post-COVID). The update stresses that POTS/MCAS testing should be targeted to clinical presentation, not applied universally. Gastroenterologists seeing DGBI patients should screen for joint hypermobility with the Beighton score and apply the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria (or refer). GI evaluation should otherwise mirror the general-population DGBI approach (positive symptom-based diagnosis, limited noninvasive testing), with select extras: earlier celiac testing, anorectal manometry/balloon expulsion/defecography for evacuation symptoms (high pelvic floor dysfunction prevalence, especially rectal hyposensitivity), and earlier gastric motor testing in those with coexisting POTS (abnormal gastric emptying may be more common).

Management is largely supportive, symptom-focused, and multidisciplinary, following general DGBI/motility principles plus targeted treatment of POTS (fluid/salt, exercise, compression garments, and pharmacotherapy — fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta-blockers) and MCAS (H1/H2 antagonists and mast-cell stabilizers, trigger avoidance). Opioids should be avoided. Diet (gastroparesis/small-particle diet for upper-GI–predominant symptoms; low-FODMAP or gluten/dairy-free for lower-GI; low-histamine) is used with nutritional counseling to avoid restrictive eating.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Verbatim Best Practice Advice statements (no evidence grade per source):**

1. Clinicians should be aware of the observed associations between hEDS or HSDs and POTS and/or MCAS and their overlapping GI manifestations; while theoretical explanations exist, experimental evidence of the biological mechanisms that explain relationships is limited and evolving.
2. Testing for POTS/MCAS should be targeted to patients presenting with clinical manifestations of POTS/MCAS, but universal testing for POTS/MCAS in all patients with hEDS/HSDs is not supported by the current evidence.
3. Gastroenterologists seeing patients with DGBI should inquire about joint hypermobility and strongly consider incorporating the Beighton score for assessing joint hypermobility into their practice as a screening tool; if the screen is positive, gastroenterologists may consider applying 2017 diagnostic criteria to diagnose hEDS or offer appropriate referral to a specialist where resources are available.
4. Testing for POTS through postural vital signs (eg, symptomatic increase in heart rate of 30 beats/min or more with 10 minutes of standing during an active stand or head-up tilt table test in the absence of orthostasis) and referral to specialty practices (eg, cardiology or neurology) for autonomic testing should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and refractory GI symptoms who also report orthostatic intolerance after exclusion of medication side effects and appropriate lifestyle or behavioral modifications (eg, adequate hydration and physical exercise) have been attempted, but is not required for all patients with hEDS/HSDs who report GI symptoms alone.
5. In patients presenting to gastroenterology providers, testing for mast cell disorders including MCAS should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and DGBI who also present with episodic symptoms that suggest a more generalized mast cell disorder (eg, visceral and somatic pain, pruritus, flushing, sweating, urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, tachycardia, abdominal cramping, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, urogynecological and neurological complaints) involving 2 or more physiological systems (eg, cutaneous, GI, cardiac, respiratory, and neuropsychiatric), but current data do not support the use of these tests for routine evaluation of GI symptoms in all patients with hEDS/HSDs without clinical or laboratory evidence of a primary or secondary mast cell disorder.
6. If MCAS is suspected, diagnostic testing with serum tryptase levels collected at baseline and 1–4 hours following symptom flares may be considered by the gastroenterologist; increases of 20% above baseline plus 2 ng/mL are necessary to demonstrate evidence of mast cell activation.
7. If a diagnosis of MCAS is supported through clinical and/or laboratory features, patients should be referred to an allergy specialist or mast cell disease research center where additional testing (eg, urinary N-methylhistamine, leukotriene E4, 11β-prostaglandin F2) may be performed.
8. Diagnostic evaluation of GI symptoms consistent with DGBI in patients with hEDS/HSDs and comorbid POTS and/or MCAS should follow a similar approach to the evaluation of DGBI as in the general population including the use of a positive symptom-based diagnostic strategy and limited noninvasive testing.
9. Testing for celiac disease may be considered earlier in the diagnostic evaluation of patients with hEDS/HSDs who report a variety of GI symptoms and not only limited to those with diarrhea. There is insufficient research to support routine testing for disaccharidase deficiencies or other diet-mediated mechanisms as causes of GI symptoms in hEDS/HSDs.
10. Diagnostic testing for functional defecation disorders with anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion test, or defecography should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and lower GI symptoms such as incomplete evacuation, given the high prevalence of pelvic floor dysfunction, especially rectal hyposensitivity, in this population.
11. In patients with hEDS/HSDs and comorbid POTS who report chronic upper GI symptoms, timely diagnostic testing of gastric motor functions (eg, measurement of gastric emptying and/or accommodation) should be considered after appropriate exclusion of anatomical and structural diseases, as abnormal gastric emptying may be more common than in the general population.
12. Medical management of GI symptoms in hEDS/HSDs and POTS/MCAS should focus on treating the most prominent GI symptoms and abnormal GI function test results. In addition to general DGBIs and GI motility disorder treatment, management should also include treating any symptoms attributable to POTS and/or MCAS.
13. Treatment of POTS may include increasing fluid and salt intake, exercise training, and use of compression garments. Special pharmacological treatments for volume expansion, heart rate control, and vasoconstriction with integrated care from multiple specialties (eg, cardiology, neurology) should be considered in patients who do not respond to conservative lifestyle measures.
14. When MCAS is suspected, patients can benefit from treatment with histamine receptor antagonists and/or mast cell stabilizers, in addition to avoiding triggers such as certain foods, alcohol, strong smells, temperature changes, mechanical stimuli (eg, friction), emotional distress (eg, pollen, mold), or specific medications (eg, opioids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, iodinated contrast).
15. Besides general nutritional support, special diets including a gastroparesis diet (ie, small particle diet) and various elimination diets (eg, low fermentable carbohydrates, gluten- or dairy-free, low-histamine diets) can be considered for improving GI symptoms. Dietary interventions should be delivered with appropriate nutritional counseling or guidance to avoid the pitfalls of restrictive eating.
16. Management of chronic GI symptoms in patients with hEDS/HSDs who do not exhibit symptoms consistent with POTS or MCAS should align with existing approaches to management of DGBI and GI motility disorders in the general population, including integrated multidisciplinary care involving multiple specialties, where appropriate (eg, cardiology, rheumatology, dietician, psychology).

**Supporting data / definitions:**
- hEDS = 80–90% of all EDS; part of broader HSD spectrum. 2017 international consensus criteria: (1) generalized hypermobility by Beighton score; (2) ≥2 of connective-tissue features / family history / musculoskeletal complications; (3) absence of unusual skin fragility (exclude other EDS/connective tissue/joint disorders).
- POTS = HR increase ≥30 bpm within 10 min of upright posture (≥40 bpm in adolescents 12–19) without orthostatic hypotension; symptoms ≥6 months. GI symptoms (nausea, pain, early satiety) most predictive of abnormal GI motility.
- MCAS classification: primary (clonal, CD25+/KIT D816V), secondary (IgE-mediated/other), idiopathic. Activation = serum tryptase rise of baseline +20% + 2 ng/mL collected 1–4 h post-flare.
- Association data: in 139 MCAS patients with refractory GI symptoms — 23.7% had EDS, 25.2% POTS, 15.1% both; 37.5% of hEDS/HSD patients reported POTS (survey, n=616); >60% of hEDS/HSDs had ≥1 GI symptom (those with POTS more likely to have fibromyalgia, IBS, GERD, dysmotility). Up to 40% of POTS patients self-report preceding viral URI/GI infection; acute and long COVID-19 associated with POTS.
- Endoscopy: complication rates (eg, perforation) NOT increased in hEDS/HSDs except vascular EDS.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Creates the disease-script page [[hypermobile-ehlers-danlos-syndrome]] (1-disease-scripts/other).
- Connects to [[disorders-of-gut-brain-interaction]] (DGBI overlap, shared evaluation/management framework), [[gastroparesis]] (gastric emptying testing in coexisting POTS; gastroparesis/small-particle diet), [[celiac-disease]] (earlier serologic testing), [[irritable-bowel-syndrome]] (IBS overlap; low-FODMAP diet), and [[anorectal-manometry]] (functional defecation disorder testing).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No direct contradictions with existing wiki content (net-new disease entity). POTS, MCAS, and dysautonomia do not yet have dedicated wiki pages (referenced as plain text on the new disease script).
- Mechanistic links between hEDS/HSDs, POTS, and MCAS are explicitly described as theoretical and evolving; most management is expert opinion with few clinical trials.

- **Authors:** Tatyana Kushner, Stanley M. Cohen, Joseph Ahn, Robert J. Wong
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.07.037](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.07.037)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Commentary)

## Summary
AGA Commentary on hepatitis delta virus (HDV) — a defective RNA virus that replicates only in the presence of HBV, occurring as coinfection or superinfection in chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Concurrent HDV markedly increases the risk of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and liver-related mortality versus HBV monoinfection. The update emphasizes that HDV is underdiagnosed: testing rates among people with CHB are low (often <11%) and the diagnostic cascade (reflexing anti-HDV–positive patients to HDV RNA) frequently breaks down. The authors **suggest universal HDV screening of all patients with HBV** (aligning with EASL/APASL/WHO), using **anti-HDV antibody as the initial test and HDV RNA to confirm viremia**; double-reflex laboratory testing dramatically improves completion. All HDV patients should undergo noninvasive fibrosis/cirrhosis assessment (FIB-4, VCTE) and HCC surveillance. The only US-available therapy is **pegylated interferon-α** (SVR ~23%–57%, but ~50% relapse); **bulevirtide** (entry inhibitor) is EMA-approved and available in the US only via an expanded-access program, with several agents (BJT-778, tobevibart+elebsiran, lonafarnib) in trials.

## Key Findings / Claims
- **Virology/risk:** HDV requires HBV (HBsAg) to replicate; coinfection (acute, with HBV) vs superinfection (on existing CHB). HDV accelerates progression to cirrhosis, HCC, and liver-related death; ~50%–70% of anti-HDV–positive patients have detectable HDV RNA (active infection).
- **Who to screen:** Authors **suggest universal anti-HDV screening of all HBsAg/HBV patients** (EASL, APASL, WHO 2024 align; one-time universal testing is cost-effective). Retest those with ongoing risk behaviors, high-prevalence-area residence, or new ALT elevation/decompensation.
- **Testing cascade:** **anti-HDV Ab first → if positive, HDV RNA** to confirm viremia. Automated reflex anti-HDV on HBsAg-positive samples raised testing from 8% → 93%; **double reflex** (anti-HDV on all HBsAg+, HDV RNA on all anti-HDV+) should be implemented. HDV antigen and anti-HDV IgM are **not** advised (limited availability/sensitivity/specificity). US HDV RNA testing is send-out (Quest, ARUP, LabCorp, CDC); assay variability remains a limitation.
- **Staging/monitoring:** Assess for cirrhosis with noninvasive testing — **VCTE** AUROC 0.90 (vs FIB-4 0.88, APRI 0.83); ≥14.0 kPa cutoff (sens 0.78, spec 0.86, NPV 0.93). FIB-4 + VCTE for fibrosis. **HCC surveillance for all HDV patients.**
- **Current treatment — peg-IFN-α-2a/2b** (only US-available): 48-week SVR 23%–57%; relapse ~50% even after prolonged therapy (up to 9 years later); responders have improved survival/fewer liver-related events. **Contraindicated in advanced liver disease** and major extrahepatic disease; significant neuropsychiatric/hematologic toxicity. Per AASLD HBV guidance, peg-IFN-α weekly ×12 months for elevated HDV RNA + elevated ALT; add a **nucleos(t)ide analogue** if HBV DNA elevated (NAs lack direct anti-HDV activity).
- **Emerging treatment — bulevirtide** (sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide / entry inhibitor, daily SC): MYR-301 phase 3 — 45%–48% on-treatment response (≥2-log HDV RNA decline and/or ALT normalization) at 48 wk; MYR-204 combination with peg-IFN raised post-treatment undetectable HDV RNA to 46% (vs 12% monotherapy). EMA-approved (2 mg) since 2020; in the US available only via Gilead **expanded-access program** (NCT06780579) for compensated cirrhosis. Other trial agents: **BJT-778 (brelovitug)** anti-HBsAg mAb, **tobevibart + elebsiran** (SOLSTICE/ECLIPSE), **lonafarnib** (farnesyltransferase inhibitor), peg-IFN-λ (discontinued), nucleic acid polymers.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Creates [[hepatitis-d]] disease script (HDV).
- Updates [[chronic-hepatitis-b]] — universal HDV screening of HBV patients; link to HDV page.
- Cross-links: [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]], [[liver-transplantation]], [[nutrition-in-liver-disease]].

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Goes **beyond** prior AASLD risk-based HDV testing by suggesting **universal** anti-HDV screening of all HBV patients (consistent with EASL/APASL/WHO); the authors note US guidelines may be updated to reflect this. Surfaced on the [[hepatitis-d]] and [[chronic-hepatitis-b]] pages.

- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Commentary; narrative, no formal Best Practice Advice statements)

## Summary

Practical commentary on submucosal lifting (injection) agents for endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD/POEM). Submucosal injection creates a cushion separating the lesion from the muscularis propria (MP); adding a blue contrast agent demarcates margins and helps detect MP injury during EMR.

## Key Findings / Claims (narrative)

- **Purpose:** cushion separates lesion from MP; contrast (**indigo carmine** or **methylene blue**) demarcates lesion margins and signals MP injury.
- **Agent choice:** "homemade" normal saline ± contrast remains acceptable; saline dissipates quickly, prompting viscous/FDA-approved agents (the first FDA-approved agent and later proprietary gels). In a non-inferiority context, saline was non-inferior to other injection-based resection methods for relevant outcomes.
- **Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs):** minimal submucosal fibrosis — lift adequately with **any** solution, including saline.
- **ESD requires submucosal injection regardless of agent**; injecting into the lesion is avoided during ESD to reduce obscuring submucosal bleeding. **POEM** typically uses normal saline.
- **Adjuncts:** dilute **epinephrine** added for cold EMR and EMR with electrocautery to reduce bleeding/improve visualization.
- **Technique:** prime the needle catheter (avoid air injection); central injection domes the lesion over submucosal fluid; **dynamic injection** (moving the needle within the submucosa) shapes the mound and maximizes separation from MP; larger lesions resected by serial inject-and-snare.
- Papillectomy generally does not require injection (saline with contrast may reassure against MP involvement).

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[polypectomy-emr]] — adds lifting-agent selection and injection technique.
- [[endoscopic-submucosal-dissection]] — injection mandatory for ESD; avoid intralesional injection.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Commentary (no formal ratings). No clear superiority of proprietary agents over saline for routine EMR of most lesions; agent choice driven by lesion size/fibrosis, predicted histology, and endoscopist preference.

# AGA 2025 Clinical Practice Update on Nonampullary Duodenal Lesions

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Bourke MJ, Lo SK, Buerlein RCD, Das KK. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Nonampullary Duodenal Lesions: Expert Review. *Gastroenterology* 2025;168(1):169–175. doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.008.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.008)
- **Authors:** Michael J. Bourke, Simon K. Lo, Ross C. D. Buerlein, Koushik K. Das
- **Year:** 2025 (received May 27, 2024; accepted October 7, 2024)
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastroenterology* 2025;168(1):169–175 (AGA Institute — Clinical Practice Update, Expert Review)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.008](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.008)
- **Type:** AGA Institute Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review (Best Practice Advice statements; **no formal evidence/strength ratings** — systematic review not performed; drawn from literature review + expert opinion)

---

## Summary

Nonampullary duodenal polyps are found in up to **5% of upper endoscopies** — vast majority incidental in asymptomatic patients. Most are benign; **adenomas account for 10%–20%** of these lesions. Duodenal adenomas (DAs) arise sporadically (seen in up to **0.5%** of patients) or with a genetic condition ([[familial-adenomatous-polyposis|FAP]] or *MUTYH*-associated polyposis); **>90% of FAP patients** eventually develop 1 or many DAs. Most DAs contain only low-grade dysplasia, but **up to 20% progress to high-grade dysplasia and ~5% to cancer**, so endoscopic resection is generally recommended.

The Update describes how patients should be **evaluated and risk-stratified**, best approaches to **endoscopic resection and surveillance**, and **management of complications**. International guidelines recommend all DAs be considered for endoscopic resection, but this carries a **~15% adverse-event rate** (predominantly bleeding and perforation) with substantial local recurrence on surveillance. Because the time course to malignant transformation is prolonged and resection morbidity is high, patient comorbidities and anticipated longevity must be weighed. Technique is individualized: **piecemeal cold-snare resection** for flat lesions <20 mm (minimal recurrence, less bleeding); **conventional hot-snare EMR + thermal ablation of the margin** for lesions >20 mm or with bulky Paris Is components. Postprocedural bleeding (usually first 48 h, risk proportional to size, >25% for lesions >3 cm) and perforation are the major complications. Initial surveillance at **6 months**. FAP duodenal disease is managed by **Spiegelman staging**.

---

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice statements (verbatim, complete):**

1. Non-neoplastic duodenal lesions (eg, metaplastic foveolar epithelium and gastric heterotopia) may mimic neoplastic adenomatous pathology. Careful optical evaluation and pathologic correlation may be necessary to exclude dysplasia. Nondysplastic lesions do not require endoscopic resection unless they are symptomatic or bleeding.

2. Ideal duodenal endoscopic inspection includes identification of the major and minor papilla with photodocumentation to ensure no involvement by the lesion. Adding a clear distal attachment device to a forward-viewing gastroscope improves visualization of the papilla and the medial wall. A side-viewing duodenoscope should be used when the major and minor papilla are not visible with the gastroscope and for most lesions on the medial wall of the duodenum within 5 cm of the ampulla.

3. All duodenal polyps should be described according to their size, Paris morphology, suspected histologic layer of origin (mucosal lesion or subepithelial lesion), duodenal location (D1–4) and orientation (anterior, posterior, medial, or lateral wall), and proximity/relationship to the major papilla to facilitate therapeutic planning and subsequent surveillance.

4. Given the high frequency of concomitant colonic adenomas in patients with duodenal adenomas, on identification of a duodenal adenoma, a colonoscopy should be performed if a high-quality examination has not been performed in the last 3 years.

5. Routine small bowel investigation (ie, capsule endoscopy) is not advised in patients with sporadic and nonsporadic duodenal adenomas. Periodic small bowel inspection with capsule endoscopy may be of benefit in patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

6. Definitive treatment of duodenal adenomas by endoscopic resection is less morbid, resource-intensive, and expensive than surgery and is therefore the preferred treatment option.

7. Due to the risk of malignant transformation, all sporadic duodenal adenomas should be considered for endoscopic resection. However, in comparison with colonic adenomas, the time course to malignant transformation may be much prolonged, and the risk of resection-related morbidity much greater. Therefore, the comorbidities and anticipated longevity of the patient must be carefully factored into the decision-making process.

8. The approach to endoscopic duodenal resection (ie, hot vs cold and conventional vs underwater endoscopic mucosal resection) should be individualized to reduce bleeding risk, based on lesion size, morphology, patient comorbidities, and endoscopic comfort level with specific techniques. Piecemeal cold snare resection for flat duodenal adenomas mitigates postprocedural bleeding risk and, for lesions <20 mm, is effective and carries a minimal risk of recurrence. In patients with comorbidities with flat nonbulky lesions measuring <20 mm, cold snare resection can be considered.

9. Currently, duodenal adenomas >20 mm or with large Paris subtype Is components should be removed by conventional hot snare endoscopic mucosal resection. Thermal ablation of the post–endoscopic mucosal resection margin to mitigate the risk of recurrence to <2%–5% is safe and effective and should be considered.

10. Endoscopists performing duodenal polyp resection should be aware of the increased risk of postprocedural bleeding (compared with elsewhere in the gastrointestinal tract), which usually occurs in the first 48 hours after the procedure, with the risk proportional to the lesion size. For lesions >3 cm, bleeding risk is >25% and may be life-threatening and associated with hemodynamic compromise; however, after resuscitation, endoscopic hemostasis is generally effective.

11. Evaluation of the postpolypectomy/endoscopic mucosal resection defect is critical to identify concerns for postprocedural duodenal perforation, which, if unrecognized and left untreated, may be life-threatening and often mandates surgery.

12. Initial endoscopic surveillance for a completely resected duodenal adenoma should be undertaken at an interval of 6 months. Although usually diminutive, recurrence is often scarred and not amenable to conventional snare resection and may require avulsion techniques to achieve cure.

13. Nonampullary duodenal adenomas associated with familial adenomatous polyposis should be considered for endoscopic resection based on size (≥1 cm), morphologic characteristics, advanced histology (ie, high-grade dysplasia), and/or based on Spiegelman criteria.

**Supporting quantitative data (from the narrative):**

- **Prevalence/malignant potential:** nonampullary duodenal polyps in up to 5% of upper endoscopies; adenomas = 10%–20% of these. Sporadic DAs in up to 0.5% of patients. FAP: >90% eventually develop DAs. Most DAs low-grade dysplasia; up to 20% → HGD, ~5% → cancer. Covert adenocarcinoma within a DA is rare (≤1%).
- **Progression (BPA 7):** in 1 study, 20.9% (9 of 43) of incidental adenomas progressed to HGD at 6 months, incl. 4.7% (n=2) to carcinoma in situ; lesions initially ≥20 mm and proximal to the ampulla were associated with histologic progression.
- **Concomitant colonic neoplasia (BPA 4):** colonic neoplasia risk 2–7-fold greater than general population. In a prospective study: colonic polyps 61% (DA group) vs 37% (controls); advanced colonic adenomas (HGD, >10 mm, or villous) 18% vs 5%. Small-bowel polyp risk in DA patients is negligible — capsule not needed for screening, but colonoscopy is mandatory.
- **Endoscopic vs surgical resection (BPA 6):** in a modeling study of 102 large DAs (mean 40 mm), endoscopic resection had less morbidity (18% vs 31%), shorter hospital stay (median 1 vs 4.75 days), and was less costly (mean $11,093 vs $19,358).
- **Recurrence — conventional hot-snare EMR:** 10%–15% at 6 months, size-dependent. **Thermal ablation of the post-EMR margin (EMR-T):** recurrence 1 of 49 (2.3%) vs 19 of 108 (17.6%) with conventional EMR (median lesion 30 mm).
- **Underwater EMR** (lesions ≤20 mm): recurrence 2%–3%, perforation <1%, delayed bleeding <2%.
- **Cold-snare EMR (CS-EMR)** of large DAs (median 30 mm, n=50) vs EMR-T: lower intraprocedural bleeding (2.0% vs 37%) and postpolypectomy bleeding (4.0% vs 16.7%); 2 immediate perforations (4.0%) closed with clips; but **higher recurrence at 6 months (24.4% vs 2.3%)** — recurrence related to primary-lesion size, so CS most attractive for lesions <15 mm, especially with comorbidities.
- **Bleeding (BPA 10):** duodenal postprocedural bleeding usually in first 48 h, proportional to size; 25% for lesions ≥30 mm; >25% and potentially life-threatening for lesions >3 cm.
- **Perforation:** hot-snare excision carries ~1% perforation risk; ESD associated with high perforation rates (thin duodenal muscularis propria) with no therapeutic advantage over piecemeal EMR; clip closure of the EMR defect is generally only effective for defects ≤15 mm.
- **Periprocedural care (BPA 11):** high-risk patients (multiple comorbidities, anticoagulation, bulky lesions ≥30 mm, significant intraprocedural bleeding, possible/closed perforation) → admit for observation. Clear-liquid diet overnight, advance as tolerated; twice-daily PPI for 6–8 weeks; individualize resumption of anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy — hold ≥48 h after resection if acceptable. Insufficient data to support prophylactic hemostatic spray/topical agents.
- **Surveillance (BPA 12):** initial at 6 months; after a negative 6-month exam, general practice is to repeat at 1 year and, if clear, annually for 2–3 years (few data on optimal timing).
- **Non-neoplastic / other entities:** non-neoplastic lesions (metaplastic foveolar epithelium, gastric heterotopia, inflammatory/pseudopolyps) most frequent in the duodenal bulb. **Brunner gland hamartomas** — uncommon, benign, often solitary pedunculated, up to 2–5 cm, from lobular proliferation of Brunner glands; resection unnecessary unless symptomatic or large (>2 cm) causing obstruction/pain/bleeding; large lesions may cause GI hemorrhage with iron deficiency; rare dysplasia. **Duodenal hamartomas** — associated with Peutz-Jeghers, Cowden, juvenile polyposis; solitary PJ-type polyps can occur without PJ syndrome; endoscopic resection generally recommended. **Subepithelial lesions** (GIST, NET, lipoma, leiomyoma) covered in a prior CPU.
- **FAP duodenal disease (BPA 13):** DAs tend to spare the duodenal bulb, mostly involve the descending duodenum with decreasing severity distally. Most adenomas flat/subtle. Tissue confirmation important, but repeated/aggressive forceps biopsy or submucosal tattooing is discouraged (avoid interference with future mucosectomy). Deep enteroscopy/capsule reserved for advanced polyposis or polyps extending toward the ligament of Treitz. Chromoendoscopy increases detection and upstages severity but clinical value not established. Surveillance may begin at age 25; **Spiegelman scoring** guides interval and management (Table 1). Stage IV (score 9–12) → surgical consult + surveillance q6–12mo; HGD and lesion size ≥10 mm are risk factors for duodenal cancer (~4% overall). Polyp removal may down-stage the Spiegelman score.

**Table 1 — Spiegelman Classification for Duodenal Polyps in FAP:**

| Variable | 1 Point | 2 Points | 3 Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| No. of polyps | 1–4 | 5–20 | >20 |
| Polyp size, mm | 1–4 | 5–10 | >10 |
| Histology | Tubulous | Tubulovillous | Villous |
| Dysplasia | Mild | Moderate | Severe |

| Stage | Spiegelman score | Surveillance | Risk of adenocarcinoma, % |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 4 y | — |
| I | 1–4 | 2–3 y | — |
| II | 5–6 | 2–3 y | 2.3 |
| III | 7–8 | 6–12 mo | 2.4 |
| IV | 9–12 | Surgical consult, 6–12 mo | 36 |

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Cold-snare vs hot-snare EMR tradeoff:** CS-EMR nearly eliminates bleeding but has much higher recurrence for large lesions (24.4% vs 2.3%) — the Update resolves this by lesion size (CS for flat lesions <20 mm / <15 mm; hot-snare EMR + thermal ablation for >20 mm).
- **No formal evidence ratings** — Best Practice Advice statements do not carry GRADE-style quality/strength ratings (systematic review not performed), unlike the [[asge-2015-ampullary-duodenal-adenomas]] guideline.
- **Optimal long-term surveillance timing** beyond the 6-month exam is expert-opinion-driven; few data.
- **Spiegelman thresholds** (this Update) are consistent with those cited on [[familial-adenomatous-polyposis]] via [[acg-2015-hereditary-gi-cancer]]; adenocarcinoma-risk percentages by stage differ across source cohorts (e.g., Stage IV 36% here vs higher lifetime figures elsewhere) — cohort-dependent.
- **ESD** is not advised in the duodenum here (high perforation, no advantage over piecemeal EMR), consistent with [[asge-2015-ampullary-duodenal-adenomas]].

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Caldera F, Kane S, Long M, Hashash JG. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Noncolorectal Cancer Screening and Vaccinations in Patients With Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Expert Review. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2025;23(5):695–706.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2024.12.011)
- **Authors:** Freddy Caldera, Sunanda Kane, Millie Long, Jana G. Hashash
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.cgh.2024.12.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cgh.2024.12.011)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — expert review, Best Practice Advice)

## Summary

AGA Clinical Practice Update providing 13 Best Practice Advice (BPA) statements for the noncolorectal-cancer screening, vaccination, and general health maintenance of adult patients with IBD. Colorectal cancer screening is explicitly out of scope (covered separately). Because this was an expert review and not a systematic review, the statements carry no formal evidence grade or strength rating.

Key thrust: novel biologics and small molecules improve IBD outcomes but raise rates of serious/opportunistic infection and certain cancers, so gastroenterologists must share responsibility (with primary care) for cancer screening, vaccination, bone health, and mental health rather than assuming these are handled elsewhere. The update covers age-appropriate general cancer screening (breast, prostate, lung per USPSTF), cervical dysplasia, skin cancer (melanoma + nonmelanoma), and anal cancer, then the adult immunization schedule with IBD-specific nuances (live-vaccine avoidance on immune-modifying therapy, hepatitis B seroprotection workup, high-dose influenza, pneumococcal, RSV, recombinant herpes zoster, HPV). It closes with bone densitometry indications and annual depression/anxiety screening.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Verbatim Best Practice Advice statements (no evidence grade per source):**

1. All adult patients with IBD should receive age-appropriate cancer screening.
2. Adult women with IBD should follow age-appropriate screening for cervical dysplasia. Data are insufficient to determine whether patients receiving combined immunosuppression or thiopurines require more frequent screening. Shared decision making and individual risk stratification are encouraged.
3. All adult patients with IBD should follow skin cancer primary prevention practices by avoiding excessive exposure to the sun's ultraviolet radiation. Patients on immunomodulators, anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) biologic agents, or small molecules should undergo a yearly total body skin exam (TBSE). Patients with any history of thiopurine use should continue with a yearly TBSE even after thiopurine cessation.
4. At every colonoscopy, a thorough perianal and anal examination should be performed. Special attention should be made to inspection of the anal canal of patients with perianal Crohn's disease, with anal stricture, with human papillomavirus (HPV), with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and who engage in anoreceptive intercourse.
5. Gastroenterology clinicians should discuss age-appropriate vaccines with adult patients who have IBD and share responsibility with primary care providers for administering these vaccines. Patients with IBD should follow the adult immunization schedule advised by the CDC for all vaccines with the exception of live vaccines; patients receiving immune-modifying agents should be counseled against receiving live vaccines; immunization history to the 2 live pediatric vaccines (varicella and MMR series) is presumptive evidence of immunity. All adults 18 to 26 years of age should receive the HPV vaccine series, and those between 27 and 45 years of age should be vaccinated if they are likely to have a new sexual partner.
6. Inactivated vaccines are safe in patients with IBD, and their administration is not associated with exacerbation of IBD activity. We suggest that patients receive vaccines at the earliest opportunity and preferably be off corticosteroids or at the lowest tolerable corticosteroid dose.
7. All adult patients with IBD should be evaluated for latent hepatitis B infection. Patients who have previously completed a full hepatitis B vaccine series but are not seroprotected (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) should receive a single challenge dose of hepatitis B vaccine; 4 to 8 weeks after this challenge dose, their anti-HBs levels should be measured to evaluate for an amnestic response. An amnestic response (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL, seroprotection) suggests immunologic memory and no further doses are needed. If no amnestic response is observed, the patient should complete a second full 2- or 3-dose series of hepatitis B vaccination.
8. All adult patients with IBD should receive an annual inactivated influenza vaccine. Patients receiving anti-TNF monotherapy or who are solid organ transplant recipients can benefit from a high-dose influenza vaccine. Adults 65 years of age and older should receive a high-dose, recombinant, or adjuvanted influenza vaccine. Live attenuated intranasal vaccines should be avoided.
9. All adult patients with IBD 19 to 64 years of age should receive an initial pneumococcal vaccine, with a subsequent second pneumococcal vaccine administered at 65 years of age and older.
10. All adult patients with IBD who are 60 years of age and older should receive a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine. There is no preference for any of the available RSV vaccines.
11. All adult patients 19 years of age and older receiving immune-modifying therapies, or with plans to initiate immune-modifying therapies, should receive a recombinant herpes zoster vaccine series, regardless of their prior varicella vaccination status.
12. Bone densitometry should be considered in patients with IBD, regardless of age, when risk factors for osteopenia and osteoporosis are present. These risk factors include low body mass index (<20 kg/m²), >3 months of cumulative corticosteroid exposure, current smoking, postmenopausal status, or hypogonadism. In the absence of other factors, bone densitometry should be considered for postmenopausal women and men 65 years or older.
13. All adult patients with IBD should be screened for depression and anxiety annually. Patients who screen positive for depression or anxiety should be referred to the appropriate specialist, be it their primary care physician or a mental health specialist.

**Supporting data:**
- General cancer screening per USPSTF: breast (women ≥40, every other year; other societies q1–2y), prostate (individualized, men 55–69), lung (high-risk adults 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years, current or quit within 15 years).
- Cervical: per USPSTF, women 21–29 cytology q3y; 30–65 cytology q3y, high-risk HPV testing q5y, or cotesting q5y. Dutch cohort — CIN2+ risk rose per year of immunomodulator exposure (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08–1.25). Meta-analysis (Mann et al, 74,310 IBD vs >2M reference) — no significant increased cervical cancer risk (HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.94–1.63) regardless of subtype or anti-TNF/thiopurine use; slightly elevated low-grade cervical lesion risk (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.04–1.28).
- Anal cancer: mostly squamous cell. Incidence 10.2/100,000 person-years in UC, 7.7 in CD; further increased in anal/perianal Crohn's (19.6/100,000). Risk factors: smoking, persistent HPV, HIV, MSM, women with HPV-associated genital cancers, solid organ recipients. Screening tools: digital anorectal exam, cytology, high-risk HPV testing ± genotyping; anal cytology not yet used for routine non-HIV screening.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[ibd-preventive-care]] with net-new content: anal cancer surveillance (BPA 4) and the perianal/anal exam at every colonoscopy; thiopurine-cessation TBSE persistence; HPV vaccination ages; hepatitis B challenge-dose / amnestic-response algorithm; bone densitometry risk-factor thresholds; pneumococcal age sequencing; RSV at ≥60.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Melanoma screening:** the existing [[ibd-preventive-care]] page (per ACG 2025) recommends annual full-skin melanoma screening for ALL IBD patients regardless of biologic use. This AGA CPU (BPA 3) ties yearly TBSE to patients on immunomodulators, anti-TNF, or small molecules (plus any thiopurine history even after cessation), rather than universally. Both are guideline-tier and same publication year; the page retains the broader ACG recommendation and notes the AGA framing.
- **RSV age:** AGA BPA 10 sets RSV vaccination at ≥60; the existing page (per ACG/ACIP) lists ≥75 and 50–74 with high-risk features. Both surfaced; per-population ACIP detail retained, AGA's ≥60 IBD-specific advice added.
- **Cervical screening frequency:** AGA finds data insufficient to mandate more frequent cervical screening on immunosuppression (BPA 2), whereas the existing page describes annual screening on immune-modifying therapy (ACG). Contradiction flagged; AGA's "insufficient data / shared decision making" qualifier added alongside.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Davis JPE, Lim JK, Francis FF, Ahn J. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Management of Portal Vein Thrombosis in Patients With Cirrhosis: Expert Review. *Gastroenterology* 2025;168(2):396–404.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.038)
- **Authors:** Jessica P. E. Davis, Joseph K. Lim, Fadi F. Francis, Joseph Ahn
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology (AGA Institute)
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.038](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2024.10.038)
- **Type:** guideline (AGA Clinical Practice Update — Expert Review; Best Practice Advice, unrated)

## Summary

AGA Expert Review Clinical Practice Update on the evaluation and management of **nonmalignant PVT in cirrhosis**. PVTs are common (5-year incidence ~11%), associated with advanced portal hypertension and mortality, and management is challenging because of competing risks of PVT-associated complications vs bleeding risk of anticoagulation (AC). Noncirrhotic PVT, malignant PVT, and hepatic venous thrombosis are **outside scope**.

The core management framework stratifies by **chronicity (recent = <6 months vs chronic = >6 months), degree of lumen occlusion (<50% vs >50%/complete), vascular bed involvement, and intestinal ischemia**. Recent + >50% occlusive or main-PV/mesenteric involvement favors AC; recent + minimally occlusive (<50%) intrahepatic-branch thrombi can be observed with 3-monthly imaging; chronic complete occlusion with cavernous transformation is generally not anticoagulated. Intestinal ischemia mandates urgent AC. Spontaneous recanalization occurs in ~40% untreated; recurrent thrombosis after AC withdrawal in up to 38%.

VKA, LMWH, and DOACs are all reasonable; choice is individualized by Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) class. **DOACs may be used in CTP class A and with caution in class B; not advised in class C.** Avoid delays in AC initiation (delay reduces odds of recanalization). Do not defer AC for variceal screening — screen and treat varices per usual, but AC can proceed. PVR-TIPS is reserved for those with additional TIPS indications (refractory ascites, variceal bleeding) or to enable transplant technical feasibility. Because no systematic review was performed, the 11 Best Practice Advice statements are **unrated**.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice statements (verbatim, all unrated):**

1. Asymptomatic patients with compensated cirrhosis do not require routine screening for PVT.
2. Patients with cirrhosis with PVTs identified on Doppler ultrasound should undergo cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the diagnosis, evaluate for malignancy, and document the degree of lumen occlusion, clot extent, and chronicity.
3. Patients with cirrhosis and PVT do not require a hypercoagulable workup in the absence of additional thromboemboli or laboratory abnormalities or family history suggestive of thrombophilia.
4. Patients with cirrhosis and PVT with evidence of intestinal ischemia require urgent anticoagulation to minimize ischemic injury. If available, these patients should be managed by a multidisciplinary team, including gastroenterology and hepatology, interventional radiology, hematology, and surgery.
5. Consider observation, with repeat imaging every 3 months until clot regression, in patients with cirrhosis without intestinal ischemia and recent (<6 months) thrombosis involving the intrahepatic portal vein branches or when there is <50% occlusion of the main portal vein, splenic vein, or mesenteric veins.
6. Anticoagulation should be considered in patients with cirrhosis without intestinal ischemia who develop recent (<6 months) PVT that is >50% occlusive or involves the main portal vein or mesenteric vessels. Patients who have increased benefit of recanalization include those with involvement of more than 1 vascular bed, those with thrombus progression, potential liver transplantation candidates, and those with inherited thrombophilia.
7. Anticoagulation is not advised for patients with cirrhosis with chronic (>6 months) PVT with complete occlusion with collateralization (cavernous transformation).
8. Patients with cirrhosis and PVT warrant endoscopic variceal screening if they are not already on nonselective beta-blocker therapy for bleeding prophylaxis. Avoid delays in the initiation of anticoagulation for PVT, as this decreases the odds of portal vein recanalization.
9. Vitamin K antagonists, low-molecular-weight heparin, and direct oral anticoagulants are all reasonable anticoagulant options for patients with cirrhosis and PVT. Decision making should be individualized and informed by patient preference and Child-Turcotte-Pugh class. Direct oral anticoagulants may be considered in patients with compensated Child-Turcotte-Pugh class A and Child-Turcotte-Pugh class B cirrhosis and offer convenience as their dosages are independent of international normalized ratio monitoring.
10. Patients with cirrhosis on anticoagulation for PVT should have cross-sectional imaging every 3 months to assess response to treatment. If clot regresses, anticoagulation should be continued until transplantation or at least clot resolution in nontransplantation patients.
11. Portal vein revascularization with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (PVR-TIPS) may be considered for selected patients with cirrhosis and PVT who have additional indications for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting, such as those with refractory ascites or variceal bleeding. Portal vein revascularization with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting may also be considered for transplantation candidates if recanalization can facilitate the technical feasibility of transplantation.

**Supporting data / thresholds:**
- Epidemiology: 5-year PVT incidence in cirrhosis ~11%; risk factors — portal hypertension, slow portal flow, metabolic syndrome, HCC.
- Natural history: spontaneous recanalization ~40% untreated; recurrent thrombosis after AC withdrawal up to 38% (within 2–5 months); no independent contribution of PVT to cirrhosis progression outside transplant setting in one large cohort.
- Diagnosis: Doppler US 89–93% sensitivity, 92–99% specificity; confirm/characterize with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI; differentiate bland thrombus from HCC tumor-in-vein (clot appearance, proximity to tumor, enhancement).
- "Recent" PVT pragmatically defined as **<6 months** (PVTs not recanalized within 6 months are unlikely to recanalize with AC).
- Cavernous transformation can appear as early as 1–3 weeks after acute PVT — collateralization alone cannot date chronicity.
- Intestinal ischemia complicates a minority (pre-existing collaterals protect); mortality up to 10–20%; features — pain out of proportion, sepsis, elevated lactate, mesenteric fat stranding/dilated loops; timely AC reduces bowel resection and mortality.
- AC and recanalization: meta-analysis OR 4.8 (2.7–8.7) for recanalization; LMWH ± VKA 71% vs 42% recanalization vs no treatment; DOAC vs VKA 87% vs 44% (RR 1.67, 1.02–2.74); AC does not increase portal-hypertensive bleeding; NSBB/variceal ligation may proceed on AC.
- Timing: AC within 6 months of diagnosis correlated with recanalization (RR 3.3, 1.2–9.4); within 2 weeks even better.
- Duration/monitoring: reimage q3 months; discontinue for futility in nonresponders after 6 months; continue after resolution in transplant-listed patients. Platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L associated with bleeding risk (individualize); thromboelastography a promising bleeding-risk tool.
- DOAC cautions: rivaroxaban small hepatotoxicity risk; avoid in CTP class C; reversal agents available (andexanet alfa / idarucizumab / 4-factor PCC).
- PVR-TIPS: revascularization ~98% in complete/near-complete occlusion in expert single-center series; data limited/low-MELD, low generalizability.

## Summary

Commentary on sclerosing mesenteritis (SM) — a rare idiopathic fibroinflammatory disorder of the bowel mesentery (spectrum includes mesenteric panniculitis, "misty mesentery," retractile/liposclerotic mesenteritis). Found on ~0.6%–1.1% of CT scans; up to ~60% of patients with CT findings are asymptomatic. Most patients identified on imaging never require treatment; management is presentation-based.

## Key Findings / Claims (narrative)

- **Clinical features:** abdominal pain most common; fever (5%–15%), unintentional weight loss (~20%); palpable mass often absent. Complications: bowel obstruction, mesenteric vascular compromise, protein-losing enteropathy, ascites.
- **Diagnosis (imaging-led):** CT signs — "misty mesentery," **fat ring sign** (preserved fat halos around central mesenteric vessels), and a **tumoral/fibrotic pseudocapsule**. No single sign is diagnostic; diagnosis is usually made on characteristic CT in the right clinical context **without biopsy**.
- **Differential:** lymphoma, carcinoid, peritoneal carcinomatosis, desmoid, IgG4-related disease, treatment-related changes (e.g., after immune checkpoint inhibitors).
- **Biopsy:** consider when atypical features raise malignancy concern (e.g., a mesenteric mass, calcified mass with bowel retraction, new/accompanying lymphadenopathy); surgical biopsy with IgG4 staining may be preferred when needed.
- **Treatment thresholds:** only ~1%–6% of patients with SM imaging findings require treatment; asymptomatic → observe.
- **Pharmacotherapy:** **prednisone** monotherapy 30–40 mg/day (typically start 40 mg/day × 3–4 months, then taper ~5 mg/week); **tamoxifen 10 mg twice daily** is the most commonly used therapy, alone or with prednisone (prednisone tapered after ~3 months, tamoxifen continued). Alternatives: thalidomide, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate. Treat concomitant GI disorders.
- **Severe disease:** bowel obstruction managed nonoperatively when feasible; surgical bypass if refractory. Surgery does not cure SM; complete resection often impossible due to vascular involvement. Recurrence can occur; surveillance imaging detects it.

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[sclerosing-mesenteritis]] — new disease-script page.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No formal evidence ratings (commentary). Optimal drug regimen/duration not established; treatment evidence for symptom relief is limited.

- **Authors:** Sahil Khanna, Jessica R. Allegretti, Jana G. Hashash, Paul Feuerstadt
- **Year:** 2026
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2026;171:184–192
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2026.03.008](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2026.03.008)

## Summary

AGA Expert Review on managing *Clostridioides difficile* infection (CDI) specifically in patients with IBD, who face higher CDI risk, greater severity, and higher recurrence than non-IBD patients. CDI drives IBD flares, hospitalization, intensified/failed therapy, and higher surgical rates, creating dilemmas around antibiotic choice and timing of IBD therapy.

Key shifts from general CDI guidance: **fidaxomicin is preferred over vancomycin** for an initial CDI episode in IBD (metronidazole should not be used), a **multistep toxin-based assay** is required because NAAT alone over-diagnoses colonization (common in IBD), and **immunosuppressive IBD therapy should be continued** during acute CDI. **Microbiome-based therapies** (FDA-approved fecal microbiota live-jslm [RBL] and fecal microbiota spores live-brpk [VOS], or unapproved FMT) are advised after ≥1 recurrence. Probiotics are not advised for prevention.

12 Best Practice Advice statements (no formal GRADE ratings).

## Key Findings / Claims

**Best Practice Advice (verbatim):**

1. In patients with IBD who have new or worsening diarrhea, CDI should be excluded, especially among those with colonic involvement, as they are at increased risk of CDI. Clinicians should consider and treat CDI in patients with end ileostomy or ileo-anal pouch anastomosis with worsening diarrhea.
2. In patients with IBD and suspected CDI, a multistep toxin-based assay should be used for diagnostic evaluation.
3. In patients with IBD and recent CDI who have been treated successfully with antibiotics, recurrent diarrhea should prompt retesting for CDI.
4. In patients with IBD who develop an initial episode of CDI, clinicians should preferentially use fidaxomicin or use vancomycin if fidaxomicin is unavailable or cost-prohibitive. Metronidazole should not be used.
5. Clinicians should strongly consider hospitalization for patients with IBD and CDI who demonstrate features of severe colitis or systemic toxicity (eg, more than 6 bowel movements per day, severe abdominal pain, marked leukocytosis, hemodynamic instability, or other evidence of sepsis).
6. When selecting an immunosuppressive therapy to treat IBD, no class or mechanism of action has a differential risk of CDI and, therefore, clinicians should choose the therapy that is best to treat the IBD.
7. In patients with IBD and acute CDI, concurrent treatment of IBD is critical and clinicians should continue therapy with the required immunosuppressive therapies (ie, immunomodulators, biologics, or small molecules). Steroids can also be used if deemed necessary while CDI is treated with antibiotics.
8. Clinicians should consider endoscopic evaluation for IBD activity and exclusion of concomitant cytomegalovirus infection if symptoms persist 48–72 hours after initiation of treatment for CDI.
9. Clinicians may consider loperamide in patients with improving inflammation and infection but ongoing diarrhea.
10. Clinicians should offer microbiome-based therapies (eg, fecal microbiota, live-jslm, fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk, or unapproved fecal microbiota transplantation) to patients with IBD with at least 1 recurrence of CDI to prevent future infection.
11. In patients with IBD, clinicians should not advise probiotics for primary or secondary prevention of CDI.
12. In patients with IBD and a history of CDI who are receiving systemic antibiotics, clinicians may consider oral vancomycin prophylaxis as secondary prevention.

As the newer same-tier guideline, the AGA 2026 preference is what the page asserts; the ACG vancomycin pathway remains acceptable when fidaxomicin is unavailable/cost-prohibitive.
