## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Pasha SF, Acosta RD, Chandrasekhara V, et al). Routine laboratory testing before endoscopic procedures. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2014;80(1):28-33.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.01.019)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2014
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2014;80(1):28-33
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.01.019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.01.019)
- **Type:** Guideline (ASGE Standards of Practice; GRADE)

## Summary

ASGE guideline against reflexive, protocol-driven laboratory testing before endoscopy. Most outcomes data are extrapolated from the surgical/anesthesia literature, where routine preoperative testing rarely alters management: unsuspected chemistry abnormalities appear in only 0.2-1.0% of healthy patients and do not change anesthetic or procedural care. When tests are ordered on the basis of history/exam, up to 30% are abnormal and often change management — arguing for **selective, risk-based testing** rather than universal panels.

The guideline sets the wiki's framework for pre-endoscopy labs: an abnormal PTT does not reliably predict periprocedural bleeding; coagulation studies, chest radiography, ECG, blood type/screen, hemoglobin/hematocrit, urinalysis, and chemistries should be individualized to patient and procedural risk. It is referenced by other ASGE procedural documents (eg, enteral feeding) that state "routine laboratory testing before endoscopy is not indicated."

## Key Findings / Claims

- Routine preoperative/pre-endoscopy chemistry testing rarely yields management-altering abnormalities in patients without a suggestive history (unsuspected abnormalities 0.2-1.0%).
- Selective testing (ordered from clinical suspicion) yields abnormalities in up to ~30% and more often changes management.
- Abnormal PTT does not reliably predict periprocedural bleeding.
- Mild renal impairment does not affect outcomes with moderate/deep sedation; renal-function testing is not required for endoscopy on that basis alone.
- In insulin-requiring diabetes, preprocedural blood glucose may be warranted.

## Recommendations (verbatim)

1. Recommend endoscopists pursue preprocedure testing **selectively** based on medical history, physical examination, and patient and procedural risk factors. (High/strong)
2. Recommend **against** routine testing with coagulation studies, chest radiography, ECG, blood typing or screening, hemoglobin/hematocrit, urinalysis, and chemistry tests before endoscopy in healthy patients; individualize based on patient and procedural risk factors. (High/strong)
3. Suggest pregnancy testing be considered before endoscopy and fluoroscopy in female patients of childbearing age with uncertain pregnancy history or history suggestive of current pregnancy (absent prior hysterectomy, bilateral tubal ligation, or ≥1 year amenorrhea/menopause). (Moderate/conditional)
4. Suggest coagulation studies before endoscopy in patients with active bleeding, known/suspected bleeding disorder, medication risk (anticoagulant use, prolonged antibiotics), prolonged biliary obstruction, history of abnormal bleeding, malnutrition, or other conditions associated with acquired coagulopathies. (Moderate/conditional)
5. Suggest a chest radiograph before endoscopy in patients with new respiratory symptoms or decompensated cardiac failure. (Moderate/conditional)
6. Recommend blood typing and screening before endoscopy when transfusion is considered likely (active bleeding or anemia). (High/strong)
7. Suggest testing hemoglobin/hematocrit before endoscopy in patients with preexisting anemia, ongoing bleeding, or high risk of significant blood loss during the procedure. (High/conditional)
8. Suggest selective chemistry testing before endoscopy in patients with significant endocrine, renal, or hepatic dysfunction before using medications that may further impair function. (Moderate/conditional)

## Relevance to Wiki

- **[[preprocedure-testing]]** — new concept page built from this guideline (selective, risk-based pre-endoscopy labs; pregnancy testing before fluoroscopy).
- Cross-links to **[[endoscopy-sedation]]** and periprocedural **[[anticoagulation-gi-bleeding]]** (coagulation testing indications).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No direct conflict with existing wiki content. The selective-testing principle aligns with the ASGE sedation and enteral-feeding documents already ingested.

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of endoscopy in the patient with lower GI bleeding. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2014;79:875-85.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2013.10.039)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2014
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2013.10.039](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2013.10.039)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE recommendations)

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice guideline on endoscopy in lower GI bleeding (LGIB), spanning occult bleeding, chronic scant hematochezia, melena, and severe acute hematochezia. **Colonoscopy** is the test of choice for occult bleeding and for chronic intermittent scant hematochezia in patients >50 or with iron-deficiency anemia/neoplasia risk/alarm features; EGD is added when no colonic source is found or upper symptoms/IDA/NSAID use are present. For melena or severe hematochezia with hemodynamic instability, an **initial EGD** excludes a high-risk upper source before colonoscopy. In severe hematochezia, **colonoscopy within 24 hours after rapid bowel preparation** is suggested. Endoscopic hemostasis is detailed for diverticular bleeding (epinephrine injection + thermal coagulation or clips; clip/tattoo for relocalization) and angioectasias (APC preferred). Severe hematochezia that cannot be stabilized or where endoscopy fails warrants surgical/radiologic (angiographic embolization) consultation.

Largely corroborates the newer [[acg-2023-lgib|ACG 2023]] LGIB guideline (added here as a complementary endoscopic-technique source; newer ACG risk-stratification and timing content is retained).

## Key Findings / Claims

- Colonoscopy is first-line for occult GI bleeding and chronic scant hematochezia in higher-risk patients.
- EGD complements colonoscopy when the colon is non-diagnostic, especially with upper symptoms, IDA, or NSAID use.
- Younger patients with scant hematochezia and no alarm features: DRE + flexible sigmoidoscopy may suffice.
- Melena → EGD first, then colonoscopy if EGD negative.
- Severe hematochezia + hemodynamic instability → initial EGD to exclude high-risk upper lesion, then colonoscopy.
- Severe hematochezia → colonoscopy within 24 h after rapid bowel prep.
- Diverticular bleeding: epinephrine injection + thermal coagulation or clip placement; place clip/tattoo adjacent for future localization.
- Angioectasia bleeding: APC is the preferred endoscopic treatment.
- Multidetector CT/CTA has largely replaced nuclear RBC scan for localizing severe LGIB; superselective embolization achieves ~85% hemostasis in diverticular bleeding (early rebleed ~22%).
- Unstable or endoscopy-refractory severe hematochezia → surgical + radiologic consultation; elective surgery preferred (lower mortality than emergent).

## Recommendations (verbatim)

1. We recommend colonoscopy in patients with occult GI bleeding. *(high quality)*
2. We recommend EGD in patients with occult GI bleeding if a bleeding source is not identified in the colon, especially in those patients with upper GI symptoms, iron deficiency anemia, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. *(moderate-high quality)*
3. We suggest small-bowel evaluation after negative EGD and colonoscopy results in patients with occult GI bleeding who have persistent anemia. *(moderate quality)*
4. We recommend colonoscopy for the evaluation of chronic intermittent scant hematochezia in patients aged >50 years and for patients who have iron deficiency anemia, risk factors for colorectal neoplasia, or the alarm symptoms of weight loss or bowel habit changes. *(moderate-high quality)*
5. We suggest that in younger patients presenting with chronic intermittent scant hematochezia without alarm symptoms, a digital rectal examination and flexible sigmoidoscopy may be sufficient evaluation. *(moderate quality)*
6. We recommend EGD in the initial evaluation of patients with melena followed by colonoscopy if the EGD result is negative. *(high quality)*
7. We recommend an initial EGD in patients with severe hematochezia and hemodynamic instability to evaluate for a high-risk upper GI lesion, followed by colonoscopy if the EGD result is negative. *(high quality)*
8. We suggest colonoscopy within 24 hours of admission after a rapid bowel preparation in the evaluation of patients with severe hematochezia. *(moderate-high quality)*
9. We recommend endoscopic treatment with epinephrine solution injection combined with thermal coagulation or endoscopic clip placement as the preferred management in patients presenting with diverticular bleeding. *(high quality)*
10. We recommend endoscopic clip or tattoo placement adjacent to a bleeding diverticulum if identified at colonoscopy for future localization in the event of recurrent bleeding. *(moderate-high quality)*
11. We recommend endoscopic treatment with argon plasma coagulation as the preferred management in patients with bleeding angioectasias. *(high quality)*
12. We recommend surgical and radiologic consultation in patients presenting with severe hematochezia who cannot be stabilized for endoscopy or in whom endoscopic evaluation has failed to reveal a bleeding source. *(quality not graded in source)*

## Relevance to Wiki

- Added as a complementary endoscopic-technique source to [[acute-lower-gi-bleeding]] (colonoscopy is the test of choice for most LGIB).
- Reinforces APC for angioectasias and epinephrine + thermal/clip for diverticular bleeding.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Superseded on risk stratification and resuscitation thresholds by the newer [[acg-2023-lgib|ACG 2023]]; older content not used to overwrite newer recommendations.

# ASGE 2015: The Role of Endoscopy in Ampullary and Duodenal Adenomas

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee; Chathadi KV, Khashab MA, Acosta RD, et al. The role of endoscopy in ampullary and duodenal adenomas. *Gastrointestinal Endoscopy* 2015;82(5):773–781. doi:10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.027.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.027)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee — Krishnavel V. Chathadi, Mouen A. Khashab, Ruben D. Acosta, Vinay Chandrasekhara, Mohamad A. Eloubeidi, Ashley L. Faulx, Lisa Fonkalsrud, Jenifer R. Lightdale, John R. Saltzman, Aasma Shaukat, Amy Wang, Brooks D. Cash, John M. DeWitt (Chair)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastrointestinal Endoscopy* 2015;82(5):773–781 (American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.027)
- **Type:** Guideline (ASGE Standards of Practice)

---

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice guideline on endoscopic evaluation and management of **ampullary** (major duodenal papilla) and **nonampullary duodenal adenomas**. Both can be sporadic or arise in genetic syndromes (FAP, Peutz-Jeghers) and both carry malignant potential. Endoscopic resection has become a viable alternative to surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy/Whipple or transduodenal ampullectomy) in selected cases, with lower adverse-event rates than local surgical excision.

Pre-treatment evaluation: a **side-viewing duodenoscope** is generally needed to visualize the papilla; biopsy of suspicious lesions is required before resection to confirm adenoma and exclude cancer (sample away from the pancreatic duct orifice to avoid pancreatitis; ≥6 specimens or sampling within 10 days of sphincterotomy reduces false-negatives, which range 16–60% for carcinoma). **EUS / intraductal US** is reserved for large ampullary lesions or those with features concerning for malignancy and is superior to CT/MRI/transabdominal US for tumor (T) staging. **ERCP** with biliary and pancreatic duct evaluation is performed at the time of papillectomy to assess intraductal extension; <1 cm of ductal extension does not necessarily preclude endoscopic therapy.

Endoscopic resection of the papilla is termed **endoscopic papillectomy** (true "ampullectomy" is a surgical term requiring ductal reimplantation). En bloc snare resection with electrocautery is preferred when the lesion can be fully ensnared (shorter time, complete pathology, less residual fibrosis); piecemeal resection is used for lesions >2 cm. Submucosal injection, chromoendoscopy, sphincterotomy, and ablative therapies (APC most common, 50–60 W) are adjuncts. **Prophylactic pancreatic duct stenting plus rectal indomethacin** reduce post-procedure pancreatitis. Papillectomy success is 46–92% with recurrence up to 33%; all patients require post-resection surveillance.

For **nonampullary duodenal polyps**, the approach mirrors right-colon polypectomy given the thin duodenal wall. EMR is the mainstay; **ESD is not recommended beyond the duodenal bulb** (perforation rates 23–35% in high-volume series). Lesions with >33% circumferential involvement should be considered for surgery. Patients with sporadic ampullary or duodenal adenomas have higher colorectal neoplasia risk and should be offered screening colonoscopy. Search covered 1980–December 2013; recommendations graded by GRADE evidence quality.

---

## All Recommendations (Verbatim, with GRADE Evidence Quality)

Evidence-quality symbols (GRADE): 4444 = High; 444B = Moderate; 44BB = Low; 4BBB = Very low. Recommendation strength: "we recommend" = stronger; "we suggest" = weaker.

1. We recommend that biopsy specimens be obtained and evaluated from ampullary lesions suspicious for neoplasia before attempted endoscopic resection. **(Moderate — 444B)**
2. We recommend EUS for large ampullary lesions or duodenal polyps with features concerning for malignancy before endoscopic or surgical resection. **(Moderate — 444B)**
3. We suggest ERCP with both biliary and pancreatic duct evaluation at the time of endoscopic papillectomy to assess for evidence of extension into either ductal system. **(Low — 44BB)**
4. We recommend prophylactic pancreatic duct stent placement and rectal indomethacin during papillectomy to reduce the risk of postprocedural pancreatitis. **(Moderate — 444B)**
5. We recommend that patients undergoing endoscopic removal of ampullary and duodenal neoplasms be included in an endoscopic surveillance program to ensure complete tissue removal and assess for disease recurrence. **(Moderate — 444B)**
6. We suggest that patients with sporadic ampullary or duodenal adenomas be offered screening colonoscopy. **(Low — 44BB)**

---

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Surgical morbidity/mortality:** Whipple/transduodenal ampullectomy associated with anastomotic dehiscence/fistula in up to 9%/14% and mortality 1–9%. Local surgical excision adverse-event rate (~29%) appears higher than endoscopy (~14%).
- **Ampullary biopsy:** diagnostic (adenoma + carcinoma) rates 45–80%; false-negative for carcinoma 16–60%. Minimize false-negatives with ≥6 specimens or biopsy within 10 days of sphincterotomy; orient forceps parallel to folds to reduce fibrosis.
- **Features suggesting malignancy / surgical referral:** firmness, ulceration, friability, **non-lifting of the periampullary component with submucosal injection** (failure to lift = strongest predictor of malignancy in one study). Many authors avoid endoscopic resection for lesions ≥4 cm.
- **Imaging:** EUS superior to CT/MRI/transabdominal US for T staging; MRI superior to EUS for nodal staging; intraductal US may visualize the tumor better than EUS but can overstage. Lesions <1 cm without malignant features may not require US before resection.
- **ERCP/intraductal extension:** <1 cm of CBD or PD extension does not preclude endoscopic therapy; balloon dilation/catheters can expose intraductal tissue for resection.
- **Papillectomy technique:** en bloc snare + electrocautery preferred when lesion fully ensnarable; piecemeal for >2 cm or residual tissue. No proven superiority of snare type, current type, or snare orientation. Larger-channel therapeutic duodenoscope eases instrument passage. Retrieve specimens immediately; glucagon may reduce peristalsis; CO₂ insufflation advantageous if perforation.
- **Post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis:** prophylactic PD stenting reduces PEP (one small RCT, n=19, of stenting after papillectomy positive); rectal indomethacin + temporary PD stenting lower PEP risk/severity in high-risk populations. Prophylactic biliary stenting not routinely recommended unless inadequate biliary drainage or microperforation concern.
- **Ablation:** APC (50–60 W) most common for residual/recurrent superficial tissue; PD stent usually placed before ablating near the PD orifice; ablated tissue is not available for pathology — biopsy suspicious areas before ablation.
- **Outcomes:** papillectomy clinical success 46–92%; recurrence up to 33%. Predictors of long-term success: age >48 y, lesion ≤24 mm, male sex, absence of polyposis syndrome (e.g., FAP). Intraductal growth → lower cure, more surgery.
- **Surveillance:** all post-papillectomy patients undergo surveillance endoscopy with scar biopsy, typically 1–6 months after the index procedure, then every 3–12 months for ≥2 years; endpoints not established.
- **Nonampullary duodenal polyps:** EMR is mainstay (approach like right colon given thin wall); submucosal injection cushion for flat lesions; lack of lift suggests malignancy/prior manipulation. **ESD beyond the bulb not recommended** (perforation 23–35%; same Japanese group reported no perforations with EMR). Cold-snare polypectomy described for lesions >1 cm to avoid cautery injury. >33% circumferential involvement → consider surgery. Giant (>3 cm) hemicircumferential LSTs have higher adverse-event (bleeding) rates (26.3% vs 3.2% for <3 cm). EUS role unclear but may affect management of polyps >2 cm.
- **CRC risk:** sporadic ampullary/duodenal adenomas are associated with increased colorectal neoplasia → offer screening colonoscopy.

---

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates the disease-script page [[ampullary-adenoma]] (ampullary and nonampullary duodenal adenoma; sporadic vs FAP-associated; endoscopic papillectomy; duodenal EMR; surveillance).
- Cross-links to [[familial-adenomatous-polyposis]], [[peutz-jeghers-syndrome]], [[ercp]], [[endoscopic-ultrasound]], [[upper-endoscopy]], [[colonoscopy]].

---

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No clinically significant conflicts with existing wiki content. Spigelman staging of duodenal polyposis is **not** addressed in this 2015 guideline (the prior ASGE FAP-specific guideline covers FAP duodenal surveillance); FAP-specific Spigelman staging should be sourced from the FAP guideline, not this document.
- Guideline is from a 1980–2013 literature search; later ASGE/ESGE papillectomy guidance may supersede technical details if ingested.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Khashab MA, Chithadi KV, Acosta RD, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee). Antibiotic prophylaxis for GI endoscopy. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;81(1):81-89. doi:10.1016/j.gie.2014.08.008.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.08.008)
- **Authors:** Khashab MA, Chithadi KV, Acosta RD, Bruining DH, Chandrasekhara V, Eloubeidi MA, Fanelli RD, Faulx AL, Fonkalsrud L, Lightdale JR, Muthusamy VR, Pasha SF, Saltzman JR, Shaukat A, Wang A, Cash BD, DeWitt JM (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2015;81(1):81-89
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.08.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.08.008)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE-based clinical practice guideline)

Update of the 2008 ASGE document; literature search 1975–2013. Recommendations graded by GRADE (4444 high, 444B moderate, 44BB low, 4BBB very low).

## Summary
ASGE Standards of Practice Committee guideline on periprocedural antibiotics for GI endoscopy, addressing both prevention of infective endocarditis (IE) and prevention of local/remote infections. Endoscopy can cause transient bacteremia (highest with esophageal dilation 12–22%, variceal sclerotherapy up to 52%, and instrumentation of obstructed bile ducts), but clinically significant infection is extremely rare — among millions of procedures only ~25 temporally associated IE cases have been reported, and there is no causal link between endoscopy and IE nor evidence that prophylaxis prevents it. Transient bacteremia from routine daily activities (brushing, flossing, chewing) often exceeds endoscopy-associated rates.

**Antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT indicated solely to prevent IE for any GI endoscopic procedure**, regardless of cardiac risk lesion, consistent with the AHA's shift away from procedure-based IE prophylaxis. The exception: patients with high-risk cardiac conditions who also have an established GI infection where enterococci may be part of the flora may receive coverage (directed at the infection, not the procedure).

Prophylaxis IS warranted in specific scenarios to prevent local infection: ERCP with anticipated **incomplete biliary drainage** (and after liver transplant or known/suspected obstruction with possible incomplete drainage); **PEG/PEJ** placement (parenteral cefazolin); **EUS-FNA of cystic lesions** (mediastinal, pancreatic/peripancreatic); and **all cirrhotic patients admitted with GI bleeding** (antibiotics started at admission regardless of endoscopy — ceftriaxone IV, or oral norfloxacin if intolerant). Prophylaxis is NOT recommended for ERCP with complete drainage and no obstruction, EUS-FNA of solid lesions, synthetic vascular grafts/nonvalvular cardiovascular devices, or orthopedic prostheses; it is suggested for lower-GI endoscopy in continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients.

## Key Findings / Claims

### Bacteremia risk by procedure
- **High:** esophageal dilation (bougienage 12–22%; higher with malignant strictures and multiple dilators), variceal sclerotherapy (up to 52%, mean ~14.6%), instrumentation of obstructed bile ducts.
- **Low:** diagnostic EGD ± biopsy, colonoscopy ± biopsy/polypectomy, EUS-FNA of solid lesions (within range of diagnostic EGD), EVL.
- Routine daily activity (brushing/flossing/chewing) causes transient bacteremia often exceeding endoscopy rates — a key rationale against procedure-based IE prophylaxis.

### Prophylaxis to prevent local infection (Table 3)
| Patient condition | Procedure | Goal | Antibiotic prophylaxis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bile duct obstruction, no cholangitis | ERCP with complete drainage | Prevent cholangitis | **Not recommended (4444)** |
| Bile duct obstruction, no cholangitis | ERCP with incomplete drainage | Prevent cholangitis | **Recommended; continue after procedure (444B)** |
| Solid lesion, upper GI | EUS-FNA | Prevent local infection | **Not recommended (4444)** |
| Solid lesion, lower GI | EUS-FNA | Prevent local infection | **Not recommended (444B)** |
| Mediastinal cysts | EUS-FNA | Prevent cyst infection | **Suggested (44BB)** |
| Pancreatic cysts | EUS-FNA | Prevent cyst infection | **Suggested (44BB)** |
| All patients | PEG/PEJ feeding-tube placement | Prevent peristomal infection | **Recommended (4444)** |
| Cirrhosis with acute GI bleeding | Required for all, regardless of procedure | Prevent infectious AEs, reduce mortality | **On admission (4444)** |
| Synthetic vascular graft / nonvalvular CV device | Any endoscopy | Prevent graft/device infection | **Not recommended (4444)** |
| Prosthetic joints | Any endoscopy | Prevent septic arthritis | **Not recommended (444B)** |
| Peritoneal dialysis | Lower GI endoscopy | Prevent peritonitis | **Suggested (44BB)** |

### Recommendations (GRADE)
1. We recommend against the routine administration of antibiotic prophylaxis solely for prevention of IE. **(444B)**
2. We suggest that patients with high-risk cardiac conditions (Table 2) and established GI tract infections in which enterococci may be part of the infecting bacterial flora should receive antibiotic coverage. **(44BB)**
3. We recommend against antibiotic prophylaxis before ERCP when obstructive biliary tract disease is not suspected or complete biliary drainage is anticipated. **(4444)**
4. We recommend that antibiotic prophylaxis be administered before ERCP in patients who have had liver transplantation or who have known or suspected biliary obstruction, where there is a possibility of incomplete biliary drainage. Antibiotics that cover biliary flora such as enteric gram-negative organisms and enterococci should be used and continued after the procedure if biliary drainage is incomplete. **(444B)**
5. We recommend against antibiotic prophylaxis before diagnostic EUS or EUS-FNA of solid lesions of the GI tract. **(444B)**
6. We suggest antibiotic administration prior to EUS-FNA of mediastinal cysts. **(44BB)**
7. We suggest administration of prophylactic antibiotics before EUS-FNA of pancreatic or peripancreatic cysts. **(44BB)**
8. We recommend administration of parenteral cefazolin (or an antibiotic with equivalent microbial coverage) to all patients before PEG/PEJ tube placement. **(4444)**
9. We recommend that all patients with cirrhosis admitted with GI bleeding should have antibiotic therapy instituted at admission with intravenous ceftriaxone (or an antibiotic with equivalent microbial coverage [eg, oral norfloxacin] in patients allergic to or intolerant of ceftriaxone). **(4444)**
10. We recommend against administration of antibiotic prophylaxis before GI endoscopic procedures for patients with synthetic vascular grafts or other nonvalvular cardiovascular devices (eg, implantable electronic devices). **(4444)**
11. We recommend against antibiotic prophylaxis for patients with orthopedic prosthesis undergoing any GI endoscopic procedure. **(444B)**
12. We suggest administration of antibiotic prophylaxis before endoscopy of the lower GI tract in patients undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis. **(4BBB)**

### Additional points
- IE prophylaxis: high-risk cardiac conditions (Table 2) include prosthetic cardiac valve/prosthetic repair material, prior IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD (incl. palliative shunts/conduits), completely repaired CHD with prosthetic material/device within 6 months, repaired CHD with residual defects at/adjacent to a prosthetic patch/device, and cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy. Even for these, prophylaxis is not given solely for the endoscopic procedure.
- **PEG/PEJ:** cefazolin ~30 min before placement reduces peristomal infection; MRSA decolonization where endemic.
- **EUS-FNA cysts:** antibiotics (eg, fluoroquinolone) before and often 3–5 days after FNA of cystic lesions; rationale is cyst-infection prevention.
- **Cirrhosis + GI bleed:** Cochrane meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 1241 patients) — antibiotics reduce infections, rebleeding, and mortality; start at admission regardless of whether/when endoscopy occurs.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Anchors the new concept page [[antibiotic-prophylaxis-endoscopy]] (when periprocedural prophylaxis is and is not indicated).
- Reinforces cirrhosis-GI-bleed prophylaxis on [[antibiotic-prophylaxis-cirrhosis]], [[portal-hypertension]], [[variceal-upper-gi-bleeding]], and [[spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis]].
- Adds periprocedural infection guidance to [[ercp]], [[endoscopic-ultrasound]], [[pancreatic-cysts]], and gastrostomy/PEG placement (see [[asge-2025-gastrostomy-tubes|ASGE 2025 gastrostomy guideline]]).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No causal link between endoscopy and IE and no evidence prophylaxis prevents it — basis for recommending against procedure-based IE prophylaxis (aligns with AHA).
- AAOS 2009 statement recommending prophylaxis for all joint-replacement patients before invasive procedures was later withdrawn for lack of evidence; ASGE recommends against prophylaxis for orthopedic prostheses.
- Evidence for EUS-FNA cyst prophylaxis and peritoneal-dialysis prophylaxis is low/very-low quality.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Chandrasekhara V, et al; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of endoscopy in benign pancreatic disease. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;82(2):203-214.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.04.022)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Chandrasekhara V, Chathadi KV, Acosta RD, et al.)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.04.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.04.022)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement (GRADE) on the endoscopic evaluation and treatment of benign pancreatic disease — idiopathic [[acute-pancreatitis]] (including idiopathic recurrent acute pancreatitis, IRAP), sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD), autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), and [[chronic-pancreatitis]] (dominant duct strictures, pancreatolithiasis, pancreatic-duct leaks).

Key themes: ERCP is **not** a diagnostic test for a single episode of acute pancreatitis; EUS is the preferred low-risk tool to interrogate idiopathic disease, especially in older patients in whom occult malignancy must be excluded. The landmark practice point is that **ERCP must not be used to evaluate type 3 SOD** (recurrent/chronic pain alone) — a high-quality recommendation rooted in the harm/no-benefit signal later confirmed by EPISOD. Post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis (rectal indomethacin and/or pancreatic-duct stenting in high-risk patients) is strongly recommended. In chronic pancreatitis, endoscopic therapy (ERP with dilation/stenting, ESWL for refractory stones, stenting for PD leaks) is appropriate within a multidisciplinary framework.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE quality of evidence; 4444 = high, 444B = moderate, 44BB = low, 4BBB = very low):**

1. We suggest EUS for the evaluation of idiopathic AP for patients older than 40 years of age if history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and abdominal imaging with MRI or CT are unrevealing. (Low)
2. We recommend against diagnostic ERCP for a single episode of AP. (Moderate)
3. We suggest that ERCP with sphincter of Oddi manometry may be considered for the evaluation of idiopathic acute recurrent pancreatitis (suspected type 2 pancreatic SOD) when findings on EUS and/or MRCP are normal and without suspicion for biliary stones, sludge, or CP. Alternate strategies include ERCP with empiric biliary and/or pancreatic sphincterotomy. (Low)
4. We recommend biliary and/or pancreatic sphincterotomy in patients with type 1 pancreatic SOD or patients with type 2 pancreatic SOD confirmed by manometry. (Moderate)
5. We recommend against the use of ERCP for the evaluation of recurrent or chronic abdominal pain interpreted as type 3 SOD. (High)
6. We recommend the use of rectal indomethacin and/or PD stenting for the prevention of post-ERCP pancreatitis in high-risk patients. (High)
7. We recommend EUS-guided tissue biopsy for suspected but unproved cases of AIP. Although FNA is useful for excluding underlying malignancy in older patients, larger gauge core tissue devices may be required to confirm the diagnosis of AIP. (Moderate)
8. We suggest ePFT and/or EUS without pancreatic biopsy for the diagnosis of CP not readily evident by previous noninvasive imaging. (Low)
9. We recommend ERP with dilation and/or plastic stent placement for the treatment of symptomatic dominant PD strictures for individuals in whom multidisciplinary review considers endoscopic therapy as the preferred initial therapy. (High)
10. We recommend the adjunctive use of ESWL for patients with symptoms attributed to pancreatolithiasis refractory to standard endoscopic stone extraction techniques. (Moderate)
11. We recommend that ERP with stenting be the first-line therapy for the management of PD leaks. (High)

**Other points:**
- ePFT = endoscopic pancreatic function testing; EUS criteria can diagnose early CP not seen on cross-sectional imaging.
- For suspected AIP, core-tissue devices (not just FNA) may be needed to confirm; FNA's main role is to exclude malignancy in older patients.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[acute-pancreatitis]] — no diagnostic ERCP for a single episode; EUS for unexplained AP in patients >40 with negative workup; SOD typing (treat type 1, manometry-confirmed type 2; do NOT scope type 3); rectal indomethacin ± PD stent for post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis.
- Updates [[chronic-pancreatitis]] — EUS/ePFT for imaging-occult CP; ERP dilation/stenting for dominant PD strictures; adjunctive ESWL for refractory pancreatolithiasis; ERP+stent first-line for PD leaks.
- Cross-links [[ercp]] and [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] (diagnostic and therapeutic roles).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Older (2015) than [[asge-2023-post-ercp-pancreatitis|ASGE 2023 post-ERCP pancreatitis prevention]] and [[asge-2024-chronic-pancreatitis-endoscopy|ASGE 2024 chronic pancreatitis endoscopy]]; for detailed PEP-prophylaxis algorithms and CP endotherapy the newer ASGE documents govern. This source contributes the type-3-SOD prohibition and the idiopathic-AP/IRAP evaluation framework. Its type-2 SOD manometry recommendation predates the EPISOD trial's negative findings for SOD type III — the type-3 prohibition (rec 5) aligns with EPISOD; the type-2 manometry pathway is now applied selectively.

Several of its core recommendations are **directly contradicted** by the 2025 statement (4 L as criterion standard, the 3–8 h second-dose window, multi-day low-residue diet, simethicone, non-simethicone adjuncts) — see [[#Contradictions / Open Questions]]. Per source priority, entity pages assert the 2025 claims. Captured here for landmark reference and for the **non-conflicting detail it still uniquely supplies**: the product-level preparation table, the bowel-preparation scoring scales, and agent-specific safety cautions.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee; Saltzman JR, Cash BD, Pasha SF, et al. Bowel preparation before colonoscopy. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;81:781-794.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.09.048)
- **Authors:** John R. Saltzman, Brooks D. Cash (Chair), Shabana F. Pasha, Dayna S. Early, V. Raman Muthusamy, Mouen A. Khashab, Krishnavel V. Chathadi, Robert D. Fanelli (SAGES representative), Vinay Chandrasekhara, Jenifer R. Lightdale, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy); Volume 81, No. 4
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.09.048](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.09.048)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice Committee guideline updating a prior ASCRS/ASGE/SAGES consensus document and technology status evaluation report on bowel preparation before [[colonoscopy]]. Literature search: PubMed, January 1975 – March 2014. Recommendations graded with GRADE.

Frames inadequate preparation as a driver of failed lesion detection, increased adverse-event risk, and incomplete colonoscopy — citing incomplete colonoscopy rates of 10%–20%, with inadequate prep the single most common reason (~25% of failed colonoscopies in one 8910-procedure audit). Defines the ideal preparation (empties the colon rapidly, no gross or histologic mucosal alteration, no discomfort or fluid/electrolyte shifts, safe, convenient, tolerable, inexpensive) and concedes that **no currently available preparation has all these characteristics**.

Its central positions are split dosing and 4 L PEG-ELS. Split dosing (part of the dose on the day of the procedure) yields higher-quality examinations, increases adenoma detection, and improves tolerance; the second dose should fall **3 to 8 hours** before the procedure and be complete **≥2 hours before sedation** (per ASA fasting guidance) to limit aspiration risk. The guideline names **4 L split-dose PEG-ELS the "current criterion standard"** — a position the 2025 statement reverses.

The durable value of this document is descriptive rather than prescriptive: a product-level comparison of the nine commercially available preparations (composition, volume, FDA status, 2015 pricing, dosing) and the three validated preparation-quality scales.

## Key Findings / Claims — Recommendations

All **9 recommendations, verbatim**, with GRADE quality of evidence as given. (The source renders quality as circle glyphs; mapped per its Table 1: ⊕⊕⊕⊕ High, ⊕⊕⊕◯ Moderate, ⊕⊕◯◯ Low, ⊕◯◯◯ Very low.)

1. "We recommend that bowel preparations be individualized by the prescribing provider for each patient based on efficacy, cost, safety, and tolerability considerations balanced with the patient's overall health, comorbid conditions, and preferences." (**High quality**)
2. "We recommend that verbal counseling regarding preparation administration be provided to patients along with written instructions that are simple and easy to follow and in their native language." (**Moderate quality**)
3. "We suggest intensive education and more aggressive than standard bowel preparation regimens be considered for patients with predictors for inadequate preparation." (**Low quality**)
4. "We recommend a low-residue diet be used in conjunction with FDA-approved purgatives for bowel preparation before colonoscopy." (**Moderate quality**)
5. "We recommend split-dose regimens for all patients and/or same day preparations for afternoon colonoscopies with a portion of the preparation taken within 3 to 8 hours of the procedure to enhance colonic cleansing and patient tolerance." (**Moderate quality**)
6. "We recommend that sodium phosphate and magnesium citrate preparations not be used in the elderly or patients with renal disease or taking medications that alter renal blood flow or electrolyte excretion." (**High quality**)
7. "We recommend against the use of metoclopramide as an adjunct to oral bowel preparation." (**Moderate quality**)
8. "We recommend that endoscopists document the quality of the bowel preparation at the time of colonoscopy with regard to adequacy." (**High quality**)
9. "We recommend that patients with inadequate preparation be offered a repeat colonoscopy within 1 year." (**Moderate quality**)

## Bowel Preparation Scales (Table 3)

| Scale | Scored on | Range | Anchors |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aronchick Scale** | Whole colon (segments not evaluated) | 1–5 | 1 Excellent (>95% mucosa seen); 2 Good (clear liquid over ≤25% mucosa, >90% seen); 3 Fair (semisolid stool not suctionable, >90% seen); 4 Poor (semisolid stool not suctionable, <90% seen); 5 Inadequate (repeat preparation needed) |
| **Ottawa Bowel Preparation Scale** | Each of 3 segments (right, transverse/descending, sigmoid/rectum), 0–4 each, **plus** whole-colon fluid score (0 small, 1 moderate, 2 large) | 0 (excellent) – 14 (very poor) | Per segment: 0 Excellent (mucosal detail clearly visible); 1 Good (minimal turbid fluid); 2 Fair (must suction liquid to view); 3 Poor (must wash and suction for reasonable view); 4 Inadequate (solid stool not cleared) |
| **Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS)** | Each of 3 segments (right, transverse, left), 0–3 each, **after all cleansing maneuvers** | 0 (very poor) – 9 (excellent) | 0 Unprepared segment, stool cannot be cleared; 1 Portion of mucosa seen, other areas obscured by retained material; 2 Minor residual material, mucosa generally well seen; 3 Entire mucosa well seen |

- Aronchick is a global rating best suited to **comparing different preparations** (assesses quality on initial inspection); Ottawa validated against Aronchick; BBPS found both valid and reliable.
- Prep quality should be graded **after** efforts to remove residual effluent and debris are complete.
- USMSTF definition of an adequate examination cited here: one allowing confidence that lesions other than small (≤5 mm) polyps were generally not obscured by residual colonic contents.

## Key Findings / Claims — Supporting Detail

**Agent-specific safety and performance (largely still applicable):**
- **PEG-ELS:** 5%–15% do not complete it (palatability, volume). No significant physiologic change in weight, vital signs, electrolytes, chemistries, or CBC. **Does not alter colonic mucosal histology** — usable in suspected [[inflammatory-bowel-disease]] without obscuring diagnosis or tissue analysis. Generally safe in pre-existing electrolyte imbalance and where sodium load is poorly tolerated (renal failure, congestive heart failure, advanced liver disease with [[ascites]]). Works best ingested quickly (240 mL every 10 min); chilling improves palatability. Reported adverse events: nausea ± vomiting, abdominal pain, rare pulmonary aspiration, Mallory-Weiss tear, pancreatitis, colitis, lavage-induced pill malabsorption, cardiac arrhythmia, SIADH exacerbation.
- **Adding prokinetics or bisacodyl to 4 L PEG-ELS does not improve tolerance or cleansing**; adding enemas does not improve efficacy and increases discomfort.
- **PEG-SD (PEG-3350 + sports drink):** hyposmotic, **not FDA approved** for colonoscopy prep, **not equivalent** to FDA-approved 2 L isosmotic PEG-ELS — despite wide use. Versus FDA-approved 2 L PEG-ELS, changes from baseline in serum Na, K, Cl were significantly greater with PEG-SD; hyponatremia 3.9% vs 2.2% (OR 1.82, 95% CI 0.45–8.62; not statistically significant). One study suggested a lower adenoma detection rate with 2 L PEG-SD/bisacodyl vs 4 L PEG-ELS.
- **Ascorbic-acid PEG:** use cautiously in G6PD deficiency (ascorbic acid may provoke hemolysis).
- **OSS:** noninferior to 2 L PEG-ELS with ascorbic acid; vs 4 L SF-PEG-ELS, less bloating and more frequent excellent preparation (71.4% vs 34.3%, P = .01). Vs split-dose sodium picosulfate/magnesium citrate (n = 338): higher successful prep (94.7% vs 85.7%, P = .006) and more excellent preps (54% vs 26%, P < .001), with no difference in treatment-emergent adverse events. Limited safety data.
- **Sodium picosulfate/magnesium citrate:** stimulant (picosulfate) + osmotic (magnesium citrate) mechanism. Phase 3 trials achieved adequate preparation in only **83%–84.2%**. Rare hyponatremia and clinically significant electrolyte disturbance.
- **Magnesium citrate:** not FDA approved as a colonoscopy prep; limited stand-alone efficacy data; magnesium toxicity (bradycardia, hypotension, nausea, drowsiness) with deaths reported — **not recommended for routine preparation**.
- **Sodium phosphate:** brand-name aqueous form voluntarily withdrawn; **FDA box warning on the prescription tablet form**. Acute phosphate nephropathy (age- and dose-related, reported even without underlying disease); hyperphosphatemia in up to 40% of healthy patients completing prep; also elevated BUN, increased plasma osmolality, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia, seizures.
- **Bisacodyl:** can cause cramping and has been associated with [[colon-ischemia|ischemic colitis]] — 5 and 10 mg doses recommended when used adjunctively. The only FDA-approved 2 L PEG-ELS + bisacodyl regimen was discontinued by the manufacturer in 2013.
- **Metoclopramide:** reduced nausea/bloating in one study but did not improve cleansing; a second showed no advantage for either tolerance or cleansing → recommended against (Rec 7).
- **Simethicone:** does **not** significantly change preparation quality, but reduces adherent bubbles, which may enhance visualization.
- **Senna:** no difference vs bisacodyl as a PEG-ELS adjunct; improves prep quality and reduces PEG-ELS volume required.

**Administration and logistics:**
- Clear liquids may be taken up to **2 hours** before the procedure; preparation must be complete **≥2 hours before sedation** (ASA guidance) to avoid aspiration — institutional policies may vary. See [[endoscopy-sedation]].
- Red liquids should be avoided (mistaken for blood / obscure mucosal detail).
- Unclear whether a clear liquid diet the day before offers any advantage over a low-fiber diet for prep quality; low-residue diets are at least as effective as clear liquids and improve satisfaction. In hospitalized patients, clear liquid diet before the purgative was the **only dietary modification that improved prep quality**.
- Split-dosing is recommended for **both morning and afternoon** procedures; for afternoon procedures the prep may be given entirely on the morning of the examination (superior quality/tolerability, less impact on activities of daily living, better sleep). Hospitalized patients prefer split-dosing though prep quality did not differ vs morning-only.
- When educated on the benefit, the vast majority of patients are willing to wake at 2–3 AM to complete a split-dose regimen.
- **NG tube administration:** PEG-ELS gut lavage via NG tube is the most effective cleansing method in infants and children, and is an option when patients cannot drink or have a significant swallowing disorder. **High-dose (6–8 L) PEG-ELS via NG tube is effective as rapid preparation in [[acute-lower-gi-bleeding]].** Risk of severe, life-threatening adverse events including aspiration; prokinetics/antiemetics and avoiding over-rapid instillation improve tolerability.
- **Pediatrics:** no national standards; topic deferred to a prior ASGE guideline.
- Patient education significantly improves prep quality — written instructions in the patient's native language, visual aids, educational booklets, and smartphone applications all described.

**Inadequate preparation:**
- **The most important predictor of inadequate preparation is a previous inadequate preparation.** Other predictors: later colonoscopy start time, failure to follow instructions, hospitalized status, procedural indication of [[chronic-idiopathic-constipation|constipation]], tricyclic antidepressant use, male sex, history of cirrhosis, stroke, or dementia; [[obesity]] may also predict poor prep. Additional factors: non-English speaking, Medicaid insurance, single and/or inpatient status, polypharmacy (especially constipating medications such as opiates), advanced age, diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, poor adherence, erroneous purgative timing, longer appointment wait times.
- Fewer than 20% of patients with inadequate preparation reported failing to follow instructions.
- Consequences: missed lesions, cancelled procedures, increased procedural time and cost, potential increase in adverse events. With **fair** preps, 28%–42% had adenomas found when repeated within 3 years, including up to 27% with advanced adenomas. Adenoma and advanced-adenoma **miss rates were 35% and 36%** for colonoscopies repeated in <1 year. Intraprocedural cleansing accounts for an estimated **17% of total colonoscopy procedural time**.
- Patients with persistent brown effluent before the procedure should be considered for large-volume enemas or additional oral preparation before proceeding.
- No standardized approach to an inadequately prepped colon found at intubation. Anecdotal approaches: instilling an enema through the colonoscope then reattempting after evacuation, or additional oral preparation then reattempting — both require recovery from sedation and resedation. Irrigation devices permit more aggressive water instillation than standard pumps or syringe flushing.
- Immediate repeat after additional/more aggressive preparation is preferred in most patients; otherwise repeat **within 1 year**, with a **shorter interval if advanced neoplasia is discovered** in an inadequately prepped colon. When instructed to repeat the following day, 47% complied — significantly higher than for later intervals.

## Relevance to Wiki

- **[[colonoscopy]]** — the page's Bowel Preparation section already asserts the 2025 positions and should continue to. This source contributes only non-conflicting material: the **preparation-quality scales** (Aronchick / Ottawa / BBPS) and the **product-level preparation table**, which remain useful now that 2025 holds no single purgative superior and leaves agent selection to patient factors.
- **[[acute-lower-gi-bleeding]]** — supports high-dose (6–8 L) PEG-ELS via NG tube as rapid preparation for urgent colonoscopy.
- **[[colonoscopy-surveillance]]** — corroborates repeat within 1 year after inadequate preparation, with a shorter interval when advanced neoplasia is found in an inadequately prepped colon; concordant with the 2025 12-month figure.
- **[[inflammatory-bowel-disease]]** — PEG-ELS does not alter colonic mucosal histology and so may be used in suspected IBD without compromising diagnosis or tissue analysis.
- Historical anchor for the ASGE line of bowel-prep guidance alongside [[acg-2014-bowel-cleansing]]; both are superseded by the 2025 multi-society statement.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

**Superseded by [[usmstf-2025-bowel-prep]] / [[acg-2025-bowel-prep]] (2025 wins per source priority — Guidelines tier, newer publication date):**

| Topic | ASGE 2015 | USMSTF/ACG 2025 | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Preparation volume** | 4 L split-dose PEG-ELS is the **"current criterion standard"**; highest-quality preps achieved with 4 L | **No single purgative is superior** (Strong/High); **2 L regimens preferred over 4 L** (Weak/Moderate) | 2025 wins — 4 L is no longer the reference standard; it is retained only within the high-risk protocol |
| **Second-dose timing** | Portion taken **within 3 to 8 hours** of the procedure (Rec 5) | Second portion **begins 4–6 h before**, completed **≥2 h before** procedure start (Strong/Moderate) | 2025 wins — narrower window; the 2015 3 h and 8 h extremes are out |
| **Diet** | **Low-residue diet** with FDA-approved purgatives (Rec 4); text describes low-residue diets "often recommended for **several days** before the procedure" | **Limit dietary modification to the day before** for average-risk ambulatory patients (Strong/High); low-residue or full liquids for early/midday meals | 2025 wins — multi-day restriction now reserved for **high-risk** patients only (2025 Rec 23: restrict vegetables/legumes 2–3 days prior) |
| **Simethicone** | "Simethicone does **not** significantly change the quality of the bowel preparation" — no recommendation issued | **Suggest adjunctive oral simethicone ≥320 mg** (Weak/Moderate) | 2025 wins — direct reversal on a positive recommendation |
| **Non-simethicone adjuncts** | Bisacodyl / magnesium citrate / senna presented favorably as volume-reducing adjuncts to PEG-ELS | **Against routine use of non-simethicone adjuncts** (Weak/Low) | 2025 wins — bisacodyl retained only in the specific high-risk 4 L regimen (2025 Rec 25) |
| **Quality target** | Document prep quality "with regard to adequacy" (Rec 8) — **no numeric target** | Track adequate-prep rate at **endoscopist AND unit** level; **target >90%** (Strong/Moderate) | 2025 wins and is additive (note [[acg-2014-bowel-cleansing]] set ≥85% per-physician; 2025 raised it to >90% and added the unit level) |

**Concordant / additive (2015 still corroborates):**
- Split-dose for all patients; same-day acceptable for afternoon colonoscopy (2015 Rec 5 ≈ 2025 Recs 9–10). 2025 adds that same-day is **inferior** for morning colonoscopy (Weak/Low) — 2015 is silent, not conflicting.
- Verbal + written instructions in the patient's native language (2015 Rec 2 ≈ 2025 Rec 1).
- Individualize prep by efficacy/cost/safety/tolerability and comorbidity (2015 Rec 1 ≈ 2025 Rec 7).
- Intensified education and more aggressive regimens for predictors of inadequate prep (2015 Rec 3 ≈ 2025 Recs 23–24).
- Avoid NaP and magnesium citrate in the elderly/renal disease (2015 Rec 6) ≈ 2025's generalized "against hyperosmotic regimens in patients at risk for volume overload or electrolyte disturbances" (Strong/High).
- Against metoclopramide (2015 Rec 7) — subsumed by 2025's against-routine-non-simethicone-adjuncts.
- Grade prep quality only after residual debris is cleared (2015 text ≈ 2025 Rec 16).
- Repeat within 1 year after inadequate prep (2015 Rec 9 ≈ 2025 Rec 22's 12 months). 2025 additionally requires **≤3 months** when the colonoscopy was prompted by an abnormal noncolonoscopic CRC test — 2015 has no counterpart.

**Open questions carried by this source:**
- Whether a clear liquid diet the day before confers any advantage over a low-fiber diet — unresolved in 2015; 2025 permits either.
- Safety of PEG-SD combined with bisacodyl "has not been well reported"; whether bisacodyl adds benefit or only side effects was explicitly unclear in 2015 — 2025 resolves against routine use.
- Limited safety data for OSS (no serious adverse effects reported at the time).
- No standardized approach to the inadequately prepped colon found at intubation; 2025 addresses this with same-day salvage maneuvers (Weak/Moderate).
- Widely used PEG-SD (Miralax/Gatorade) remains **not FDA approved** for colonoscopy preparation and is not equivalent to isosmotic 2 L PEG-ELS — a caution not carried forward explicitly in the 2025 statement and still worth surfacing.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of deep enteroscopy in the management of small-bowel disorders. Gastrointest Endosc. 2015;82(4):600-607.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.046)
- **Authors:** Khashab MA, Pasha SF, Muthusamy VR, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.046](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.06.046)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary
ASGE position statement on deep enteroscopy (DE) for small-bowel disorders. DE encompasses double-balloon enteroscopy (DBE), single-balloon enteroscopy (SBE), and spiral enteroscopy (SE) — the techniques of choice for tissue acquisition and therapy in the midgut (ampulla of Vater to ileocecal valve). DBE (introduced 2001, Yamamoto) is the most studied and most effective for total enteroscopy. Video capsule endoscopy (VCE) remains first-line for small-bowel evaluation in obscure GI bleeding (OGIB); DE is reserved for positive VCE findings, surgically altered anatomy, high suspicion of angiectasias, tissue diagnosis of tumors, or Crohn's disease abnormalities within reach.

Depth of intubation with DBE: 240–360 cm past ligament of Treitz (antegrade) and 102–140 cm past ileocecal valve (retrograde). Antegrade route for proximal two-thirds, retrograde for distal one third (based on capsule transit times). Total enteroscopy = intubation of entire small bowel by one or both routes; DBE total enteroscopy rate 0–86% (highest in Asian populations). Pooled DE adverse-event rate for all indications: minor 9.1%, major 0.72%. Interventions during DE: biopsy, mucosal injection, polypectomy, stricture dilation, hemostasis (APC, electrocoagulation, hemoclips), and foreign-body/retained-capsule retrieval.

## Key Findings / Claims
- DBE, SBE, and SE all have diagnostic and therapeutic capability; DBE most established.
- SBE potential advantages over DBE: shorter setup, single-balloon cycle, simpler control panel, non-latex balloon.
- SE uses rotate-to-advance technology; swift exam, stability, mucosal inspection on insertion and withdrawal.
- NaviAid (through-the-scope balloon on a standard adult colonoscope) is a newer device with limited data — no recommendation yet.
- Short DBE model used for difficult ileocolonoscopy, ERCP in altered anatomy, proximal small-bowel endoscopy.

## Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE)
1. We recommend DE as an effective and safe technique for small-bowel examination. *(High)*
2. We recommend DBE as the most effective deep enteroscopy technique for achieving total enteroscopy. *(Moderate)*
3. We suggest either DBE or SBE for retrograde enteroscopy. *(Low)*
4. We recommend VCE as the first-line diagnostic tool for small-bowel evaluation in patients with OGIB. DE may be considered when positive findings are identified on VCE. *(Very low)*
5. We suggest that in select circumstances (eg, surgically altered anatomy or high suspicion for small-bowel angiectasias) DE may be considered as the initial small-bowel diagnostic procedure in patients with OGIB. *(Low)*
6. We suggest that DE be used for tissue diagnosis and therapeutic interventions in patients with small-bowel tumors detected by other diagnostic tests (eg, VCE) or in those with high suspicion for tumors despite initial negative testing. *(Low)*
7. We suggest that DE be considered in Crohn's disease patients with abnormalities seen on other imaging studies, if these abnormalities are within reach of the enteroscope. DE allows endoscopic and histologic evaluation and the potential for therapeutic interventions such as hemostasis, stricture dilation, or foreign body retrieval. *(Low)*

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[device-assisted-enteroscopy]] — adds non-bleeding indications (small-bowel tumors, Crohn's disease) and total-enteroscopy definition.
- Supports [[small-bowel-bleeding]] and [[capsule-endoscopy]] algorithm (VCE-first, DE for positive findings).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Older (2015) source; obscure GI bleeding (OGIB) terminology has since been refined to small-bowel bleeding by newer ASGE/ACG documents already ingested. No conflicts — technique data is complementary.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of ERCP in benign diseases of the biliary tract. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;81(4):795-803.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.11.019)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Chathadi KV, Chandrasekhara V, et al.)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.11.019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.11.019)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement on [[ercp|ERCP]] for benign biliary disease. ERCP has evolved into an almost exclusively therapeutic procedure; cross-sectional imaging (US, CT, MRCP, EUS) and intraoperative cholangiography select patients for therapeutic ERCP. Successful endoscopic cholangiography with relief of obstruction should be achievable in >90% of patients.

Core indications covered: [[choledocholithiasis]] (stone extraction, mechanical/cholangioscopy-guided lithotripsy for difficult stones, endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation), benign [[biliary-stricture|biliary strictures]] (dilation + stenting; evolving role of fully covered SEMS), postoperative bile leaks (ERCP is first-line), sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (treat type I, do not perform ERCP for type III — EPISOD trial), and congenital choledochocele/choledochal cyst. Post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis with rectal indomethacin ± pancreatic stent is recommended for high-risk patients including suspected SOD.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE quality of evidence):**

1. We recommend that diagnostic ERCP not be undertaken for the evaluation of pancreaticobiliary-type pain in the absence of objective abnormalities on other pancreaticobiliary imaging or laboratory studies. (Moderate)
2. We recommend that routine ERCP before laparoscopic cholecystectomy not be performed in the absence of objective signs of biliary obstruction or stone. (Moderate)
3. We recommend that ERCP in patients with acute biliary pancreatitis be limited to those with concomitant cholangitis or biliary obstruction. (High)
4. We recommend ERCP with dilation and stent placement for benign biliary strictures. (Moderate)
5. We recommend that ERCP be undertaken as first-line therapy for postoperative biliary leaks. (High)
6. We suggest that cholangioscopy be considered as an adjunctive technique for the management of difficult bile duct stones not amenable to removal after sphincterotomy with or without balloon dilation or mechanical lithotripsy. (Low)
7. We suggest that cholangioscopy with directed biopsy be considered as an adjunctive technique for the characterization of biliary strictures. (Low)
8. We recommend ERCP with sphincterotomy for patients with type I SOD. (Moderate)
9. We recommend against the performance of ERCP for the evaluation or treatment of type III SOD. (High)
10. We recommend rectal indomethacin with or without a pancreatic stent for prophylaxis against post-ERCP pancreatitis when ERCP is performed in patients with suspected SOD. (Moderate)

**Other points:**
- Sensitivity/specificity of ERCP for CBD stones >95%, but small stones may be missed (cholangiography false-negative up to 13%).
- Difficult stones: mechanical lithotripsy, peroral cholangioscopy with electrohydraulic or laser lithotripsy (clears 83%-100% of difficult extrahepatic stones); endoscopic papillary large-balloon (≥12 mm) dilation + sphincterotomy gives high clearance with low (2.3%) PEP rate.
- Bile leaks: ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy and/or stenting is the preferred strategy.
- Fully covered SEMS for refractory benign strictures: larger caliber and longer patency allow fewer procedures than serial multiple-plastic-stent exchanges; role still evolving (RCTs needed).
- Surgically altered anatomy (Roux-en-Y, Billroth II): device-assisted (balloon) enteroscopy-ERCP or EUS-guided biliary access by experts when standard access fails.
- EPISOD trial: sphincterotomy did not benefit type III SOD and carried significant adverse-event rates.

## Relevance to Wiki

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Evans JA, et al; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of endoscopy in the management of premalignant and malignant conditions of the stomach. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;82(1):1-8.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.03.1967)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Evans JA, Chandrasekhara V, Chathadi KV, et al.)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.03.1967](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.03.1967)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement (GRADE) on the endoscopic management of premalignant and malignant gastric conditions — a revision/expansion of the 2006 ASGE upper-GI premalignant-surveillance document. Covers gastric polyps (fundic gland, hyperplastic, adenomatous; sporadic vs FAP/Lynch), [[gastric-intestinal-metaplasia|gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM)]] and metaplastic atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, gastric carcinoids (types 1–4), [[gastric-adenocarcinoma|gastric adenocarcinoma]] (biopsy, EUS staging, palliation of malignant gastric outlet obstruction), gastric MALT lymphoma, and gastric [[gastrointestinal-stromal-tumor|GISTs]]/subepithelial lesions.

Core themes: gastric polyp histology cannot be predicted endoscopically → biopsy/resect; hyperplastic and adenomatous polyps carry malignant potential (FGPs do not, except in FAP); GIM and pernicious anemia confer increased gastric-cancer risk and warrant individualized surveillance; gastric cancer requires adequate biopsy sampling (≥7) and EUS for locoregional staging; EUS ± FNA is the cornerstone for evaluating gastric subepithelial lesions. Note this is an **older** document — for current gastric-premalignant surveillance the page's primary recommendations follow [[acg-2025-gastric-premalignant|ACG 2025]], [[aga-2020-gastric-intestinal-metaplasia|AGA 2020 GIM]], [[aga-2021-atrophic-gastritis|AGA 2021 atrophic gastritis]], and [[aga-2026-gastric-polyps|AGA 2026 gastric polyps]]; this source contributes the endoscopic-technique and staging detail.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE quality of evidence; ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high, ⊕⊕⊕◯ moderate, ⊕⊕◯◯ low, ⊕◯◯◯ very low; "recommend" = strong, "suggest" = conditional/weak):**

1. We recommend solitary gastric polyps undergo biopsy or be resected when possible. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
2. We suggest polypectomy of fundic gland polyps 1 cm or larger, hyperplastic polyps 0.5 cm or larger, and adenomatous polyps of any size when possible. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
3. We suggest surveillance endoscopy 1 year after removing adenomatous gastric polyps. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
4. In the setting of multiple polyps, we recommend biopsy or resection of the largest polyps and representative biopsy specimens be taken from others. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
5. In the setting of multiple hyperplastic or adenomatous polyps, we suggest systematic sampling of the surrounding nonpolypoid gastric mucosa to assess for H pylori and metaplastic atrophic gastritis. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
6. We suggest sampling and, when feasible, resection of large gastric polyps in patients with FAP to confirm histology and to assess for dysplasia. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
7. We suggest surveillance endoscopy for patients with GIM who are at increased risk of gastric cancer due to ethnic background or family history. Optimal surveillance intervals have not been extensively studied and should be individualized. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
8. We recommend endoscopic resection and surveillance endoscopy for patients with confirmed GIM with HGD when feasible. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
9. We suggest endoscopy within 6 months of the diagnosis of pernicious anemia or the development of upper GI symptoms in patients with pernicious anemia. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
10. We recommend EUS for local staging of gastric carcinoids. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
11. We suggest endoscopic resection of small (<1 cm) type 1 and type 2 gastric carcinoids that do not demonstrate aggressive features such as angioinvasion, muscular wall invasion, high proliferative index, and/or metastatic disease and endoscopic surveillance thereafter every 1 to 2 years. We suggest endoscopic removal for type 3 and 4 gastric carcinoids (isolated and <1 cm in diameter). (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)
12. We recommend at least 7 biopsy samples be obtained of gastric masses or the heaped-up edges of ulcers suspicious for gastric adenocarcinoma. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
13. We recommend EUS and when applicable, EUS-FNA to locally stage gastric cancer. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
14. We recommend endoscopically placed self-expanding metal stents for the palliation of malignant gastric outlet obstruction due to gastric cancer in patients with poor performance status or nonoperable anatomy. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
15. We recommend EUS with or without FNA in the evaluation of gastric submucosal lesions. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
16. We suggest annual EUS surveillance of GISTs smaller than 2 cm if surgical resection is not performed to determine progression of size or change in echo features. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)

**Other points:**
- Gastric polyp histology cannot be reliably distinguished by endoscopic appearance → biopsy/polypectomy when detected. 70%–90% of gastric epithelial polyps are FGPs or hyperplastic.
- **FGPs:** associated with long-term PPI use; **not** an increased cancer risk in the absence of FAP. **Hyperplastic polyps:** dysplasia/focal cancer in 5%–19%; risk factors for dysplasia = size >1 cm, pedunculated morphology. **Adenomatous polyps:** malignant potential; recurrence up to 2.6% after complete endoscopic excision; cancer in 1.3% on follow-up. Endoscopic submucosal resection reduces recurrence vs EMR but increases adverse events.
- Gastric polyps occur with H pylori and environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis → polypectomy + treat H pylori.
- Gastric subepithelial/submucosal lesions arising from the muscularis propria can be removed endoscopically only by practitioners with dedicated training and skill.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[gastric-polyps]] — additive endoscopic thresholds: resect FGP ≥1 cm, hyperplastic ≥0.5 cm, adenoma any size; surveillance 1 y after adenoma removal; sample surrounding nonpolypoid mucosa (H pylori + atrophic gastritis); largest-polyp + representative sampling when multiple.
- Updates [[gastric-intestinal-metaplasia]] / [[gastric-premalignant-conditions]] — individualized surveillance for high-risk GIM (ethnicity/family history); endoscopic resection + surveillance for GIM with HGD.
- Updates [[atrophic-gastritis]] (pernicious-anemia context) — endoscopy within 6 months of pernicious-anemia diagnosis or new upper-GI symptoms (gastric carcinoid/adenocarcinoma risk).
- Updates [[gastric-adenocarcinoma]] — ≥7 biopsies of masses/ulcer edges; EUS ± FNA for locoregional staging; SEMS for palliation of malignant gastric outlet obstruction.
- Updates [[gastroenteropancreatic-neuroendocrine-tumors|gastric carcinoid]] management — EUS staging; resection criteria by type (1/2 <1 cm without aggressive features; isolated type 3/4 <1 cm).
- Cross-links [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] and [[gastrointestinal-stromal-tumor|GIST/subepithelial lesions]] — EUS ± FNA for subepithelial lesions; annual EUS surveillance of GIST <2 cm if unresected.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Older than** the current gastric guidelines on the wiki ([[acg-2025-gastric-premalignant|ACG 2025]], [[aga-2020-gastric-intestinal-metaplasia|AGA 2020 GIM]], [[aga-2021-atrophic-gastritis|AGA 2021]], [[aga-2026-gastric-polyps|AGA 2026 gastric polyps]]). Where they specify GIM risk-stratification, staging systems (OLGA/OLGIM), and surveillance intervals, those newer documents govern the page's primary recommendations; this 2015 source contributes endoscopic technique/sampling and staging/palliation detail only — it does not overwrite the newer surveillance schemes.
- Predates routine endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) adoption for early gastric cancer in Western practice — see [[asge-2023-esd|ASGE 2023 ESD]] for current early-gastric-cancer resection criteria.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Shergill AK, Lightdale JR, Bruining DH, et al. The role of endoscopy in inflammatory bowel disease. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;81(5):1101–1121.e13.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.10.030)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Amandeep K. Shergill, Jenifer R. Lightdale, et al.)
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.10.030](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.10.030)
- **Type:** guideline (ASGE Standards of Practice; GRADE-rated)

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement on the role of endoscopy across the full arc of IBD care: **diagnosis and subtyping, small-bowel evaluation, disease-activity/mucosal-healing assessment, postoperative recurrence, dysplasia surveillance, and endoscopic therapy of strictures.** For diagnosis, colonoscopy **with ileoscopy** plus multi-site mucosal biopsies is the cornerstone and distinguishes CD from UC in ~90% of cases; ileoscopy is key to separating true CD ileitis from UC backwash ileitis, and a cecal/periappendiceal patch in UC should not be misread as CD. Small-bowel CD is evaluated with capsule endoscopy (after a patency capsule or cross-sectional enterography when obstruction is possible) and device-assisted enteroscopy for reachable lesions; EUS aids characterization of perianal fistulizing CD.

For surveillance, the guideline endorses screening colonoscopy 8 years after colitis onset, then surveillance every 1–3 years, with **chromoendoscopy and targeted biopsies as the preferred dysplasia-detection technique** (random biopsies remain a reasonable alternative when chromoendoscopy yield is limited) — content that aligns with and predates the [[asge-2015-scenic-ibd-dysplasia|SCENIC]] consensus. It recommends the Montreal Classification for standardized phenotyping, pouch surveillance for highest-risk patients (prior dysplasia/cancer), neoterminal-ileum evaluation 6–12 months after resection to risk-stratify recurrence (Rutgeerts score), and **endoscopic balloon dilation for symptomatic benign IBD strictures ≤4 cm**. A UC colon stricture is malignant until proven otherwise.

## Key Findings / Claims
- Colonoscopy + ileoscopy + multi-site biopsy is the diagnostic cornerstone; differentiates CD vs UC in ~90%.
- Ileoscopy distinguishes CD ileitis (extensive/patchy, ulcers, stricture, worse than cecal inflammation) from UC backwash ileitis (short, contiguous, mild, no stricture; seen in up to 25% of UC pancolitis).
- Cecal/periappendiceal patch in otherwise normal right colon in UC is not CD and does not change UC outcomes.
- Stricturing disease is rare in UC → raises possibility of CD or malignancy; a UC colon stricture is malignant until proven otherwise (consider surgery if it cannot be fully examined/biopsied).
- Small-bowel CD: capsule endoscopy after negative ileocolonoscopy in non-obstructive suspected CD; obtain patency capsule / SBFT / CTE / MRE first if known small-bowel CD; enteroscopy for reachable lesions; EUS for perianal fistula characterization.
- Mucosal healing is an increasingly important treatment target; endoscopy assesses activity and response.
- Postoperative CD: endoscopy of the neoterminal ileum 6–12 months after resection risk-stratifies recurrence (Rutgeerts score) and guides therapy.
- Dysplasia surveillance: screening colonoscopy at 8 years; then q1–3 years; chromoendoscopy with targeted biopsies preferred; management of dysplastic lesions by resectability (proctocolectomy if not endoscopically resectable, dysplasia at base, or invisible HGD/multifocal LGD).
- Pouch surveillance: highest-risk patients (prior dysplasia/cancer) considered for annual pouchoscopy with proximal (pouch) and distal (anal transition zone) biopsies; PSC, refractory pouchitis, type C pouch mucosa may warrant surveillance.
- Endoscopic balloon dilation: effective for symptomatic benign CD/anastomotic strictures ≤4 cm (durable response ~58% in one systematic review, avoiding surgery).

### Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE evidence quality)
1. We recommend colonoscopy with ileoscopy for the initial evaluation of IBD and for differentiating IBD subtypes. *(high quality)*
2. We recommend mucosal biopsy specimens from multiple sites during the initial endoscopic evaluation of IBD. *(high quality)*
3. We recommend flexible sigmoidoscopy in patients with IBD when colonoscopy is contraindicated and to evaluate for other inflammatory etiologies before escalating therapies in patients with refractory disease. *(moderate quality)*
4. We recommend that EGD be performed in pediatric patients with suspected IBD at the time of ileocolonoscopy. *(moderate quality)*
5. We recommend CE to evaluate the small intestine in patients with suspected CD who have no obstructive symptoms and negative ileocolonoscopy results. *(moderate quality)*
6. We recommend that a patency capsule, small-bowel follow-through, CT enterography, or magnetic resonance enterography be performed before CE in patients with known small-bowel CD involvement. *(moderate quality)*
7. We recommend CE in patients with known CD and unexplained symptoms only when abnormalities detected with CE will alter management. *(moderate quality)*
8. We suggest enteroscopy in patients with IBD who have abnormalities within reach of the enteroscope seen on other imaging studies to facilitate endoscopic and histologic evaluation and the potential for therapeutic interventions. *(moderate quality)*
9. We suggest EUS for characterizing and managing fistulous perianal CD in conjunction with other imaging modalities. *(low quality)*
10. We recommend the Montreal Classification System be used to standardize reporting of disease extent and IBD phenotypes for both UC and CD. *(moderate quality)*
11. We recommend endoscopic and histologic assessment of the pouch and afferent limb in symptomatic patients. *(high quality)*
12. We suggest endoscopic evaluation of the neoterminal ileum 6 to 12 months after surgery in order to risk-stratify patients whose medical management may be affected by endoscopic recurrence. *(moderate quality)*
13. We recommend that all patients with UC or CD colitis undergo a screening colonoscopy 8 years after disease onset to (1) re-evaluate extent of disease and (2) initiate surveillance for colorectal neoplasia. *(moderate quality)*
14. We recommend surveillance colonoscopy be performed every 1 to 3 years beginning after 8 years of disease in patients with UC with macroscopic or histologic evidence of inflammation proximal to and including the sigmoid colon and for patients with Crohn's colitis with greater than one-third of colon involvement. *(moderate quality)*
15. We recommend chromoendoscopy with targeted biopsies as the preferred surveillance technique to maximize dysplasia detection. *(moderate quality)*
16. We suggest that chromoendoscopy-targeted biopsies are sufficient for dysplasia surveillance in patients with IBD and that consideration should be given to taking two biopsies from each colon segment for histologic staging to assess extent and severity of inflammation. *(low quality)*
17. We suggest that random biopsies with targeted biopsies of any suspicious appearing lesions remain a reasonable alternative for dysplasia surveillance if the yield of chromoendoscopy is reduced by significant underlying inflammation, significant pseudopolyposis, or poor preparation or if chromoendoscopy is not available. *(low quality)*
18. We recommend that patients with IBD whose polypoid dysplastic lesions have been removed completely receive endoscopic surveillance at 1 to 6 months and at 12 months, with yearly surveillance thereafter. *(moderate quality)*
19. We suggest that patients with IBD whose non-polypoid dysplastic lesions have been removed completely receive endoscopic surveillance at 1 to 6 months and at 12 months, with yearly surveillance thereafter. *(low quality)*
20. We recommend proctocolectomy in patients with IBD if a detected lesion is not endoscopically resectable, if there is evidence of dysplasia at the base of the lesion, or if endoscopically invisible HGD or multifocal LGD is found in the colon during a high-quality chromoendoscopy examination. *(moderate quality)*
21. We recommend IBD-associated benign strictures ≤4 cm in length manifesting obstructive symptoms be managed with endoscopic balloon dilation when feasible. *(low quality)*

*GRADE symbols in the source: ⨁⨁⨁⨁ high, ⨁⨁⨁◯ moderate, ⨁⨁◯◯ low, ⨁◯◯◯ very low.*

## Relevance to Wiki
- [[crohns-disease]] — diagnostic ileoscopy, CE algorithm for small-bowel CD, EUS for perianal fistula, neoterminal-ileum (Rutgeerts) postoperative evaluation, endoscopic balloon dilation of benign strictures ≤4 cm.
- [[ulcerative-colitis]] — colonoscopy + ileoscopy diagnosis, backwash-ileitis vs CD distinction, cecal patch, UC stricture is malignant until proven otherwise.

- [[colonoscopy]], [[capsule-endoscopy]], [[device-assisted-enteroscopy]], [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] — modality roles in IBD; mucosal healing as a treatment target.

- 2015 document; dysplasia-surveillance content overlaps the [[asge-2015-scenic-ibd-dysplasia|SCENIC]] consensus (same year) — keep the surveillance algorithm on the SCENIC page rather than duplicating. Therapeutic IBD management has advanced since 2015; this guideline informs the **endoscopic** role only and should not override newer pharmacologic guidelines ([[acg-2025-crohns]], [[acg-2025-uc]], [[aga-2024-uc-pharm]], [[aga-2025-crohns-pharm]]).
