## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Laine L, Kaltenbach T, Barkun A, et al. SCENIC international consensus statement on surveillance and management of dysplasia in inflammatory bowel disease. Gastrointest Endosc 2015;81(3):489-501.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.12.009)
- **Authors:** Loren Laine, Tonya Kaltenbach, Alan Barkun, Kenneth R. McQuaid, Venkataraman Subramanian, Roy Soetikno; SCENIC Guideline Development Panel
- **Year:** 2015
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (co-published with Gastroenterology); jointly sponsored by ASGE and AGA
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2014.12.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2014.12.009)
- **Type:** guideline (international consensus statement, GRADE methodology)

## Summary

SCENIC (**S**urveillance for **C**olorectal **E**ndoscopic **N**eoplasia **D**etection and Management **i**n **I**nflammatory Bowel Disease Patients: **I**nternational **C**onsensus) is a joint ASGE/AGA international consensus addressing two questions: (1) how surveillance colonoscopy for dysplasia should be performed, and (2) how dysplasia found at colonoscopy should be managed. It marks the paradigm shift from the older model (where most dysplasia was thought invisible, justifying ≥32 random biopsies) to the modern recognition that **most dysplasia in IBD is visible** with current video endoscopy.

The panel standardized terminology (modified Paris classification): dysplasia is described as **visible** (polypoid — pedunculated/sessile; or nonpolypoid — superficial elevated/flat/depressed, with descriptors for ulceration and distinct vs indistinct border) or **invisible** (found on random/non-targeted biopsy). The terms **DALM, adenoma-like, and non-adenoma-like were explicitly abandoned**. "Endoscopically resectable" requires distinct margins, apparent complete removal, histologic confirmation of complete removal, and dysplasia-free biopsies of adjacent mucosa.

For detection, the panel favored **high-definition over standard-definition** white-light colonoscopy and **chromoendoscopy** (methylene blue or indigo carmine dye spray) over white-light, while finding insufficient evidence to recommend narrow-band imaging (NBI) over white-light or over chromoendoscopy. For management, the major shift is away from reflexive colectomy: after complete endoscopic removal of resectable polypoid or nonpolypoid visible dysplasia, **continued surveillance colonoscopy is favored over colectomy**. Endoscopically invisible dysplasia confirmed by a GI pathologist warrants referral to an endoscopist with IBD-surveillance/chromoendoscopy expertise.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, Table 2 — strength; quality of evidence):**

*Detection of dysplasia on surveillance colonoscopy*
1. When performing surveillance with white-light colonoscopy, **high definition is recommended rather than standard definition** (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).
2. When performing surveillance with standard-definition colonoscopy, **chromoendoscopy is recommended rather than white-light colonoscopy** (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).
3. When performing surveillance with high-definition colonoscopy, **chromoendoscopy is suggested rather than white-light colonoscopy** (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence).
4. When performing surveillance with standard-definition colonoscopy, **narrow-band imaging is not suggested in place of white-light colonoscopy** (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence).
5. When performing surveillance with high-definition colonoscopy, **narrow-band imaging is not suggested in place of white-light colonoscopy** (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).
6. When performing surveillance with image-enhanced high-definition colonoscopy, **narrow-band imaging is not suggested in place of chromoendoscopy** (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).

*Management of dysplasia discovered on surveillance colonoscopy*
7. After complete removal of endoscopically resectable **polypoid** dysplastic lesions, **surveillance colonoscopy is recommended rather than colectomy** (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence).
8. After complete removal of endoscopically resectable **nonpolypoid** dysplastic lesions, **surveillance colonoscopy is suggested rather than colectomy** (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence).
9. For patients with endoscopically **invisible dysplasia** (confirmed by a GI pathologist), **referral is suggested to an endoscopist with expertise in IBD surveillance using chromoendoscopy with high-definition colonoscopy** (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence).

**Supporting data points:**
- HD vs SD colonoscopy: dysplasia found in ~2× as many patients (adjusted prevalence ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.1–4.5).
- Chromoendoscopy vs SD white-light: meta-analysis RR 1.8 (1.2–2.6) for proportion of patients with dysplasia, absolute increase 6% (3%–9%); chromoendoscopy adds a mean ~11 min to the procedure.
- HD chromoendoscopy vs HD white-light (tandem): dysplasia in 21% vs 9% (P = .007).
- IBD interval cancers (6–36 mo post-colonoscopy) far exceed non-IBD patients (15.1% Crohn's, 15.8% UC vs 5.8% non-IBD) — current surveillance misses clinically relevant neoplasia.

**Terminology (Table 1):** visible (polypoid: pedunculated/sessile; nonpolypoid: superficial elevated/flat/depressed; descriptors: ulcerated, distinct/indistinct border) vs invisible dysplasia; DALM/adenoma-like/non-adenoma-like abandoned.

## Relevance to Wiki
- `[[ulcerative-colitis]]` and `[[crohns-disease]]` — defines how CRC-dysplasia surveillance colonoscopy should be performed (HD + chromoendoscopy) and managed (resect-and-survey over colectomy for resectable visible dysplasia).
- `[[colonoscopy]]` — IBD-surveillance technique (HD, dye-spray chromoendoscopy, targeted + random biopsy debate).
- `[[colorectal-cancer]]` — IBD-related CRC pathway (dysplasia → cancer).
- `[[primary-sclerosing-cholangitis]]` — PSC-IBD high-risk annual surveillance already cites chromoendoscopy when only SD available.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- SCENIC did not address **surveillance intervals** or risk stratification (timing left to other guidelines, e.g. ACG/AGA).
- Whether the extra lesions found by chromoendoscopy carry the same CRC risk as historically described dysplasia is unknown.
- The role of **random biopsies** when HD chromoendoscopy is used was not resolved (panel did not eliminate random biopsies); subsequent guidelines continue to debate targeted-only vs targeted + random.

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Acosta RD, Abraham NS, Chandrasekhara V, et al). The management of antithrombotic agents for patients undergoing GI endoscopy. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2016;83(1):3-16.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.09.035)
- **Authors:** Ruben D. Acosta, Neena S. Abraham, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee; John M. DeWitt, Chair)
- **Year:** 2016 (literature search through December 2014; erratum *Gastrointest Endosc* 2016;83[3]:678)
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2016;83(1):3-16
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.09.035](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.09.035)
- **Type:** Guideline (ASGE Standards of Practice; GRADE)

## Summary

ASGE Standards-of-Practice guideline on periprocedural management of anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents (APAs). It frames the decision around four factors: procedure urgency, procedure bleeding risk, the drug's effect on bleeding, and the thromboembolic risk of interrupting therapy. It provides a duration-of-action / reversal reference table for every antithrombotic class, a procedure bleeding-risk dichotomy (high vs low), and a CV-risk × bleeding-risk management matrix (Table 13) for the elective setting, plus separate guidance for urgent/emergent bleeding.

This is an **older tier-1 source**; the newer **[[acg-cag-2022-anticoag-gi-bleeding]]** (2022 ACG/CAG) governs the wiki's periendoscopic and acute-bleeding recommendations where they overlap. ASGE 2016's net-new contribution to the wiki is its **drug-specific duration-of-action / hold-interval / reversal reference table** and specific pre-procedure hold intervals, which were added to **[[anticoagulation-gi-bleeding]]** without overwriting the ACG/CAG framework.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Procedure bleeding risk (Table 3).** High-risk: polypectomy, biliary/pancreatic sphincterotomy, variceal treatment, PEG/PEJ placement, EUS-FNA, endoscopic hemostasis, tumor ablation, cystgastrostomy, ampullary resection, EMR, ESD, pneumatic/bougie dilation, therapeutic balloon enteroscopy, POEM, Zenker's therapy. Low-risk: diagnostic EGD/colonoscopy/flex sig (incl. mucosal biopsy), ERCP with stent without sphincterotomy, push/diagnostic balloon enteroscopy, capsule endoscopy, enteral stent deployment (controversial), EUS without FNA, APC, Barrett's ablation. *PEG on ASA or clopidogrel monotherapy is low risk (not DAPT); EUS-FNA of solid masses on ASA/NSAIDs is low risk.*
- **Duration of action / reversal (Table 2, erratum-corrected).** Aspirin 7-10 d (hold, ± platelets if urgent); NSAIDs varies; dipyridamole 2-3 d; cilostazol 2 d; thienopyridines: clopidogrel/prasugrel 5-7 d, ticagrelor 3-5 d, ticlopidine 10-14 d; GPIIb/IIIa: tirofiban 1-2 s, eptifibatide 4 h, abciximab 24 h; vorapaxar 5-13 d; warfarin 5 d (reverse: vitamin K, PCC); UFH IV 2-6 h / SQ 12-24 h (protamine, partial); LMWH 24 h (protamine ± rVIIa); fondaparinux 36-48 h; factor Xa inhibitors and dabigatran per renal function (reverse: charcoal if last dose <2-3 h, nonactivated/activated PCC; dabigatran also HD).
- **Elective setting (Table 13).** Continue warfarin and NOAC for low-bleeding-risk procedures regardless of CV risk. For high-bleeding-risk procedures: discontinue AC; restart warfarin same day; delay reinitiating NOAC until hemostasis; if high CV risk, add bridge therapy. APAs: continue ASA/NSAIDs; hold thienopyridines ≥5 days before high-risk procedures (ticagrelor 3-5 d, others 5-7 d) or switch to ASA monotherapy.
- **Bridging** decisions in moderate-risk patients should be individualized (Table 5 mechanical valve / VTE risk).
- **Urgent/emergent bleeding.** Hold anticoagulants to achieve hemostasis; give 4-factor PCC + vitamin K (ACCP) or FFP (AHA/ACC accepts either) for life-threatening warfarin-associated bleeding; endoscopic therapy need not be delayed if INR <2.5; give UFH (short half-life) after successful hemostasis of high-risk stigmata; consult the prescriber before stopping APAs in patients with recent (<1 y) drug-eluting stent, <30 d bare-metal stent, or <90 d ACS.
- **Elective procedures should be deferred** in patients with recently placed intracoronary stents / ACS until the minimum DAPT duration (ACCF/ACG) has elapsed.

## Recommendations (verbatim)

**A. Elective procedures — patients on anticoagulants**
1. Recommend elective endoscopic procedures be deferred until short-term anticoagulation (eg, warfarin for VTE) is completed. (High/strong)
2. Suggest discontinuing anticoagulation (warfarin, NOACs) for the drug-specific interval if high-risk endoscopic procedures are planned in a patient at low thromboembolic risk. (Low/conditional)
3. Suggest continuing warfarin and NOAC periendoscopically in patients undergoing low-risk procedures. (Low/conditional)
4. Suggest bridge therapy for patients undergoing high-risk procedures who are at high thromboembolic risk. (Low/conditional)
5. Suggest warfarin be restarted the same day as the procedure in all patients without ongoing bleeding. (Low/conditional)
6. Suggest reinitiation of NOACs after high-risk procedures be delayed until adequate hemostasis is ensured; if NOACs cannot be restarted within 12-24 h after a high-risk procedure in a high-thrombotic-risk patient, consider UFH bridge thromboprophylaxis. (Low/conditional)

**A. Elective procedures — patients on APA therapy**
1. Suggest low-dose ASA and NSAIDs may be continued safely periendoscopically. (High/conditional)
2. Recommend thienopyridines be continued for all low-risk procedures. (High/strong)
3. Recommend discontinuing thienopyridines ≥5-7 days before a high-risk procedure (or switching to ASA monotherapy), continued until the thienopyridine can be safely resumed. (High/strong)
4. Recommend elective procedures be deferred in patients with recently placed intracoronary stents and/or ACS until the minimum antithrombotic therapy duration is complete. (High/strong)
5. Suggest thienopyridines be withheld ≥5-7 days (ticagrelor 3-5 d) before high-risk procedures and that ASA be continued in patients requiring dual APA. (High/conditional)

**B. Urgent/emergent procedures — anticoagulants**
1. Recommend patients with acute GI bleeding on anticoagulation have agents held to facilitate hemostasis. (High/strong)
2. Recommend either 4-factor PCC + vitamin K or FFP for life-threatening GI bleeding on warfarin (ACCP advocates PCC only; AHA/ACC supports either). (High/strong)
3. Suggest endoscopic therapy not be delayed in patients with serious GI bleeding and INR <2.5. (Low/conditional)
4. Suggest patients who require anticoagulation receive UFH (short half-life) after successful endoscopic hemostasis for high-risk stigmata. (Low/conditional)

**B. Urgent/emergent procedures — APA therapy**
1. Recommend consultation with the prescribing specialist before stopping APAs in significant GI bleeding for patients with (1) recent (<1 y) drug-eluting intracoronary stent, (2) <30 days after bare-metal stent, or (3) <90 days of ACS. (High/strong)
2. Recommend APAs be held after discussion with cardiology in patients with life-threatening or serious GI bleeding. (High/strong)

## Relevance to Wiki

- **[[anticoagulation-gi-bleeding]]** — added the drug-specific duration-of-action / hold-interval / reversal reference table and pre-procedure hold intervals as net-new content complementing the ACG/CAG 2022 framework.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Bridging.** ASGE 2016 suggests bridge therapy for high-thrombotic-risk patients undergoing high-bleeding-risk procedures. The newer **[[acg-cag-2022-anticoag-gi-bleeding]]** (informed by BRIDGE/PERIOP-2) suggests **against** routine bridging except for mechanical heart valves. **Newer ACG/CAG governs the wiki claim**; ASGE 2016's bridging stance is noted here as superseded.
- **Reversal-agent emphasis.** ASGE 2016 endorses 4F-PCC/FFP more readily for warfarin-related bleeding; ACG/CAG 2022 reserves reversal agents for life-threatening hemorrhage and suggests against routine FFP. Wiki follows ACG/CAG 2022.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of endoscopy in the diagnosis and treatment of inflammatory pancreatic fluid collections. Gastrointest Endosc 2016;83(3):481-488.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.11.027)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Muthusamy VR, Chandrasekhara V, et al.)
- **Year:** 2016
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.11.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.11.027)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement on endoscopic management of inflammatory pancreatic fluid collections (PFCs) following [[acute-pancreatitis|acute pancreatitis]], using the revised Atlanta classification (acute peripancreatic fluid collection, pancreatic pseudocyst, acute necrotic collection, walled-off necrosis [WON]). Before drainage, alternative diagnoses (cystic neoplasm, pseudoaneurysm) must be excluded and the collection wall allowed to mature.

Drainage is indicated for symptomatic or rapidly enlarging pseudocysts, infected PFCs failing conservative management, and symptomatic sterile necrosis >8 weeks out. Endoscopic transmural drainage (EUS-guided) is preferred as initial therapy over surgery for pseudocysts; for WON, a step-up approach (transmural/percutaneous drainage before transmural necrosectomy or surgery) is recommended. WON drainage is less successful and higher-risk than pseudocyst drainage. Procedures require surgical and interventional-radiology backup.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE quality of evidence):**

1. We recommend that endoscopic drainage of PFCs be performed only after sufficient exclusion of alternative diagnoses, such as cystic pancreatic neoplasms and pseudoaneurysms. (High)
2. We recommend waiting for maturation of the cyst wall of PFCs before endoscopic intervention. (Moderate)
3. We recommend drainage of symptomatic pancreatic pseudocysts. (Moderate)
4. We suggest drainage of rapidly enlarging pancreatic pseudocysts. (Low)
5. We recommend drainage of all infected PFCs in patients who fail to improve with conservative management alone. (High)
6. We recommend drainage of symptomatic sterile necrosis lasting more than 8 weeks after the onset of acute pancreatitis. (Moderate)
7. We suggest that routine FNA of PFCs is not required to diagnose infected necrosis. (Low)
8. We recommend that endoscopic drainage be considered for initial therapy before surgical drainage of pancreatic pseudocysts. (Moderate)
9. We recommend using EUS for transmural drainage of PFCs in the absence of a luminal bulge or when portal hypertension is suspected. (High)
10. We recommend initial endoscopic transmural and/or percutaneous drainage of WON before consideration of endoscopic transmural necrosectomy or surgical drainage. (Moderate)
11. We recommend that endoscopic drainage of PFCs be performed only with the availability of surgical and interventional radiology support. (High)
12. We suggest using CO2 when performing transmural drainage procedures. (Low)

**Other points:**
- Endoscopic WON drainage achieves nonsurgical resolution in 70%-80%; success lower and adverse events higher than for pseudocysts (systematic review: 81% clinical success, 36% adverse events, 6% mortality; mean ~4 interventions/patient).
- Disconnected duct syndrome can result from main-duct disruption in the body/tail; long-term indwelling transmural stents may reduce recurrence.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[acute-pancreatitis]] (#Necrotizing Pancreatitis / fluid-collection sections) — drainage indications and thresholds, pre-drainage workup (exclude neoplasm/pseudoaneurysm), EUS use when no bulge or portal hypertension, endoscopy-before-surgery for pseudocysts.
- Cross-links [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] (transmural drainage), [[pancreatic-cysts]] (differential to exclude before drainage).

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Older (2016) than [[acg-2024-acute-pancreatitis|ACG 2024 acute pancreatitis]], which governs the step-up approach and LAMS-based necrosectomy on the [[acute-pancreatitis]] page; concordant overall. This source adds explicit drainage indications/thresholds and the pre-drainage diagnostic checklist.

- **Year:** 2016
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2015.09.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2015.09.009)
- **Type:** guideline

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice statement (GRADE) on endoscopy in solid pancreatic neoplasia — [[pancreatic-cancer|pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)]], pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, solid pseudopapillary tumors, and metastases. Covers diagnostic imaging (EUS + pancreas-protocol multidetector CT, selective MRI/PET-CT), [[endoscopic-ultrasound|EUS]]-guided tissue acquisition (FNA/FNB), the limited role of preoperative ERCP, and endoscopic palliation (biliary/gastroduodenal stenting, EUS-guided celiac plexus neurolysis, fiducial placement). Also endorses EUS + MRCP screening of high-risk individuals.

This is an **older** ASGE document — superseded for tissue-acquisition technique by [[asge-2024-solid-pancreatic-masses|ASGE 2024: EUS-guided sampling of solid pancreatic masses]] and for screening by [[asge-2022-pancreatic-cancer-screening|ASGE 2022 pancreatic cancer screening]]. It contributes the endoscopic-palliation framework (celiac plexus neurolysis, stenting, fiducials) and the "no preoperative ERCP for resectable PDAC" principle as net-new, non-conflicting detail.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Recommendations (verbatim, with GRADE quality of evidence; ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high, ⊕⊕⊕◯ moderate, ⊕⊕◯◯ low, ⊕◯◯◯ very low; "recommend" = strong, "suggest" = conditional):**

1. We recommend that imaging evaluation of patients with suspected solid pancreatic neoplasia include EUS and multidetector pancreas protocol CT scans with selective use of MRI and PET-CT when appropriate. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
2. We recommend that EUS be performed for evaluation of pancreatic masses and suspected malignancy, particularly when CT detection or evaluation of resectability is equivocal. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
3. We recommend that biopsy of a suspected primary or metastatic pancreatic tumor should be individualized based on need for preoperative chemotherapy, resectability, and feasibility of surgery. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕⊕)
4. We suggest that EUS-guided celiac plexus neurolysis be considered in patients with pancreatic cancer–related pain. (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
5. We do not recommend preoperative ERCP in patients with obstructive jaundice because of resectable adenocarcinoma of the pancreas in the absence of cholangitis unless a substantial delay in operative resection of a symptomatic patient is anticipated. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
6. We recommend that patients with symptomatic, unresectable adenocarcinoma of the pancreas with biliary and/or gastroduodenal obstruction undergo attempted palliation with endoscopic stent placement as the preferred therapeutic modality. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
7. We recommend EUS ± FNA for localization and characterization of suspected pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and metastatic solid pancreatic neoplasia. (strong, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
8. We suggest EUS-guided fiducial placement into a pancreatic malignancy if image-guided radiation therapy is considered. (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕◯)
9. We suggest that screening with EUS and MRCP should be offered to high-risk individuals for pancreatic cancer. (conditional, ⊕⊕◯◯)

**Other points:**
- EUS-FNA sensitivity for pancreatic malignancy is high; a linear-array echoendoscope outperforms radial for lesion detection. EUS-FNB (core) and rapid on-site evaluation improve adequacy.
- Preoperative biliary drainage before pancreaticoduodenectomy is associated with increased perioperative complications — avoid routine preop ERCP when prompt resection is feasible.
- High-risk-individual screening should occur within a multidisciplinary program (genetics, GI, radiology, surgery, pathology).

## Relevance to Wiki
- Updates [[pancreatic-cancer]] — endoscopic palliation menu (SEMS for malignant biliary/gastroduodenal obstruction; EUS-guided celiac plexus neurolysis for tumor-related pain; EUS-guided fiducials for image-guided RT); avoid preoperative ERCP for resectable PDAC with obstructive jaundice absent cholangitis.
- Corroborates [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] roles — EUS ± FNA/FNB for diagnosis, staging, and NET localization; EUS therapeutics (neurolysis, fiducials).
- Corroborates [[pancreatic-cancer-screening]] / [[asge-2022-pancreatic-cancer-screening|ASGE 2022]] — EUS + MRCP for high-risk individuals.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- **Older than** [[asge-2024-solid-pancreatic-masses|ASGE 2024 (solid pancreatic mass sampling)]] and [[asge-2022-pancreatic-cancer-screening|ASGE 2022 (pancreatic cancer screening)]]; where those specify FNB-needle selection, ROSE, and screening eligibility/intervals, the newer documents govern. This 2016 source contributes the endoscopic-palliation and preop-ERCP-avoidance content, which the newer documents do not duplicate.

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. The role of endoscopy in the management of suspected small-bowel bleeding. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2017;85:22-31.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2016.06.013)
- **Authors:** Gurudu SR, Bruining DH, Acosta RD, et al.; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (DeWitt JM, Chair)
- **Year:** 2017
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2016.06.013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2016.06.013)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE recommendations)

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice guideline on the endoscopic evaluation of **suspected small-bowel bleeding** (formerly obscure GI bleeding). Endorses the shift to anatomic terminology and a stepwise algorithm: exclude upper/lower sources (repeat EGD/colonoscopy when recurrent symptoms) → **video capsule endoscopy (VCE) as the initial small-bowel test** → device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) or push enteroscopy for therapy of positive findings or when VCE is unavailable/nondiagnostic. Cross-sectional imaging (multiphase CTE/MRE) is reserved for suspected small-bowel neoplasm or obstruction; CTA or RBC scan localizes active bleeding to guide angiography in stable patients; angiography with embolization is recommended for hemodynamically unstable bleeding.

Corroborates the [[acg-2015-small-bowel-bleeding|ACG 2015]] approach. Notes that DAE may be the *initial* small-bowel procedure in select circumstances (high suspicion of angiectasias, surgically altered anatomy). For non-localizable chronic angiectasia bleeding, hormonal therapy is abandoned (ineffective in RCTs); octreotide and low-dose thalidomide may reduce transfusion/iron needs.

## Key Findings / Claims

- Endorses anatomic terms (overt/occult small-bowel bleeding) over "obscure GI bleeding."
- VCE is the recommended initial small-bowel test for overt or occult bleeding; positive findings → push enteroscopy (if within reach) or DAE.
- DAE or push enteroscopy when VCE unavailable/nondiagnostic in overt bleeding.
- DAE may be the initial small-bowel procedure when angiectasias are highly suspected or in surgically altered anatomy.
- Multiphase CTE or MRE when small-bowel neoplasm is suspected.
- Hemodynamically unstable suspected small-bowel bleeding → angiography with selective embolization after resuscitation.
- Hemodynamically stable active bleeding → CTA or RBC scan to localize and time angiography.
- Lesions within endoscopic reach: treat with electrocautery, APC, injection, or mechanical hemostasis (clips/bands).
- After negative evaluation, stable patients with iron deficiency may be managed with iron therapy and clinical follow-up.
- Hormonal therapy for angiectasias abandoned (no RCT efficacy); octreotide and low-dose thalidomide reduce transfusion needs in chronic angiectasia blood loss.

## Recommendations (verbatim)

1. For patients with signs or symptoms consistent with recurrent upper or lower GI sources of bleeding, we suggest repeating EGD and colonoscopy, respectively, before small-bowel evaluation. *(moderate quality)*
2. We suggest VCE as the initial test for patients with overt or occult small-bowel bleeding. Positive VCE results should be followed with push enteroscopy if within reach or DAE. *(moderate quality)*
3. We suggest DAE or push enteroscopy if VCE is unavailable or nondiagnostic in patients with overt small-bowel bleeding. *(moderate quality)*
4. We suggest that in select circumstances (eg, high level of suspicion of small-bowel angiectasias or in patients with surgically altered anatomy) DAE may be considered as the initial small-bowel diagnostic procedure in patients with small-bowel bleeding. *(moderate quality)*
5. We suggest that after an appropriate negative evaluation, clinically stable patients without recurrent bleeding may be treated with iron therapy and clinically followed if iron deficiency is present. *(moderate quality)*
6. We suggest multiphase CTE or MRE in patients with obscure bleeding and suspected small-bowel neoplasms. *(high quality)*
7. Following appropriate hemodynamic resuscitation, we recommend angiography for selective embolization in patients who present with hemodynamically unstable suspected small-bowel bleeding. *(high quality)*
8. We suggest a CTA or RBC scan for localization of the bleeding site and to guide timing of angiography in hemodynamically stable patients with suspected active small-bowel bleeding. *(moderate quality)*

## Relevance to Wiki

- Corroborates and is added as a source to [[small-bowel-bleeding]], [[capsule-endoscopy]], and [[device-assisted-enteroscopy]].
- Reinforces VCE-first algorithm and the role of DAE as initial procedure in select anatomy.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Aligns with [[acg-2015-small-bowel-bleeding|ACG 2015]]; no substantive conflict. The newer ACG content is retained where more detailed.

# ASGE 2017: The Role of Endoscopy in Subepithelial Lesions of the GI Tract

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee; Faulx AL, Kothari S, Acosta RD, et al. The role of endoscopy in subepithelial lesions of the GI tract. *Gastrointestinal Endoscopy* 2017;85(6):1117–1132. doi:10.1016/j.gie.2017.02.022.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.02.022)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee — Ashley L. Faulx, Shivangi Kothari, Ruben D. Acosta, Deepak Agrawal, David H. Bruining, Vinay Chandrasekhara, Mohamad A. Eloubeidi, Robert D. Fanelli (SAGES), Suryakanth R. Gurudu, Mouen A. Khashab, Jenifer R. Lightdale (NASPGHAN), V. Raman Muthusamy, Aasma Shaukat, Bashar J. Qumseya, Amy Wang, Sachin B. Wani, Julie Yang, John M. DeWitt (Chair)
- **Year:** 2017
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastrointestinal Endoscopy* 2017;85(6):1117–1132 (American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2017.02.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.02.022)
- **Type:** Guideline (ASGE Standards of Practice)

---

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice guideline on **subepithelial lesions (SELs)** — tumors originating from the muscularis mucosa, submucosa, or muscularis propria. SELs are most common in the stomach (~1 in 300 endoscopies), usually small (<2 cm) and incidental; <15% are malignant at presentation. Management centers on diagnosis and determination of malignant potential. **EUS is the most accurate imaging test**, delineating the 5 wall layers (1st/2nd = mucosa incl. muscularis mucosa; 3rd = submucosa; 4th = muscularis propria; 5th = serosa/adventitia), distinguishing intramural from extramural lesions (up to 30% of suspected SELs are extramural), and superior to CT/MRI for small (<2 cm) lesions. High-frequency (20–30 MHz) miniprobes improve subcentimeter and proximal-colon assessment.

The document characterizes each lesion type by endoscopic and EUS appearance (Table 2): **GIST** (4th layer, hypoechoic), **leiomyoma** (esophageal, 2nd/3rd/4th), **lipoma** (3rd layer, hyperechoic, pillow sign 98% specific), **GI neuroendocrine neoplasms** (carcinoid; 2nd/3rd), **granular cell tumor** (2nd/3rd, S-100+), **pancreatic rest** (antral, umbilicated), **duplication cyst** (anechoic), and others (varices, glomus tumor, lymphangioma, inflammatory fibroid polyp, Brunner's gland hyperplasia, metastasis, lymphoma). GISTs originate from interstitial cells of Cajal, stain CD117/DOG1+, and have malignant potential stratified by size, mitotic rate, and location (gastric vs small-bowel tables). EUS-FNA cannot reliably assess mitotic rate, so final malignant potential is determined by surgical pathology.

Tissue acquisition is challenging because SELs lie deep to the epithelium. Techniques: standard biopsy (low yield), bite-on-bite (30–40%), jumbo biopsy, unroofing, single-incision needle-knife (SINK, 93% yield), and EUS-FNA/FNB (FNB ≥ FNA for immunohistochemistry). Endoscopic resection/ligation and tunneling techniques include ESMR (ESMR-C, ESMR-L), ESD, submucosal tunneling endoscopic resection (STER), and endoscopic full-thickness resection (EFTR). Surgery is indicated for symptomatic or malignant lesions and those with metastatic risk; asymptomatic benign lesions (lipoma, vascular, cysts, pancreatic rests, leiomyomas) need no intervention or follow-up. Recommendations graded by GRADE evidence quality.

---

## All Recommendations (Verbatim, with GRADE Evidence Quality)

Evidence-quality symbols (GRADE): 4444 = High; 444B = Moderate; 44BB = Low; 4BBB = Very low. Recommendation strength: "we recommend" = stronger; "we suggest" = weaker.

1. We suggest that EUS be used to further characterize indeterminate SELs. **(Moderate — 444B)**
2. We suggest surveillance EUS for gastric GI stromal tumors <2 cm in size. **(Low — 44BB)**
3. We recommend surgery for gastric and colorectal GI stromal tumors >2 cm in size and those with high-risk features. **(Moderate — 444B)**
4. We recommend that rectal GI neuroendocrine neoplasms <1 cm in size may be managed by local endoscopic or transanal excision. **(Moderate — 444B)**
5. We suggest EUS for staging of rectal GI neuroendocrine neoplasms >1 cm. Endoscopic or transanal excision may be considered for rectal tumors 1 to 2 cm in diameter that do not invade the muscularis propria. **(Low — 44BB)**
6. We recommend surgical resection for GI neuroendocrine neoplasms identified in the jejunum and ileum. **(Moderate — 444B)**
7. We recommend that asymptomatic leiomyomas do not require endoscopic surveillance or therapy unless symptomatic. **(Moderate — 444B)**
8. We recommend that GI lipomas do not require follow-up or therapy unless symptomatic. **(Moderate — 444B)**
9. We suggest that lesions arising from the muscularis propria be sampled with FNA or fine-needle biopsy for histologic evaluation. **(Low — 44BB)**
10. We suggest that a firm, round subepithelial lesion with central umbilication along the greater curve of the antrum of the stomach be considered diagnostic for a pancreatic rest. Further investigation with EUS and follow-up is not required. **(Low — 44BB)**
11. We suggest that lesions with malignant potential requiring treatment can be removed either endoscopically or surgically based on the type of lesion, size, location, patient preference, and available expertise. **(Low — 44BB)**

---

## Key Findings / Claims

- **EUS layers:** 1st/2nd = mucosa incl. muscularis mucosa; 3rd = submucosa; 4th = muscularis propria; 5th = serosa/adventitia. EUS distinguishes intramural vs extramural (up to 30% extramural). Low-frequency EUS (<10 MHz) cannot reliably see the muscularis mucosa; 20–30 MHz miniprobes improve subcentimeter and proximal-colon imaging.
- **GIST:** most common GI mesenchymal neoplasm (~4.3/million/yr US); arise from interstitial cells of Cajal; stomach 60–70%, small intestine 20–30%, colon 5%, esophagus <5%. Spindle (70%)/epithelioid (20%)/mixed (10%); CD117+ in 95%, DOG1+ (useful when CD117−). EUS-FNA cannot reliably assess mitotic rate → malignant potential determined by surgical pathology. Small-intestine GISTs more aggressive (40–50% malignant vs 20–25% gastric). EUS malignant features (inconsistent across studies): size >3 cm, irregular margins; less consistent — echogenic foci, cystic spaces, heterogeneity, ulceration.
- **Gastric GIST malignant-potential table (size × mitotic rate; metastasis/mortality):** see [[gastrointestinal-stromal-tumor]] and [[subepithelial-lesion]].
- **Leiomyoma:** benign smooth-muscle tumor, mostly esophageal (90% in lower/middle third), from muscularis mucosa or propria; CD117−/CD34−, desmin+/SMA+ (distinguishes from GIST). Resect only if symptomatic.
- **Lipoma:** colon and gastric antrum; yellow, soft, pillow sign 98% specific (low sensitivity); homogeneous hyperechoic from submucosa. No tissue/surveillance needed unless symptomatic; negligible malignant potential.
- **GI neuroendocrine neoplasms (carcinoids):** originate from mucosa, penetrate submucosa; standard mucosal biopsy usually diagnostic. **Gastric types:** Type I (multifocal, chronic atrophic gastritis/hypergastrinemia/pernicious anemia, low metastatic potential); Type II (Zollinger-Ellison/MEN-1, intermediate; nodal mets 10–30% if >2 cm); Type III (sporadic, often metastatic, 5-yr survival <50%, manage surgically). EMR for type I/II lesions <2 cm; lesions <1 cm may not need removal.
- **Rectal NET:** size-based — <1 cm/submucosal/no LVI: local endoscopic or transanal excision (5-yr survival 98.9–100%); 1–2 cm: EUS then endoscopic/transanal excision if no MP invasion; >2 cm: surgery with lymph node dissection (up to 80% nodal disease). Nodal-metastasis incidence for 11–19 mm tumors 17–81%. Proposed surveillance: EUS at 3 months then every 6 months for 3 years (NCCN: no follow-up for fully resected <1 cm).
- **Duodenal NET:** managed like rectal carcinoids; <1 cm well-differentiated → endoscopic polypectomy/EMR; refer for surgery if angioinvasion, MP invasion, or grade 2/3. Nodal risk 2% (<1 cm), 4.7% (1–2 cm), 20% (>2 cm).
- **Jejunal/ileal NET:** surgical resection recommended (mid-gut metastatic disease incurable); follow-up ≥7 years.
- **Pancreatic rest:** heterotopic pancreas, greater-curve antrum, central umbilication; firm SEL with umbilication considered diagnostic — EUS not required. EUS (when done): heterogeneous/hypoechoic, any layer.
- **Granular cell tumor:** nerve-sheath (Schwann cell) tumor, mostly esophageal; "submucosal pill," grayish-yellow; S-100+; mucosal/submucosal, hypoechoic homogeneous. Malignant transformation rare (>4 cm). Subcentimeter lesions safe to surveil; endoscopic resection (snare/EMR/ESD) may obviate surveillance.
- **Duplication cyst:** congenital, GI-epithelium-lined; anechoic, 3–5 layer wall, submucosal or extrinsic; avoid FNA when clearly anechoic (infection risk; use antibiotic prophylaxis if FNA needed). No surveillance data; resect only if symptomatic.
- **Other SELs:** metastasis (stomach body/fundus, central depression, biopsy diagnostic >90%); varices (anechoic, Doppler+, can occur in duodenum/rectum); glomus tumor (antrum, MP, hypervascular, actin+/vimentin+, CD117−); inflammatory fibroid polyp; Brunner's gland hyperplasia; lymphangioma; lymphoma.
- **Tissue acquisition yields:** standard pinch biopsy rarely sufficient; bite-on-bite 30–40%; jumbo forceps higher yield for submucosal lesions but bleeding 35.7% (34.9% needed hemostasis); SINK 93%; ESMR 87% (vs bite-on-bite 17%). EUS-FNA accuracy for GIST 46–93%; FNB (22G core) yield 75% vs FNA 20% — FNB salvages nondiagnostic FNA. FNA accuracy plateaus after the 4th pass; stylet, suction, fanning, and ROSE have unproven incremental benefit. Partial-resection/jumbo techniques risk perilesional fibrosis complicating later resection.
- **Endoscopic resection:** ESMR (≤20 mm, mucosa/submucosa; ESMR-C cap, ESMR-L ligation — bleeding up to 9%; caution in duodenum and for MP lesions). ESD for MP lesions (gastric MP ESD complete resection 92%, perforation 14% — all managed endoscopically); limited for >5 cm (perforation up to 19%). STER (mucosal incision ≥5 cm proximal; preserves mucosa; en bloc 78–100%, adverse events 9.4–33%). EFTR for MP-infiltrating lesions up to 4 cm; requires secure defect closure.
- **Management algorithm (Fig 3):** EUS triages extramural vs intramural; hyperechoic + pillow sign → lipoma (observe); anechoic Doppler+ → varix; anechoic Doppler− → cyst; 2nd/3rd-layer hypoechoic → tissue (EMR/EUS-FNA/FNB/bite-on-bite/unroofing/jumbo/SINK), treat by histology; 4th-layer ≥2 cm or symptomatic/suspicious → ESD/STER/EFTR vs surgery; <2 cm asymptomatic → surveillance 3–12 months.

# ASGE 2018 — Endoscopic Eradication Therapy for BE-Associated Dysplasia and Intramucosal Cancer

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Wani S, Qumseya B (co-first authors), Sultan S, Agrawal D, Chandrasekhara V, Harnke B, Kothari S, McCarter M, Shaukat A, Wang A, Yang J, Dewitt J; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. ASGE Guideline: Endoscopic Eradication Therapy for Patients with Barrett's Esophagus-Associated Dysplasia and Intramucosal Cancer (2018). Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2018;87(4):907-931 (DOI 10.1016/j.gie.2017.10.011).](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.10.011)
- **Authors:** Wani S, Qumseya B (co-first authors), Sultan S, Agrawal D, Chandrasekhara V, Harnke B, Kothari S, McCarter M, Shaukat A, Wang A, Yang J, Dewitt J; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2018
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2018;87(4):907-931 (DOI 10.1016/j.gie.2017.10.011)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2017.10.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.10.011)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE methodology, official ASGE recommendations)

## Summary

This ASGE guideline addresses the role of endoscopic eradication therapy (EET) in the management of [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's esophagus]] (BE)-related neoplasia — high-grade dysplasia (HGD), low-grade dysplasia (LGD), and intramucosal cancer (IMC/T1a EAC). In this document EET refers to endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) of visible lesions plus radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of the remaining flat Barrett's segment, unless stated otherwise. It is the companion to the 2019 ASGE screening/surveillance guideline.

The panel answered 7 PICO questions and issued 7 GRADE-based recommendations (Table 4). Core messages: confirm dysplasia with an expert GI pathologist; offer EET (vs surveillance) for confirmed LGD (conditional) and HGD (strong); recommend EET over esophagectomy for HGD/IMC (strong, on the basis that lymph-node metastasis risk is 0% for HGD and ~2% for IMC); resect all visible lesions endoscopically before ablation (strong); ablate the remaining flat BE segment after EMR (conditional); do NOT routinely perform complete EMR of the entire BE segment (strong against — higher stricture/bleeding/perforation than focal EMR + RFA with equivalent eradication); and continue surveillance after complete eradication of intestinal metaplasia (CE-IM) (conditional).

The goal of EET is **CE-IM** — absence of endoscopically visible BE plus no intestinal metaplasia on surveillance biopsies. Most patients achieve CE-IM within ~3 ablation sessions. EET is cost-effective for HGD and confirmed/stable LGD (not for NDBE). The basic premise allowing EET over surgery is the very low lymph-node metastasis risk in mucosal disease; submucosal (T1b sm2-3) cancer, poor differentiation, and lymphovascular invasion shift the balance toward esophagectomy (LN metastasis risk ≥20%).

## Key Findings / Claims (Recommendations — near-verbatim, with strength and quality)

**Summary of recommendations (Table 4):**

1. **Statement 1 (Conditional, Low quality):** In BE patients with LGD and HGD being considered for EET, we suggest confirmation of diagnosis by at least 1 expert GI pathologist or panel of pathologists compared with review by a single pathologist.
2. **Statement 2a (Conditional, Moderate quality):** In BE patients with LGD, we suggest EET compared with surveillance; however, patients who place a high value on avoiding adverse events related to EET may choose surveillance as the preferred option.
3. **Statement 2b (Strong, Moderate quality):** In BE patients with confirmed HGD, we recommend EET compared with surveillance.
4. **Statement 3 (Strong, Very low quality):** In BE patients with HGD/IMC, we recommend against surgery compared with EET.
5. **Statement 4 (Strong, Moderate quality):** In BE patients referred for EET, we recommend endoscopic resection of all visible lesions compared with no endoscopic resection of visible lesions.
6. **Statement 5 (Conditional, Low quality):** In BE patients with visible lesions who undergo endoscopic resection, we suggest ablation of the remaining Barrett's segment compared with no ablation.
7. **Statement 6 (Strong, Very low quality):** In BE patients with dysplasia and IMC referred for EET, we recommend against routine complete endoscopic resection of entire Barrett's segment compared with endoscopic resection of visible lesion followed by ablation of remaining Barrett's segment.
8. **Statement 7 (Conditional, Very low quality):** In BE patients with dysplasia and IMC who have achieved CE-IM after EET, we suggest surveillance endoscopy versus no surveillance.

**Pre-EET general statements (ungraded good practice):** Before embarking on EET, patients should have a clear understanding of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to EET; clinicians should obtain informed consent including discussion of natural history of BE, progression rates to EAC, surveillance and treatment options, risks/benefits of each approach, and the frequency of EET sessions and duration of follow-up. Patient comorbidities and life expectancy should be considered.

**Supporting evidence by question:**

- **Q1 — Expert pathology confirmation:** LGD confirmed by expert/panel pathologists carried a higher cumulative progression to HGD/EAC than unconfirmed studies (15.7% [12.7%-19.3%] vs 8.1% [5.3%-12%], P=.004) and higher incidence rate (.031 vs .012/person-year). Expert review changed the pathologic diagnosis in 55% (31%-77%) of cases, most often downgrading (36% [18%-59%]). Interobserver agreement among expert pathologists: κ NDBE .22, LGD .11, HGD .43. Duits et al: progression risk rose dramatically when all 3 pathologists agreed on LGD (OR 47.14; 95% CI 13.10-169.70).
- **Q2a — EET vs surveillance in LGD:** RR of progression with RFA vs surveillance .14 (22 studies, 2746 pts); pooled from 2 RCTs RR .16 (95% CI .04-.57; P=.001). Cumulative progression: surveillance 12.6% (9.8%-15.9%) vs RFA 1.7% (1.1%-2.6%). For confirmed LGD, absolute risk ~25/100 over up to 84 mo on surveillance; treating 100 with EET → 21 fewer with HGD/EAC and ~9 (mostly treatable stricture) adverse events. **Confirmed LGD** and **persistent LGD** (LGD on 2 consecutive endoscopies) are the reproducible progression risk factors.
- **Q2b — EET vs surveillance in HGD:** RR of progression .42 (95% CI .24-.73; P=.0002) from 2 RCTs; indirect comparison cumulative progression surveillance 34% (25.5%-43.8%) vs EET 7.4% (4.5%-11.7%), RR .22. HGD adverse-event subanalysis 10.6% (5.7%-19.1%).
- **EET safety (RFA ± EMR, 37 studies, 9200 pts):** overall serious adverse event rate **8.8% (6.5%-11.9%)**; **stricture 5.6% (4.2%-7.4%)** (most common), bleeding 1% (.8%-1.3%), perforation 0.6% (.4%-.9%). Adverse events significantly higher for RFA *with* EMR vs RFA alone (RR 4.4; P=.015; 22.2% vs 5%).
- **Q3 — EET vs esophagectomy (HGD/IMC):** No difference in complete eradication of HGD/IMC (RR .96; .91-1.01) or in 1-, 3-, 5-year survival (5-yr RR .88; .74-1.04) or EAC-related mortality. Neoplasia recurrence higher with EET (RR 9.5; 3.26-27.75 — 2 more per 100). Major adverse events fewer with EET (RR .38; .20-.73; 16 fewer per 100). LN metastasis risk: 0% in HGD, up to 2% in IMC. Esophagectomy preferred for **T1b sm2-3 submucosal cancer, poorly differentiated cancer, lymphovascular invasion** (LN metastasis risk ≥20%). Esophagectomy operative mortality ~2%. >95% of recurrences after EET are successfully re-treated endoscopically.
- **Q4 — EMR of visible lesions:** EMR changed the pathologic diagnosis in **39% (34%-45%)** of patients, mostly **upstaging**. EMR provides larger/deeper specimens (to muscularis mucosa/submucosa) improving staging accuracy and interobserver agreement. EMR safety: in 681-patient cohort (2513 EMRs) no perforations, bleeding 1.2%, stricture 1%. "Visible lesions" = nodularity, ulceration, plaques, depression, or mucosal discoloration; resect all "no matter how subtle."
- **Q5 — Ablation of remaining flat BE after EMR:** Pech et al — metachronous neoplasia 16.5% (EMR + ablation) vs 29.9% (EMR alone), P=.0014; lack of ablation predicted recurrence (RR 2.5; 1.52-3.85). Manner RCT (EMR + APC vs EMR alone) stopped early: recurrence 3% vs 36.7%. Achieving CE-IM was protective for mortality (OR .4; .3-.6).
- **Q6 — Focal EMR + RFA vs complete EMR (cEMR) of entire segment:** Equivalent complete eradication of neoplasia (EMR+RFA 93.4% vs cEMR 94.9%) and CE-IM, but cEMR caused significantly more strictures (OR 4.73; 1.61-13.85), bleeding (OR 6.88; 2.19-21.62), and perforation (OR 7.00; 1.56-31.33). No difference in recurrence. cEMR may be acceptable in select cases (multifocal disease, diffuse nodularity, select short-segment BE).
- **Q7 — Surveillance after CE-IM:** Pooled recurrence (Fujii-Lau): any recurrence **7.5/100 patient-years**, IM recurrence **4.8/100 patient-years**, dysplasia recurrence **2.0/100 patient-years**; most recurrences within the first 3 years. CE-IM defined by 1-2 consecutive negative endoscopies (no standardized number). Post-CE-IM surveillance intervals are driven by expert opinion/low-quality evidence; a suggested schedule for **HGD/IMC**: every 3 months in year 1, then every 6 months in year 2, then annually; for **LGD**, surveillance every ~6 months ×2 then annually was referenced. Biopsy technique after CE-IM not standardized.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Updates [[barretts-esophagus]] therapeutics: screening-independent dysplasia management — expert pathology confirmation, EET indications by grade, EMR-first for visible lesions, focal EMR + ablation over complete EMR, EET over esophagectomy for HGD/IMC, post-CE-IM surveillance.
- Anchors [[endoscopic-eradication-therapy]] (EET technique, RFA/cryotherapy, CE-IM goal, adverse-event rates, recurrence).
- Cross-links to [[radiofrequency-ablation|RFA]], [[polypectomy-emr|EMR]], [[esophageal-adenocarcinoma]], [[upper-endoscopy]].

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Largely concordant with [[acg-2022-barretts]], [[aga-2024-barretts-eet]]. ASGE 2018 issues a *strong recommendation against esophagectomy* for HGD/IMC (very low quality), reflecting low LN-metastasis risk — consistent with later AGA/ACG positions.
- Post-CE-IM surveillance intervals are based on expert opinion; ACG 2022 and AGA give more explicit interval schedules — defer to those for exact timing.
- No RCT of EET vs esophagectomy exists and none is anticipated.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Early DS, Lightdale JR, Vargo JJ II, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee). Guidelines for sedation and anesthesia in GI endoscopy. Gastrointest Endosc 2018;87(2):327-337. doi:10.1016/j.gie.2017.07.018.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.07.018)
- **Authors:** Early DS, Lightdale JR, Vargo JJ II, Acosta RD, Chandrasekhara V, Chathadi KV, Evans JA, Fisher DA, Fonkalsrud L, Hwang JH, Khashab MA, Muthusamy VR, Pasha SF, Saltzman JR, Shergill AK, Cash BD, DeWitt JM (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee)
- **Year:** 2018
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2018;87(2):327-337
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2017.07.018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2017.07.018)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE-based clinical practice guideline)

Endorsed by AASLD, ACG, and AGA. Update of 3 prior ASGE sedation documents; literature search through August 2017. Recommendations graded by GRADE quality of evidence (4444 high, 444B moderate, 44BB low, 4BBB very low).

## Summary
ASGE Standards of Practice Committee guideline on sedation and anesthesia across the full continuum used for GI endoscopy. Sedation is a drug-induced depression of consciousness on a continuum from minimal sedation (anxiolysis) → moderate ("conscious") sedation → deep sedation → general anesthesia. Because patients move unpredictably along this continuum, providers must be able to **rescue** a patient who becomes more deeply sedated than intended.

Pre-procedural work-up: informed consent, history/focused exam (snoring/OSA, drug allergies, prior sedation reactions, last oral intake, tobacco/alcohol/substance use), airway assessment (Mallampati class), ASA physical-status classification (I–V, +E), and NPO/fasting to limit aspiration (ASA: ≥2 h clear liquids, ≥6 h light meal). A documented pre-procedural assessment and time-out are required quality metrics.

Minimal/moderate sedation is safely delivered by endoscopists for ASA class I–III patients, typically a **benzodiazepine + opioid** (midazolam favored for fast onset, short duration, amnestic effect; fentanyl favored over meperidine). Reversal agents — **naloxone** (opioids) and **flumazenil** (benzodiazepines) — must be available in every unit. Adjuncts (diphenhydramine, promethazine, droperidol) can deepen sedation in select cases (droperidol has a black-box QTc warning).

Propofol-mediated sedation (NAAP/NAPS, balanced propofol sedation, or anesthesia-provider/MAC) has shorter sedation and recovery times; propofol has no reversal agent, so deep sedation and rescue skills are required. Monitoring of BP, SpO₂, and HR is required for all sedated procedures; **capnography** should be considered for deep sedation (reduces transient hypoxemia). Anesthesia-provider assistance should be considered for prolonged/therapeutic procedures needing deep sedation, anticipated sedative intolerance, severe comorbidity (ASA IV/V), or airway-obstruction risk. Routine anesthesia for low-risk EGD/colonoscopy has not shown a safety benefit and increases cost.

## Key Findings / Claims

### Levels of sedation (Table 2)
| Level | Responsiveness | Airway | Spontaneous ventilation | CV function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal (anxiolysis) | Normal to verbal | Unaffected | Unaffected | Unaffected |
| Moderate (conscious) | Purposeful to verbal/tactile | No intervention | Adequate | Usually maintained |
| Deep | Purposeful after repeated/painful stimulus | Intervention may be required | May be inadequate | Usually maintained |
| General anesthesia | Unarousable even to pain | Intervention often required | Frequently inadequate | May be impaired |

### ASA physical-status classification (Table 3)
- **I:** Normal, healthy. **II:** Mild systemic disease, no activity limit (controlled HTN/DM). **III:** Moderate–severe systemic disease, no activity limit (stable angina, DM with sequelae). **IV:** Severe systemic disease, constant threat to life (severe CHF, ESRD). **V:** Moribund, substantial risk of death within 24 h. **E:** Emergency (suffix to I–V).
- Endoscopists may deliver minimal/moderate sedation to ASA I–III; higher ASA class is associated with increased cardiopulmonary adverse events.

### When to involve an anesthesia provider (Table 4)
- Prolonged or therapeutic procedures requiring deep sedation
- Anticipated intolerance to standard sedatives
- Increased adverse-event risk from severe comorbidity (ASA IV or V)
- Increased airway-obstruction risk from an anatomic variant

### Recommendations (GRADE)
1. We recommend that all patients undergoing endoscopic procedures be evaluated to assess their risk of sedation related to pre-existing medical conditions. **(4444 — high)**
2. We recommend that the combination of an opioid and benzodiazepine is a safe and effective regimen for achieving minimal to moderate sedation for upper endoscopy and colonoscopy in patients without risk factors for sedation-related adverse events. **(4444 — high)**
3. We suggest using an appropriate adjunctive agent (eg, diphenhydramine, promethazine, or droperidol) in combination with conventional sedative drugs in select clinical circumstances. **(44BB — low)**
4. We recommend that providers undergo specific training in the administration of endoscopic sedation and possess the skills necessary for the diagnosis and management of sedation-related adverse events, including rescue from a level of sedation deeper than that intended. **(4444 — high)**
5. We recommend the routine monitoring of blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and heart rate in addition to clinical observation for changes in cardiopulmonary status during all endoscopic procedures using sedation. Supplemental oxygen should be considered for moderate sedation and should be administered during deep sedation; supplemental oxygen should be administered if hypoxemia is anticipated or develops. **(4444 — high)**
6. We suggest that capnography monitoring be considered for patients undergoing endoscopy targeting deep sedation. **(44BB — low)**
7. We recommend anesthesia provider–administered sedation be considered for complex endoscopic procedures or patients with multiple medical comorbidities or at risk for airway compromise. **(444B — moderate)**
8. We suggest that endoscopists use propofol-based sedation (endoscopist-directed or anesthesia-provider administered) when it is expected to improve patient safety, comfort, procedural efficiency, and/or successful procedure completion. **(44BB — low)**

### Additional points
- **NPO/aspiration:** ASA — minimum 2 h after clear liquids, 6 h after a light meal; no universally accepted fasting standard. With impaired gastric emptying or emergencies, weigh aspiration risk in choosing target sedation depth, delaying the procedure, or protecting the airway with intubation.
- **Capnography:** detects depressed respiration before transient hypoxemia; reduced transient hypoxemia in a >500-patient colonoscopy RCT under deep sedation; not shown to improve safety in moderate sedation.
- **Reversal agents:** naloxone (opioid antagonist) and flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist) must be readily available; propofol has no specific reversal agent.
- **Cost/utilization:** endoscopist-directed propofol more cost-effective than anesthesia-administered; anesthesia utilization for low-risk EGD/colonoscopy continues to rise without demonstrated safety benefit and tracks reimbursement patterns; no difference in adenoma detection rate by sedation provider.

## Relevance to Wiki
- Anchors the new concept page [[endoscopy-sedation]] (sedation continuum, ASA class, propofol vs benzodiazepine/opioid, capnography, NPO, reversal agents).
- Adds periprocedural sedation context to [[upper-endoscopy]], [[colonoscopy]], [[ercp]], and [[endoscopic-ultrasound]].

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- No direct data link fasting duration to aspiration risk; fasting thresholds are extrapolated from ASA preoperative guidance.
- Capnography benefit established for deep but not moderate sedation; link between transient hypoxemia and serious cardiopulmonary events not established.
- Routine anesthesia-assisted sedation for low-risk procedures lacks a demonstrated safety benefit but utilization continues to grow.

# ASGE 2019 — Screening and Surveillance of Barrett's Esophagus

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Qumseya B, Sultan S, Bain P, Jamil L, Jacobson B, Anandasabapathy S, Agrawal D, Buxbaum JL, Fishman DS, Gurudu SR, Jue TL, Kripalani S, Lee JK, Khashab MA, Naveed M, Thosani NC, Yang J, DeWitt J, Wani S. ASGE guideline on screening and surveillance of Barrett's esophagus. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2019;90(3):335–359.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.05.012)
- **Authors:** Qumseya B, Sultan S (co-first authors), Bain P, Jamil L, Jacobson B, Anandasabapathy S, Agrawal D, Buxbaum JL, Fishman DS, Gurudu SR, Jue TL, Kripalani S, Lee JK, Khashab MA, Naveed M, Thosani NC, Yang J, DeWitt J, Wani S (Chair); ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2019
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2019;90(3):335-359
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2019.05.012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.05.012)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE methodology, official ASGE recommendations)

## Summary

This ASGE guideline addresses **screening and surveillance** of [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's esophagus]] (BE), the companion to the 2018 ASGE EET guideline. It uses GRADE methodology across 6 PICO questions covering surveillance of nondysplastic BE (NDBE), screening of at-risk populations, and advanced imaging/sampling adjuncts (chromoendoscopy, confocal laser endomicroscopy, EUS, WATS-3D, volumetric laser endomicroscopy).

Key positions: surveillance endoscopy is suggested for NDBE (conditional, very low quality — no RCT exists; benefit may be inflated by lead-/length-time bias). There is insufficient evidence on whether screening reduces mortality, but if screening is performed it should target an **at-risk population** — high risk = family history of EAC or BE; moderate risk = GERD plus ≥1 additional risk factor (age >50, obesity/central adiposity, smoking, male sex). For surveillance imaging, **chromoendoscopy (dye-based or virtual) plus Seattle-protocol biopsies is strongly recommended over white-light + Seattle alone** (moderate quality; ~9% absolute / ~30% relative increase in dysplasia detection). Routine **CLE is suggested against** (conditional, low). **EUS is strongly recommended against** for routinely differentiating T1a vs T1b mucosal/submucosal disease (moderate; high false-positive rate, EUS T1a-vs-T1b sensitivity only 41%). **WATS-3D as an adjunct to Seattle-protocol biopsies is suggested** (conditional, low). There is **no recommendation** for or against **VLE**.

The guideline endorses (without re-grading) NDBE surveillance every **3-5 years** based on the low NDBE progression rate (0.1%-0.3%/year), and the **Seattle protocol**: 4-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm (no prior dysplasia) or every 1 cm (prior dysplasia), plus targeted biopsies of any mucosal abnormality.

## Key Findings / Claims (Recommendations — near-verbatim, with strength and quality)

**Summary of recommendations (Table 4):**

1. **Statement 1 (Conditional, Very low quality):** In patients with nondysplastic BE, we suggest performing surveillance endoscopy compared with no surveillance.
2. **Statement 2 (No graded strength / NA quality):** There is insufficient evidence on the effectiveness of screening for BE. However, if screening endoscopy for BE is performed, we suggest a screening strategy that identifies an at-risk population. An at-risk population is defined as individuals with a family history of EAC or BE (high risk) or patients with GERD plus at least 1 other risk factor (moderate risk). [Additional risk factors: age >50, obesity/central adiposity, history of smoking, male sex.]
3. **Statement 3 (Strong, Moderate quality):** In patients with BE undergoing surveillance, we recommend using chromoendoscopy, including virtual chromoendoscopy and Seattle protocol biopsy sampling, compared with white-light endoscopy with Seattle protocol biopsy sampling.
4. **Statement 4 (Conditional, Low quality):** In patients with BE undergoing surveillance, we suggest against routine use of confocal laser endomicroscopy compared with white-light endoscopy with Seattle protocol biopsy sampling.
5. **Statement 5 (Strong, Moderate quality):** In BE patients with high-grade dysplasia/IMC or nodules, we recommend against routine use of EUS to differentiate mucosal vs submucosal disease.
6. **Statement 6a (Conditional, Low quality):** In patients with known or suspected BE, we suggest using WATS-3D in addition to Seattle protocol biopsy sampling compared with white-light endoscopy with Seattle protocol biopsy sampling.
7. **Statement 6b (No recommendation / NA quality):** In patients with BE undergoing surveillance, there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine use of VLE.

**Supporting evidence by question:**

- **Q1 — NDBE surveillance vs none (Codipilly SR/MA):** Unadjusted EAC-related mortality lower with surveillance (RR .60; .50-.71); EAC patients with prior BE diagnosis had lower EAC mortality (RR .73; .57-.94). **Lead-time adjustment eliminated the mortality benefit** (El-Serag HR 1.72 [.78-2.07]; Tramontano HR .89 [.78-1.01]; pooled adjusted HR .85 [.75-.95]). All-cause mortality unadjusted HR .75 (.59-.94); RR .48 (.37-.63) in EAC patients with prior BE. Surveillance associated with earlier-stage diagnosis (RR 2.11; 1.08-4.11). Adverse events of diagnostic EGD very low (1/200 to 1/10,000). NDBE EAC progression 0.1%-0.3%/year → supports **3-5 year** NDBE surveillance intervals. Diagnostic EGD AEs: cardiopulmonary 1/170-1/10,000; perforation 1/2500-1/11,000.
- **Q2 — Screening / at-risk population:** No studies compared screening vs no screening. Panel used a ≥10% BE prevalence threshold to recommend screening. Risk factors (Table 6): GERD OR 2.9 (4.5 if GERD ≥2 weeks); family history of BE/EAC OR 12; male-to-female ratio 2.13; obesity OR 1.15 (NS adjusting for GERD) but central adiposity OR 1.44 (1.2-1.74); ever-smoking OR 1.42 (1.15-1.76), 1.96 adjusted. BE risk increases ~1.2% per additional risk factor. <10% of EAC patients have a prior BE diagnosis; ~40% of EAC patients report no prior GERD; ~50% of short-segment BE patients have no GERD symptoms. PPI (OR .55) and statins (OR .48) linked to lower progression. AspECT-type trial: high-dose PPI + aspirin improved composite of all-cause mortality/HGD/EAC (time ratio 1.59; 1.14-2.23). AGA Clinical Practice Update recommended against alternative (non-endoscopic) screening tests at the time. Endoscopic screening of GERD patients cost-effective at <$100,000/QALY.
- **Q3 — Chromoendoscopy (CE/VC) + Seattle vs WLE + Seattle:** Absolute increase in dysplasia detection **9% (4.1%-14%; P<.001)**; relative increase **30.3% (16.2%-44.3%)**. No significant difference VC vs dye-based CE. Performance (ASGE Technology Committee): conventional dye CE sensitivity 91.9%, NPV 95.5%, specificity 89.9%; acetic acid sensitivity 96.6%, NPV 98.3%, specificity 84.6% (met PIVI thresholds); NBI/VC sensitivity 94.2%, NPV 97.5%.
- **Q4 — CLE:** Absolute increase in dysplasia detection 10.2% (1.4%-19.1%; CI near zero); relative increase **not significant** (36%; -5.4% to 77.5%). Overall CLE sensitivity 90.4%, NPV 96.2%, specificity 89.9% — did not meet PIVI thresholds (endoscope-based CLE met thresholds but is no longer available). High false-positive rate in low-prevalence settings (16.3% at 5% prevalence; 12% at 30%). RCT prevalence (19%-35%) far exceeds community surveillance prevalence → limited real-world yield.
- **Q5 — EUS for T1a vs T1b:** Pooled sensitivity **41% (35%-48%)**, specificity 89% (86%-91%), accuracy 75% (59%-86%) for differentiating mucosal vs submucosal disease. High false-positive rate (6% at high prevalence to 10.5% at low prevalence); ~one-third of EUS-positive "advanced disease" calls are false positives. Reinforces ASGE 2018 position: resect all visible lesions with EMR/ESD first as the diagnostic/staging step rather than relying on EUS. (EUS remains relevant for confirmed/advanced EAC and nodal assessment.)
- **Q6a — WATS-3D added to Seattle protocol:** Relative increase in dysplasia detection **48% (34%-60%)** overall; 47% (32%-61%) in patients with prior dysplasia; absolute increase 10.6% (1.5%-19.8%) (history of dysplasia) and ~2% in known/suspected BE without dysplasia history. Much of the additional detection is LGD (absolute LGD increase ~1.8%); the clinical meaning of "LGD on cytology" vs histologic LGD is uncertain. Exceeded the expert-derived 27% threshold. No safety/cost-effectiveness data identified.
- **Q6b — VLE:** Evidence insufficient/evolving (VLE with laser marking promising but immature) — no recommendation.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Updates [[barretts-esophagus]] diagnostics/surveillance: at-risk screening criteria, NDBE 3-5 year surveillance and the Seattle protocol, chromoendoscopy/virtual chromoendoscopy as a strong adjunct, recommendations against routine CLE and EUS (T1a/T1b), WATS-3D as adjunct, and caution on lead-/length-time bias in surveillance evidence.
- Cross-links to [[upper-endoscopy]] (screening modality), [[esophageal-adenocarcinoma]], [[gerd]] (screening trigger), [[endoscopic-ultrasound|EUS]], [[endoscopic-eradication-therapy]].

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Concordant with [[acg-2022-barretts]] and [[aga-2025-barretts-surveillance]] on the Seattle protocol, chromoendoscopy, and risk-factor-based screening. ASGE 2019 is more cautious than some societies on accepting non-endoscopic screening devices (Cytosponge/capsule) — ACG 2022 explicitly endorses them as an acceptable alternative.
- ASGE 2019 does NOT require intestinal metaplasia for a BE diagnosis in its framing, whereas ACG/AGA require IM with goblet cells — note the international disagreement.
- Surveillance mortality benefit largely disappears after lead-time adjustment; no RCT (BOSS trial result awaited at publication).

# ASGE Guideline: Endoscopic Management of Choledocholithiasis (2019)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Buxbaum JL, Abbas Fehmi SM, Sultan S, Fishman DS, Qumseya BJ, Cortessis VK, Schilperoort H, Kysh L, Matsuoka L, Yachimski P, Agrawal D, Gurudu SR, Jamil LH, Jue TL, Khashab MA, Law JK, Lee JK, Naveed M, Sawhney MS, Thosani N, Yang J, Wani SB. ASGE guideline on the role of endoscopy in the evaluation and management of choledocholithiasis. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2019;89(6):1075–1105.e15.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2018.10.001)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2019
- **Journal:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2019;89(6):1075–1105.e15
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2018.10.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2018.10.001)
- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline risk-stratifies suspected common bile duct (CBD) stones and defines the diagnostic and therapeutic endoscopic pathway, including stone-clearance techniques and the role of early [[ercp]] in gallstone pancreatitis.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Risk stratification (revised from 2010):**
  - **High (>50%)** — any of: CBD stone on US/cross-sectional imaging; total bilirubin **>4 mg/dL** *and* dilated CBD; ascending cholangitis → proceed directly to **[[ercp]]**.
  - **Intermediate (10–50%)** — any of: abnormal liver tests; age **>55 y**; dilated CBD → confirm first with **EUS or MRCP** (or IOC / intraoperative US) to avoid unnecessary ERCP.
  - **Low (<10%)** — no predictors → cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiogram as needed.
  - Dilated CBD = **>6 mm** (gallbladder in situ) / **>8 mm** (post-cholecystectomy). Bilirubin >4 alone *or* dilation alone is only intermediate — the combination is high-risk. **Gallstone pancreatitis dropped** as a criterion (no correlation with persistent stones).
- **EUS and MRCP** have comparable high accuracy for detecting CBD stones; choose by availability/expertise.
- **Large/difficult stones:** **endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation after sphincterotomy** improves clearance over sphincterotomy alone; consider mechanical lithotripsy/cholangioscopy-guided lithotripsy.
- **Gallstone pancreatitis:** **early ERCP** for concurrent **cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction** (not routinely for uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis).

---

## Clinical Relevance

ERCP for high-probability stones, EUS/MRCP to triage intermediate-probability cases, large-balloon dilation for big stones, and early ERCP only when cholangitis/obstruction complicates [[acute-pancreatitis|gallstone pancreatitis]]. Core to [[ercp]] practice and biliary obstruction workup.

---

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Lee JK, Agrawal D, Thosani N, et al. ASGE guideline on the role of endoscopy for bleeding from chronic radiation proctopathy. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2019;90:171-82.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.234)
- **Authors:** Lee JK, Agrawal D, Thosani N, et al.; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee (Wani SB, Chair)
- **Year:** 2019
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.234](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.234)
- **Type:** guideline (systematic review + GRADE recommendations)

## Summary

ASGE Standards of Practice systematic review (literature 1946–2017) of endoscopic therapy for bleeding from **chronic radiation proctopathy**, a common late sequela of pelvic radiation (bladder, cervical, prostate, rectal cancer) affecting up to 30% of irradiated patients. Distinguishes **acute** radiation proctopathy (≤3 months, superficial epithelial depletion with acute inflammatory infiltrate, usually self-limiting) from **chronic** radiation proctopathy (≥3 months, median onset 8–12 months; obliterative/ischemic endarteritis, submucosal fibrosis, neovascularization, and relative *lack* of inflammatory infiltrate).

Endoscopy is the principal diagnostic tool — findings include mucosal pallor, edema, friability, spontaneous bleeding, and telangiectasias. **Biopsy is discouraged** because sampling can create non-healing ulcers or fistulas; biopsy only when needed to exclude other proctitis (infection, IBD).

Evidence is limited (mostly small observational series, few comparative trials), but pooled analyses found argon plasma coagulation (APC, ~87% clinical success), bipolar electrocoagulation (~88%), heater probe, and radiofrequency ablation (RFA) all effective for rectal bleeding. No modality proven superior. The panel suggests *against* 4% formalin compared with APC (higher adverse-event rate), and found insufficient evidence on newer-generation cryoablation.

## Key Findings / Claims

- Up to 30% of patients receiving pelvic radiation develop radiation proctopathy.
- Acute vs chronic distinguished by timing (3 months) and histology (acute inflammatory infiltrate vs obliterative endarteritis/fibrosis/neovascularization).
- Acute proctopathy: manage supportively (hydration, antidiarrheals, discontinuation of radiation); usually self-limited.
- Chronic proctopathy bleeding: medical/supportive therapy often insufficient → endoscopic therapy is the mainstay.
- Endoscopic findings: pallor, edema, friability, spontaneous bleeding, telangiectasias; biopsy discouraged (non-healing ulcer/fistula risk).
- **APC:** pooled clinical success 87% (95% CI 85–90%); 1–3.7 treatment sessions, typically 3–4 weeks apart; reported power 25–80 W (median 50 W), argon flow 0.6–2.5 L/min (median 1.5 L/min); pooled serious AE rate 4%; **colonic explosion reported with inadequate bowel prep → adequate bowel preparation required**; avoid "painting" (target individual vessels) to prevent confluent ulcers.
- **Bipolar electrocoagulation:** pooled clinical success 88%; comparable to APC and heater probe.
- **Heater probe** and **RFA:** effective in available series.
- **4% formalin:** suggested *against* vs APC (higher AE rates), though comparably effective for bleeding control.
- **Cryoablation (newer-generation):** insufficient evidence for or against.
- No mandate to treat "cosmetic" bleeding (minor bleeding without anemia).

## Recommendations (verbatim)

1. In patients with chronic radiation proctopathy, we suggest argon plasma coagulation, bipolar electrocoagulation, heater probe, and radiofrequency ablation for treatment of bleeding from chronic radiation proctopathy. There is insufficient evidence to recommend a specific endoscopic modality over another for treatment of bleeding from chronic proctopathy. *(Conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence)*
2. In patients with chronic radiation proctopathy, we suggest against the use of 4% formalin compared with argon plasma coagulation because of higher adverse event rates compared with argon plasma coagulation for treatment of bleeding from chronic radiation proctopathy. *(Conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence)*
3. In patients with chronic radiation proctopathy, there is insufficient evidence for or against the use of the newer-generation cryoablation system for treatment of bleeding from chronic radiation proctopathy.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates new disease script [[radiation-proctopathy]] (colorectal inflammation/injury).
- Links to [[acute-lower-gi-bleeding]] DDx (radiation proctopathy as a cause of hematochezia); APC is the most commonly used endoscopic therapy.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- No validated diagnostic criterion or unified endoscopic grading system for radiation proctopathy.
- Evidence base limited to small uncontrolled series; no head-to-head modality superiority established.

## Bibliographic Info

ASGE guideline on the management of achalasia. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2020;91(2):213–227.e6.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.231)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2020
- **Journal:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 2020;91(2):213–227.e6
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.231](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2019.04.231)
- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline addresses diagnosis confirmation and definitive therapy for [[achalasia]]. Diagnosis is confirmed by [[high-resolution-manometry]] (Chicago classification); endoscopy/barium support it. Definitive options are graded therapies that disrupt the lower esophageal sphincter.

---

## Key Recommendations

- Confirm diagnosis with **[[high-resolution-manometry]]**; exclude pseudoachalasia (EGD ± EUS/imaging).
- **Definitive therapies** of comparable efficacy: **[[poem]]**, **pneumatic dilation (PD)**, and **laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM)** — select by achalasia subtype, surgical risk, and local expertise (**POEM** favored for **type III/spastic** disease given a tailorable myotomy).
- **Botulinum toxin injection** reserved for **poor candidates** for myotomy/dilation (temporary effect, repeat needed).
- Counsel on **post-treatment reflux** (highest after POEM; LHM usually paired with partial fundoplication) and arrange surveillance.

---

## Clinical Relevance

POEM, pneumatic dilation, and Heller myotomy are the durable options (botox for frail patients); subtype guides choice and reflux is the key trade-off. Supports the [[achalasia]] and [[poem]] notes; updated by SAGES 2024 POEM guidance.
