- **Authors:** Kohli DR, Amateau SK, Desai M, Chinnakotla S, Harrison ME, Chalhoub JM, Coelho-Prabhu N, Elhanafi SE, Forbes N, Fujii-Lau LL, Kwon RS, Machicado JD, Marya NB, Pawa S, Ruan W, Sheth SG, Thiruvengadam NR, Thosani NC, Qumseya BJ; ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2023
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Gastrointestinal Endoscopy* 2023;97(4):607–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2022.10.007
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2022.10.007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2022.10.007)
- **Type:** guideline (GRADE-based clinical practice guideline)

## Summary

This ASGE Standards of Practice Committee guideline provides an evidence-based, GRADE-framework approach to the management of biliary strictures in liver transplant recipients. Bile duct strictures are a common adverse outcome after liver transplantation, associated with significant morbidity ranging from asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation to cholangitis, allograft rejection, and allograft failure. The document addresses four clinical questions developed with a multidisciplinary expert panel (transplant surgery, transplant hepatology, gastroenterology) and a patient advocate.

The four questions cover: (1) ERCP versus percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) as initial therapy; (2) covered self-expandable metal stents (cSEMSs) versus multiple plastic stents (MPSs) for therapy of strictures; (3) the role of MRCP for diagnosing post-transplant biliary strictures; and (4) antibiotics versus no antibiotics during elective ERCP. The panel notably excluded patients with cholangitis from the antibiotic question (clear existing guidelines mandate antibiotics) and, for the cSEMS question, restricted analysis to anastomotic (duct-to-duct) extrahepatic strictures in patients eligible for either treatment irrespective of foregut anatomy.

Overall, in patients with post-transplant biliary strictures the ASGE suggests **ERCP as the initial intervention** and **cSEMSs as the preferred stent for extrahepatic (anastomotic) strictures**. In patients with unclear diagnoses or intermediate probability of a stricture, the ASGE suggests **MRCP as the diagnostic modality**. Antibiotics should be administered during ERCP when complete biliary drainage cannot be ensured. All four recommendations are **conditional** ("we suggest"), reflecting limited (very low to high) quality of evidence.

The guideline focuses on patients with unaltered (duct-to-duct) foregut anatomy; patients with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (e.g., PSC recipients) may not be candidates for conventional duodenoscope ERCP, and the role of EUS-guided biliary access and percutaneous approaches in transplant recipients remains to be defined.

## Key Findings / Claims

### Question 1 — ERCP vs PTBD as initial therapy

**Recommendation 1 (verbatim):** "In liver transplant recipients with a biliary stricture, the ASGE suggests ERCP over PTBD as initial therapy for management of strictures." — *Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence.*

**Best practice advice (Table 1):**
- ERCP preferred if it is difficult for caregivers to manage percutaneous drains/catheters, risk of dislodgement of percutaneous drains/catheters, presence of multiple intrahepatic strictures in different hepatic lobes, and lack of significant biliary dilation to facilitate percutaneous drainage.
- PTBD preferred if difficult endoscopic biliary access because of various reasons including altered anatomy or increased risk of adverse events from anesthesia.

**Supporting evidence:**
- Systematic review of 4 full-text studies (all retrospective except 1 multicenter nationwide study) directly comparing ERCP and PTBD as initial therapy; 432 procedures in aggregate (275 ERCP, 157 PTBD). Patients with altered foregut anatomy (Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy) and salvage procedures were excluded.
- Allograft rejection: adjusted odds of allograft failure were **8.47 greater for PTBD** vs ERCP (95% CI 1.47–48.6; P = .017).
- PTBD associated with longer hospitalization (OR 14.4; 95% CI 3.7–25.1; P = .008), higher disposition to nursing home (OR 2.72; 95% CI 1.08–6.87; P = .03), and higher overall cost.
- One study: fewer procedures with ERCP than PTBD (2.5 ± 0.9 vs 6.1 ± 0.4; P < .01). PTBD patients had an average of 3.0 ± 0.4 additional procedures for external catheter problems (leakage 14.9%, catheter retraction 29.8%, decreased drainage 43.2%, cholangitis 6.6%, other 5.5%).
- No difference in technical success (RR 1.28; 95% CI 0.27–2.33; P = .42; I² = 53.4%), composite AEs (RR 1.12; 95% CI 0.62–2.0; P = .7; I² = 0%), adjusted inpatient mortality (OR 1.47; P = .74), nonelective 30-day readmission (OR 0.98; P = .97), or total duration of therapy (5.3 ± 0.8 months ERCP vs 6.5 ± 0.7 months PTBD; P = .31).
- Cost of hospitalization: $179,179.3 ± $123,386.6 (ERCP) vs $257,058.7 ± $201,423.3 (PTBD), P < .01.

### Question 2 — cSEMS vs MPS for extrahepatic (anastomotic) strictures

**Recommendation 2 (verbatim):** "In liver transplant recipients with biliary strictures, the ASGE suggests cSEMSs should be used instead of MPSs for initial therapy of extrahepatic biliary strictures." — *Conditional recommendation, low to moderate quality of evidence.*

**Best practice advice (Table 1):**
- Covered metal stents are most often used for extrahepatic biliary strictures, typically at the anastomosis.
- Cholangiographic findings, such as intrahepatic biliary strictures or anastomotic strictures just below the bifurcation, may preclude the use of covered metal stents.

**Supporting evidence:**
- Systematic review using existing published analyses (Visconti et al). 4 multicenter RCTs and several meta-analyses; only studies in which patients could undergo either treatment irrespective of foregut anatomy were included. 205 patients across the 4 RCTs (103 cSEMS, 102 MPS); strictures were anastomotic (duct-to-duct) and did not involve intrahepatic ducts. Follow-up ≥1 year.
- No difference in stricture resolution between cSEMS and MPS (pooled risk difference 0.01; 95% CI −0.08 to 0.10; I² = 12%).
- No difference in stricture recurrence (pooled risk difference 0.13; 95% CI −0.03 to 0.28; I² = 52%), assessed in 181 patients.
- cSEMSs associated with **fewer procedures** (mean difference −1.86; 95% CI −3.12 to −0.06; I² = 97%) and fewer days to achieve resolution (mean difference −105.07; 95% CI −202.38 to −7.76; I² = 95%).
- cSEMSs required fewer stents per patient (mean difference −10.63; 95% CI −20.82 to −0.44).
- Plastic stents were exchanged through the point of resolution, whereas metal stents were removed after a defined period of 3 to 6 months regardless of cholangiogram interpretation.
- Most common AE was stent migration, with no significant difference between SEMSs and MPSs (meta-analysis of 84 patients). Stent migration considered a procedural finding rather than an AE if the stent was recovered on schedule and the stricture resolved.
- Cost: mean treatment cost lower with cSEMS than MPS ($8288 vs $19,580; P < .01).
- Salient points: stricture location was not delineated in the 4 RCTs; cholangiographic findings such as intrahepatic strictures or anastomotic strictures just below the bifurcation may obviate the use of cSEMSs; no clear strategy for positioning across or upstream of the biliary orifice was evaluated. Indirect evidence that cSEMSs can be associated with post-ERCP pancreatitis (not reported in any RCT).

### Question 3 — MRCP as preferred diagnostic modality

**Recommendation 3 (verbatim):** "In liver transplant recipients with suspected biliary stricture, the ASGE suggests use of MRCP as a diagnostic test." — *Conditional recommendation, moderate to high quality of evidence.*

**Best practice advice (Table 1):**
- MRCP is an acceptable diagnostic test for detecting post-transplant strictures.
- Individual clinical scenarios should dictate the utility of MRCP.
- In patients with a high pretest probability for a biliary stricture or cholangitis, proceeding directly to ERCP without a diagnostic MRCP is prudent.

**Supporting evidence:**
- Systematic review of 21 studies (13 retrospective, 8 prospective); meta-analyses compared MRCP to ERCP (criterion standard).
- Sensitivity/specificity meta-analysis: 20 studies, 758 patients. Pooled **sensitivity 94.9%** (95% CI 92.4–96.6; I² = 32.8%); pooled **specificity 90.3%** (95% CI 84.7–94.0; I² = 87.8%).
- Positive predictive value: 16 studies, 584 patients; PPV 90.6% (95% CI 85.6–93.9; I² = 64.4%).
- Negative predictive value: 14 studies, 505 patients; NPV 93.7% (95% CI 86.2–97.2; I² = 81.2%).
- Accuracy: 13 studies, 508 patients; pooled accuracy 92.4% (95% CI 89.0–94.6; I² = 24.1%).
- In a population of 1000 patients with 50% pretest probability: MRCP correctly identifies 452 as no stricture and 475 as having stricture; 48 false positives, 25 false negatives.
- Overall risk of MRCP deemed low, especially vs ERCP. Limitations: incompatible metallic implants, claustrophobia.

### Question 4 — Antibiotics during elective ERCP

**Recommendation 4 (verbatim):** "In patients with post–liver transplant biliary strictures undergoing elective ERCP in whom complete biliary drainage is technically challenging to achieve (ischemic cholangiopathy, multiple strictures, failure of stenting), the ASGE suggests administration of periprocedural antibiotics over no antibiotics to reduce incidence of infectious AEs." — *Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence.*

**Best practice advice (Table 1):**
- An individualized approach for administering antibiotics based on each patient's unique biliary anatomy and clinical condition is prudent.
- Patients with inadequate drainage of the biliary tree because of strictures may benefit from preprocedural antibiotics.
- Otherwise, use of antibiotics should be discussed with the patient and transplant team before ERCP.

**Supporting evidence:**
- Patients with cholangitis excluded (clear guidelines already recommend antibiotics).
- Only 2 retrospective single-center US studies met selection criteria; 361 liver transplant recipients undergoing 959 ERCP procedures. Pooled incidence of infections 1.1% (95% CI 0.6–2.0; I² = 0). Both studies found that antibiotic administration did NOT lower the risk of infections or adverse outcomes.
- Bacteremia during ERCP is typically transient and not definitely associated with AEs. Unrestricted antibiotic use may increase multidrug-resistant organisms and antibiotic resistance (especially fluoroquinolones, already a challenge in LT patients).
- Antibiotic AEs noted: QTc prolongation, torsades de pointes, fluoroquinolone tendinitis/tendon rupture (black box warning); fluoroquinolones are weak CYP3A4 inhibitors and can increase serum tacrolimus concentration.
- Patients who may benefit from periprocedural antibiotics: stenosed intra- or extrahepatic ducts, ischemic cholangiopathy, multiple intrahepatic strictures, or those in whom contrast was injected but stricture dilation or stent placement across a stricture was unsuccessful.

### What Is New
ERCP as initial therapy for biliary strictures in post–LT patients; covered metal stents as preferred implant for strictures not involving intrahepatic ducts; preprocedural MRCP to confirm and delineate stricture location in patients with uncertain diagnosis; selection of patients for periprocedural antibiotic therapy.

### Future Directions
1. Natural history and risk factors for biliary stricture formation (ischemia from vascular insult postulated for ischemic cholangiopathy and nonanastomotic strictures; other factors — medications, donor age, allograft mismatch, pretransplant MELD — remain under investigation).
2. Optimal therapeutic approach in patients with altered foregut anatomy (Roux-en-Y, as in PSC) — role of percutaneous and EUS-guided biliary access needs evaluation.
3. Role of antibiotics during ERCP — prospective trials needed to define need, class, dose, and duration.

## Relevance to Wiki
- **[[biliary-stricture]]** (diagnostic schema): adds a dedicated post-LT anastomotic vs non-anastomotic stricture management section — ERCP-first, cSEMS over MPS, MRCP diagnosis, antibiotics.
- **[[liver-transplantation]]** (disease script): reinforces the Biliary Complications subsection; the AASLD-AST 2025 graft-complications guidance (already cited) is concordant — ERCP first-line therapy, MRCP first-line diagnosis, cSEMS = MPS resolution but cSEMS fewer procedures/lower cost/shorter duration, PTBD for failed endoscopy.
- **[[ercp]]** (procedure): post-LT stricture as a stent-strategy indication; periprocedural antibiotics when drainage incomplete.
- **[[mri-mrcp]]** (concept): high diagnostic performance of MRCP in the post-LT population.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Largely concordant with the AASLD-AST 2025 graft-complications guideline cited on [[liver-transplantation]]. One nuance: AASLD-AST states cSEMS and MPS have equivalent resolution but cSEMS needs fewer procedures (mean difference 1.69 ERCPs), shorter treatment (40 vs 80 days), 25% lower cost; the ASGE 2023 meta-analysis numbers differ slightly (mean −1.86 procedures; cost $8288 vs $19,580) but the direction is identical.
- Evidence base is weak for Q1 (very low) and Q4 (very low); both are conditional. Q3 (MRCP) is the strongest (moderate–high).
- All cSEMS data are for anastomotic duct-to-duct strictures; cSEMS may be inappropriate for intrahepatic or near-bifurcation strictures and for non-anastomotic ischemic cholangiopathy.

# ASGE Guideline: Endoscopy in Management of Chronic Pancreatitis (2024)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. ASGE Guideline: Role of Endoscopy in Management of Chronic Pancreatitis (2024). Gastrointestinal Endoscopy.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.05.016)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2024.05.016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.05.016)
- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline defines endoscopic options for painful [[chronic-pancreatitis]] — ductal decompression, stone management, and pain-directed neurolysis — and where surgery is preferred. It weighs [[ercp]]-based endotherapy and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) against surgical drainage.

---

## Key Recommendations (conditional)

- In patients with an **obstructed main pancreatic duct and no surgical contraindication**, **surgery (drainage)** is suggested as it provides more durable pain relief than endotherapy; **endotherapy** is reserved for those with contraindications to or who decline surgery.
- For **pancreatic duct stones**, **ESWL ± [[ercp]]** for ductal clearance and decompression.
- For pain, **EUS-guided celiac plexus block** is suggested **over** percutaneous approaches, but with modest/limited efficacy (<60% achieve relief) — use selectively.
- For main-duct lesions, **ERCP with or without pancreatoscopy**; consider **fully-covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS)** for refractory benign pancreatic duct strictures.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Frames a stepwise approach to painful [[chronic-pancreatitis]]: favor surgical drainage for durable relief in good operative candidates, use ERCP/ESWL endotherapy and EUS celiac block selectively. Connects to [[ercp]] technique and [[endoscopic-ultrasound]]-guided interventions.

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Desai M, Ruan W, Thosani NC, et al. American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy guideline on the diagnosis and management of GERD: methodology and review of evidence. *VideoGIE* 2025;10:81–137.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vgie.2024.10.001)
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.vgie.2024.10.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vgie.2024.10.001)

Desai M, Ruan W, Thosani NC, et al. American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy guideline on the diagnosis and management of GERD: methodology and review of evidence. *Gastrointest Endosc* 2025;10:81–137. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vgie.2024.10.001>

- Prepared by: ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- GRADE methodology; evidence panel convened March 10, 2023
- Literature search through December 2022
- Updates the prior 2015 ASGE GERD guideline
- Published open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

## Summary

57-page evidence review and guideline covering six PICO questions on [[gerd|GERD]]: (1) indications for [[upper-endoscopy|upper endoscopy]] including in post-sleeve gastrectomy and post-[[poem|POEM]] patients; (2) criteria for high-quality endoscopy and reporting; (3) lifestyle interventions; (4) PPI therapy vs placebo; (5a) TIF 2.0 vs medical therapy; (5b) combined TIF + hiatal hernia repair (cTIF) vs medical therapy; and (6) radiofrequency energy (Stretta) vs medical therapy. Recommendations are graded using GRADE (strong/conditional; high/moderate/low/very low quality of evidence).

## Key Findings / Claims

### Definition and Epidemiology

- GERD defined as troublesome heartburn and/or regurgitation; affects ~one-third of the U.S. adult population
- Incidence rising in parallel with obesity prevalence
- Guideline explicitly excludes patients with known GI motility disorders ([[gastroparesis]], scleroderma, autonomic dysfunction)

### Endoscopy Indications (Q1)

- **Strong, moderate evidence**: Upper endoscopy recommended for alarm symptoms — dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting, unexplained iron deficiency anemia
- **Conditional, low evidence**: Endoscopy suggested for [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's esophagus]] risk factors (family history of BE/EAC; GERD + age >50, male sex, white race, smoking, or obesity) and for infants/children with suggestive symptoms
- **Post-sleeve gastrectomy (SG), conditional, very low**: Endoscopy if symptomatic; asymptomatic screening at 3 years then every 5 years (pooled BE rate post-SG 11.4%, crossing the ASGE 10% screening threshold); de novo GERD rate 45%, esophagitis rate 39.1% vs 21.9% pre-SG
- **Post-POEM, conditional, very low**: Endoscopy if symptomatic GERD; best practice advice to consider periodic endoscopy even if asymptomatic given high GERD rate (~19–29% esophagitis pooled); BE rate very low (1/2342 patients at 36 months in one meta-analysis)

### High-Quality Endoscopy Reporting (Q2)

- **Strong, very low evidence**: Require documentation and photo-documentation of:
  - Erosive esophagitis graded by Los Angeles (LA) classification
  - Barrett's esophagus described by Prague C&M classification
  - Peptic stricture (if present)
  - GEJ landmarks: top of gastric folds, Z-line, diaphragmatic impression
  - Hiatal hernia size; Hill grade or American Foregut Society (AFS) grade in forward view and retroflexion
  - Existing fundoplication (if present)
- Observational data showed esophagitis graded in only 42% of reports and hiatal hernia measured in only 51%

### Lifestyle Modifications (Q3)

- **Strong, low evidence**: Recommend weight loss (overweight/obese), smoking cessation, head of bed elevation, and avoiding meals within 3 hours of bedtime
- Weight loss: dose-dependent GERD symptom improvement; 81% of subjects in one RCT showed reduced GERD scores after 6-month weight-loss program (BMI 34.7 to 30.2)
- Head of bed elevation: significant reduction in reflux episodes and AET
- Alcohol, citrus/spicy foods: insufficient evidence for recommendations
- Data overall very low quality due to small sample sizes and inability to pool

### PPI Therapy (Q4)

- **Strong, moderate evidence**: PPIs at lowest dose for shortest duration while discussing long-term management
- PPI vs placebo: OR 4.2 for symptom relief (95% CI 3.25–5.48); OR 11.4 for esophagitis healing (95% CI 8.17–16.3) — Zhang 2017 network meta-analysis, 98 RCTs, ~46,000 patients
- PPI safety (Moayyedi 2019 large RCT, n=17,598, mean 3-year follow-up): no significant increase in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, CKD, C. diff, pneumonia, fractures, or dementia; only confirmed adverse event is modest increase in enteric infections (OR 1.33)
- **Conditional, very low evidence**: Test CYP2C19 polymorphism in suboptimal PPI responders; rapid metabolizers have OR 1.6 for PPI refractoriness
- Best practice advice: de-escalate after >6 months; discuss risks/benefits; H2RAs acceptable as adjunct/PRN; potassium-competitive acid blockers (PCABs, e.g., [[vonoprazan]]) likely more potent for erosive esophagitis but long-term data not yet available

### TIF 2.0 (Transoral Incisionless Fundoplication) (Q5a)

- **Conditional, low evidence**: Suggest TIF evaluation for confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia ≤2 cm and Hill grade I or II who meet any of: chronic GERD ≥6 months, long-term PPI use ≥6 months, refractory GERD, regurgitation-predominant GERD, patient preference to avoid long-term PPI
- Refractory GERD defined as persistent troublesome symptoms despite double-dose PPI for ≥8 weeks with documented pathologic reflux
- PPI discontinuation: RCT pooled RR 12.7 (77.6% vs 6.3% at 6 months); cohort studies: 98.8% on PPI at baseline vs 28.6% at ~19 months post-TIF
- Symptom resolution (6-month RCTs): 68.2% vs 32.4%, RR 2.12 (1.27–3.54)
- Durable symptom resolution at 5 years: 86.4% (1 RCT)
- Acid exposure time: significantly lower vs sham (MD –2.38), but not significantly lower vs PPI (MD +2.61)
- Overall adverse events higher with TIF vs PPI/sham (37.8% vs 14.3%); serious adverse events not statistically different (8% vs 1.9%); perforation 0.9%, bleeding 0.6%, pneumothorax 0.5%; 1 death at 20 months unrelated
- Post-TIF dysphagia: pooled 3.6%
- Cost: TIF 2.0 (~$13,979) < LNF (~$17,658) but > PPI (~$10,931); cost-effective with ICUR of $3,047/0.29 QALY

### cTIF — Combined Hiatal Hernia Repair + TIF (Q5b)

- **Conditional, very low evidence**: Suggest cTIF evaluation in multidisciplinary review for confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia >2 cm and Hill grade III or IV
- Cohort data only (7 studies, n=358); no RCTs yet (NCT04795934 ongoing)
- PPI use: 94.6% at baseline → 37.5% at follow-up; GERD-HRQL MD 21.87 improvement
- Serious adverse events 0.56%; dysphagia 5.6%

### Stretta — Radiofrequency Energy to LES (Q6)

- **Best practice advice only** (no GRADE recommendation): Stretta can be considered for confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia <2 cm and Hill grade I or II when TIF and surgical fundoplication are not available or feasible
- RCT evidence: no statistically significant PPI discontinuation advantage, no significant AET reduction, no significant symptom resolution benefit vs sham/PPI
- Cohort data suggest partial benefit (47% PPI discontinuation at 25 months); GERD-HRQL improvement in cohorts
- Reimbursement challenges and lack of adoption limit utility

### Novel Endoscopic Therapies

- GERDx (EFTP), MUSE, antireflux mucosectomy (ARMS), antireflux mucosal ablation (ARMA), resection and plication (RAP): insufficient controlled data; panel declined to recommend
- MUSE: serious AE rates 3.5–13.9% (empyema, hemorrhage, perforation) — not recommended over TIF 2.0
- ARMS: clinical response 80.1%; dysphagia/stricture 11.4% — RCT underway
- Investigational use only; ongoing RCTs expected to provide future guidance

## Recommendations

| Recommendation | Strength | Evidence Quality |
|---|---|---|
| **Endoscopy Indications** | | |
| Perform upper endoscopy for alarm symptoms (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting, unexplained iron deficiency anemia) | Strong | Moderate |
| Consider endoscopy for Barrett's esophagus risk factors (family Hx BE/EAC; GERD + age >50, male sex, white race, smoking, or obesity) | Conditional | Low |
| Post-sleeve gastrectomy: perform endoscopy if symptomatic; consider asymptomatic screening at 3 years then every 5 years | Conditional | Very Low |
| Post-POEM: perform endoscopy if symptomatic GERD; consider periodic endoscopy even if asymptomatic | Conditional | Very Low |
| **High-Quality Endoscopy Reporting** | | |
| Document and photo-document: LA classification for erosive esophagitis, Prague C&M for Barrett's, GEJ landmarks, hiatal hernia size, Hill grade, fundoplication if present | Strong | Very Low |
| **Lifestyle Modifications** | | |
| Recommend weight loss, smoking cessation, head of bed elevation, and avoiding meals within 3 hours of bedtime | Strong | Low |
| **PPI Therapy** | | |
| Use PPIs at lowest dose for shortest duration while discussing long-term management | Strong | Moderate |
| Consider testing CYP2C19 polymorphism in suboptimal PPI responders | Conditional | Very Low |
| **TIF 2.0 (Transoral Incisionless Fundoplication)** | | |
| Evaluate for TIF 2.0 in confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia <=2 cm and Hill grade I or II in patients with chronic GERD >=6 months, long-term PPI use, refractory GERD, regurgitation-predominant GERD, or preference to avoid long-term PPI | Conditional | Low |
| **cTIF (Combined TIF + Hiatal Hernia Repair)** | | |
| Evaluate for cTIF in multidisciplinary review for confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia >2 cm and Hill grade III or IV | Conditional | Very Low |
| **Stretta (Radiofrequency Energy)** | | |
| Stretta can be considered for confirmed GERD with hiatal hernia <2 cm and Hill grade I or II when TIF and surgical fundoplication are not available or feasible | Best Practice Advice | — |

## Relevance to Wiki

- Primary source for `wiki/disease-scripts/foregut-and-motility-diseases/ge-junction/gerd.md`
- Informs therapeutics hierarchy: lifestyle → PPI → TIF/cTIF vs surgery based on hiatal hernia size and Hill grade
- Endoscopy quality standards (LA grading, Prague classification, Hill/AFS grading) relevant to GEJ evaluation section
- Post-SG and post-POEM surveillance protocols are newly codified in this guideline
- Links conceptually to `[[achalasia]]` (post-POEM GERD risk), `[[laryngopharyngeal-symptoms]]` (cTIF data includes LPR cohort), and `[[hrm-antireflux-surgery]]` (manometry role pre-TIF)
- Substantial reflux testing content supports a dedicated `wiki/concepts/reflux-testing.md` page

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- TIF vs PPI on AET: TIF better vs sham but not better than PPI for AET normalization — raises questions about mechanism of symptom benefit
- RCT heterogeneity for TIF is high; multiple device iterations (TIF 1.0 through 2.0) and techniques over the study period confound pooled estimates
- cTIF evidence is entirely observational with only one ongoing RCT; positioning relative to laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication (LNF) is not yet defined
- Stretta: RCT data show no significant benefit, but cohort data suggest modest benefit — discrepancy likely due to small RCT sample sizes and high risk of bias
- PCABs (vonoprazan): data emerging after guideline evidence cutoff; positioning relative to PPIs will require guideline update
- CYP2C19 testing: principle endorsed but not widely implemented; real-world utility unclear
- Long-term PPI safety: prospective RCT data reassuring for most outcomes studied, but observational associations with dementia, gastric cancer persist (very low certainty); creates patient anxiety
- Next guideline update anticipated ~2029 or sooner if significant new data (e.g., cTIF RCT results)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline addresses tissue acquisition and palliation for solid pancreatic masses using [[endoscopic-ultrasound|EUS]]. The headline change: **EUS fine-needle biopsy (FNB) needles are preferred over fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** for diagnosis.

---

## Key Recommendations (conditional)

- **EUS-FNB over FNA** for tissue acquisition of solid pancreatic masses (higher diagnostic yield/adequacy, more tissue for ancillary testing; fewer passes).
- Reasonable to use **22-gauge** needles; **rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE)** is not mandatory when FNB is used.
- For malignant distal biliary obstruction from a pancreatic head mass, **self-expandable metal stents** over plastic stents for durable drainage (coordinate with [[ercp]]).

---

## Clinical Relevance

Cements **EUS-FNB as the first-choice sampling technique** for solid pancreatic masses, reducing reliance on ROSE, and supports metal stents for malignant biliary obstruction. Core to the pancreatic-mass diagnostic pathway and adjacent to [[pancreatic-cysts]] evaluation.

# ASGE Guideline: Role of Therapeutic EUS in Biliary Tract Disorders (2024)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee. ASGE Guideline: Role of Therapeutic EUS in Biliary Tract Disorders (2024). Gastrointestinal Endoscopy.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.03.027)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee
- **Year:** 2024
- **Journal:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2024.03.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.03.027)
- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This guideline defines the role of **therapeutic [[endoscopic-ultrasound|EUS]]** for biliary access and gallbladder drainage when conventional [[ercp]] fails or is not feasible. It positions EUS-guided biliary drainage (EUS-BD) — via choledochoduodenostomy (EUS-CDS) or hepaticogastrostomy (EUS-HGS) — and EUS-guided gallbladder drainage (EUS-GBD) as effective alternatives to percutaneous (PTBD) approaches in selected patients.

---

## Key Recommendations (all conditional)

- **After failed [[ercp]]** in distal malignant [[biliary-stricture|biliary obstruction]], **EUS-BD** is favored over PTBD given comparable/better effectiveness with fewer reinterventions (discuss with surgical team if surgery is planned).
- **EUS-CDS vs EUS-HGS:** either may be used; choose by anatomy — **EUS-CDS** preferred when tumor compromises gastric puncture sites for HGS; **EUS-HGS** preferred when duodenal involvement/gastric outlet obstruction compromises CDS.
- **Acute cholecystitis** in nonsurgical candidates needing gallbladder drainage: **EUS-GBD** is favored over percutaneous cholecystostomy where expertise exists (durable, fewer reinterventions).

---

## Clinical Relevance

Establishes therapeutic EUS as a mainstream rescue/primary route for biliary and gallbladder drainage in malignant obstruction and high-risk cholecystitis, complementing rather than replacing [[ercp]]. Decisions hinge on anatomy, malignancy, and local expertise. Relevant to malignant [[biliary-stricture]] and [[cholangiocarcinoma]] palliation.

# ASGE Guideline: Gastrostomy Feeding Tubes (2025)

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [ASGE Standards of Practice Committee — Kohli DR, Abidi WM, Cosgrove N, Machicado JD, Desai M, Forbes N, et al. ASGE Guideline: Gastrostomy Feeding Tubes (2025). Gastrointestinal Endoscopy.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.08.044)
- **Authors:** ASGE Standards of Practice Committee — Kohli DR, Abidi WM, Cosgrove N, Machicado JD, Desai M, Forbes N, et al.
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal:** Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.gie.2024.08.044](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2024.08.044)
- **Type:** GRADE-based Standards of Practice guideline

---

## Summary

This ASGE guideline addresses endoscopic enteral access, comparing **percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG)** with interventional-radiology gastrostomy (IR-G), the timing of feeding, and periprocedural antithrombotic management. It supports PEG as the default modality and earlier feeding than historically practiced. Placement is performed via [[upper-endoscopy]] and supports [[nutrition-in-hospitalized-patients|enteral nutrition]] in patients who cannot meet needs orally.

---

## Key Recommendations

- **Rec 1:** In patients with **normal foregut anatomy** needing enteral access, **PEG is preferred over IR-G** as the initial gastrostomy technique.
- **Early feeding:** Tube feeding can be **safely started within 4 hours** of gastrostomy.
- **Rec 2a:** On **antiplatelet therapy**, suggests **against routine withholding** of antiplatelet agents before PEG.
- **Rec 2b:** On **anticoagulants**, periprocedural management is **individualized** (managed differently from antiplatelets, balancing thrombotic vs bleeding risk).
- **Rec 3:** PEG tubes may be placed via **transoral "pull" or transcutaneous** techniques; tightening the external bumper for ~24 h is reasonable.

---

## Clinical Relevance

Codifies PEG-first enteral access, feeding within 4 hours, and no routine interruption of antiplatelet agents — reducing delays and unnecessary antithrombotic holds. Decisions about anticoagulants intersect with broader periprocedural bleeding-risk management in [[anticoagulation-gi-bleeding]], and downstream care supports [[nutrition-in-hospitalized-patients]].
