## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Carlson DA, Pandolfino JE, Yadlapati R, Vela MF, Abrahão L Jr, Aziz Q, Babaei A, Bredenoord AJ, Cisternas D, Compean DG, Coss-Adame E, Costilla VC, Crowell MD, Fischella PM, Gyawali CP, Jadcherla SR, Johansson J, Kahrilas PJ, Keller J, Mack T, Maddela C, Mittal R, Quigley EMM, Rao SSC, Roman S, Sarr MG, Tatum R, Tolone S, Zerbib F, Simren M (19 voting experts plus co-authors). Dallas Consensus on the Classification of Esophageal Motility Abnormalities: FLIP Panometry (v2.0). Gastroenterology 2025;168:1114–1127.](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.234)
- **Authors:** Carlson DA, Pandolfino JE, Yadlapati R, Vela MF, Abrahão L Jr, Aziz Q, Babaei A, Bredenoord AJ, Cisternas D, Compean DG, Coss-Adame E, Costilla VC, Crowell MD, Fischella PM, Gyawali CP, Jadcherla SR, Johansson J, Kahrilas PJ, Keller J, Mack T, Maddela C, Mittal R, Quigley EMM, Rao SSC, Roman S, Sarr MG, Tatum R, Tolone S, Zerbib F, Simren M (19 voting experts plus co-authors)
- **Year:** 2025
- **Journal/Publisher:** Gastroenterology 2025;168:1114–1127
- **DOI:** [10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.234](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2025.01.234)
- **Received:** November 18, 2024. **Accepted:** January 9, 2025.
- **Type:** Consensus (modified Delphi methodology; 40 consensus statements; ≥80% agreement threshold)

## Summary

The Dallas Consensus v2.0 updates and formalizes the [[flip-panometry|FLIP Panometry]] Motility Classification for esophageal motility assessment using the functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP). FLIP panometry provides simultaneous measurement of esophagogastric junction (EGJ) opening and the contractile response (CR) of the esophageal body during balloon distension — two axes that together define a 6-category motility classification matrix. This version refines and expands the original Dallas Consensus, clarifying thresholds, simplifying criteria, and adding normative data from large multi-center series.

The classification is built on two independent axes. EGJ opening is assessed by the EGJ distensibility index (EGJ-DI) and maximum EGJ diameter at 70 mL, yielding three categories: Reduced EGJ Opening (REO), Non-Reduced EGJ Opening (NEO), or Inconclusive. The contractile response to distension is categorized as Absent, Diminished, Disordered, Normal, or Spastic, based on the character, propagation, pressure, and timing of esophageal contractions during FLIP. Crossing these two axes produces the 6 FLIP Panometry Motility Classifications: Normal, Hypocontractility, Possible Spasm, Spastic Obstruction, Obstruction with Normal Contractility, and Non-spastic Obstruction.

Key clinical applications are established by large evidence bases: a Normal FLIP pattern (NEO + Normal CR) carries a high negative predictive value for major esophageal motor disorders, with 92% of subjects showing normal [[high-resolution-manometry|HRM]] and 0% having [[achalasia]] (n=722). Non-spastic Obstruction (REO + Absent/Diminished CR) shows 92% correspondence with manometric EGJ outflow disorder and 77% with abnormal timed barium esophagram. The consensus formalizes FLIP as a clinically valid and increasingly preferred test at centers with expertise in panometry interpretation.

## Key Findings / Claims

**Standardized FLIP Protocol:**

- 16-cm EndoFLIP catheter
- Stepwise inflation: 50 mL → 60 mL → 70 mL (≥30 seconds at each volume)
- Sensor positioning: ≥2 impedance sensors below the crural diaphragm at all distension volumes
- EGJ-DI calculation: median of 3 measurements at 60 mL; omit first 5 seconds to allow stabilization
- Maximum EGJ diameter: measured at 70 mL

**EGJ Opening Classification (at 60 mL for EGJ-DI; at 70 mL for max diameter):**

| Category | EGJ-DI | Max EGJ Diameter |
|---|---|---|
| REO (Reduced) | <2 mm²/mmHg | AND <12 mm at 70 mL |
| NEO (Non-Reduced) | ≥2 mm²/mmHg | AND ≥16 mm at 70 mL |
| Inconclusive | Between REO and NEO thresholds | — |

**Contractile Response (CR) Categories:**

| Category | Definition |
|---|---|
| Absent | No discernible antegrade contractions |
| Diminished | Some contractile activity but not meeting Normal; 60 mL pressure <40 mmHg |
| Disordered | Contractile activity not meeting Normal or Spastic; 60 mL pressure ≥40 mmHg |
| Normal | >1 distinct antegrade contraction ≥6 cm axial extent and ≥10 mmHg; includes RAC (≥6 consecutive antegrade at 6±3/min) |
| Spastic | Simultaneous occluding contractions (SOCs): non-propagating, lumen-occluding, >10s, pressure >35 mmHg; OR sustained LES contractions (>5s with pressure increase) |

*Note: Repetitive retrograde contractions (RRC) removed from spastic criteria in v2.0.*

**FLIP Panometry Motility Classification v2.0 (6-category matrix):**

| EGJ Opening | Contractile Response | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| NEO | Normal | **Normal** |
| NEO | Diminished or Absent | **Hypocontractility** |
| NEO | Disordered or Spastic | **Possible Spasm** |
| REO | Spastic | **Spastic Obstruction** |
| REO | Normal | **Obstruction with Normal Contractility** |
| REO | Diminished or Absent | **Non-spastic Obstruction** |

*Inconclusive EGJ Opening: report EGJ-DI value; clinical context determines interpretation.*

**Evidence Base for Key Classifications:**

| Pattern | n | Key Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Normal FLIP | 722 | 92% normal HRM; 0% achalasia; high NPV for major motor disorder |
| Non-spastic Obstruction | 202 | 92% manometric EGJ outflow disorder; 77% abnormal TBE |
| REO overall | — | PPV >75% for EGJOO |
| Normal FLIP (NPV) | — | NPV >90% for major obstruction or spasm |

**Clinical Application Rules:**

- Normal FLIP at adequate distension (70 mL) effectively excludes achalasia and major obstructive motor disorders
- REO with Absent/Diminished CR (Non-spastic Obstruction) = functionally equivalent to manometric EGJOO; warrants same workup/treatment pathway
- REO with Normal CR (Obstruction with Normal Contractility) suggests mechanical obstruction (e.g., tight wrap post-fundoplication, ring/web) rather than primary motor disorder
- FLIP may be performed at time of endoscopy, offering advantage over HRM when sedation is already planned
- Spastic classifications (Possible Spasm, Spastic Obstruction) correlate with spastic motor patterns on HRM ([[distal-esophageal-spasm|DES]], [[hypercontractile-esophagus|jackhammer]]) but clinical significance requires correlation

**Protocol Modifications from v1.0:**

- Spastic CR: RRC removed as defining criterion; SOCs and sustained LES contractions retained
- Pressure threshold added: 60 mL pressure <40 mmHg = Diminished CR; ≥40 mmHg = Disordered CR
- Max diameter threshold for NEO raised to ≥16 mm (from ≥12 mm in some prior formulations)
- RAC now defined explicitly: ≥6 consecutive antegrade contractions at 6±3 per minute

## Recommendations

| Recommendation | Strength | Evidence Quality |
|---|---|---|
| **FLIP Protocol** | | |
| The standard FLIP protocol uses a 16-cm EndoFLIP catheter with stepwise inflation to 50 → 60 → 70 mL (≥30 seconds each); EGJ-DI is calculated as the median of 3 measurements at 60 mL (omitting first 5 seconds) | Consensus Statement | — |
| At least 2 impedance sensors must be positioned below the crural diaphragm at all distension volumes | Consensus Statement | — |
| **EGJ Opening Classification** | | |
| EGJ-DI <2 mm²/mmHg AND max diameter <12 mm at 70 mL = Reduced EGJ Opening (REO); EGJ-DI ≥2 mm²/mmHg AND max diameter ≥16 mm = Non-Reduced EGJ Opening (NEO); values between thresholds = Inconclusive | Consensus Statement | — |
| **Clinical Interpretation** | | |
| A Normal FLIP pattern (NEO + Normal CR) has NPV >90% for major esophageal motor disorders and effectively excludes achalasia | Consensus Statement | — |
| Non-spastic Obstruction (REO + Absent/Diminished CR) should be managed equivalently to manometric EGJOO given 92% correspondence | Consensus Statement | — |
| Obstruction with Normal CR (REO + Normal CR) suggests mechanical obstruction (tight wrap, ring, web) rather than a primary motor disorder | Consensus Statement | — |
| FLIP may be performed at the time of endoscopy when sedation is already planned, offering a practical advantage over HRM in appropriate patients | Consensus Statement | — |
| **Spastic Patterns** | | |
| Spastic classifications (Possible Spasm, Spastic Obstruction) correlate with spastic HRM patterns but require clinical correlation; PPV <75% in spastic domains limits independent diagnostic utility | Consensus Statement | — |
| Repetitive retrograde contractions (RRC) should no longer be used as a criterion for spastic CR (removed in v2.0) | Consensus Statement | — |

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates need for a new procedure page: [[flip-panometry]]
- Informs [[achalasia]] — FLIP provides complementary motility assessment; Normal FLIP excludes achalasia
- Future pages: functional-lumen-imaging.md, egjoo.md (EGJ outflow obstruction as a diagnostic schema)
- The FLIP Panometry Classification v2.0 should be referenced in any HRM/motility workup page

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Inconclusive EGJ Opening category lacks clear management guidance; consensus defers to clinical context — gap in decision algorithm
- FLIP requires specialized hardware and expertise in panometry interpretation; availability limits generalizability
- Correlation between FLIP motility classifications and patient symptoms/outcomes is based largely on cross-sectional data; longitudinal outcome studies (e.g., post-treatment response by FLIP class) remain limited
- Role of FLIP in diagnosing spastic disorders (Possible Spasm, Spastic Obstruction) is less established than its role in obstructive disorders; some classifications in the spastic domain have PPV <75%
- FLIP-based assessment of hypercontractile disorders (jackhammer esophagus) not fully addressed in this consensus

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [de-Madaria E, et al. Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis. N Engl J Med 2022;387:989-1000.](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202884)
- **Authors:** de-Madaria E, Buxbaum JL, Maisonneuve P, et al., for the ERICA Consortium
- **Year:** 2022
- **Journal/Publisher:** New England Journal of Medicine
- **DOI:** [10.1056/NEJMoa2202884](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202884)
- **Type:** RCT (multicenter, open-label, parallel-group, superiority; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04381169)

## Summary
Open-label RCT at 18 centers across four countries (India, Italy, Mexico, Spain) comparing **aggressive vs moderate goal-directed fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's** in patients presenting with acute pancreatitis of any severity. Aggressive arm: 20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/hr. Moderate arm: 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolemic (no bolus if normovolemic) then 1.5 mL/kg/hr; both adjusted at 12/24/48/72 hr per clinical status. Primary outcome: progression to moderately severe or severe pancreatitis during hospitalization. Main safety outcome: fluid overload.

The trial was **halted early** at the first planned interim analysis (249 of a planned 744 patients) for between-group safety differences without an efficacy signal. This provides the primary-evidence basis for the shift away from historically recommended early aggressive hydration toward moderate, goal-directed resuscitation now reflected in ACG 2024.

## Key Findings / Claims
- No difference in progression to moderately severe/severe pancreatitis: **22.1% (aggressive) vs 17.3% (moderate)**; adjusted RR 1.30 (95% CI 0.78–2.18), P = 0.32.
- **Fluid overload roughly tripled with aggressive resuscitation: 20.5% vs 6.3%**; adjusted RR 2.85 (95% CI 1.36–5.94), P = 0.004.
- Median hospitalization 6 days (aggressive) vs 5 days (moderate).
- Bottom line: early aggressive fluid resuscitation caused more harm (fluid overload) without improving clinical outcomes.

## Relevance to Wiki
- `[[acute-pancreatitis]]` → Therapeutics / Fluid Resuscitation: primary-evidence support for moderate, goal-directed LR resuscitation over aggressive hydration.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Corroborates (does not conflict with) the existing `[[acg-2024-acute-pancreatitis]]` moderately-aggressive/goal-directed recommendation. Older observational data and small trials favoring vigorous hydration are superseded by this RCT.
- Excluded severe organ failure at baseline in some strata; optimal resuscitation in patients presenting with established severe disease remains less defined.

## Bibliographic Info
- **Article:** [Feuerstadt P, et al. SER-109, an Oral Microbiome Therapy for Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection. N Engl J Med 2022;386:220-9.](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2106516)
- **Authors:** Feuerstadt P, Louie TJ, Lashner B, et al.
- **Year:** 2022
- **Journal/Publisher:** New England Journal of Medicine
- **DOI:** [10.1056/NEJMoa2106516](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2106516)
- **Type:** RCT (phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled; ECOSPOR III, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03183128)

## Summary
Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of **SER-109**, an orally administered microbiome therapeutic composed of **purified Firmicutes spores**, in patients with **recurrent C. difficile infection** (≥3 episodes inclusive of the qualifying episode). After standard-of-care antibiotic treatment (vancomycin or fidaxomicin) had resolved symptoms, patients received SER-109 or placebo (four capsules daily for 3 days). Rationale: antibiotics kill toxin-producing vegetative bacteria but not spores and do not repair the disrupted microbiome; restoring spore-forming Firmicutes shifts bile-acid metabolism (raising secondary bile acids) to inhibit C. difficile spore germination.

SER-109 was later FDA-approved (2023) as the first orally administered fecal microbiota spore product for prevention of recurrent CDI (marketed as VOWST / fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk).

## Key Findings / Claims
- Recurrence up to 8 weeks: **12% (SER-109) vs 40% (placebo)**; relative risk 0.32 (95% CI 0.18–0.58), P < 0.001.
- Benefit consistent across strata — age <65 (RR 0.24) and ≥65 (RR 0.36); prior vancomycin (RR 0.41) and fidaxomicin (RR 0.09).
- Safety similar to placebo; most adverse events mild-to-moderate and gastrointestinal.
- SER-109 dose species detected as early as week 1, associated with bile-acid profiles that inhibit C. difficile spore germination.

## Relevance to Wiki
- `[[clostridioides-difficile]]` → Therapeutics / Recurrent CDI: adds FDA-approved oral microbiome (live biotherapeutic) option alongside FMT and bezlotoxumab.

## Contradictions / Open Questions
- Complements `[[aga-2024-fmt]]` (fecal microbiota-based therapies) — no conflict; SER-109 is a defined-consortium spore product rather than conventional donor stool FMT.
- Enrolled patients required prior antibiotic symptom resolution; efficacy as primary (non-recurrent) therapy not addressed.

## Summary
Phase 2 double-blind RCT of **once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide vs placebo** over 9 weeks of outpatient treatment in **48 non–treatment-seeking adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD)** (dose escalated 0.25 → 0.5 → 1.0 mg/week). Primary outcome was laboratory alcohol self-administration (pre- vs post-treatment at 0.5 mg/week); secondary/exploratory outcomes included prospective drinking and craving. First prospective human trial testing the preclinical/observational signal that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol intake.

Relevant to GI/hepatology given the rising burden of alcohol-associated liver disease; semaglutide use for AUD is **off-label** and investigational (phase 2, small sample), justifying larger trials rather than practice change.

- **Reduced laboratory alcohol self-administration** — grams consumed (β −0.48; 95% CI −0.85 to −0.11; P = .01) and peak breath alcohol concentration (β −0.46; 95% CI −0.87 to −0.06; P = .03), medium-to-large effect sizes.
- No effect on average drinks/calendar day or number of drinking days, but **reduced drinks per drinking day** (β −0.41; P = .04) and **weekly alcohol craving** (β −0.39; P = .01); predicted greater reductions in heavy drinking over time.
- Reduced **cigarettes/day** in the subgroup with current cigarette use (β −0.10; P = .005).
- Interpretation: initial prospective evidence that low-dose semaglutide reduces craving and some drinking outcomes; larger trials needed.

- `[[semaglutide]]` → investigational/off-label use for alcohol use disorder (GLP-1RA effect on craving and consumption).
- Tangential to `[[alcohol-associated-liver-disease]]` (emerging pharmacologic angle on alcohol reduction).

- Small phase 2 sample (n = 48), non–treatment-seeking population, 9-week duration — not practice-changing; off-label. No conflict with existing wiki content (semaglutide's ingested GI indication is MASH per `[[aasld-2025-semaglutide-mash]]`).

## Bibliographic Info

- **Article:** [Shane AL, Mody RK, Crump JA, Tarr PI, Steiner TS, Kotloff K, Langley JM, Wanke C, Warren CA, Cheng AC, Cantey J, Pickering LK. 2017 Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea. *Clinical Infectious Diseases* 2017;65(12):e45–e80.](https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/cix669)
- **Authors:** Andi L. Shane, Rajal K. Mody, John A. Crump, Phillip I. Tarr, Theodore S. Steiner, Karen Kotloff, Joanne M. Langley, Christine Wanke, Cirle Alcantara Warren, Allen C. Cheng, Joseph Cantey, Larry K. Pickering
- **Year:** 2017
- **Journal/Publisher:** *Clinical Infectious Diseases* 2017;65(12):e45–e80
- **DOI:** [10.1093/cid/cix669](https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/cix669)
- **Type:** Guideline (IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline; GRADE methodology)

---

## Summary

These IDSA guidelines address the diagnosis and management of acute and persistent infectious diarrhea in infants, children, adolescents, and adults in the United States, and replace the 2001 IDSA practice guidelines on infectious diarrhea. They are broader in scope than the contemporaneous [[acg-2016-acute-diarrhea|ACG 2016 acute diarrhea guideline]] in that they cover pediatric patients, enteric (typhoid) fever, Shiga toxin–producing organisms in detail, immunocompromised hosts, vaccines, and public-health reporting. Recommendations explicitly defer to the separate IDSA/SHEA *Clostridium difficile* guidelines for CDI management.

The Panel uses GRADE throughout, grading each statement by strength (strong/weak) and evidence quality (high/moderate/low/very low). Diarrhea is defined (per WHO) as ≥3 loose or liquid stools per 24 hours or more frequently than normal; passage of formed stools and loose "pasty" stools in breastfed infants is not diarrhea. Four temporal categories are defined: **acute** (<7 days, watery or bloody/dysenteric), **prolonged** (7–13 days), **persistent** (14–29 days), and **chronic** (≥30 days). Note this differs from the ACG 2016 cutoffs (acute <14 d, persistent 14–30 d).

Core themes: obtain a detailed clinical and exposure history; reserve stool testing for patients with fever, bloody/mucoid stools, severe disease, sepsis, immunocompromise, or epidemiologic/outbreak indications; detect and characterize STEC (Shiga toxin ± O157 culture) because antibiotics are contraindicated for STEC O157 / Shiga toxin 2 producers (HUS risk); empiric antibiotics are generally NOT recommended for either bloody or watery diarrhea in immunocompetent hosts (with defined exceptions such as suspected shigellosis, ill febrile travelers, infants <3 months, and enteric-fever sepsis); rehydration with reduced-osmolarity ORS is the foundation of supportive care; and notifiable enteric pathogens must be reported to public health.

The guideline adds management points absent from the ACG acute-diarrhea guideline: enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever diagnosis and empiric therapy, blood-culture indications, HUS hematologic/renal monitoring for STEC, age-specific rules (no loperamide <18 years; ondansetron and oral zinc in children), serologic/fecal-leukocyte/lactoferrin tests should NOT be used to establish etiology, and rotavirus/typhoid/cholera vaccine guidance.

---

## All Recommendations (Complete Verbatim Text)

> Each recommendation is graded *(strength, quality of evidence)* as published.

### Clinical, Demographic, and Epidemiologic Features

**1.** A detailed clinical and exposure history should be obtained from people with diarrhea, under any circumstances, including when there is a history of similar illness in others *(strong, moderate)*.

**2.** People with diarrhea who attend or work in child care centers, long-term care facilities, patient care, food service, or recreational water venues (eg, pools and lakes) should follow jurisdictional recommendations for outbreak reporting and infection control *(strong, high)*.

**3.** People with fever or bloody diarrhea should be evaluated for enteropathogens for which antimicrobial agents may confer clinical benefit, including *Salmonella enterica* subspecies, *Shigella*, and *Campylobacter* *(strong, low)*.

**4.** Enteric fever should be considered when a febrile person (with or without diarrhea) has a history of travel to areas in which causative agents are endemic, has consumed foods prepared by people with recent endemic exposure, or has laboratory exposure to *Salmonella* Typhi or *Salmonella* Paratyphi *(strong, moderate)*.

**5.** People of all ages with acute diarrhea should be evaluated for dehydration, which increases the risk of life-threatening illness and death, especially among the young and older adults *(strong, high)*.

**6.** When the clinical or epidemic history suggests a possible Shiga toxin–producing organism, diagnostic approaches should be applied that detect Shiga toxin (or the genes that encode them) and distinguish *Escherichia coli* O157:H7 from other Shiga toxin–producing *E. coli* (STEC) in stool *(strong, moderate)*. If available, diagnostic approaches that can distinguish between Shiga toxin 1 and Shiga toxin 2 (typically more potent) could be used *(weak, moderate)*. *Shigella dysenteriae* type 1, and rarely other pathogens, may produce Shiga toxin and should be considered as a cause of HUS, especially with suggestive international travel or contact with a traveler *(strong, moderate)*.

**7.** Clinicians should evaluate people for postinfectious and extraintestinal manifestations associated with enteric infections *(strong, moderate)*.

### Diagnostics

**8.** Stool testing should be performed for *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, *Yersinia*, *C. difficile*, and STEC in people with diarrhea accompanied by fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe abdominal cramping or tenderness, or signs of sepsis *(strong, moderate)*. Bloody stools are not an expected manifestation of *C. difficile*. STEC O157 should be assessed by culture and non-O157 STEC detected by Shiga toxin or genomic assays *(strong, low)*. Sorbitol-MacConkey agar or an appropriate chromogenic alternative is recommended to screen for O157:H7 STEC; Shiga toxin detection is needed for other STEC serotypes *(strong, moderate)*.

**9.** Blood cultures should be obtained from infants <3 months of age, people of any age with signs of septicemia or when enteric fever is suspected, people with systemic manifestations of infection, immunocompromised people, people with high-risk conditions such as hemolytic anemia, and people who traveled to or had contact with travelers from enteric-fever-endemic areas with a febrile illness of unknown etiology *(strong, moderate)*.

**10.** Stool testing should be performed under clearly identified circumstances (Table 2) for *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, *Yersinia*, *C. difficile*, and STEC in symptomatic hosts *(strong, low)*. Specifically: (a) test for *Yersinia enterocolitica* in people with persistent abdominal pain (especially school-aged children with RLQ pain mimicking appendicitis who may have mesenteric adenitis) and in people with fever at epidemiologic risk (eg, infants exposed to raw/undercooked pork); (b) test for *Vibrio* species in people with large-volume rice-water stools or exposure to salty/brackish water, raw/undercooked shellfish, or travel to cholera-endemic regions within 3 days before onset.

**11.** A broader set of bacterial, viral, and parasitic agents should be considered regardless of fever, bloody/mucoid stools, or other markers of severity in the context of a possible outbreak; agent selection should be based on host and epidemiologic risk factors and ideally coordinated with public health authorities *(strong, moderate)*.

**12.** A broad differential diagnosis is recommended in immunocompromised people with diarrhea, especially with moderate-severe primary or secondary immune deficiencies, for evaluation by culture, viral studies, and parasite examination *(strong, moderate)*. People with AIDS and persistent diarrhea should undergo additional testing for organisms including *Cryptosporidium*, *Cyclospora*, *Cystoisospora*, microsporidia, *Mycobacterium avium* complex, and cytomegalovirus *(strong, moderate)*.

**13.** Diagnostic testing is not recommended in most cases of uncomplicated traveler's diarrhea unless treatment is indicated. Travelers with diarrhea ≥14 days should be evaluated for intestinal parasites *(strong, moderate)*. Test for *C. difficile* in travelers treated with antimicrobials within the preceding 8–12 weeks. IBD and postinfectious IBS should be considered *(strong, moderate)*.

**14.** Clinical consideration should be included in interpreting multiple-pathogen nucleic acid amplification test results, because these assays detect DNA and not necessarily viable organisms *(strong, low)*.

**15.** All specimens positive for bacterial pathogens by culture-independent diagnostic testing (eg, GI panels), for which isolate submission is requested/required under public health reporting rules, should be cultured in the clinical or public health laboratory to ensure outbreaks are detected and investigated *(strong, low)*. Culture may also be required where antimicrobial susceptibility results would affect care or public health responses *(strong, low)*.

**16.** Specimens from people involved in an enteric-disease outbreak should be tested for enteric pathogens per public health department guidance *(strong, low)*.

**17.** Culture-independent (including panel-based multiplex molecular) diagnostics from stool and blood, and, when indicated, culture-dependent testing should be performed when there is clinical suspicion of enteric fever (diarrhea uncommon) or diarrhea with bacteremia *(strong, moderate)*. Cultures of bone marrow (particularly valuable if antimicrobials already given), stool, duodenal fluid, and urine may help detect enteric fever *(weak, moderate)*. Serologic tests should NOT be used to diagnose enteric fever *(strong, moderate)*.

**18.** Testing may be considered for *C. difficile* in people >2 years of age with diarrhea following antimicrobial use and in people with healthcare-associated diarrhea *(weak, high)*. Testing may be considered in people with persistent diarrhea without an etiology and without recognized risk factors *(weak, low)*. A single diarrheal stool specimen is recommended for detection of toxin or a toxigenic strain (eg, NAAT) *(strong, low)*; multiple specimens do not increase yield.

**19.** The optimal specimen for laboratory diagnosis is a diarrheal stool sample (takes the shape of the container). For bacterial detection, if a timely diarrheal stool cannot be collected, a rectal swab may be used *(weak, low)*. For viral and protozoal agents and *C. difficile* toxin, fresh stool is preferred *(weak, low)*.

**20.** Fecal leukocyte examination and stool lactoferrin detection should NOT be used to establish the cause of acute infectious diarrhea *(strong, moderate)*. There are insufficient data to make a recommendation on fecal calprotectin in acute infectious diarrhea.

**21.** Serologic tests are not recommended to establish an etiology of infectious diarrhea or enteric fever *(strong, low)*, but may be considered for people with postdiarrheal HUS in which a stool culture did not yield a Shiga toxin–producing organism *(weak, low)*.

**22.** A peripheral WBC count and differential and serologic assays should not be performed to establish an etiology of diarrhea *(strong, low)*, but may be useful clinically *(weak, low)*.

**23.** Frequent monitoring of hemoglobin and platelet counts, electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine is recommended to detect hematologic and renal abnormalities that are early manifestations of HUS and precede renal injury in people with diagnosed *E. coli* O157 or another STEC infection (especially Shiga toxin 2 producers or bloody diarrhea) *(strong, high)*. Examining a peripheral blood smear for RBC fragments is necessary when HUS is suspected *(strong, high)*.

**24.** Endoscopy or proctoscopy should be considered in people with persistent, unexplained diarrhea who have AIDS, in people with certain underlying conditions, in people with acute diarrhea with clinical colitis or proctitis, and in people with persistent diarrhea who engage in anal intercourse *(strong, low)*. Duodenal aspirate may be considered in select people for suspected *Giardia*, *Strongyloides*, *Cystoisospora*, or microsporidia infection *(weak, low)*.

**25.** Imaging (ultrasonography, CT, or MRI) may be considered to detect aortitis, mycotic aneurysms, peritonitis, intra-abdominal free air, toxic megacolon, or extravascular foci of infection in older people with invasive *Salmonella enterica* or *Yersinia* infections if there is sustained fever/bacteremia despite adequate therapy, or with underlying atherosclerosis or recent-onset chest/back/abdominal pain *(weak, low)*.

### Follow-up Evaluation

**26.** Follow-up testing is not recommended in most people following resolution of diarrhea *(strong, moderate)*. Serial stool specimens (culture-dependent) for *Salmonella* Typhi/Paratyphi, STEC, *Shigella*, nontyphoidal *Salmonella*, and other bacteria are recommended in certain situations by local health authorities to enable return to child care, employment, or group activities *(strong, moderate)*. Practitioners should collaborate with local public health authorities *(strong, high)*.

**27.** Clinical and laboratory reevaluation may be indicated in people who do not respond to an initial course of therapy, and should include consideration of noninfectious conditions including lactose intolerance *(weak, low)*.

**28.** Noninfectious conditions, including IBD and IBS, should be considered as underlying etiologies in people with symptoms lasting ≥14 days and unidentified sources *(strong, moderate)*.

**29.** Reassessment of fluid and electrolyte balance, nutritional status, and optimal dose/duration of antimicrobial therapy is recommended in people with persistent symptoms *(strong, high)*.

### Empiric Management — Bloody Diarrhea

**30.** In immunocompetent children and adults, empiric antimicrobial therapy for bloody diarrhea while awaiting results is NOT recommended *(strong, low)*, except: (a) infants <3 months with suspicion of bacterial etiology; (b) ill immunocompetent people with documented fever, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and bacillary dysentery presumptively due to *Shigella*; (c) people recently traveled internationally with temperature ≥38.5°C and/or signs of sepsis *(weak, low)*.

**31.** Empiric antimicrobial therapy in adults should be either a fluoroquinolone (eg, ciprofloxacin) or azithromycin, depending on local susceptibility patterns and travel history *(strong, moderate)*. Empiric therapy for children includes a third-generation cephalosporin for infants <3 months and others with neurologic involvement, or azithromycin, depending on local susceptibility and travel history *(strong, moderate)*.

**32.** Empiric antibacterial treatment should be considered in immunocompromised people with severe illness and bloody diarrhea *(strong, low)*.

**33.** Asymptomatic contacts of people with bloody diarrhea should NOT be offered empiric treatment, but should follow appropriate infection prevention and control measures *(strong, moderate)*.

**34.** People with clinical features of sepsis suspected of enteric fever should be treated empirically with broad-spectrum antimicrobials after blood, stool, and urine culture collection *(strong, low)*; therapy should be narrowed when susceptibilities return *(strong, high)*. If no isolate is available and enteric fever is suspected, antimicrobial choice may be tailored to susceptibility patterns of the acquisition setting *(weak, low)*.

**35.** Antimicrobial therapy for infections attributed to STEC O157 and other STEC producing Shiga toxin 2 (or unknown toxin genotype) should be AVOIDED *(strong, moderate)*. Therapy for other STEC not producing Shiga toxin 2 (generally non-O157) is debatable due to insufficient evidence of benefit or potential harm *(strong, low)*.

### Empiric Management — Watery Diarrhea

**36.** In most people with acute watery diarrhea without recent international travel, empiric antimicrobial therapy is NOT recommended *(strong, low)*. An exception may be made in immunocompromised people or ill-appearing young infants. Empiric treatment should be avoided in people with persistent watery diarrhea ≥14 days *(strong, low)*.

**37.** Asymptomatic contacts of people with acute or persistent watery diarrhea should NOT be offered empiric or preventive therapy, but should follow appropriate infection prevention and control measures *(strong, moderate)*.

### Directed Management

**38.** Antimicrobial treatment should be modified or discontinued when a clinically plausible organism is identified *(strong, high)*.

### Supportive Treatment — Rehydration

**39.** Reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) is recommended as first-line therapy of mild to moderate dehydration in infants, children, and adults with acute diarrhea from any cause *(strong, moderate)*, and in people with mild-moderate dehydration associated with vomiting or severe diarrhea.

**40.** Nasogastric administration of ORS may be considered in infants, children, and adults with moderate dehydration who cannot tolerate oral intake, or in children with normal mental status who are too weak or refuse to drink adequately *(weak, low)*.

**41.** Isotonic intravenous fluids (eg, lactated Ringer's, normal saline) should be administered for severe dehydration, shock, altered mental status, and failure of ORS *(strong, high)* or ileus *(strong, moderate)*. In people with ketonemia, an initial course of IV hydration may be needed to enable tolerance of ORS *(weak, low)*.

**42.** In severe dehydration, IV rehydration should continue until pulse, perfusion, and mental status normalize and the patient awakens, has no aspiration risk, and has no ileus *(strong, low)*; the remaining deficit can be replaced with ORS *(weak, low)*. People with mild-moderate dehydration should receive ORS until clinical dehydration is corrected *(strong, low)*.

**43.** Once rehydrated, maintenance fluids should be administered; replace ongoing stool losses with ORS until diarrhea and vomiting resolve *(strong, low)*.

### Feeding

**44.** Human milk feeding should be continued in infants and children throughout the diarrheal episode *(strong, low)*.

**45.** Resumption of an age-appropriate usual diet is recommended during or immediately after the rehydration process *(strong, low)*.

### Ancillary Management

**46.** Ancillary treatment with antimotility, antinausea, or antiemetic agents can be considered once the patient is adequately hydrated, but is not a substitute for fluid and electrolyte therapy *(weak, low)*.

**47.** Antimotility drugs (eg, loperamide) should NOT be given to children <18 years of age with acute diarrhea *(strong, moderate)*. Loperamide may be given to immunocompetent adults with acute watery diarrhea *(weak, moderate)*, but should be avoided at any age in suspected or proven cases where toxic megacolon may result, in inflammatory diarrhea, or diarrhea with fever *(strong, low)*.

**48.** Antinausea and antiemetic agents (eg, ondansetron) may be given to facilitate tolerance of oral rehydration in children >4 years of age and in adolescents with acute gastroenteritis associated with vomiting *(weak, moderate)*.

### Probiotics and Zinc

**49.** Probiotic preparations may be offered to reduce symptom severity and duration in immunocompetent adults and children with infectious or antimicrobial-associated diarrhea *(weak, moderate)*.

**50.** Oral zinc supplementation reduces the duration of diarrhea in children 6 months to 5 years of age who reside in countries with a high prevalence of zinc deficiency or who have signs of malnutrition *(strong, moderate)*.

### Treatment of Asymptomatic Carriers

**51.** Asymptomatic people who practice hand hygiene and live/work in low-risk settings do not need treatment, except asymptomatic people with *Salmonella* Typhi in their stool who may be treated empirically to reduce transmission *(weak, low)*. Those in high-risk settings (healthcare, child/elderly care, food service) should be treated per local public health guidance *(strong, high)*.

### Prevention

**52.** Hand hygiene should be performed after using the toilet, changing diapers, before and after preparing food, before eating, after handling garbage or soiled laundry, and after touching animals or their feces/environments, especially in public settings such as petting zoos *(strong, moderate)*.

**53.** Infection control measures including gloves and gowns, hand hygiene with soap and water, or alcohol-based sanitizers should be followed in caring for people with diarrhea *(strong, high)*. Hand hygiene product selection should be based on the known/suspected pathogen and environment *(strong, low)*.

**54.** Appropriate food safety practices are recommended to avoid cross-contamination of foods, surfaces, and utensils during shopping, preparation, and storage; ensure foods containing meats and eggs are cooked and maintained at proper temperatures *(strong, moderate)*.

**55.** Healthcare providers should direct educational efforts toward all people with diarrhea, but particularly people with primary/secondary immune deficiencies, pregnant women, parents of young children, and the elderly *(strong, low)*.

**56.** Ill people with diarrhea should avoid swimming, water-related activities, and sexual contact with others while symptomatic, with meticulous hand hygiene *(strong, low)*.

**57.** Rotavirus vaccine should be administered to all infants without a known contraindication *(strong, high)*.

**58.** Typhoid vaccination (two vaccines—oral and injectable—licensed in the US but not recommended routinely) is recommended as an adjunct to hand hygiene and avoidance of high-risk foods/beverages for travelers to moderate-to-high-risk areas, people with intimate exposure to a documented *Salmonella* Typhi chronic carrier, and microbiologists/laboratory personnel routinely exposed to *Salmonella* Typhi cultures *(strong, high)*. Booster doses are recommended for people who remain at risk *(strong, high)*.

**59.** A live attenuated cholera vaccine (single-dose oral, available in the US) is recommended for adults 18–64 years of age who travel to cholera-affected areas *(strong, high)*.

**60.** All diseases listed in the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System, including those that cause diarrhea, should be reported to the appropriate state, territorial, or local health department, with submission of isolates of certain pathogens (eg, *Salmonella*, STEC, *Shigella*, *Listeria*) to ensure control and prevention practices may be implemented *(strong, high)*.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Temporal definitions (differ from ACG 2016):** acute <7 days; prolonged 7–13 days; persistent 14–29 days; chronic ≥30 days. WHO diarrhea definition = ≥3 loose/liquid stools per 24 h (or more than normal); loose "pasty" stools in breastfed infants are not diarrhea.
- **History first:** A detailed clinical and exposure history (food, water, travel, animal, sexual, antimicrobial, occupational, child/long-term-care exposures) drives the differential — Table 2 maps exposures to likely pathogens.
- **STEC / HUS is a central safety theme:** Detect Shiga toxin (and distinguish O157 by culture); AVOID antibiotics for O157 / Shiga toxin 2 producers; monitor CBC, smear for schistocytes, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine to catch early HUS.
- **Empiric antibiotics are generally not indicated** for immunocompetent adults/children with either bloody or watery diarrhea, with narrow exceptions: suspected bacillary dysentery (*Shigella*), ill febrile international travelers, infants <3 months, immunocompromised with severe bloody diarrhea, and sepsis suspicious for enteric fever. Adult empiric agent = fluoroquinolone or azithromycin per local susceptibility/travel.
- **Enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever** gets a dedicated workup (blood + stool + urine ± bone marrow culture; serology NOT used) and empiric broad-spectrum therapy with later narrowing.
- **Tests to avoid for etiology:** serology, peripheral WBC count, fecal leukocytes, and stool lactoferrin should NOT be used to establish the cause of acute infectious diarrhea; calprotectin—insufficient data.
- **Molecular caveat:** multiplex NAAT/GI panels detect nucleic acid, not necessarily viable organisms; positive bacterial results requiring public-health reporting should be reflex-cultured for subtyping and susceptibility.
- **Supportive care:** reduced-osmolarity ORS is first-line for mild-moderate dehydration of any cause; isotonic IV fluids (LR, NS) for severe dehydration/shock/ileus; continue breastfeeding and resume age-appropriate diet early.
- **Age-specific ancillary care:** loperamide contraindicated <18 years (and in fever/inflammatory diarrhea/toxic-megacolon risk at any age); ondansetron may aid ORS tolerance in children >4 years; oral zinc shortens diarrhea in children 6 months–5 years in zinc-deficient/malnourished settings; probiotics may modestly reduce severity/duration.
- **Vaccines:** rotavirus vaccine for all infants; typhoid vaccine for select travelers/contacts/lab staff with boosters; oral cholera vaccine for adults 18–64 traveling to affected areas.
- **Public health:** notifiable enteric diseases (*Salmonella*, STEC, *Shigella*, *Listeria*, etc.) must be reported with isolate submission; outbreak specimens tested per public-health guidance; defer CDI management to IDSA/SHEA *C. difficile* guidelines.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Temporal cutoffs differ from ACG 2016:** IDSA defines acute as <7 days (with a separate "prolonged" 7–13 day band) and persistent as 14–29 days, whereas [[acg-2016-acute-diarrhea|ACG 2016]] uses acute <14 days and persistent 14–30 days. The wiki [[acute-diarrhea]] page uses the ACG framing; both are noted.
- This is a 2017 guideline; multiplex GI PCR panels (eg, BioFire FilmArray, 22 targets) have since become widespread and largely standard, amplifying Recommendation 14's caveat about interpreting positive nucleic-acid results (colonization vs infection, multiple detections).
- CDI recommendations defer to the IDSA/SHEA *C. difficile* guidelines, which were "in development" at publication and have since been updated; see [[acg-2021-cdiff]].
- Probiotic guidance (Rec 49, weak) predates later, more cautious analyses (eg, [[aga-2020-probiotics|AGA 2020 probiotics guidance]] generally recommends against routine probiotics for most GI indications) — note the divergence.

## Summary

The Lyon Consensus 2.0 is an international expert update of the original Lyon Consensus (2018), developed using the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Methodology with 20 voting members across five rounds of voting (≥80% agreement threshold). It introduces the concept of "actionable [[gerd|GERD]]" — defined as conclusive evidence of reflux-related pathology on endoscopy and/or abnormal [[ambulatory-reflux-monitoring|reflux monitoring]] (using Lyon Consensus thresholds) in the presence of compatible troublesome symptoms — where management requires long-term acid suppression, escalation, or consideration of irreversible interventional options (fundoplication, MSA, endoscopic GERD therapies, bariatric surgery).

Key structural innovation: the framework now stratifies patients into **unproven GERD** (no prior conclusive evidence → test off therapy) vs. **proven GERD** (prior conclusive evidence + persisting symptoms → test on optimised therapy with pH-impedance).

## Key Findings / Claims

### GERD Definition

- Actionable GERD requires conclusive evidence of reflux-related pathology on endoscopy and/or abnormal reflux monitoring plus compatible troublesome symptoms.
- Typical symptoms (heartburn, oesophageal chest pain, regurgitation) alone may justify empiric antisecretory trials but are insufficient for conclusive diagnosis.
- PPI response alone is insufficient (10–25% placebo effect).

### Symptom Likelihood of Reflux Association

- **High likelihood:** Heartburn, oesophageal chest pain, regurgitation
- **Intermediate/variable:** Belching (can be part of reflux pathophysiology)
- **Low but potential:** Chronic cough, wheezing
- **Low likelihood:** Hoarseness, globus, nausea, abdominal pain, other dyspeptic symptoms in the absence of typical symptoms

### Endoscopic Evidence

- **Conclusive for GERD (off therapy):** LA grades B, C, D oesophagitis; biopsy-proven [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's oesophagus]]; peptic stricture
- **Key update from Lyon 1.0:** LA grade B is now conclusive (previously considered inconclusive/borderline). LA grade B has AET similar to grade C (8.23% vs 9.95% on wireless pH; 6.0% vs 8.7% on pH-impedance) and similar PPI response (74% vs 70%).
- **Borderline (off therapy):** LA grade A oesophagitis (found in 5–7.5% of healthy subjects)
- **Supportive adjunctive:** Hiatus hernia on endoscopy
- **Retired adjunctive:** Routine histopathological scoring, electron microscopy (dilated intercellular spaces), endoscopy-based mucosal impedance (not currently available)
- **Endoscopy timing in unproven GERD:** Perform 2–4 weeks after PPI discontinuation to maximise diagnostic yield (mucosal healing occurs in ~80% after 8 weeks of PPI)
- **On-therapy endoscopic evidence of refractory GERD:** LA grades B, C, D or recurrent peptic stricture while on optimised PPI

### Ambulatory Reflux Monitoring — Test Selection

- **Unproven GERD:** Test off antisecretory therapy
  - Preferred: prolonged wireless pH monitoring (48–96h; 96h provides highest diagnostic yield; AUC 0.63 for 96h vs 0.57 for 48h, p=0.01)
  - pH-impedance off therapy: preferred when typical symptoms + excessive belching, rumination suspected, or pulmonary symptoms being evaluated
  - Catheter-based pH monitoring: acceptable alternative when pH-impedance unavailable
- **Proven GERD with persisting symptoms:** pH-impedance monitoring on optimised antisecretory therapy (only modality able to identify refractory reflux on therapy)

### Wireless pH Monitoring Thresholds

- **AET <4.0% on all days + negative reflux-symptom association:** Excludes GERD
- **AET >6.0% on ≥2 days:** Diagnostic of GERD, supports treatment
- **AET <4.0% on all days + positive reflux-symptom association:** Meets criteria for reflux hypersensitivity
- **AET 4.0–6.0% (any study not meeting above criteria):** Inconclusive — adjunctive metrics needed

### pH-Impedance Monitoring Thresholds (off therapy)

- **AET >6% off PPI:** Diagnostic of GERD
- **Total reflux episodes <40/day:** Adjunctive evidence against pathological GERD
- **Total reflux episodes 40–80/day:** Inconclusive as stand-alone metric
- **Total reflux episodes >80/day:** Adjunctive evidence for objective GERD
- **Baseline impedance (MNBI) <1500 ohms:** Adjunctive evidence for GERD
- **Baseline impedance (MNBI) >2500 ohms:** Evidence against pathological GERD

### pH-Impedance Monitoring Thresholds (on optimised therapy — refractory GERD)

- **AET >4% AND >80 reflux episodes/day on optimised antisecretory regimen:** Evidence for actionable refractory GERD (85% symptomatic benefit from [[antireflux-surgery|ARS]]/MSA)
- MNBI on therapy may have diagnostic value; PSPW remains a research tool only

### Symptom Association Metrics

- **Symptom Association Probability (SAP) >95%:** Positive, increases confidence symptoms are linked to reflux episodes
- **Symptom Index (SI) >50%:** Positive, increases confidence symptoms are linked to reflux episodes
- Caution: reflux-symptom association relies on prompt patient reporting within a 2-minute window and may not always be reliable

### Retired Criteria (from Lyon 1.0)

- PSPW index (postreflux swallow-induced peristaltic wave): retired as adjunctive diagnostic evidence (remains research tool for phenotyping)
- Routine oesophageal biopsy analysis
- Endoscopy-based mucosal impedance assessment (devices no longer available)
- LA grade B as borderline (now promoted to conclusive)

### Manometry

- [[high-resolution-manometry|HRM]] rules out [[achalasia]] spectrum disorders in PPI non-responders
- Abnormal EGJ morphology (hiatus hernia), compromised EGJ barrier, oesophageal hypomotility ([[chicago-classification-v4|Chicago Classification 4.0]]) remain supportive but cannot diagnose GERD
- Chicago Classification updated from v3.0 to v4.0

This is the primary authoritative reference for GERD diagnosis standards in the wiki. Key pages that should cite this source:

- `[[ambulatory-reflux-monitoring]]` — directly built from this source; covers all thresholds and test selection logic
- GERD disease script — diagnostic criteria section

The Lyon 2.0 framework supersedes older binary pH-only approaches. Clinicians should note the unproven vs. proven GERD distinction drives test modality choice, and that both AET and reflux episode counts must be interpreted in the context of whether testing was on or off antisecretory therapy.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- **Wireless pH vs. catheter-based pH-impedance:** No high-quality head-to-head comparisons exist; wireless preferred for typical symptoms but pH-impedance adds value for belching/regurgitation/pulmonary symptoms
- **Regional/system variability:** Significant differences in normative impedance-pH thresholds across Diversatek (95th percentile AET 2.8%; reflux episodes 55) vs. Laborie (AET 5%; reflux episodes 78) systems, and across countries — clinical interpretation must account for this
- **Upright vs. supine reflux episode thresholds:** Insufficient data to define separate thresholds for positional or pH-specific reflux counts
- **Reflux-symptom association reliability:** SAP/SI may be unreliable due to dependence on prompt within-window patient reporting
- **Endoscopic mucosal impedance:** Novel cap device under development; normative thresholds pending — not yet clinically deployable
- **Cost-effectiveness of upfront testing** for typical symptoms requires further study
- **PSPW normative thresholds:** Variable and calculation cumbersome; clinical role remains undefined beyond research phenotyping
- **LA grade A:** Still borderline — overlaps with healthy subjects (5–7.5% prevalence in controls); insufficient on its own

## Summary

The NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers guideline covers four related malignancies on parallel pathways: **gallbladder cancer (GALL)**, **intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA, INTRA)**, **perihilar and distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (eCCA, EXTRA)**, and the shared principles of pathology, biomarker testing, systemic therapy, and radiation. Workup centers on multiphasic cross-sectional imaging, tissue diagnosis (with **core biopsy preferred over FNA**), assessment of resectability, and multidisciplinary review. Management is stage- and site-specific: surgical resection (with adequate margins and regional lymphadenectomy) for resectable disease; adjuvant therapy after resection; and systemic ± locoregional therapy for unresectable or metastatic disease.

The defining feature of biliary tract cancer management in this guideline is **molecular biomarker testing**, which is recommended for all patients with unresectable or metastatic disease who are systemic-therapy candidates. A comprehensive multi-gene panel (MGPT) — with **RNA-based testing preferred to maximize detection of gene fusions** — interrogates actionable targets including FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations, BRAF V600E, HER2 (ERBB2) amplification/overexpression, NTRK1/2/3 fusions, RET fusions, NRG1 fusions (new in this version), KRAS G12C, and the tumor-agnostic immunotherapy markers MSI-H/dMMR and TMB-H. Version 1.2026 adds NRG1 fusion to the testing tables, strengthens the preference for RNA-/transcriptome-based fusion detection, notes ctDNA as a complementary option (with the caveat that it may miss fusions), and refines liver-transplant exception criteria for unresectable iCCA.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Four pathways, shared principles.** Gallbladder cancer, iCCA, perihilar eCCA, and distal eCCA each have their own workup/treatment algorithm but share the pathology, biomarker, systemic-therapy, and RT principles pages.
- **Tissue diagnosis — core biopsy preferred over FNA** (new/expanded footnotes this version), reflecting tissue requirements for comprehensive molecular profiling.
- **Comprehensive molecular profiling is standard for advanced disease.** Recommended for all unresectable/metastatic biliary tract cancer candidates for systemic therapy. Actionable targets: **FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements** (iCCA), **IDH1 mutation** (iCCA), **BRAF V600E**, **HER2 (ERBB2)**, **NTRK1/2/3 fusions**, **RET fusions**, **NRG1 fusions** (added this version), **KRAS G12C**, and tumor-agnostic **MSI-H/dMMR** and **TMB-H**. **RNA-/transcriptome-based MGPT is the preferred assay for fusion detection** (higher sensitivity than DNA-based testing); ctDNA may complement tissue but can miss fusions.
- **First-line systemic therapy for advanced disease** is a gemcitabine + cisplatin backbone combined with a PD-L1/PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor (durvalumab per TOPAZ-1; pembrolizumab per KEYNOTE-966); carboplatin may substitute when cisplatin-ineligible. Biomarker-matched targeted agents (e.g., FGFR2-fusion and IDH1-mutation inhibitors, HER2-directed therapy, BRAF/MEK, NTRK/RET inhibitors, and immunotherapy for MSI-H/dMMR/TMB-H) are used in subsequent lines where a target is present.
- **Adjuvant therapy after resection.** Capecitabine is a category 1 adjuvant option (BILCAP); gemcitabine-based regimens and fluoropyrimidine-based chemoradiation are alternatives, with greatest benefit signaled in node-positive disease. Adjuvant therapy is given for up to ~6 months.
- **Neoadjuvant therapy** is addressed specifically for gallbladder cancer (individualized, 2–6 months with reassessment), reflecting its often advanced presentation; clinical-trial participation is encouraged given limited data.
- **Liver transplantation for iCCA.** Refined transplant-exception criteria for biopsy-proven unresectable iCCA (or mixed HCC-iCCA) in the setting of cirrhosis after locoregional/systemic therapy with a defined observation period — i.e., transplant is an option for selected patients, distinct from the established role in perihilar CCA.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Updates [[cholangiocarcinoma]] (disease script) — adds the NCCN molecular-biomarker framework (FGFR2, IDH1, HER2, BRAF, NTRK, RET, NRG1, MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H; RNA-based MGPT preferred), the gem/cis + checkpoint-inhibitor first-line backbone, adjuvant capecitabine (BILCAP), and the iCCA liver-transplant-exception pathway. **Additive only** — the page's ASGE-based tissue-acquisition content stays primary for the diagnostic-stricture workup; NCCN layers in oncologic staging and systemic therapy.
- Creates a stub for [[gallbladder-cancer]] (currently part of the biliary differential but without its own page).
- Touches [[biliary-stricture]] (presentation/DDx), [[liver-transplantation]] (iCCA and perihilar transplant), [[ercp]]/[[endoscopic-ultrasound]] (tissue acquisition), [[primary-sclerosing-cholangitis]] (CCA risk), and [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]] (mixed HCC-iCCA, iCCA differential).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Algorithm-based guideline (category 2A consensus by default), not a GRADE systematic review — strength labels differ from the ASGE biliary-stricture guidelines already cited on the cholangiocarcinoma page. The two are complementary: ASGE governs how to obtain the diagnosis; NCCN governs oncologic staging and treatment.
- Optimal assay strategy (tissue RNA-based MGPT vs ctDNA) for fusion detection remains an evolving area; ctDNA sensitivity for fusions depends on panel/partner gene.

## Summary

The NCCN Colon Cancer guideline covers workup, staging, and stage-directed treatment of colon adenocarcinoma (rectal cancer is addressed in a companion guideline). Diagnosis is by [[colonoscopy]] with biopsy; staging uses CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CEA, and TNM. Universal **mismatch-repair (MMR/MSI)** testing is recommended for all patients (Lynch screening and immunotherapy selection), and **RAS (KRAS/NRAS), BRAF V600E, HER2 (ERBB2), and NTRK** testing is recommended for metastatic disease to direct systemic therapy; **DPYD** testing is addressed before fluoropyrimidine exposure.

Management is stage-based: endoscopic resection for selected early (T1) cancers in a polyp; colectomy with en-bloc regional lymphadenectomy for localized disease; **adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX)** for stage III and high-risk stage II disease, with duration (3 vs 6 months) risk-stratified per the IDEA analyses; and biomarker-directed systemic therapy for metastatic disease, including resection/local therapy for resectable oligometastatic (especially liver-limited) disease. Biologic and targeted therapy is biomarker- and sidedness-dependent: **anti-EGFR therapy (cetuximab/panitumumab) only for RAS-wild-type, BRAF-wild-type, left-sided tumors**; **bevacizumab** broadly; **encorafenib + cetuximab** for BRAF V600E; **pembrolizumab (or nivolumab-based immunotherapy)** for MSI-H/dMMR; and HER2-directed therapy for HER2-amplified, RAS-wild-type tumors.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Universal MMR/MSI testing** for all colon cancers (Lynch syndrome screening and immunotherapy candidacy). See [[lynch-syndrome]].
- **Expanded molecular profiling for metastatic disease:** RAS (KRAS/NRAS), BRAF V600E, HER2 (ERBB2) amplification, NTRK fusions; **DPYD** testing informs fluoropyrimidine dosing/toxicity risk.
- **Localized disease:** endoscopic resection for selected favorable T1 cancers; otherwise colectomy with regional lymphadenectomy (≥12 nodes for adequate staging).
- **Adjuvant therapy:** **FOLFOX or CAPOX** for stage III and high-risk stage II; treatment duration (3 vs 6 months) is risk-stratified (IDEA). MSI-H stage II tumors generally do not benefit from single-agent fluoropyrimidine adjuvant therapy.
- **Metastatic, biomarker- and sidedness-directed:**
  - **Anti-EGFR (cetuximab/panitumumab)** only for **RAS-wild-type, BRAF-wild-type, left-sided** primaries.
  - **Bevacizumab** added to chemotherapy backbones broadly.
  - **BRAF V600E** → **encorafenib + cetuximab** (± a MEK inhibitor in some settings).
  - **MSI-H/dMMR** → **pembrolizumab** first-line (or nivolumab ± ipilimumab).
  - **HER2-amplified, RAS-wild-type** → HER2-directed therapy (e.g., trastuzumab + tucatinib/pertuzumab/lapatinib, or trastuzumab deruxtecan).
  - **KRAS G12C** → a G12C inhibitor (adagrasib/sotorasib) combined with an anti-EGFR antibody in later lines.
- **Resectable oligometastatic disease** (especially liver-limited) is treated with curative-intent resection/ablation integrated with systemic therapy.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Updates [[colorectal-cancer]] (disease script) — adds the NCCN oncologic systemic-therapy framework (universal MMR/MSI, RAS/BRAF/HER2/NTRK/DPYD biomarkers, adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX with IDEA duration, biomarker- and sidedness-directed metastatic therapy) and an original algorithm recreation. **Additive only** — the page's extensive ACG/USMSTF screening and post-resection-surveillance content remains primary.
- Connects to [[lynch-syndrome]] (universal MMR testing), [[colonoscopy]] and [[polypectomy-emr]] (diagnosis/early resection), and the hereditary-syndrome pages already cross-linked from the CRC page.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Algorithm-based guideline (category 2A by default), not a GRADE systematic review; complements the ACG/USMSTF screening and surveillance guidelines already cited on the CRC page (which govern prevention/early detection rather than oncologic treatment).
- Optimal adjuvant duration (3 vs 6 months) remains risk-stratified rather than uniform; immunotherapy's role in localized dMMR disease is evolving.

## Summary

The NCCN guideline covers esophageal and esophagogastric junction (EGJ) cancers, with separate pathways by histology — **adenocarcinoma** (distal esophagus/EGJ, arising via the [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's]] metaplasia–dysplasia sequence) and **squamous cell carcinoma** (more often mid/upper esophagus). Workup centers on [[upper-endoscopy|endoscopy]] with biopsy, endoscopic ultrasound and PET/CT for staging, and biomarker testing on advanced/metastatic disease (HER2 [ERBB2], PD-L1 CPS, and MSI-H/dMMR). Management is stage-directed: endoscopic resection ([[endoscopic-eradication-therapy|EMR/ESD]]) for early mucosal (Tis/T1a) disease; neoadjuvant or perioperative chemotherapy and/or chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy for locally advanced resectable disease; definitive chemoradiation for selected (especially SCC) patients; and biomarker-directed systemic therapy for metastatic disease.

Version 3.2026 refines perioperative therapy: in the **MATTERHORN** context, adding **durvalumab to perioperative FLOT** is positioned for selected adenocarcinoma (e.g., clinically node-negative tumors; PD-L1 CPS <1 listed as category 2B), with the explicit caveat that **diffuse-type** gastric/EGJ adenocarcinoma showed no event-free/overall survival advantage from added durvalumab. The guideline integrates HER2-directed therapy (trastuzumab first-line for HER2-overexpressing adenocarcinoma; trastuzumab deruxtecan in later lines) and checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab/pembrolizumab) into the systemic pathways, and recognizes MSI-H/dMMR tumors as candidates for immunotherapy.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Two histologic pathways.** Adenocarcinoma (EGJ/distal, Barrett's-associated) and squamous cell carcinoma (mid/upper) have distinct treatment algorithms; SCC is more radiosensitive and more often managed with definitive chemoradiation.
- **Early disease is endoscopically curable.** Tis (HGD) and T1a mucosal cancers are managed with endoscopic resection ± ablation; T1b and deeper generally require esophagectomy or chemoradiation depending on risk and fitness.
- **Locally advanced resectable disease** is treated with neoadjuvant/perioperative therapy then surgery — perioperative **FLOT** (adenocarcinoma) or neoadjuvant **chemoradiation (CROSS-type)** followed by esophagectomy; adjuvant **nivolumab** is an option after neoadjuvant chemoradiation + surgery with residual disease (CheckMate-577).
- **Perioperative durvalumab + FLOT (v3.2026).** Positioned for selected adenocarcinoma (clinically node-negative; PD-L1 CPS <1 as category 2B; diffuse-type EGJ as category 2B), reflecting MATTERHORN — with the caveat that diffuse-type disease did not show a survival advantage from added durvalumab.
- **Biomarker-directed systemic therapy for metastatic disease.** HER2 (ERBB2) testing directs first-line **trastuzumab** added to chemotherapy for HER2-overexpressing adenocarcinoma; **trastuzumab deruxtecan** is a category 1 later-line option for HER2-positive disease. PD-L1 CPS guides addition of **nivolumab or pembrolizumab** to first-line chemotherapy; **MSI-H/dMMR** tumors are immunotherapy candidates.
- **Subcutaneous pembrolizumab** (pembrolizumab–berahyaluronidase alfa) may substitute for IV pembrolizumab.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Expands [[esophageal-cancer]] (disease script) from a stub into a staged ADDT page with the NCCN workup/staging and treatment framework, including an original algorithm recreation.
- Updates [[esophageal-adenocarcinoma]] — connects the [[barretts-esophagus|Barrett's]]/EET pathway already on the page to NCCN oncologic staging and systemic therapy for invasive disease.
- Touches [[upper-endoscopy]], [[endoscopic-ultrasound]], [[endoscopic-eradication-therapy]] (staging/early therapy), [[barretts-esophagus]] (precursor), and [[gastric-adenocarcinoma]] (shared EGJ systemic therapy and biomarkers).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Algorithm-based guideline (category 2A by default), not a GRADE systematic review; complements the ACG Barrett's guideline already cited on the EAC page (which governs the precursor/early-neoplasia endoscopic pathway).
- Benefit of adding durvalumab to perioperative FLOT appears histology- and biomarker-dependent (no advantage in diffuse-type); optimal patient selection is still being defined.

## Summary

The NCCN Gastric Cancer guideline covers workup, staging, and stage-directed treatment of gastric adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis is by [[upper-endoscopy|endoscopy]] with biopsy; staging combines endoscopic ultrasound, CT, PET/CT, and diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal cytology for locally advanced disease. Biomarker testing — **HER2 (ERBB2), PD-L1 CPS, MSI-H/dMMR, and claudin 18.2** — is integral to treatment selection in advanced disease. Management is stage-based: endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD) for early, low-risk T1a tumors meeting criteria; **perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT)** with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy for resectable locally advanced disease; definitive chemoradiation/chemotherapy for unresectable disease; and biomarker-directed systemic therapy for metastatic disease.

Version 3.2026 reorganizes the systemic-therapy principles around HER2 status, makes **first-line trastuzumab** explicit for HER2-overexpressing (IHC 3+, or IHC 2+ with ISH/FISH amplification) adenocarcinoma, elevates **fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan to a category 1** second-line/subsequent option for HER2-positive disease, adds **dostarlimab as a neoadjuvant option for MSI-H/dMMR** tumors, and clarifies that for MSI-H/dMMR tumors undergoing non-operative management, immunotherapy should be given for at least one year. Gastrectomy with appropriate lymphadenectomy remains the standard even after radiologic/endoscopic complete response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, outside of prospective organ-preservation trials.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Biomarker testing is integral.** HER2 (ERBB2), PD-L1 CPS, MSI-H/dMMR, and claudin 18.2 testing guide systemic therapy in advanced/metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma.
- **Early disease.** Selected early T1a tumors meeting size/histology/depth criteria are candidates for endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD); otherwise gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.
- **Resectable locally advanced disease.** Perioperative chemotherapy — **FLOT** preferred — with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy; perioperative/neoadjuvant immunotherapy is considered for MSI-H/dMMR tumors in multidisciplinary consultation (**dostarlimab** added as a neoadjuvant option).
- **MSI-H/dMMR organ preservation.** Radiologic/endoscopic complete responses to neoadjuvant immunotherapy do not reliably predict pathologic complete response; gastrectomy remains standard outside prospective trials. If non-operative management is pursued, immunotherapy should continue for **at least 1 year**.
- **First-line metastatic therapy.** HER2-overexpressing adenocarcinoma: add **trastuzumab** to first-line chemotherapy. HER2-negative: fluoropyrimidine + platinum chemotherapy, with **nivolumab or pembrolizumab** added based on PD-L1 CPS, and **zolbetuximab** for claudin 18.2-positive tumors.
- **Later-line therapy.** **Fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan** is now a category 1 second-line/subsequent option for HER2-positive disease; other options include ramucirumab-based regimens, taxanes, irinotecan, and trifluridine/tipiracil.
- **Subcutaneous pembrolizumab** (pembrolizumab–berahyaluronidase alfa) may substitute for IV pembrolizumab.

- Reliability of imaging/endoscopy to confirm pathologic complete response in MSI-H/dMMR tumors is an open question; organ-preservation remains investigational.

## Summary

The NCCN GIST guideline covers the diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of gastrointestinal stromal tumors — the most common mesenchymal tumors of the GI tract, arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal and typically expressing **KIT (CD117) and DOG1**. Most are driven by activating **KIT** mutations (exon 11 most common) or **PDGFRA** mutations (including the imatinib-resistant **D842V** variant); a minority are **SDH-deficient ("wild-type") GISTs** (often gastric, in younger patients, associated with Carney triad and Carney-Stratakis syndrome). **Mutational testing is essential** because it predicts response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors and guides drug/dose selection.

Management is risk- and resectability-based. Localized, resectable GISTs are treated with **surgical resection** (negative margins; routine lymphadenectomy is not required). Very small (<2 cm) gastric GISTs without high-risk endoscopic-ultrasound features may be followed with surveillance. **Neoadjuvant imatinib** is used to downsize marginally resectable tumors or preserve organ function (e.g., at the EGJ, rectum, duodenum), with mutational testing first to confirm imatinib sensitivity. After resection, **adjuvant imatinib for at least 3 years** is recommended for high-risk tumors (risk estimated by size, mitotic rate, and primary site, with tumor rupture conferring high risk). For unresectable/metastatic disease, **imatinib is first-line** (with a higher dose for KIT exon 9 mutations), followed by **sunitinib, regorafenib, and ripretinib** in sequence; **avapritinib** is used for PDGFRA D842V-mutant disease.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Diagnosis & immunophenotype.** GIST is the most common GI mesenchymal tumor; typically **KIT (CD117)+ and DOG1+**. Biopsy of a suspected GIST is approached carefully (risk of rupture/seeding); EUS-guided sampling is often used for gastric lesions.
- **Mutational testing is essential** and predictive: **KIT** (exon 11 most common; exon 9 needs higher-dose imatinib), **PDGFRA** (D842V is imatinib-resistant → avapritinib), and **SDH-deficient** wild-type GIST (different biology; less TKI-responsive, indolent, consider germline/syndrome evaluation).
- **Risk stratification** uses **tumor size, mitotic rate, and primary site** (gastric GISTs behave better than small-bowel/rectal at equivalent size/mitotic rate); **tumor rupture** denotes high risk.
- **Localized disease:** surgical resection with negative margins; no routine lymphadenectomy. Small (<2 cm) gastric GISTs without high-risk EUS features may be surveilled.
- **Neoadjuvant imatinib** to downsize marginally resectable tumors or enable organ preservation; confirm imatinib-sensitive mutation first.
- **Adjuvant imatinib ≥3 years** for high-risk resected GIST.
- **Advanced/metastatic sequence:** imatinib (1st-line; exon 9 → higher dose) → sunitinib (2nd) → regorafenib (3rd) → ripretinib (4th); **avapritinib** for PDGFRA D842V. Continue TKI therapy indefinitely in responding metastatic disease; surgery/ablation may be considered for limited progression.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Creates [[gastrointestinal-stromal-tumor]] (new disease script, ADDT) — the wiki's first dedicated GIST page; resolves links from [[gastric-adenocarcinoma]] and [[esophageal-cancer]] differentials.
- Connects to [[endoscopic-ultrasound]] (subepithelial-lesion evaluation/sampling), [[upper-endoscopy]] (gastric GISTs), and [[gastroenteropancreatic-neuroendocrine-tumors]] (subepithelial differential). Complements the ACG subepithelial-lesions guideline already in the wiki.

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Algorithm-based guideline (category 2A by default), not a GRADE systematic review.
- Optimal adjuvant imatinib duration beyond 3 years and management of SDH-deficient/wild-type GIST (less TKI-responsive) remain active questions.

## Summary

The NCCN Hepatocellular Carcinoma guideline covers the workup, diagnosis, staging, and stage-directed management of HCC in the at-risk (predominantly cirrhotic or chronic-HBV) population. Diagnosis follows a non-invasive imaging pathway in at-risk patients (multiphasic contrast CT/MRI, with LI-RADS used to assign HCC probability) and reserves biopsy for indeterminate lesions or when tissue would change management. Liver function (Child-Pugh class, and increasingly ALBI), performance status, tumor burden, and vascular invasion/extrahepatic spread together drive treatment allocation, broadly aligned with the BCLC framework used elsewhere in the wiki.

Management is multidisciplinary and tiered: potentially curative options (surgical resection, ablation, and liver transplantation within accepted criteria) for limited disease with adequate liver reserve; locoregional therapy (TACE, TARE/Y90, and — emphasized in this version — external-beam/stereotactic body radiation therapy) for intermediate disease; and systemic therapy for advanced disease (macrovascular invasion, extrahepatic spread, or progression after locoregional therapy). The headline change in Version 1.2026 is in first-line systemic therapy: **ipilimumab + nivolumab was elevated to a Preferred, category 1 first-line option** (CheckMate-9DW), joining atezolizumab + bevacizumab and durvalumab + tremelimumab. The version also strengthens the role of radiation therapy (new Principles of Radiation Therapy and locoregional therapy footnotes) and adds subcutaneous substitution options for several checkpoint inhibitors.

## Key Findings / Claims

- **Diagnosis in at-risk patients is imaging-based.** In patients with cirrhosis or chronic HBV, a characteristic multiphasic CT/MRI appearance (arterial-phase hyperenhancement with washout ± capsule) supports HCC diagnosis without biopsy; LI-RADS categorizes lesions and indeterminate findings are biopsied or re-imaged. Pathologic confirmation is required outside the at-risk setting.
- **Treatment is allocated by liver function + tumor burden + performance status.** Resection is favored for limited disease with preserved function and adequate remnant without clinically significant portal hypertension; ablation for small lesions in non-surgical candidates; transplantation for patients meeting accepted criteria; locoregional therapy and/or systemic therapy for larger or advanced disease.
- **First-line systemic therapy (Preferred, all category 1):** atezolizumab + bevacizumab; durvalumab + tremelimumab; **ipilimumab + nivolumab (new this version)**. **Other Recommended (category 1):** durvalumab monotherapy, lenvatinib, sorafenib. An upper endoscopy to evaluate/manage varices is expected within ~6 months before starting atezolizumab + bevacizumab because of GI-bleed risk.
- **CheckMate-9DW caveat.** Ipilimumab + nivolumab improved overall survival vs lenvatinib/sorafenib but carried a higher rate of death during the first ~6 months and a high rate of immune-mediated toxicity (≈29% required high-dose steroids); counsel patients about early immune-mediated toxicity risk (Yau T, et al. Lancet 2025;405:1851-1864).
- **Radiation therapy emphasized.** New Principles of Radiation Therapy (HCC-H) and locoregional-therapy footnotes position EBRT/SBRT (with image guidance) as an option for tumors irrespective of location, as an alternative to ablation/embolization or when those fail or are contraindicated; SBRT is typically delivered in 3–5 fractions for a limited number of tumors with adequate uninvolved liver.
- **Subcutaneous checkpoint-inhibitor substitutions.** SC formulations (atezolizumab-hyaluronidase; nivolumab-hyaluronidase for monotherapy; pembrolizumab–berahyaluronidase alfa) may substitute for the corresponding IV agents, with their own dosing/administration instructions.
- **Pembrolizumab.** A recommended option in the subsequent-line setting; FDA-approved for MSI-H tumors, and per this version recommended regardless of MSI status in eligible patients.

## Relevance to Wiki

- Updates [[hepatocellular-carcinoma]] (disease script) — adds the NCCN first-line systemic-therapy tiering (notably ipilimumab + nivolumab as category 1 first-line) and the strengthened RT/SBRT role to the existing AASLD/AGA-based content. **Additive only** — the page's AASLD 2023/2025 and BCLC content remains the primary framework; NCCN is layered in as a concordant, newer source.
- Touches [[li-rads]] (diagnostic framework), [[liver-transplantation]] (transplant criteria), [[portal-hypertension]] (variceal screening before anti-VEGF therapy), and [[immune-checkpoint-inhibitor-hepatitis]] (irAE context).

## Contradictions / Open Questions

- Algorithm-based guideline (category 2A consensus by default), not a GRADE systematic review — strength-of-evidence labels differ from the AASLD/AGA guidance already cited on the HCC page. The two are concordant on the major pathways; NCCN's distinction is the explicit first-line tiering and the category 1 elevation of ipilimumab + nivolumab.
- NCCN and AASLD frame staging differently (NCCN's algorithm tables vs AASLD's BCLC 2022); both converge on function- and burden-based allocation.
